News.title: Boy, 11, dies after being 'shot in face' as heartbroken dad speaks out
News.content:
Boy, 11, dies after being 'shot in face' as heartbroken dad speaks out

An 11-year-old boy has died after suffering gunshot wounds to his face and neck with police continuing to investigate the incident as tributes pour in from the community

View 3 Images The boy has died after the shooting (Image: Nine)

An 11-year-old boy who was shot in the face and neck in Sydney has tragically died in hospital.

The youngster suffered a gunshot wound to his face and neck at a unit in Norwest at around 5pm on Monday, September 21 and was raced to hospital in critical condition.

Police have confirmed the boy has now died.

View 3 Images The boy was rushed to hospital in critical condition (Image: Nine )

A NSW Police spokesperson said: “About 8pm tonight (Thursday), police were informed that the boy had died from injuries sustained.

“Inquiries are continuing.”

The force believed a single shot was fired but the weapon has not been recovered.

An investigation has been launched with enquiries looking into whether the weapon may have been accidentally discharged as a result of the child handling it.

Following the announcement on Thursday evening, tributes have started to pour in on social media. A man understood to be his father, who cannot be named for legal reasons, posted: "Rip peace my baby."

The school the boy attended issued a statement saying they were “deeply saddened” by the news.

“Our thoughts and prayers are with his family, friends, classmates, and all those affected by this tragic loss,” a statement issued on Thursday night reads.

“At this difficult time, our focus is on supporting the child’s family and providing wellbeing and counselling support to our students and staff.”

On Tuesday, the Hills Police Area Commander, Superintendent Naomi Moore, said several people who were inside the property were known to police.

She said: “A number of individuals that were inside the unit at the time are well known to NSW Police, and their association with organised crime is being considered by investigators."

Three men, all aged 18, were arrested at the scene.

View 3 Images Superintendent Naomi Moore said the occupants of the property were known to police (Image: Nine)

Isaac James Bechara, 18, was taken to Riverstone Police Station and charged with concealing a serious indictable offence.

The two others were taken to Castle Hill Police Station, where they were spoken to before being released pending further inquiries.

Mr Bechara did not appear when his matter was mentioned before Blacktown Local Court on Tuesday, with his lawyer appearing on his behalf.

No application for bail was made and the matter was adjourned.

Police allege Mr Bechara failed, without reasonable excuse, to provide information that could materially assist investigators after becoming aware a serious indictable offence had been committed.

Superintendent Moore said police had previously attended the property but did not add any further detail.

“Police are aware of the premises. Police have engaged with the occupants previously,” she said.

Moore added that none of the three men arrested were related to the 11-year-old.

News.title: Thousands of Brits have to trek miles to medication as more pharmacies close
News.content:
Thousands of Brits have to trek miles to medication as more pharmacies close

Some 51 high street pharmacies have shut for good since start of 2026, and the Mirror is now campaigning to save family chemists and stop the closures

View 5 Images More pharmacies across England are closing (Image: Getty Images)

More than 280,000 people — the equivalent of a city the size of Newcastle-upon-Tyne — have seen their local pharmacies close in the first eight months of this year.

‌



New NHS data shows show 51 high street pharmacies have added to the “tidal wave” of branches shut for good in England due to chronic underfunding between January and August.

‌



The Mirror is campaigning to save family chemists and stop the closures, which are piling pressure on overstretched GPs. The relentless toll of closures has taken the network to its smallest level in 20 years.

‌



This latest startling toll of closures includes 31 pharmacies on a Government programme to maintain vital access to medicines in healthcare shortage areas have closed for good. That’s despite the government providing the sector with its second uplift in a decade in May.

Mum spent thousands taking up to 40 painkillers a day for nine years READ MORE :

View 5 Images Former prime Minister Rishi Sunak has blood pressure checked as more pharmacies close leaving people travelling miles to get medication (Image: Getty Images)

'We need to act'

Olivier Picard, chair of the National Pharmacy Association (NPA) said it was a "tidal wave". He added: “These are depressing figures and demonstrates the work to stabilise the pharmacy network that millions of patients depend on is not done yet.

‌



“We need to act to prevent the permanent closure of pharmacies becoming the new normal at a time when Government and the public wants more care closer to people’s homes

“Patients are being forced to travel long distances to access the medicines and support they need, particularly on weekends.The NHS Pharmacy Access Scheme provides additional funding to ensure there is access to pharmacy services in communities where there is no alternative nearby.”

View 5 Images Olivier Picard

‌



NPA leaders, who represent around 6,000 community pharmacies across the country, have urged the government to fundamentally reform the NHS’s contract with pharmacies which means many pharmacies cannot rely on NHS income to keep them afloat. They called on government to close the £2billion funding gap facing pharmacies.

Since 2017, some 9.9 million people have seen their local pharmacy shut, around a fifth of the adult population of England. Mr Picard added: “It is particularly concerning to see closures of pharmacies that have been singled out for additional support due to their importance to the patients that use them and the lack of available alternatives in those areas.

“We recognise this government has provided pharmacies with desperately needed funding uplifts, but much of this had to go out the door to meet soaring costs including business rates and national living wage leaving pharmacies facing a yawning gap between their costs and the funding they receive from the NHS.

‌



“We want to work with the government to fundamentally reform the pharmacy contract to achieve Ministers’ ambitions to bring care closer to home and end pharmacies being forced to dispense medicines at a loss.”

View 5 Images Pharmacies still closing down in large numbers (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Closed pharmacies include...

The closure of a former Lloyds Pharmacy in Long Rock, Penzance. This has left patients with a one-hour-twenty-minute journey by public transport to access their nearest pharmacy on a Sunday, a 17-mile round trip.

‌



Bishops Lydeard in Somerset, where the closure of the local pharmacy has left patients with a 10-mile round to trip to their nearest alternative. On the weekend, this is a one-hour-six-minute journey on public transport.

In Barnwood, Gloucester, where the closure of a Lloyds Pharmacy has left patients with a 50-minute walk to their nearest pharmacy on a weekend or a one-hour-ten-minute round trip by public transport.

In Bodmin in Cornwall where the closure of the Asda pharmacy has left patients with a 16-mile round trip to their nearest pharmacy open on a weekend, one-hour-ten-minutes on public transport.

‌



View 5 Images More pharmacies close leaving people travelling miles to get medication (Image: Getty Images)

Closures have forced patients to travel significant lengths to access emergency prescriptions.

This risks putting pressure on other parts of the health system, with some patients potentially choosing to visit Urgent Care or even Accident and Emergency departments instead.

Article continues below

Since 2017, 1500 pharmacies have shut when funding was first cut to pharmacies by the previous government.

William Pett, Interim Director of Policy and External Affairs at Healthwatch, said: “People rely on their local pharmacy for timely advice and essential medication, so closures are a real worry. "We hear from people about longer journeys to find an open pharmacy, particularly in rural areas, and this is particularly difficult for those with limited mobility or no access to transport. It is no surprise that some people end up turning to other parts of the NHS when they cannot get the help they need in their community.

“Our own research has shown that temporary and unplanned closures have disrupted care and caused anxiety for patients across the country. A plan for the future sustainability of community pharmacies is essential so the public can rely on consistent access to medicines and advice."

News.title: Owner of UK airport killed alongside friends as plane crashes in Swiss Alps
News.content:
Owner of UK airport killed alongside friends as plane crashes in Swiss Alps

Anthony Hall, 42, who was the owner of Wolverhampton Halfpenny Green Airport, Staffordshire, was one of three people killed in a plane crash in the Swiss Alps

View 4 Images Anthony Hall, 42, died in a plane crash in Switzerland (Image: Courtesy Suzanne Webb OBE / SWNS)

The family of an airport owner killed in a plane crash in the Swiss Alps have described him as a "kind, caring, generous, determined and fantastic character".

‌



Anthony Hall, 42, was on board a Cirrus SR22T which crashed high in the mountains near the town of Leukerbad in the southern canton of Valais on September 15. Owain Davies, 55, from west Wales, also sadly died, as well as a third person.

‌



The plane departed Sion airport in the Rhône Valley but crashed into a mountain slope about 10 minutes later.

‌



Mr Hall was the owner of Wolverhampton Halfpenny Green Airport in Staffordshire and the managing director of construction and recycling firm Pegasus, based near Stourbridge in the West Midlands.

View 4 Images Mr Hall was the owner of Wolverhampton Halfpenny Green Airport (Image: SWNS)

Menu for Trump's dinner with Xi revealed as Melania prepares banquet for billionaires READ MORE :

Tempers flare at Trump-Xi meeting as Chinese press clash with White House staff READ MORE :

His family have now paid tribute, telling how he was a "truly wonderful husband, devoted father and much-loved man".

‌



They added: "Tony was an exceptional businessman who achieved great things in the construction/haulage industry, and his commitment to succeed and progress never faltered.

"He was first and foremost a loving husband and an incredible dad to his daughter, whose family meant everything to him. We will miss him immensely and will remember him as the kind, caring, generous, determined and fantastic character he was."

The family of Mr Davies have told of their "unimaginable loss". Mr Davies was managing director of engineering firm Amcanu, which is based in Burry Port, Carmarthenshire.

‌



Emergency teams from the Valais Rescue Organisation, police and firefighters were sent to the scene along with three helicopters. The Swiss Transportation Safety Board has begun an investigation.

View 4 Images Owain Davies also died in the plane crash (Image: Amcanu)

Mr Hall's family stressed they were incredibly grateful for the kindness, love, and support that had been shown. They added: "Our hearts go out to those who also lost their lives in this terrible tragedy."

‌



Paying tribute, former Stourbridge MP Suzanne Webb, who was a friend of Mr Hall, described him as a "legend". She said: "Tony will always be a legend to me. What he achieved in helping build Pegasus into the success it is today, alongside the other directors, was remarkable.

"But beyond the business, Tony was great fun to be around and, quite simply, a genuinely good person. I will miss his quick wit and humour."

She added he gave "so much" to the area, particularly through his support for the Poppy Appeal and Military Vehicle Parade. "Having served in the armed forces, he gave his support willingly," she said. "His life was tragically cut short, but what he achieved after leaving the army was truly inspiring, and he did it with a passion I was always in awe of."

‌



View 4 Images Swiss authorities have launched an investigation into the cause of the crash (Image: Valais Cantonal Police)

Wolverhampton Halfpenny Green Airport also issued a tribute to its owner and director, who bought the site in 2023. He had a "clear vision" for it to become "the best general aviation airport in the country", the statement said, and "poured his time, energy and passion" into securing its future.

"Together with his co-owner, he transformed the airport, creating a thriving aviation hub for the local and wider aviation community," it continued. "His passion, determination and commitment have left a lasting mark on the airport and on the many people who had the privilege of knowing and working alongside him."

Article continues below

The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office confirmed it was "providing support to the families of two British nationals who died in Switzerland". It added officials were in contact with the local authorities and its thoughts were with the families of those who had died.

News.title: Russian beauty queen found dismembered in bags as pet dog leads police to her body
News.content:
Russian beauty queen found dismembered in bags as pet dog leads police to her body

Relatives raised the alarm after model Natalia Bozhuk disappeared on a walk with her pet dog Luna - police found her remains in bags weeks later in Russia

View 3 Images Natalia Bozhuk vanished after leaving home with her pet spaniel (Image: JamPress)

A businessman has been arrested over the alleged killing of a beauty queen whose body was found in a forest.

‌



Natalia Bozhuk, 39, vanished after leaving home with her pet spaniel. Police said her partner later hid her remains in woodland. He was caught abroad after an international hunt.

‌



The killing is alleged to have taken place in July near the Romashkovo housing estate in Odintsovo in Russia’s Moscow region.

‌



Bozhuk was a model and a Mrs Russia Universe contestant. She also worked as a stylist and had just finished a course at the Ostankino television school. She went missing after an alleged row with Pavel Kozlov, 44, on July 17.

The model went for a walk with her pet dog Luna. Relatives raised the alarm when she stopped answering her phone. Investigators said she died that day or the next.

View 3 Images Natalia Bozhuk with Pavel Kozlov (Image: JamPress)

‌



Three influencers could face years in Dubai's hellhole prisons after arrests READ MORE :

Her remains were found in bags left in woodland near an outbuilding on July 27. Police said the dog, which had stayed close to the spot for almost two weeks, helped lead them there. Investigators said the body had been cut up and hidden after the killing.

Interior Ministry spokeswoman Irina Volk said a row broke out between the pair. “During the quarrel the defendant inflicted several wounds on the woman, from which she died,” she said. “After that the attacker took measures aimed at hiding the traces of the crime.”

Kozlov flew from Moscow’s Vnukovo airport to Turkey and later went on to Northern Cyprus. He was detained on September 17. Turkish officers handed him to Russian police at Istanbul Airport on September 18.

‌



View 3 Images Natalia Bozhuk was brutally killed (Image: JamPress)

Volk said: “Today, at Istanbul International Airport, employees of the competent Turkish authorities handed over a citizen of our country. He was on the international wanted list for the murder of a model and participant in the contest Mrs Russia Universe. At present, he is in custody.”

Kozlov faces a murder charge under Article 105 and up to 15 years in prison. Local reports said he confessed after he was brought back to Russia.

Article continues below

The pair had met about six months earlier after she posted online that she was looking for a partner. Friends said he approached her in the street and courted her.

Kozlov, who was born in Tashkent, worked in finance and set up wholesale firms. He has a five-year-old daughter and a nine-year-old son.

News.title: BBC Question Time panelist Josh Babarinde makes desperate plea after RNLI volunteers abused by far-right thugs
News.content:
BBC Question Time panelist Josh Babarinde makes desperate plea after RNLI volunteers abused by far-right thugs

BBC Question Time panelist Josh Babarinde issued a desperate plea to the public after hundreds of balaclava-clad protesters descended on Dover and Portsmouth overnight on September 6 and vowed to stop migrants from leaving the port

View 3 Images Josh Babarinde is the Liberal Democrat MP for Eastbourne, and has been an MP continually since 4 July 2024. (Image: Gary Roberts/SOPA Images/Shutterstock)

A BBC Question Time panelist has called for the British public to "love our lifeboats" after RNLI crews were abused by protesters.

‌



Andy Burnham hit out at "appalling" abuse directed at hero crews after they were labelled as traitors online by far-right thugs for rescuing asylum seekers in the Channel and bringing a dinghy to safety in Portsmouth, Hants.

‌



The topic was one fo many discussed on tonight's BBC Question Time featuring; the business secretary Jonathan Reynolds; the Conservative shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately; the journalist and broadcaster Andrew Neil, the president of the Liberal Democrats Josh Babarinde and the political commentator Ash Sarkar.

‌



Discussing the recent protests Helen Whately said: "a vigilante justice approach to it I'm certain is the wrong way."

View 3 Images Balaclava-clad followers have protested in both Dover and Portsmouth in recent weeks

RNLI warned of cyber attack after volunteers abused for saving migrants by far-right thugs READ MORE :

Host Fiona Bruce said: "The people that we saw were all dressed in black wearing balaclavas... Do you condemn that?"

‌



Helen replied: "I don't want to see threatening behaviour, peaceful protests is one thing threatening protests, no that is not ok."

Josh Babarinde chimed in with a desperate plea for the public. He said: "Its one thing to protest it's another thing to intimidate and abuse our volunteer lifeboat crews, these are people who put their lives on the line for us and anyone who should get in their way is pathetic, un-patriotic and un-british we're a country that prides ourselves in bringing people together. We are a country that thought we banished hate and division some time ago and these folks only seek to threaten that."

He added: "Love our lifeboats, donate to the RNLI, stand up to this division by helping to support their work going forward."

‌



View 3 Images RNLI volunteers were labelled as traitors online by far-right thugs for rescuing asylum seekers in the Channel (Image: Barry Williams/PA Wire)

Volunteers for the organisation were told their data may have been stolen by hackers - just days after they suffered online and physical abuse for rescuing 120 migrants from a dinghy in the English Channel.

Online security experts have warned that the identities of RNLI members could have been leaked or fallen into the wrong hands after a cyber-attack on a third-party software provider. In a letter accompanying the autumn copy of its Lifeboat magazine, the charity warned supporters that their "name, contact details and records of interactions with the RNLI" could have been breached in the raid on Beacon CRM.

‌



The RNLI said it was advised last month by the provider to "assume that data held within its systems was taken" in a cyber-attack that affected around 1,500 charities in late July.

"At this stage we're not aware of any misuse of your personal information and have no evidence that your information has been published or shared," the charity added.

The RNLI has suspended its services in Portsmouth since its staff were subjected to relentless abuse and branded "traitors" by anti-migrant protesters.

Article continues below

Peter Sparkes, the charity's chief executive, condemned abuse of its volunteers as "wholly unacceptable in civilised society", adding that the RNLI worked to save lives at sea irrespective of whose they are.

BBC Question Time returns on Thursday Octoebr 1 in North London and Thursday October 8 in Peterlee.

News.title: UK's rudest place names revealed - see if you live in any of the the 35
News.content:
UK's rudest place names revealed - see if you live in any of the the 35

WARNING: - More than half of Britons believe we boast some of the most amusing road and village names globally, though they can also prove a hazard for motorists

View Image The street Bell End is in Rowley Regis, West Midlands (Image: BPM Media)

Horny Old Road, Minge Lane, Bell End and Cock Hill Lane are amongst the UK's rudest place names, a new survey has disclosed.

More than half of Britons believe we boast some of the most amusing road and village names globally, though they can also prove a hazard for motorists.

Risqué road names have distracted two thirds of drivers, with six in 10 missing their turning or exit because they were laughing and one in three nearly causing a collision.

The research was commissioned by Asda Money, which has temporarily installed "modesty" curtains over signs to help keep drivers focused on the road.

Nearly one in three (29%) have even cited a humorous place name as justification for visiting a location, reports the Daily Star.

The initiative comes as Asda Money prepares to launch its new car insurance this month in partnership with Allianz.

Yet amusing road names represent just one of the distractions vying for drivers' attention. In total, 76% confess they become distracted while driving, experiencing this an average of five times during a one-hour journey.

Beyond road signs, chatty passengers (32%), breathtaking scenery (30%), passengers repeatedly pointing things out (27%), yawning or fatigue (26%) and singing along to the radio (25%) all feature on the list.

Jenny Maden, Head of Insurance, at Asda Money, said: "Britain's road signs might make us laugh, but keeping drivers covered is serious business.

"Our partnership with Allianz, brings 'Asda Car Insurance' to our customers, with guaranteed exclusive rates available for Asda Rewards members – as well as a £25 Cashpot contribution, for a limited offer period."

News.title: Luxury British homeware store collapses into administration after 56 years
News.content:
Luxury British homeware store collapses into administration after 56 years

Luxury homeware brand Designers Guild has entered administration after facing 'trading challenges for several years' - dozens of staff have been made redundant

View Image Designers Guild has entered administration (file) (Image: Ilpo Musto/Shutterstock)

A luxury homeware brand has collapsed into administration after "not being able to find a way forward".

‌



Designers Guild, with a flagship store on the King’s Road in London, had been facing “trading challenges for several years”, it stated in an announcement on social media.

‌



The decision to appoint administrators comes less than 18 months after its brand and intellectual property assets were bought by London-listed Dunelm.

‌



Designers Guild was founded in 1970 and jointly owned by Tricia Guild and her brother Simon Jeffreys. Its homeware designs were inspired by the interiors of Britain's royal residences. Products included upholstery and home accessories.

Rick Harrison and Howard Smith from Interpath were appointed joint administrators today with the firm ceasing trading - which has led to 93 staff being made redundant.

UK coffee company plunges into liquidation after 76 years READ MORE :

Hundreds lose jobs as major UK glass firm plunges into administration READ MORE :

The company was popular in Europe and the impact of Brexit followed by the war in Ukraine has had an impact on sales.

‌



A statement from Ms Guild said: "It is with great sadness that after 56 wonderful years, Simon Jeffreys and I are closing Designers Guild Ltd."

She continued "We have been supported in the UK, Europe and worldwide by our wonderful loyal clients for over 50 years. From our small beginnings to the present day their enthusiasm and involvement with the brand has been wonderful and so many have become lifelong friends. I have always been moved by their support and love of the brand.

"Designer Guild Ltd has also been built on the creativity and vision of our many wonderful suppliers. From village producers in rural India to sophisticated contemporary mills in Italy and everything in between. All of the makers who translated our designs into beautiful fabrics, wallpapers, furniture, products and more have my enduring respect. Their skill and talent are always amazing and hugely appreciated."

‌



But she told how they have not been able to overcome the financial challenges. "Recent years have brought a succession of challenges for the business," she said. "Unfortunately despite the best efforts by our team and others over numerous months we have not been able to find a way forward, and this is a source of huge regret and sorrow for us."

A statement from Interpath read: " The Company had experienced trading challenges for several years. With a strong European customer base, the Company was particularly exposed to the impact of Brexit and the war in Ukraine, both of which weighed heavily on sales while driving up underlying costs across the business.

"In response to these increasing financial pressures, the Directors sold the Designers Guild brand and design archive to a third party in 2025, after which the Company continued to trade under a license agreement. However, the headwinds facing the business persisted. The Company faced ongoing constraints on working capital which, combined with industry-wide pressures on supply chain lead times, presented challenges in managing customer order fulfilment.

‌



"Consequently, following a review of the Company’s position, and with no solvent solutions available, the Directors took the difficult decision to file for the appointment of administrators. As a result, the business ceased to trade and, with regret, 93 members of staff have been made redundant.

"The joint administrators have retained a small number of staff to assist them as they commence an orderly wind down of the business. The administrators will now seek to explore options for the business and its assets, including any residual stock."

Rick Harrison, managing director at Interpath and joint administrator, said: “For over 50 years, Designers Guild Limited has been one of the UK’s most recognised and respected names in the world of interior design, so it’s tremendously sad that the business has not been able to overcome its recent challenges.

Article continues below

“As a matter of priority, we will be supporting those members of staff who have been impacted by insolvency, while we also explore options for the Company’s remaining assets, including leftover stock.”

News.title: Far-right activist Daniel 'Tommo' Thomas charged after 'slashing dinghy in Channel'
News.content:
Far-right activist Daniel 'Tommo' Thomas charged after 'slashing dinghy in Channel'

Danny 'Tommo' Thomas has been charged by police with criminal damage after he allegedly slashed a dinghy in the English Channel

View 2 Images Danny 'Tommo' Thomas has been charged (Image: Jonathan Buckmasterr)

Far-right activist Danny 'Tommo' Thomas has been charged after a video was shared that allegedly showed him slashing a dinghy in the Channel.

Thomas, 37, an associate of anti-immigration activist Tommy Robinson, previously uploaded footage onto his YouTube channel that appeared to show the moment he was arrested by police. He was seen getting out of his vehicle as officers approached him.

Hampshire Constabulary this evening confirmed he has been charged with one count of criminal damage. He was also charged with failing to disclose the Pin to his phone to police, under Section 53 of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000.

He was remanded into custody to appear at Basingstoke Magistrates’ Court on Friday, Hampshire police said.

Hampshire Police said: "A man has been charged in connection with an incident that occurred in the English Channel on Tuesday 22 September.

View 2 Images People gathered outside a police investigation centre in Basingstoke this evening, believing that Thomas was inside (Image: Getty Images)

"Daniel Thomas, aged 37 and of no fixed abode, has been charged with one count of criminal damage. He has also been charged with a further offence under Section 53 of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (RIPA), for allegedly failing to comply with a notice to disclose a phone PIN number to police.

"The charges follow an allegation made to police that damage had been caused to a boat in the Channel whilst an emergency responder was on board. He was remanded in custody to appear at Basingstoke Magistrates’ Court tomorrow (Friday 25 September)."

His arrest came after Thomas allegedly slashed a dinghy while a rescue worker was on board. The boat had previously carried some 50 migrants who left Normandy for the UK.

The migrants were picked up by RNLI crew after they reached the British search and rescue area. They were then transferred to a UK Border Force vessel and were later taken to Dover where they were processed.

Thomas filmed the transfer and gave commentary to the audience of some 15,000 viewers. The clip appeared to show him manoeuvring up close to the small boat before allegedly slashing it.

Several hundred people, largely wearing black, gathered outside a police investigation centre in Basingstoke this evening, believing that Thomas was inside.

They arrived together at just before 6.30pm and stood on the road outside the investigation centre and began chanting “free DT”. Most were not masked, though some could be seen wearing face coverings.

Dozens of police officers could be seen monitoring the group outside the investigation centre as the protest continued for several hours.

The demonstration was peaceful, with the group moving out of the road to make way for approaching traffic.

News.title: Anti-migrant activist charged after dinghy slashed in Channel
News.content:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been charged with criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at a dinghy in the English Channel.

The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, has also been charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone, Hampshire Police said.

He has been remanded in custody and is due to appear at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court via videolink on Friday, the force added.

Several hundred people had gathered outside a police investigation centre in Basingstoke on Thursday evening believing Thomas was inside.

The demonstration, which seemed to pass off peacefully, began shortly before 18:30 BST. Protesters stood on the road outside the building and could be heard chanting "free DT".

The crowd began to disperse at about 21:45 BST after they learned of the charges against Thomas.

News.title: From weeks to hours - the rapid new test transforming brain tumour diagnosis
News.content:
A rapid new test for brain tumours that the NHS has started using can slash the time it takes for an accurate diagnosis from up to eight weeks to two hours.

The test, which is used by doctors to diagnose which type of tumour a patient has, should mean patients can start treatment including radiotherapy and chemotherapy sooner, and are spared weeks of uncertainty.

Steve Palmer, 55, from Nottingham, is among those to benefit from the new technology - and it meant surgeons were able to get his result while they were still operating to remove his tumour.

"Getting that quick diagnosis removed weeks of anxiety," he told the BBC.

NHS England said that the genomic test, which works by quickly analysing the genetic code of a sample of the tumour, will be piloted in specialist centres around England.

There are around 150 different types of brain tumour ranging from slow-growing to aggressive cancers, each of which can respond differently to treatment.

Steve was diagnosed with a brain tumour after he collapsed at the gym, and the test revealed it to be a grade 4 glioblastoma.

"It wasn't the result I wanted to hear but it means I can get on with the next phase of treatment and recovery, and get on with fighting whatever it is I've got to fight," he told the BBC.

Consultant neurosurgeon Stuart Smith, who led Steve's operation at Queens Medical Centre, part of Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust, told the BBC the test "seems almost magical."

"The diagnosis of brain tumours relies on molecular and genetic analysis but it can take up to six to eight weeks to get the full information back. Here it is done while we are still operating."

Diagnosing the type of tumour while the patient is still on the operating table could impact how surgeons operate. Smith explained: "For some tumour types, which are curable, surgery needs to be as radical as possible to remove every last bit of tumour that we can find.

"Other types, sadly, are too aggressive, and beyond what surgery can remove, so we would be more cautious in order to lower the risk of causing damage to the brain."

News.title: New policies, election speculation: What to expect from Burnham's first Labour conference as PM
News.content:
Andy Burnham had plenty to say about where the government - and the country - was going wrong at last year's Labour conference in Liverpool.

But that was at a fringe meeting on the sidelines of the main event.

Now, as Labour leader and prime minister, he is the main event - and it is down to him to show party members and the wider public that he has some answers.

Earlier this week, he said his debut leader's speech would leave nobody in any doubt about "what I'm trying to do in this role".

"People are going to know the direction I want to take this country and I will set it down quite clearly," he told reporters en route to the UN General Assembly in New York.

An internal No 10 note has set out the broad themes he will explore when he takes to the stage in Liverpool on Tuesday - including setting out long-term solutions to build a belief that the future can be brighter.

The slogan for this year's conference is "Hope Again".

So in his speech he is likely to point to his forthcoming 10 Year Plan for the UK â which, he says, will have "making life more affordable" at its core.

As for the specifics of what he will say, some of it will be very familiar to anyone who was listening to his conference fringe speech 12 months ago.

News.title: Just how hot and dry was your summer? Use our postcode lookup to find out
News.content:
Where does the data come from?

This lookup uses data from the HadUK Grid dataset (opens in new tab), which is produced by the Met Office Hadley Centre. HadUK Grid is one of the main products used by scientists to monitor and research the UKâs changing climate.

The data for 2026 is provisional, with fewer observations feeding into calculations due to lags in data availability. As such, the precise values could change slightly in future as more data comes available. The historical averages are calculated over a 30-year period from 1991-2020, which matches the standard period used by the UNâs World Meteorological Organization.

The HadUK dataset displays temperature and rainfall data across a uniform grid covering the entire landmass of the UK. The data does not cover the Channel Islands. Every value on the grid is an estimate for the centre point of a 1km by 1km grid box, the most detailed climate data publicly available for the UK. The values are created using observations from land-based weather stations across the country, and by taking into account additional factors such as altitude, terrain and distance from the coast to scientifically âfill in the gapsâ between weather stations.

What do we mean by your area?

Weâve matched every active postcode in the UK to its nearest 1km by 1km grid cell in the HadUK dataset.

The results displayed for your area represent a mean average of that grid cell and the surrounding grid cells to your location. For most areas, this represents a 5km square centred on your postcode. Along irregular coastlines and on small islands, the nearest grid cells are chosen to match the shape of the coastline or island, but no cells are further than 7km away.

This approach aims to avoid sharp jumps between neighbouring locations which may occasionally arise due to uncertainties in the data, while still making use of the most detailed dataset available to capture local weather conditions across the UK's varied geography.

What does your areaâs weather data represent?

The average temperature represents the mean average of the selection of grid cells across the month or season.

The maximum temperature is the mean average of the daily maximums recorded across all nearest grid cells for the month or season; the minimum temperature is the mean average of the daily minimums.

The rainfall is the total amount of rain for the month or season, averaged across the selection of grid cells.

To calculate the number of days above the heatwave threshold, we first averaged the daily maximum temperature for each grid cell with its nearest grid cells on every day. Using the Met Officeâs heatwave thresholds (opens in new tab), we determined how many maximum daily temperatures exceeded the threshold for your location, based on the centre of your grid cell. Your areaâs heatwave threshold may be approximate if your postcode is near a county boundary.

This is not the same as the number of days spent in an official heatwave, where the threshold has to be met or exceeded for at least three consecutive days.

Acknowledgements

Methodology support from Dan Hollis, Amy Doherty and Oli Claydon, UK Met Office.

News.title: 'We are living a constant nightmare,' mother of poison seller victim tells hearing
News.content:
The mother of a British victim of poison seller Kenneth Law has said his death and the way that he died had "destroyed" their family.

Tanya Whitaker broke down at the start of her video statement about the death of her son, Samuel, shown on the second day of a four-day sentencing hearing of Law in Ontario, saying: "He barely had a chance."

The University of Warwick student was found collapsed outside his halls after taking poison sold by Law, who has admitted 14 counts of aiding suicide in Canada. British authorities have confirmed 79 UK victims also died after using his products.

Debbie Cornish echoed Whitaker's sentiments, telling the hearing that her family was "still fighting" to stay together years on from her daughter Danielle's death.

A plea deal with Canadian authorities means Law will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths, but impact statements from their families are being read this week.

"The enormity of losing a child is catastrophic," Whitaker told a Canadian court on Thursday. "Samuel was just 19 when he was handed the tools that ended his precious life."

She continued: "It has broken me completely and utterly. It has broken us as a family and me as a mother.

"Our son died alone at university 100 miles away from his family. We will never be able to forgive ourselves for this happening."

News.title: Poland says fire at Starlink station is sabotage as Denmark warns of rising Russian threat
News.content:
A fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland was a deliberate "act of sabotage", a government minister has said.

Polish Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said the fire in the Masovian Voivodeship province was "deliberately designed to disable the station... disrupting internet access for various institutions, including the Ukrainian army".

He told Polish public broadcaster TVP Info an investigation was ongoing but "many indications suggest" the attack fits into a "new Russian doctrine of attack". The Kremlin has not commented.

Meanwhile, Denmark's intelligence service issued a new threat assessment saying it expects Russia to escalate hybrid warfare in the coming months.

It said an attack remained "highly unlikely" but warned of "a low but growing risk" that Russia could launch a limited military attack against Nato countries.

In recent weeks a number of European Nato members have said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine, which Moscow denies.

Earlier this month, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, while France has ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.

Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary - for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation.

Proxies are often used to carry out the attacks and Russia always denies involvement, despite growing evidence to the contrary.

News.title: Xi visit to Washington all pomp but little progress so far
News.content:
"The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come," he said.

The marching bands and military flyovers on Thursday may serve a larger purpose, however â at least for Trump.

"This is a little bit of intentional pageantry to talk up the positive vibes of the summit," Jennifer Welch, chief economic analyst for Bloomberg Economics, told the BBC. "This is very much how President Trump sees the summit and the role he plays in the US-China relationship, as ballast to provide stability."

Even so, there is still an edge to some of Xi's rhetoric, she notes.

In remarks at the White House, the Chinese leader again mentioned the "Thucydides trap" â a theory that shifts in global power tend to lead to conflict between rising and declining nations.

"China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust," Xi said.

The obstacles in the way of reaching any substantive agreement between the two nations are significant, however. When Trump and Xi met in Beijing in May, the men agreed to form boards of trade and investment to oversee economic interactions, and little more.

On Wednesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a year-long trade "truce" between the two nations that had kept tariffs lower would be extended another two months. Financial analysts expect a further extension could come before this week's summit ends, given that neither side wants a renewal of last year's trade war.

The outlook for progress is much dimmer on other topics, like the US war with Iran, the Ukraine war and regulating AI.

China's reneging on promises to buy more American agricultural products and to also sell more rare earth minerals to the US is helping cloud the outlook. China, meanwhile, is watching to see if Trump follows through on a proposed sale of American weapons to Taiwan, which has been on hold for months.

News.title: Catterick Garrison fire could burn through night, authorities say
News.content:
Firefighters expect to work all night as a fire blazes at the military barracks accommodation block in Catterick Garrison, North Yorkshire.

North Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service said in a statement that multiple crews were at the scene, along with an appliance from County Durham and Darlington.

"The incident is expected to be ongoing throughout the night," the statement said.

Unverified videos and images shared online show flames and smoke rising up from a building as bystanders watch.

The BBC has asked the Ministry of Defence for comment.

Hipswell and Colburn councillor Kevin Foster told local media that details were limited at this stage.

"My immediate concern is for the safety and wellbeing of everyone at the camp, including our military personnel, their families and the emergency services responding to the incident," he said.

This is a developing story.

News.title: Sex offender bailed to flat near playground
News.content:
A sex offender jailed for taking thousands of pictures of children and using AI software to "nudify" them was repeatedly allowed to return to his home overlooking the playground he targeted.

It meant victims of Zafer Dogan, from Enfield in north London, were living close to the 32-year-old, who admitted multiple offences.

Met Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley spoke outside Wood Green Crown Court after Dogan was jailed for two years and four months, where Sir Mark criticised the "unfathomable decisions" of the justice system.

"The children should be put first, not the paedophile," he said.

A government spokesperson said the law is clear that bail "should only be used where necessary and proportionate, including to protect victims, witnesses and the public".

"These were awful crimes and our thoughts are with the victims and their loved ones," the spokesperson said.

They added that the government had introduced "tough new laws" to ban AI tools that are designed to create child sexual abuse images and stop the "vile material being created in the first place".

Remand and bail decisions are made by independent judges or magistrates.

News.title: Crashed RAF jet steered to 'avoid built-up areas' before pilots ejected, commander says
News.content:
An RAF jet was steered to "avoid built-up areas" before two pilots ejected out of the aircraft, an air force commander has said.

Gp Capt Gez Currie, Station Commander, said: "The aircraft would have been aimed in a direction that the pilot believed was open field, in order to avoid built-up areas and anybody on the ground."

The Hawk T2 aircraft had been flying out of the RAF Valley station on Anglesey on Wednesday when it plummeted to the ground in nearby Pencarnisiog, narrowly avoiding homes.

The trainee and an experienced professional, who parachuted out of their plane moments before it crashed, are expected to make a full recovery after they were treated for minor injuries.

Hawk operations have been paused by the RAF as a "precautionary measure" while investigations into the crash are ongoing - the Red Arrows are included in the pause as the aerobatics display team use the T1.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) confirmed that the squadron of Hawk jets at RAF Leeming, in Yorkshire, has also "paused" flying.

News.title: Man jailed for throwing bottle at migrant protest
News.content:
Judge Daniel Sawyer told Somerville that his sentence would act as a deterrent to others following subsequent protests in the area.

Describing him as a "thug", he told the defendant: "Police officers dedicate their lives to the protection of the public regardless of their own views, the very least they can expect is that those who engage in protests treat them with respect and the courts punish those who assault them."

The court heard Sommerville, from Portsmouth, was among a large group of demonstrators protesting at the arrival of the migrants.

They were brought ashore by the RNLI after being picked up in the Channel. A number of volunteer lifeboat crew members were subject to online abuse following the incident.

Prosecutor Edward Warren said Somerville was part of an "initially peaceful and lawful" gathering of a number of people on Ferry Road.

At shortly before 23:30 BST, he was with a large group of men as they were held up by the police line.

The court was told he was identified in police body-worn video as throwing a small bottle and swearing at police.

When later interviewed by police, he said he had found the bottle on the ground and was going to throw it into a nearby bush, but was angry and so threw it up into the air.

Defence barrister Helen Easterbrook said Somerville had been "caught up" in the disturbances.

She said he had been attempting to be a "calming influence" on the crowd but had thrown the bottle "in frustration".

Four other men are awaiting sentence having also been charged with violent disorder following the protest in Eastney.

News.title: NHS trust to review 4,500 more breast cancer cases after failings
News.content:
Hospital chiefs in County Durham have agreed to review up to a further 4,500 breast cancer cases after failings including delayed diagnoses and unnecessary surgeries were found.

Hundreds of patients suffered harm under County Durham and Darlington NHS Foundation Trust, according to a review of cases dating back to 2023.

The BBC previously investigated the failings and has spoken to multiple women affected, including one who said she felt "mutilated" and the trust's mistakes were "absolutely unforgivable".

Ahead of agreeing to expand the review to cases dating back to 2015, members of the trust's board offered "sincere" apologies for the failings and harm caused.

At an extraordinary meeting of the board held in Durham, board chair Alison Marshall said: "I would like to offer a sincere apology to all the women and their families who have been affected by the failings in our breast services.

"I can't imagine the impact that has had."

She said they could "not turn back the clock" but would be "open, honest and transparent" about the failings.

Chief nurse Gill Hunt told the board concerns were first raised in 2015 after a "service reconfiguration" and loss of breast surgical trainee posts.

Over the following years patients and bodies such as the Northern Cancer Alliance, Care Quality Commission and NHS England raised multiple issues, she said.

The key "themes" included treatment "not aligned to best practice", excessive surgery and delayed diagnosis, she said.

The trust's breast surgery lookback review began in April 2025 by examining cases between January 2023 and February 2025.

Hunt said 538 cases had been reviewed so far with 321 having experienced some form of harm, including one death.

News.title: Firm fined £1m after man killed by window that fell from luxury penthouse
News.content:
Ferris said her husband's death was "so sudden" and "out of the blue".

She said in a statement read out in court: "If somebody had done something differently â anything â it would have changed our lives. We wouldn't be in this position.

"I know it wasn't just one person, but one person could have changed this.

"What those companies did killed my husband.

"The thought this could have happened to anybody is always with me. It could have been a child."

She also told the court that 400 people attended her husband's funeral, and said "he is missed by so many it was unbelievable".

At the time of the incident, television host and fellow West Ham fan James Corden paid tribute to Mick Ferris on Twitter, saying: "He was a huge West Ham fan and has passed away in the most sudden of circumstances."

He added: "Tell your loved ones you love them today."

Health and Safety Executive principal inspector James Goldfinch said: "The fact lessons had not been learnt from a near miss the year before makes what happened on that day all the more galling.

"For a window to fall once was quite extraordinary, for it to fall again was simply criminal."

News.title: Greek PM urges Burnham to return Elgin Marbles permanently
News.content:
The Greek prime minister has called on Andy Burnham to find the "political will" to send the Parthenon sculptures back to Greece.

Kyriakos Mitsotakis wrote in the Guardian that returning the classical treasures, also known as the Elgin Marbles in the UK, would "send a powerful signal" but would require "courage".

The sculptures have been on display in the British Museum since the 19th Century, though Greece has long disputed the legality of their removal.

Mitsotakis and his government have previously held talks with the British Museum about the sculptures, but the two have so far failed to reach an agreement, with Greek authorities seeking their permanent return.

The Greek PM used the recent fanfare generated by the loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum to restate his country's claim to the Elgin Marbles.

"Nobody would seriously contemplate cutting what survives of the tapestry in two and displaying half in London and half in Bayeux, and claiming this was an adequate way to understand it," he wrote on Thursday, external.

"Yet that is exactly what happened to the Parthenon sculptures."

His comments come after British Museum director Nicholas Cullinan suggested that the recent arrangement struck between the UK and France, after decades of rejected requests to borrow the medieval embroidery, offered hope of a deal with Greece over the Elgin Marbles.

Mitsotakis said he was "surprised at the recent suggestion from the museum that the Bayeux Tapestry loan might provide a template for an agreement over the Parthenon sculptures", adding: "I do not believe it does."

"Greece cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum's ownership of the sculptures, or a scheme that would mean we 'borrow' parts of our own monument," he wrote.

Instead, he urged Burnham to stand by his previous comments on the sculptures and find a way of returning them for good.

This would be a "decisive step", Mitsotakis said, that would "reunite the sculptures and transform a historic dispute into a unique act of cultural friendship".

Back in 2023, several years before he returned to government and became prime minister, Burnham said the sculptures should be returned to Greece with "no strings attached".

For years, he supported a change in the law to allow for this. But last month, he told the Financial Times that "ultimately it's an issue for the British Museum", adding that "legally that's where that issue rests".

News.title: Police in Scotland arrest 36 in raids on Vietnamese crime gangs linked to human trafficking
News.content:
One of Scotland's biggest police operations has targeted a Vietnamese organised crime group linked to human trafficking and cannabis farms.

About 300 officers took part in simultaneous early-morning raids, leading to the arrest of 36 people and the discovery of 14 cannabis-growing operations.

In total, police searched or checked 47 addresses in Aberdeen, Dundee, Falkirk, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Ayrshire, Lanarkshire, Midlothian and the Scottish Borders.

Police Scotland allege the gang is involved in "poly-criminality," including human trafficking, drug production, fraud, money laundering and organised immigration crime.

The force says the activities first came to light after Vietnamese criminals were connected to 150 cannabis farms discovered in Scotland last year.

Around 120 people had been arrested - so-called "gardeners"- and drugs worth Â£26m were seized.

News.title: They said it: Leaders at the UN, in their own words
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Many leaders saying many things about many topics that matter to them, to their regions, to the world: That’s what the U.N. General Assembly invariably produces each year.

And each year, certain voices dominate. Here, The Associated Press takes the opposite approach and spotlights some thoughts from leaders who might have not captured the headlines and airtime on Thursday, the third day of the 2026 General Debate.

___

“The time for simply setting out goals is behind us.”

—Mia Amor Mottley, president of Barbados, on climate change

___

"A United Nations that delivers for all cannot mean an organization that responds loudly to some crises and quietly to others."

—Janez Jansa, prime minister of Slovenia

___

“Power earns trust only when it respects law.”

—András Baka, president of Hungary

___

“Narrow self-interest is breaking the bonds of solidarity.”

—Micheál Martin, Taoiseach of Ireland

___

“Please allow me to quote the great African writer Chinua Achebe, who said the following: ’When we gather in the village under the moonlight, it’s not because of the moon. Each person can see the moon in his own backyard. We gather because it is good to do so.'”

—Azali Assoumani, president of The Comoros

News.title: CNN and MS NOW blocked from covering Xi’s arrival at state dinner, networks say
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The White House has blocked CNN and MS NOW from covering Chinese President Xi Jinping’s arrival at the White House for a state dinner with Donald Trump, according to the networks.

CNN and MS NOW both said their reporters were denied access to cover Xi’s arrival Thursday night at the North Portico of the White House, despite a federal judge temporarily reversing Trump’s ban on the outlets covering such events.

A reporter and producer with CNN were stopped by a press wrangler when they tried to enter the greeting ceremony between Trump and first lady Melania and Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, the network reported.

The White House reportedly told CNN shortly before the event that it could cover Xi’s arrival but only with a photojournalist and audio technician, despite other networks being allowed to bring reporters and producers.

open image in gallery The White House has blocked CNN and MS NOW from covering Chinese President Xi Jinping’s arrival at the White House for a state dinner with Donald Trump, according to the networks ( AFP via Getty Images )

MS NOW White House reporter Laura Barrón-López said she was also stopped by a press wrangler when trying to cover Xi’s arrival.

“I was told, ‘I’m sorry, I can’t let you in,’” Barrón-López told MS NOW host Symone Sanders Townsend, recalling the incident.

“The big question is — is this going to continue? Are we not going to be credentialed into these daily events?” Barrón-López asked.

The Independent has reached out to the White House for comment.

The news of reporters continuously being barred from covering White House events came hours after Trump slammed CNN and MS NOW for skipping Xi’s arrival at the White House Thursday morning to attend a press conference and an Oval Office meeting.

open image in gallery CNN and MS NOW both said their reporters were denied access to cover Xi’s arrival Thursday night at the North Portico of the White House, despite a federal judge temporarily reversing Trump’s ban on the outlets covering such events ( Getty Images )

CNN and MS NOW “refused to cover one of the Biggest and Most Beautiful Events to take place in many years, the arrival at the White House of the Highly Respected President of China, Xi Jinping, and his beautiful wife, Madam Peng,” Trump raged on Truth Social Thursday afternoon.

The president suggested that the outlets didn’t cover Xi’s arrival Thursday morning because of their perceived vendetta against him.

“The event was magnificent — Actually made for Television but, because they’re Fake News, and because they knew how good it would be, they didn’t want credit to be given to ‘TRUMP,’ they refused to be there. That’s why they have such poor Ratings,” he wrote.

A rotating press pool usually covers White House events for major TV networks, but the pool has abstained from filming in solidarity with the outlets Trump banned.

open image in gallery Trump prohibited CNN, MS NOW and Politico from covering events at the White House last Friday because of their unfavorable coverage ( Getty Images )

Trump prohibited CNN, MS NOW and Politico from covering events at the White House just days before because of their unfavorable coverage.

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” the president wrote last Friday.

The three outlets subsequently filed a lawsuit to regain access to the White House, arguing the ban violated their First Amendment rights. In an early morning ruling Thursday, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the Trump administration to temporarily reinstate the outlets’ press badges.

Despite Kelly’s order, reporters from the three outlets were denied entry Thursday morning. A White House official later told the court that the press office started “reinstating” press badges that morning.

By Thursday afternoon, the outlets’ reporters regained access to the White House. But after reporters from CNN and MS NOW were blocked from covering Xi’s White House arrival Thursday night, it’s unclear whether their access will continue to be challenged and how that will play out in court.

News.title: US weighs new limits on Cuban travel at the UN as Havana decries Trump's economic squeeze
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Trump administration was considering imposing new restrictions on Cuban officials who travel to the United Nations, another step to squeeze the government in Havana as its top diplomat accused the United States on Thursday of unleashing collective punishment on Cuba’s people with its intensifying measures.

Even as a sizable Cuban delegation was approved to come to the U.N. General Assembly this week, the State Department is now weighing “strict controls” on the officials who plan to return next month for an annual U.N. vote on the decadeslong U.S. economic embargo on Cuba.

That is according to U.S. officials and an internal document obtained by The Associated Press. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because a decision on the details of what the restrictions will entail has not yet been finalized.

Potential plans to further restrict officials in New York for diplomatic work come as Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez bemoaned the “lack of progress” in negotiations between Havana and Washington. He also blasted the oil blockade that the Trump administration imposed on the Caribbean island nation in January.

“What defines the present status of the Cuba-U.S. relations is the brutal tightening of the economic and financial blockade and the total oil siege imposed on our country, which is equivalent to a naval blockade,” Rodríguez said in Spanish during an AP interview on the sidelines of the annual U.N. General Assembly gathering of world leaders.

His comments, made through a translator, follow President Donald Trump's wide-ranging U.N. address Tuesday, when he again called Cuba a “failed state" and said he was “seeking a fundamental ⁠change in the situation in Cuba.”

His administration has been trying to force changes to Cuba’s political system by cutting off fuel to the island, leading to massive power outages that affect basic activities such as cooking, water supply, and internet and telephone service.

“Communism will never be coming to America, but freedom ​will be coming to Cuba," Trump said at the U.N.

US-Cuba negotiations once again reach an impasse

Rodríguez, who has served as foreign minister since 2009, said that while no meetings now are scheduled with U.S. officials, “Cuba remains willing to keep these channel of contacts open.”

He refused to say when the last talks took place, noting that while past conversations have been “respectful,” the public statements and policy decisions made by U.S. officials afterward have been “extremely aggressive."

Millions of people have lost access to electricity as Cuba’s power grid has collapsed at least six times since the U.S. energy blockade began at the start of the year. The restrictions prevent Cuba from importing fuel needed to operate its thermoelectric power plants or replacement parts to maintain infrastructure that in many cases has become obsolete.

Other U.S. measures have included imposing more economic penalties on industries in the already heavily sanctioned country and broadening enforcement of laws that bar Americans who visit the island from dealings with government-owned or -affiliated businesses.

"These measures hamper some processes that could lead to discussion of things in the common interests of both nations," Rodríguez said.

Havana has recently integrated historic economic reforms, opening up the island to the private sector. Officials, including Rodríguez, have said these are not concessions to the U.S., but they are moving in the direction the Trump administration wants.

Cuban delegation could face new obstacles to visit United Nations

Rodríguez and other members of his government are planning to return to New York next month for the annual U.N. General Assembly vote on the U.S. economic embargo against Cuba — a vote that has historically condemned American policy toward the island by overwhelming margins.

Cuban officials already face heavy restrictions in New York and Washington due to their U.S. designation as a state sponsor of terrorism, with travel and commuting limited to a 25-mile radius of the U.N. headquarters in Manhattan.

But any new U.S. travel restrictions could make it more difficult or impossible for Cuban officials to attend the vote, which has been taking place for more than three decades.

Last year, Washington’s isolation on the issue was softened as countries like Argentina, Ukraine and Hungary — all closely allied with the Trump administration — rejected the Cuban-backed effort even as friction has grown in the region around American military actions there.

While General Assembly resolutions are not legally binding, they reflect world opinion.

Rodríguez told the AP last year that the U.S. had mounted a pressure campaign to influence the vote. He said then that Havana had heard from other countries, mainly in Europe, that the State Department was encouraging them to vote against the resolution.

In response, a State Department spokesperson said last year that “the Cuban regime does not deserve the backing of America’s democratic allies.”

News.title: It's been an intense hurricane season in the Pacific and there's still a long way to go
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

It’s already been an intense hurricane season in the Pacific Ocean — and there’s still quite a ways to go.

Tropical storms have spawned in what seems like assembly-line fashion in recent weeks, as El Nino conditions that emerged in June have caused waters to grow warmer than normal, setting off a chain of unusual weather around much of the world.

“It’s ramping up to be perhaps the strongest El Nino on record,” University of Miami hurricane expert Brian McNoldy said.

The number of hurricanes in the eastern Pacific has already surpassed what occurs in a typical season. This week alone, Hurricane Polo drenched Mexico’s Pacific Coast as it seesaws between Category 4 and 5. And in storm-weary Hawaii, there’s the potential for catastrophic flooding from a growing Tropical Storm Nolo.

During El Nino, low-level surface winds blowing from east to west across the Pacific are weakened or sometimes reversed. It causes a shift in the jet stream and drives record global heat, severe droughts, wildfires and shrinking water supplies.

El Ninos don’t follow a regular schedule, occurring every two to seven years on average. Some can be mild. Others can pack a punch. McNoldy predicted that the current El Nino will peak during the coming winter but linger into 2027.

“It doesn’t turn off right away,” he said.

While the focus is on the increased number of Pacific storms, El Ninos conversely curtail hurricane activity in the Atlantic Ocean: Tropical weather activity in the Atlantic has been virtually silent this year.

A turbocharged hurricane year in the Pacific

Thanks to El Nino, both the eastern Pacific and the central Pacific have seen four more tropical storms than is normal to date with more than two months left in the hurricane season, said Matthew Rosencrans, lead hurricane season forecaster with NOAA’s National Weather Service.

From 1991 to 2020, there were an average of 15 named storms in the eastern Pacific per season, which runs from May 15 to Nov. 30.

But surpassing the yearly average in September? “That's a different story,” Rosencrans said.

What also sets this year’s El Nino-fueled storms apart is that three Pacific hurricanes have reached Category 5 strength, tying a record set in 2002, also during an El Nino, he said.

The most active season on record in the eastern Pacific was 1992, when there were 25 named storms, Rosencrans said. For the central Pacific, it was 14 in 2015.

In 2015 there were nine major hurricanes, of Category 3 or higher, in the eastern Pacific, but no reported deaths. Due to El Nino, forecasters said the eastern Pacific storms formed farther west and tracked more westward, remaining over the open ocean throughout their cycle.

During another strong El Nino in 1997, hundreds of people died when Hurricane Pauline tore across Mexico’s Pacific coast. That same year Tropical Storm Nora gave landlocked southwestern Arizona an unusual soaking. And a December storm in Southern California caused flooding that swept cars into a storm channel and prompted evacuations of some mobile home parks.

In 1998, El Nino was blamed for flooding in China that killed 4,150 people, most along the Yangtze River.

Hawaii finds itself in the crosshairs again

The state has felt the wrath of two hurricanes over the past month. Lala in August and Lowell in early September combined to destroy or damage more than 510 homes and cause $168 million in damage to public infrastructure. Lala also caused $21.5 million in damage to 38 schools.

Assuming Tropical Storm Nola follows current forecasts for it to strengthen dramatically in the coming days south of the islands, that will make it three. Forecasters say the storm could drop rainfall amounts on Hawaii that are measured in feet, not inches.

On top of that, heavy rains in March caused the worst flooding to hit Hawaii in two decades. That was followed in May by a magnitude-6.0 earthquake, prompting Gov. Josh Green to remark that this year has been “unlike anything I can recall.”

Two hurricanes came within 200 miles (320 kilometers) of Hawaii in 1957, but that did not happen again for more than a half century. Then it occurred in 2014, 2016 and 2018 before this year's predicted trifecta.

Meteorologists often worry about “preparedness fatigue,” when communities gear up for storms that never arrive or fall short of their potential strength. But John Bravender, a weather service warning coordination meteorologist, said 2026 has yielded a different type of weariness in Hawaii.

“The fact that we’ve had these damaging impacts that keep happening, and as we’re recovering from them, we have to get ready for the next event — that’s a new one that really drains the resources and leads to this overall sense that this is a very busy hurricane season for us,” he said.

Residents understand the risks and are getting more accustomed to preparing.

“I think community members realize how dangerous the weather can be, how important it is for them to be self-sufficient, have food, water and also look out for their neighbors,” Bravender said.

___

Associated Press writer Gabriela Aoun Angueira contributed.

Far-right activist Daniel Thomas has been charged with criminal damage after allegedly slashing a dinghy in the English Channel earlier this week.

The anti-migrant agitator – known to his supporters as Danny Tommo – has also been charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone when requested by the police.

The 37-year-old, of no fixed abode, was remanded into custody to appear at Basingstoke Magistrates’ Court on Friday, Hampshire police said in a statement.

The force said in a statement on Thursday evening: “The charges follow an allegation made to police that damage had been caused to a boat in the Channel whilst an emergency responder was on board.”

Chris Derrick from the Crown Prosecution Service said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute Daniel Thomas following an investigation by Hampshire Constabulary into an incident on Tuesday September 22.

“Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue criminal proceedings.

open image in gallery Protesters gathered calling for the release of Danny Tommo ( PA )

“We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial.”

It comes after around 300 people gathered outside a police investigation centre calling for his release earlier on Thursday evening.

The protesters, who were mostly in black, and some with hoods or face coverings, arrived at the centre in Basingstoke, Hampshire, just before 6.30pm after social media posts urged them to be there at that time.

The group mainly consisted of men, with some carrying Union flags.

Some chanted “free DT”, with others taking mobile phone footage of the protest.

About a dozen police officers stood between the crowd and the entrance to the police investigation centre but the demonstration was peaceful.

It follows an anti-migrant protest in Gosport on Tuesday, when hundreds gathered in the belief that a boat of asylum-seekers, which had travelled from France, would be brought to shore.

Six people were arrested by officers during the evening, the force said.

open image in gallery Supporters of Danny Tommo gather outside Basingstoke Police Station ( Getty )

The boat eventually docked in Dover, Kent, at around 12.30am on Wednesday after 51 migrants on board reportedly refused help from a French ship and spent 33 hours at sea.

The government on Wednesday said it must “push further and harder” to stop migrants crossing the Channel after more than 700 people arrived in the UK – the highest number for a single day so far this year.

Education secretary Lucy Powell said not every migrant boat could be intercepted after two vessels landed undetected on British shores within two days.

Home secretary Shabana Mahmood said the failure to intercept the two boats was “not acceptable” and has ordered an urgent review by the Border Security Command.

The Home Office recorded 781 arrivals in 10 boats on Wednesday, suggesting an average of 78 people per boat.

It brings the provisional total for Channel crossings for the year so far to 18,565.
