News.title: Cheese and butter prices could soar after heatwave hits milk production
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Analysis of industry figures shows that British dairy farmers supplied 240 million fewer litres of milk than expected over the UK’s record hot summer.

Daily delivery records from agricultural holdings across the nation indicate the extreme temperatures had an unprecedented effect on output, according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU).

In reviewing data from the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB), researchers observed that producers delivered four fewer days’ worth of milk than anticipated between May and August.

Throughout those four months, deliveries dropped further beneath expected benchmarks on 87 individual days when compared against equivalent dates between 2008 and 2025.

The deficit became increasingly widespread as summer continued, affecting 25 days in June followed by every day of July and August, totalling 31 days in each respective month.

In total, the ECIU said dairy farmers lost more than £83 million worth of milk, which was enough milk to fill more than a billion school milk cartons.

It comes after the UK experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, with five intense heatwaves alongside historic dry spells that triggered widespread drought declarations and hosepipe bans across much of the nation.

Because of the weather, farmers in England and Wales have seen poor grazing conditions, stunted harvests and heat strain on livestock.

But while they delivered significantly less than expected over summer and the size of the UK milking herd hitting record lows this year, the ECIU said UK milk production could still hit near record levels in 2026.

open image in gallery Because of the weather, farmers in England and Wales have seen poor grazing conditions, stunted harvests and heat strain on livestock ( Getty/iStock )

Farmers built up a cushion earlier in the year that has partially offset the litres lost over the summer.

But more widely, the consolidation of dairy farms in recent years has allowed for economies of scale and mechanisation to increase milk outputs while the herd size reduces.

The drop in expected milk deliveries is unlikely to lead to any noticeable impact on supplies or prices, although there could be a very slight knock-on effect on dairy products such as skimmed milk powder, cheese and butter.

But the ECIU warns that the figures show how climate impacts can severely hit the amount UK dairy farms are expected to produce, ultimately squeezing the already tight incomes of farmers even further.

Tom Cantillon, ECIU senior analyst, said: “With the UK dairy herd shrinking, future shocks like this will become progressively harder to recover from.”

Milk is an “unforgiving product in farming” because it cannot be stored or stockpiled, and a dip in expected yield cannot be made up for in autumn, he added.

Earlier this week, farmers told the Press Association that food and milk producers in England and Wales have come under increasing pressure from the extreme heat and drought, while Scottish producers say they are looking north to fill in the gaps.

Mr Cantillon said: “For months, UK dairy farms produced below a normal summer, and by August the scale of the impact was regularly worse than anything seen in 18 years.”

“The missing £83 million from farmers’ pockets has gone in a year when many were already milking at a loss.

open image in gallery Farmers built up a cushion earlier in the year that has partially offset the litres lost over the summer ( PA )

“The costs don’t stop now that the rain has come. A second bad year for grass has pushed farmers into their winter forage early, with feed prices to follow.”

Mr Cantillon argued that farmers need help to roll out climate resilience measures such as more shade, trees and water.

But he also warned that summers “keep getting worse until we cut emissions to net zero and bring the climate back into balance”.

Elsewhere, the ECIU found that grass growth for the season to date as of September 4 stands at 86% of the 2019-2024 average, with the lost growth to date being enough to feed the national cattle herd for two months.

Many farmers have already begun giving winter feed to cattle, forcing them to supplement their winter feed stores with supplies sourced elsewhere and leaving them more exposed to soaring hay, silage and other feed prices in the colder months.

Debbie Wilkins, a dairy and beef farmer in Gloucestershire, said: “This has been a difficult summer.”

“We’ve been able to produce enough food for the winter, though the situation is still not ideal because cows eating grass in fields is far cheaper than paying contractors to make silage and then dealing with the costs and labour of maintaining slurry stores, cleaning out sheds, changing bedding and so on.

“The costs pile up when you have to bring the cows indoors, and the loss of milk production compounds the issue.”

Ruth Grice, a dairy farmer in Leicestershire, also called this summer was “very challenging”.

“Dairy farmers have been hit by a double whammy of significant increases in operational costs, while milk prices remained really low as a hangover from the enormous volumes of milk produced last year and at the start of this year.

“It’s an incredibly volatile time to be a UK dairy farmer, as there are so many more climate unknowns than there were even five years ago.”

News.title: UK food exports tumble amid high costs and Middle East impact
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

UK food and drink exports plunged by more than a 10th over the first half of the year because of increased costs and the conflict in the Middle East, according to new figures.

Data from the Food and Drink Federation (FDF) trade organisation also revealed that high levels of food imports resulted in a widening trade deficit for the industry compared with other nations.

The organisation’s latest trade snapshot report showed that food and drink exports from the UK declined by 11.7% in the first half of 2026 compared with the first half of last year, dropping to the third lowest level on record.

Exports of roughly four billion kg were only “marginally above” levels at the height of the Covid-19 pandemic and in the aftermath of the 2001 foot-and-mouth disease outbreak, the FDF said.

Exports to the EU continued a recent downward trend, with declines of 4.9% in Ireland and 4.6% in France, two of the UK’s largest export markets.

The decline was linked to additional costs and the increased complexity of trading with the nations since Brexit.

Non-EU exports meanwhile fell by 6.9%, with the ongoing war in Iran and disruption across the Middle East weighing on trade to the region.

Exports to the UAE fell by 23.4% as a result.

Tariff measures in the US also continued to impact food exports to the region, with a decline of 16.5% for the half-year.

The data also showed that food and drink imports into the UK increased to their second highest level on record, behind the first half of 2025.

Karen Betts, chief executive of the FDF, said: “Our food and drink trade deficit is growing and is now the largest it’s been in over 25 years.

“In a world beset by conflict and the ever-increasing impacts of climate change, this poses some stark questions about our food security.

“The pressures on manufacturers are significant and growing, with the cost of everything they need to make food going up, from energy and ingredients, to logistics, packaging and labour.

“Constantly changing regulation and high compliance costs are adding to this and making UK businesses uncompetitive both here and abroad.”

News.title: Buttler injury derails England chase and sends Sri Lanka series to decider
News.content:
Enter Buttler to play a wonderful counter-attack, whacking Wellalage for four and six and dumping leg-spinner Sachindu Colombage over the rope twice as he raced to 41 off 22 balls.

Buttler was at a crossroads after the T20 World Cup in February. Despite England making the semi-finals, he averaged just 10 in the tournament to complete a third poor World Cup in a row. A break with his family, and a very good Indian Premier League, where he made a crucial technical correction, changed his fortunes.

Matthew Hayden, the batting coach at the Gujarat Titans, asked him whether he was watching the ball closely enough. Buttler discovered that, now 36, he is a right-eye dominant batsman, so with Hayden’s help he opened up his stance to give himself a better view of the ball. A summer rich in runs has followed with an average of 51 for England and a strut back in his body language. The injury has surely ended Buttler’s summer and there are worries that he could be out of the Pakistan ODI triangular tournament next month as well, just to add to the night’s woes.

This was not a vintage England performance. Atkinson made a crucial error on the boundary, dropping a straightforward chance off Kusal Mendis on 17. It kickstarted Mendis, who went on the charge smashing 51 in 24 balls. He put on 137 in 120 balls with Kuminda Mendis. Josh Tongue had an off day going at seven an over and Jofra Archer was given similar treatment, although he bowled better than figures suggest, as anything wayward with pace on the ball was hit away.

Overton was more effective with his cutters and slower balls, while Ahmed did at least bag a couple of wickets, credit for keeping his head after some early rough treatment. Kusal Mendis was given out leg before on 99 but overturned the decision and stroked a four next ball for a deserved hundred.

Thanks for joining me. A global rout in bond markets deepened overnight as traders expect the US to keep raising interest rates.

Japan’s 10-year bond yield surged to 3.08pc on Thursday, its highest level since 1996, as markets responded to stronger than expected US economic data and higher oil prices.

It followed sharp rises in the US on Wednesday, when the yield on 10-year Treasuries – a benchmark of global borrowing costs – surged as high as 5.12pc, up from 4.96pc. It was the biggest jump since the “liberation day” tariff turmoil in April last year.

Bonds were sent into turmoil as traders bet that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates three times by April next year in an effort to bring down inflation. Money markets suggest there is a 70pc chance of the Fed following this month’s first rate rise in three years with a second in October.

This followed closely watched industry data on Wednesday, known as PMIs, showed US private sector activity jumped unexpectedly to a five-year high in September.

Meanwhile, oil prices spiked 3.9pc on Wednesday to move back above $100 a barrel, risking an inflationary spiral in the world economy.

Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “The main driver was a strong batch of PMIs, along with a rebound in oil prices, which both led to mounting speculation about faster rate hikes.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) US borrowing costs hit highest since 2007 on fears economy overheating | Yield on 10-year Treasuries soars amid inflation concerns as oil prices rise

2) Diesel prices surge as Trump mulls 90-day US export ban | Pump prices could exceed £3 per litre in Britain if Washington imposes ‘catastrophic’ block on exports

3) England’s first new reservoir in 30 years delayed despite drought warnings | Havant Thicket, in Hampshire, will now be completed in 2034, five years after initially planned

4) Timpson customers ask for extra belt holes after weight-loss jabs | Boss of key cutting chain credits Ozempic and Mounjaro after surge in requests

5) Chinese carmaker’s new EV battery will charge in under five minutes | Geely says its latest system is fastest in industry as brands approach ‘physical limit’

What happened overnight

Debt markets were in turmoil after Japanese bond yields hit 30-year highs.

As Tokyo markets reopened after a three-day holiday, the benchmark 10-year Japanese government bond yield jumped to its highest level since 1996.

This came after a steep sell-off in the US market overnight. Oil prices remained around $103 a barrel and the dollar held gains after Tehran’s leader vowed to never surrender following a warning by Donald Trump that he could “annihilate” Iran.

Japan’s benchmark stock market, the Nikkei 225 rose 1pc to 65,645.10, as some chipmakers got a boost from the recent interest in AI. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.7pc to 8,702.00.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng lost 0.3pc to 24,762.39, while the Shanghai Composite dipped 0.9pc to 4,545.09. Trading was closed in South Korea for the Chuseok autumn harvest holiday.

News.title: Zelensky lashes out at EU
News.content:
Volodymyr Zelensky lashed out at the European Union over its moves to weaken sanctions on Russian oligarchs.

In his address to the UN General Assembly, the Ukrainian leader warned that beyond making life “more comfortable” for Russians, “it also gives the war more time for Putin to send poor people into the kill zone. So Russia’s revenues must remain a target.”

His criticism came after France and Luxembourg successfully pushed for sanctions exemptions for Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, Russian oligarchs, on Tuesday.

Kyiv branded the decision “shameful and unjustifiable”. The men are known to share close ties to Vladimir Putin and have net worths of $14bn and $16bn, respectively.

In his fourth address to the UN as a wartime leader, Mr Zelensky said it was paramount that the international community increased pressure on the Kremlin to stop “the madness” of the war spreading.

Under pressure from Donald Trump to halt attacks on Russian energy targets, Mr Zelensky defended his country’s aerial offensive for successfully depriving Putin of revenue for his war.

“When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time. And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he said.

‘End the war before winter’

Washington has recently attempted to revive the long-stalled negotiations between Ukraine and Russia. On Tuesday, Mr Zelensky implored Mr Trump to help Kyiv end the war “before winter”.

Mr Trump appeared optimistic, suggesting an agreement would happen “more quickly than people understand”.

Sergei Lavrov, the Russian foreign minister, told the UN Security Council on Wednesday that Russia was prepared to negotiate for a lasting peace but would not “pause the war”.

Mr Zelensky sought to remind world leaders that the conflict was not constrained within Ukraine’s borders at a time when the global community was distracted by a myriad of conflicts and crises.

Citing the support of Iran and North Korea for Russia, he warned that Putin’s war kept “spreading further”.

“Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land, take more territory and take another country instead of simply stopping and running his own country,” Mr Zelensky said at the UN.

He noted that fighters from at least 47 countries were helping to prosecute Moscow’s war against Ukraine and urged leaders to prevent their citizens from being dragged into the conflict.

After Mr Zelensky’s address, reports emerged that Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s envoy, was on his way to the US where he would meet Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the Trump administration representatives.

Sources told Reuters that the meeting would take place in New ‌York on the sidelines of the UN summit.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, also confirmed Mr Trump had invited his Russian counterpart to attend the G20 summit of world leaders in Miami in December.

News.title: Male contraceptives could hit pharmacies in ‘three to five years’, says WHO
News.content:
Game-changing contraceptives for men could be on pharmacy shelves as soon as 2029, according to the World Health Organization.

Speaking to the Telegraph, Dr James Kiarie, head of the UN agency’s contraception and fertility care unit, said he expects male birth control to be available in just a few years, in a major expansion of contraceptive options for men.

“In three to five years, we will actually have a method available, [so] men can be more than supporters of their female partners in using contraception – men can actually be users,” he said.

On Tuesday, the WHO released its first Target Product Profiles (TPPs) for these products, setting out guidelines for the desired and minimum standards any male contraceptive product must meet.

“[The TPPs] signals that this is a priority issue for the WHO,” said Dr Kiarie.

“Currently men do not have much option in terms of their contraceptive methods. They have to either use condoms… [or] they have to use withdrawal, which has a high failure rate, or they have to use vasectomy, which is a permanent method.”

At the moment, the most advanced new product is called NES/T. It is a daily hormonal gel that is applied to the shoulders and upper arms, and suppresses sperm production without affecting testosterone levels.

Other candidates include injectable hydrogels that block sperm travel, an approach that has been described as a “reversible vasectomy”. ADAM, developed by Contraline, is in phase 1 trials while Next Life Sciences is set to trial a similar product called Plan A.

A third option is YCT-529 – the first non-hormonal, daily male birth control pill. It is currently in phase 1b and 2a clinical trials.

Dr Kiarie said it was important to have multiple options as “there’s no one size fits all” approach, but warned development could take longer than five years if clinical trials face unexpected hurdles.

News.title: England learn more in scrappy Sri Lanka win than in summer of white-ball walkovers
News.content:
You do not expect spinners to dominate at Chester-le-Street, but this hot summer has produced strange events, none more so than Jacks recording the second-best figures by an England spinner in one-day international cricket having previously only taken three wickets in 16 games at home.

Sachindu Colombage, Sri Lanka’s debutant leggie who was playing club cricket in East Anglia a year ago, laid down a marker as he impressed with three for 44 starting with the wicket of Root, his first dismissal in one-day international cricket since February.

England’s 89-run win was completed by Jacks taking three for none in four balls as Sri Lanka were bowled out for 176, their run chase a timid effort when they had a sniff of victory after restricting England to 265 and preventing them from hitting a six for the first time in an innings since 2019.

Vice-captain Jacks has evolved under Harry Brook’s leadership from an opening batsman to middle-order finisher who can chip in with the ball. “He is just a good leader with bat ball and in the field. He is buying into everything we want to do,” Brook said. “We are always talking about adapting to conditions and he has done it really well since coming back in. He could have moaned and groaned about batting in the middle order and playing as an all-rounder but has accepted that will be his place for a long time.”

Brook thought England made “just about par” on a very dry pitch and was reluctant to shower too much praise on batting consultant Kevin Pietersen, whose spin class the day before concentrated on making runs on a slow surface. “It will take time, more than one day. He’s not a miracle worker but it helps the more opportunity we get,” Brook said.

England were stretched and Pietersen will be happy. He told them to think about their approach, that in this type of game “rotation of strike is incredibly important”. He was right, they ran well, apart from Rehan Ahmed, and did not hit a six in an innings for the first time in seven years.

When England batsmen tried to force the pace they perished. Ben Duckett, Root and Brook all had opportunities to build an innings without seeing it through and it required Jacks to tip the total to more than 250. He batted within himself at first, but hit four fours in a row in the 47th over in a late burst that took England to a winning score.

News.title: Africa faces new threat as chronic disease rate leaps
News.content:
Chronic ailments like heart disease, cancers and diabetes now account for almost half of deaths in Africa and will soon overtake the continent’s infectious disease toll, new research has found.

Between 1990 and 2023 the proportion of deaths caused by non-communicable diseases (NCDs) almost doubled, from 25 per cent to 45 per cent, with heart disease and strokes now the leading killers.

The shift is not unexpected: public health experts have long warned that although African countries are making huge strides cutting infectious disease deaths through vaccinations, better sanitation and improved healthcare, lifestyle changes pose a new threat.

But the continent is not necessarily ready to tackle this “epidemiological transition”, researchers warned, in a study published in the Lancet Global Health journal on Tuesday.

“Although the epidemiological transition is well recognised, the speed and scale of NCD growth in Africa is particularly concerning,” they wrote.

“Health systems face increasing demands for chronic disease management, yet low-resource settings remain poorly equipped, underfunded, and unable to provide adequate preventive or treatment services.”

News.title: Zika mosquitoes still breeding in London
News.content:
Dr Medlock said there is still “no conclusive” evidence about how the insects arrived, but it’s possible that someone brought them back from holiday in their luggage, or that mosquito eggs were hidden on a tropical plant.

The mosquitoes are very temperature sensitive – they typically survive and multiply between 25C and 30C – and the UK has historically been too cold. But the species are gradually making their way north through Europe, after successive summers of record heat.

As temperatures drop in the coming weeks, the UKHSA hopes London’s invasive mosquitoes will die off naturally – though an unprecedented El Niño has made the predicament more challenging.

“This is a tropical mosquito, so the model has convinced me this won’t survive the winter,” Dr Medlock said. “Although we’ve got El Niño, [so] it’s very mild – it’s certainly warm enough still in East London [for the insects to survive].”

Diseases such as dengue and Zika virus do not typically circulate in Britain, but an infected traveller returning from a country where the diseases are present could carry the virus back with them.

If an invasive mosquito then bit an infected person, it could potentially catch and spread on the disease to others.

Several countries in Europe, including France, Italy and Spain, have started to see local transmission of mosquito-borne viruses, including dengue fever and West Nile virus, in recent years as the climate becomes more suitable for mosquitoes to survive and multiply.

Just last week, a third person died in Frankfurt, Germany, from malaria despite having no travel history, after mosquitoes infected with the disease were imported into the country on an aeroplane and subsequently infected eight people over the summer.

“We [already] see imported cases of malaria, dengue and chikungunya each year, with significant associated mortality and morbidity,” Dr Phillip Veal, a consultant in public health at the UKHSA, said.

“But if we [in Britain] follow the pattern of Europe, and all models suggest we will, Aedes albopictus and other Aedes species may become established. We’ve got a window of opportunity to do something, to prepare, to be ready, to fulfil our mission of protecting the public,” Dr Veal said.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

News.title: Tax rises ‘virtually inevitable’ after £8bn borrowing blow
News.content:
Tax rises are “virtually inevitable” after official figures showed the Treasury has borrowed £8bn more than expected so far this year.

Economists said the Chancellor faced an “uncomfortable” Budget after the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said spending outstripped tax receipts by £18.3bn in August, £3.5bn more than expected.

It means John Healey, the Chancellor, has borrowed £77.3bn so far this financial year, which is £8.1bn more than forecast.

Reacting to the figures, Emma Reynolds, the Chief Secretary to the Treasury, warned of “tough decisions” in Mr Healey’s Budget.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said: “The jump in borrowing in August compared to last year sets the stage for what is likely to be a much trickier Budget than Andy Burnham or Healey anticipated when they came to power.

“Another round of tax rises in October now looks inevitable.”

Philip Shaw, an economist at Investec, added: “We suspect that some tax increases are virtually inevitable.”

Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said the Chancellor would need to raise up to £14bn to restore the £24bn of fiscal headroom left by his predecessor Rachel Reeves to balance the books.

The Government’s debt interest bill soared to £8.8bn last month, according to the ONS, the biggest August figure since records began in 1997.

So far this year, the Treasury has spent £50bn on debt interest – £2bn more than forecast in March.

Nick Ridpath, an economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: “Debt interest spending is a worryingly large share of overall government spending.

“Both higher borrowing costs and higher inflation make life harder for a Chancellor who is looking to bring down borrowing and to spend more on government priorities.”

Higher prices caused by the Iran war mean the Chancellor must pay more interest on the country’s huge stock of inflation-linked debt.

Inflation is also pushing up the welfare bill. The Government spent almost £30bn in August on benefits, 7pc more than a year ago.

Despite this, the Treasury continued to see substantial tax receipts. Income tax, capital gains, and National Insurance receipts stood at £231bn in the financial year to August.

That is £16.6bn higher than the same period a year ago.

Inheritance tax receipts also grew. They have risen to £3.8bn so far this financial year, a £100m increase compared with a year ago.

Ms Reynolds, the Treasury minister, said: “At a time when debt interest costs billions of pounds that could otherwise be spent on improving lives, we must always know where the money is coming from to pay for public services.

“That is why we are committed to meeting our fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.”

The figures also showed total debt rose to £2.985tn in August, taking the level just shy of £3tn.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Labour has lost control of the public finances.

“It takes a rare fiscal incontinence to have both the highest tax take in history and see borrowing still shoot up.”

Sports.title: Harry Kane tipped to play at next World Cup weeks before he turns 37 by England boss Thomas Tuchel
Sports.content:
Next

HARRY KANE has been tipped by England boss Thomas Tuchel to star at the next World Cup — weeks before he turns 37.

The veteran Three Lions captain faces Spain in the Nations League on Saturday night.



And Tuchel said: “No problem, age is just age, it doesn’t matter.

“It is only about quality — and he still has a long way to go.”



The Wembley clash with the world champions represents the first step towards a home Euros in 2028.

But Tuchel believes Kane, 33, who has scored 85 goals for his country, will carry on through to the 2030 World Cup in Spain, Portugal and Morocco.



The German said: “He’s getting better and better.

“He has added a level of physicality.

“He is so committed to the high press and being involved in every part of the match.

“Be it deep build-up, be it finishing, be it build-up play in the middle block, be it defending.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

“He is the full package.”

Kane is just four games away from equalling goalkeeper Peter Shilton’s record of 125 England caps.

Earlier this week, he said: “Right now, I am feeling that I want to play for as long as I can here.



“It is easy at my age to start thinking about retirement.

“But I am trying to extract everything I can from the last two, five or ten years.”

Kane hit 73 goals for Bayern Munich and England last term — and is a contender for next month’s Ballon d’Or.

Asked if his skipper should win, Tuchel told ITV Sport: “After this season, yes, 70-plus goals, three titles with Bayern Munich.”

Sports.title: Former Premier League stadium set to host charity match after last-minute change
Sports.content:

GOODISON PARK is set to host a charity match despite Everton replacing it with the Hill Dickinson Stadium.

The iconic Premier League venue is still standing and is now the home of the Toffees’ women’s team.



The inaugural Game4Hope was booked to be played at the modern home of Everton on Saturday.

The club have confirmed that the venue has now been changed to Goodison.



A statement was released on social media confirming the change.

It also assured fans with tickets that they do not need to take any action.

It said: “Supporters who have already purchased tickets or Premium packages for Game4Hope at Hill Dickinson Stadium do not need to take any action at this stage.

“Everton’s Fan Centre and Premium teams will contact all existing purchasers directly with further information about their revised ticketing and package arrangements for the event at Goodison Park.

“With Cahill, Rivaldo, Cafu, Seedorf and some of the most recognisable names from Everton and Liverpool’s recent history preparing to grace the Goodison turf, alongside live music, celebrity guests and entertainment for the whole family – supporters are encouraged to secure their place now to avoid disappointment.”

The match is being held to help fight homelessness across Merseyside and further afield.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Legends from both Everton and cross-city rivals Liverpool will feature in the match alongside celebrities and other football icons.

Players who will feature include Leighton Baines, Gareth Barry, Phil Jagielka, Yakubu, Robbie Fowler, David James, Ryan Babel, Jari Litmanen, John Aldridge, Joleon Lescott and Louis Saha.

The Rest of the World squad will include the likes of Brazil icon Cafu, Dutch star Clarence Seedorf and Jaap Stam.



Boxer Tony Bellew, Big Zuu, Molly McCann, Still Ryan and John Bishop are all also involved in the event.

There will be a half-time show performed by rapper Tinie Tempah.

Sports.title: Wayne Rooney reveals all behind his incredible body transformation and shoots down claims he is using fat jabs
Sports.content:
Next

WAYNE ROONEY has revealed all about his incredible body transformation.

The Manchester United and England legend has enjoyed a stunning glow-up over the last few months.



Rooney, 40, stunned fans during the World Cup when he appeared as a pundit on the BBC.

The retired footballer had a clean look combined with a tan and a sharp-looking suit.



SunSport exclusively revealed that his wife Coleen, 40, had been helping him transform that life.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo left devastated after wildly celebrating Portugal goal vs Wales – only for it to be ruled out
Sports.content:
Next

HEARTBROKEN Cristiano Ronaldo was in utter disbelief after his Nations League goal was disallowed.

It was an Al Nassr striker who scored for Portugal… but it was not Ronaldo.



Joao Felix’s deflected 20-yard shot clinched a 1-0 Nations League triumph

over Craig Bellamy‘s battling Wales.

All the pre-match talk in Lisbon focused on Ronaldo’s future with the

41-year-old setting himself the target of 1,000 career goals before he

retires.



Ronaldo drew a blank on a frustrating night here back at his first

ground of Sporting where he started out before his first spell at

Manchester United.

He saw four first half chances go begging, missed a second half sitter

as the ball came off his shin six yards out before having career goal

number 980 ruled out by VAR for offside.



Even the footballing legend, who was winning his 234th international cap, showed he is human.

As a result, Ronaldo remains on 979 career goals with 146 of those

coming for his country.

Every Ronaldo touch was applauded wildly by the enthusiastic home

crowd inside the Jose Alvalade.

Ronaldo – marked by Ben Cabango of Swansea in the Championship – sent

an early warning in the tenth minute.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

But the former Real Madrid and Juventus superstar dragged a

left-footed shot wide from a tight angle after Felix’s precise pass.

Ronaldo had an even better chance minutes later only for Neco Williams

to produce a block as the ball went out for a corner.

Portugal, with five Champions League winners and three Ballon d’Or

nominees – Bruno Fernandes, Nuno Mendes and Vitinha – in Jorge Jesus’

first starting line-up were dominant.

Manchester City defender Ruben Dias headed over before Chelsea winger Pedro Neto prodded wide at the back post.



Despite being on the back foot, Bellamy and Wales would have been

happy with how the visitors navigated the opening 20 minutes,

particularly with the impressive way Liverpool’s Lewis Koumas held the

ball up.

But Felix broke the deadlock midway through the first half when

left-back Mendes stormed past Ethan Ampadu before supplying Felix 30

yards out.

The ex-Chelsea forward hit his right-footed effort from outside the

penalty box and Davies’ deflection took the ball past Danny Ward into

the corner although the Dragons keeper should have done better with the shot.

Ronaldo saw a free-kick hit the wall and Wales fans responded with

“You’re just a s*** Gareth Bale!”, in reference to their greatest player who played alongside CR7 at the Bernabeu.



Ronaldo then had a tame shot at Ward and he walked away frustrated

with himself as he failed to get a clean connection on a bobbly pitch.

Yet the goalscoring phenomenon was fuming after he failed to convert

Ruben Neves’ 50th minute cross.

Neves flashed the ball across the box where Ronaldo was unmarked but

he leaped to cushion the ball home at the back post only for it to

bounce off his leg and sail over the crossbar.

Ronaldo, normally as cool as a cucumber, could not believe he had

missed and the home fans instantly chanted his name in a bid to lift

his spirits.



But his luck did not change even when he beat Ward just before the hour mark.

Ronaldo raced on to a Bruno Fernandes pass and rolled the ball beyond

Wrexham keeper Ward but his ‘Siuuu’ celebration was cut short as VAR

chalked off the goal.

Ronaldo had another shot straight at Ward but that was his final

contribution as he received a standing ovation when Goncalo Ramos

replaced him in the 68th minute.



With Ronaldo on the sidelines, Wales came so close to an equaliser.

Brennan Johnson’s effort from an acute angle hit the bar before

Koumas’ follow-up shot was blocked by Dias on the line.

Sports.title: Ex-Spurs ace Sebastien Bassong charged with dodging £7 Tube fare by using fake travelcard & tailgating through barriers
Sports.content:
Next

FORMER Tottenham footballer Sebastien Bassong has been accused of evading a £7 Tube train fare by using a dodgy travelcard and tailgating through ticket barriers.

The ex-Premier League star is said to have avoided tapping in to pay for a trip on the London Underground and was halted by a revenue officer.



Bassong, 40, claims he did not realise the travel pass he had been given was not valid.

Employee Adebukola Anifowose said in a witness statement: “I observed Mr Bassong pretend to tap an Oyster card enclosed in a white wallet before tailgating through the wide-aisle gate behind another male. When requested to produce the card used at the barrier, Mr Bassong presented a Transport for London Staff Nominee Pass without the required accompanying photocard.



“System checks later confirmed that the pass did not belong to him and had last been used in October 2025.”

He explained it was established that the pass was registered to his male companion’s ex-girlfriend who claimed to be a Docklands Light Railway driver.



Mr Anifowose added: “No valid ticket was shown for being in thecompulsory ticket area. The fare avoided was £7.”

The Frenchman, now a TV pundit, is being prosecuted by Transport for London. Bassong, of New Southgate, North London, was told to respond to the charge by September 15 but has failed to do so.

He has now told The Sun: “I didn’t know about the prosecution and I haven’t received a letter.

“I was using a card given to me, and I was stopped, and I didn’t know it wasn’t good enough.



“I use the Tube every day. I’m a good citizen.”

The star, who played international football for Cameroon, was previously in trouble with the law when he was caught doing 110mph in a Maserati supercar in 2017.

He joined Newcastle United from French club Metz in 2008 before joining Spurs a year later.

The 6ft 4in centre-half played 45 times before moving to Wolves on loan and then Norwich City, where he spent five years.

He joined Peterborough in 2018 but left for Greek club Volos without making an appearance.

Sports.title: Gareth Southgate’s old coach says England call-up would be ‘too soon’ for U21 striker & fears days of No9 could be over
Sports.content:
Next

GARETH SOUTHGATE’S former England coach says it is the correct call to keep Will Lankshear with the Under-21s.

The red-hot striker, 21, has made a blistering start to life at Championship side Middlesbrough with eight goals already since his £10m arrival from Tottenham.



Three Lions legend Michael Owen believes the striker should have been called up by Thomas Tuchel so that the England boss could take a closer look at the in-form star as he searches for Harry Kane’s long-term successor.

Instead, Lankshear is preparing to make his U21s debut in Friday’s Euro qualifier against Kazakhstan at Molineux.



While Owen may not agree with it, but fellow Premier League scoring icon Jimmy Floyd Hasselbaink says the decision to put him with Lee Carsley’s squad is right.

The Dutchman, who joined ex-Three Lions manager Southgate’s staff in 2023, told Sun Sport via MrQ: “It’s too soon for Lankshear. He needs to play first at the highest level first.



“Don’t get me wrong, he’s doing really well, and I’m happy he’s doing well at my old club, Middlesbrough, as well. But England will really be a step too big for him right now.

“There are still other players in front of him right now. So he’s doing well, but he needs to keep on going and keep developing.

“Hopefully Middlesbrough get promoted, and then he has got a year of playing in the Premier League, playing all the other top teams. Then he can really show us what he is about.”

As well as Lankshear, Hasselbaink says there are several others who could potentially take over from Kane in both the short or long-term.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

And he even warned that the days of England playing with a regular No.9 may have to end once the skipper hangs up his boots.

He added: “Harry is getting older, and it is something to think about. But England have got different kinds of strikers to Harry. Dominic Calvert-Lewin is now playing really well and is in the England team again.

“There’s Liam Delap too. Yeah, it didn’t work out for him at Chelsea, but he’s got a chance at Nottingham Forest now, and he’s started okay there. He scored a goal, and hopefully he can pick up his career again.



“Hopefully, in the near future, a new striker who we don’t know about yet from the youth comes up.

“Or maybe it will be the case that England have to play a little bit differently if Harry Kane goes and you don’t have a focal No.9.

“It hurts me to say this as a No.9 myself, but you can play and win games without a No.9. It’s just one of the ways to win.”

Sports.title: Virgil van Dijk goes wild at referee as Germany score highly controversial goal while Holland star is down injured

VIRGIL VAN DIJK blew a gasket after Germany controversially took the lead against the Netherlands in their Nations League clash.

The Oranje went 1-0 down in the 32nd minute of their Group B clash in Amsterdam on Tuesday night.



Borussia Dortmund‘s Felix Nmecha gave the visitors the lead with a tap-in inside the six-yard box.

But he found the back of the net while Sunderland hitman Bryan Brobbey lay stricken on the turf.



And to say Van Dijk, who had a goal ruled out by VAR in the 13th minute, was furious would be an understatement.

The Liverpool skipper fumed immediately after Nmecha broke the deadlock and led his team’s protestations towards the Germans as they celebrated.



And he also vented his anger at referee Alejandro Jose Hernandez Hernandez, repeatedly pointing at the official as he verbally gesticulated.

The Netherlands’ fury at the referee not stopping play for Brobbey’s injury divided footie fans.

One wrote on X: “There was zero need to play out the ball, TBH.”

Another said: “It’s a competitive Nations League match.

Another chimed in: “Netherlands said, ‘We’re not letting that slide’ 😭🔥.”

Sports.title: Alcaraz felt burnt out after too much exposure on and off the court
Sports.content:
Carlos Alcaraz has admitted feeling burnt out due to being exposed to a lot of commitments before he suffered a lengthy layoff due to an injury sustained in April.

The Spaniard, who won the Australian Open title at the start of the year, was forced to miss more than four months from tennis because of a right wrist injury.

Alcaraz returned at the US Open where he reached the quarter-finals before losing a five-set thriller to American Ben Shelton, which finished at 3.33am local time.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the US Open quarter-final between Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcaraz

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch this incredible point from the match between Alcaraz and Shelton in New York

Due to the demanding nature of the calendar, the former world No 1 has said he plans to take longer breaks from the game in the future and skip some tournaments.

"With the breaks I cannot plan them in advance," Alcaraz told Sky's Jacquie Beltrao at London's O2. "It depends how I feel mentally and physically.

"The tennis calendar has been super tight. There are more important tournaments and even more Masters 1000 events over two weeks, so it's pretty long. You have to be focused from the first day until the last, plus all the Grand Slams and everything else so it depends on how many matches I've been playing.

"If I'm injured or mentally a bit down I'm going to need those breaks. I realise it will be better to take it before getting injured."

"You expose yourself in every tournament, but not only when you go on the court, it's every time you go out for dinner, the people who stop you, the people rolling with the cameras. Sometimes that is hard to deal with when you expose yourself at that level," the seven-time Grand Slam champion said.

Sports.title: Late Gakpo strike denies Klopp winning start with Germany
Sports.content:
Cody Gakpo hit a stoppage-time volley to earn the Netherlands a 1-1 draw against Germany in their Nations League Group A2 opener on Thursday, denying Jurgen Klopp victory in his first match as Germany boss.

Former Liverpool manager Klopp took charge in July after their surprise early exit from the World Cup against Paraguay in the last 32 under Julian Nagelsmann.

His side appeared set to give him the perfect start after Felix Nmecha put Germany ahead, but Gakpo finished off a swift counter-attack in the closing stages to level the contest.

Image: Jurgen Klopp's first game as Germany boss ended in a draw

The result also gave Xavi Hernandez something to celebrate in his first game in charge of the Netherlands. He was appointed in August after Ronald Koeman stepped down following the Dutch side's elimination at the same stage of the World Cup.

Germany suffered an early blow when Jamal Musiala was ruled out before kick-off, after experiencing muscle pain - and they were given a scare when Virgil van Dijk headed in from a corner inside the first 15 minutes.

Image: Arsenal's Kai Havertz picked up an injury in Amsterdam

The goal was ruled out following a VAR review, however, with the Netherlands captain adjudged to have fouled Germany goalkeeper Marc-Andre ter Stegen.

Klopp's side were hit by another injury in the 30th minute when Arsenal's Kai Havertz was forced off, but they took the lead just two minutes later.

Philipp Treu's cutback found Nmecha, who made no mistake from close range to put Germany ahead.

Image: Sunderland's Brian Brobbey was also taken off injured

The Netherlands had an injury concern of their own to contend with soon after, with Sunderland's Brian Brobbey taken off with what appeared to be a hamstring injury.

Germany almost doubled their advantage before half-time when Karim Adeyemi somehow failed to find the target from inside the six-yard box.

The Netherlands increased the pressure after the break and created a succession of chances, with Ter Stegen producing several important saves to preserve his side's lead.

Germany eventually succumbed in the closing stages, though, as Gakpo's late volley completed the Netherlands' comeback and secured an opening point.

Haaland brace fires Norway to winning start

Image: Erling Haaland scored for Norway against Denmark

Erling Haaland scored twice as Norway beat Denmark 3-2 in their UEFA Nations League Group A4 fixture in Oslo.

Fulham's Oscar Bobb put Norway in front after 14 minutes and Haaland made it 2-0 on 18 minutes.

Brentford's Mikkel Damsgaard, however, halved the deficit with a stunning free-kick and former Man Utd striker Rasmus Hojlund struck on the hour to level it at 2-2.

But Haaland struck with 16 minutes of the 90 remaining to seal the win, taking his tally to 64 senior international goals in just 56 appearances.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

Sports.title: João Félix strike for Portugal enough to sink Wales but Ronaldo fever falls flat
Sports.content:
There was a comic-strip feel to another eventful evening in the kingdom of Cristiano Ronaldo. Where to start? It was the 67th minute when his No 7 went up on the fourth official’s board, the cue to remove the captain’s armband from his left bicep before departing to a universal ovation, but for the pocket of Wales supporters.

The referee, Donatas Rumsas, hurried him off the pitch but Ronaldo, his hair glazed copper, was presumably ruminating on a series of missed chances, a sitter from a few yards at the start of the second half, and his disallowed goal, after skating offside to latch on to a Bruno Fernandes pass. The grandiose “Siu” celebration went to waste, though try telling that to the locals who worship him.

In the end, Portugal began their defence of the Nations League with a narrow victory courtesy of another Al-Nassr forward, João Felix’s deflected first-half strike from the edge of the box beating Danny Ward in goal.

Many of the Wales squad have been lightly raced of late, but they could have snatched a late equaliser when Brennan Johnson hit the crossbar and Rúben Dias desperately denied Lewis Koumas, who again impressed Craig Bellamy. For Wales, this was an exhaustive physical effort and afterwards the head coach, citing his own experiences as a player, referenced how mentally sapping games against elite opposition can prove. “I needed an ice pack on my head,” Bellamy said.

All eyes were on Ronaldo, back playing in Lisbon for the first time since last October, at the José Alvalade Stadium where he made his name as a teenager. The 41-year-old started, as Jorge Jesus promised he would, and despite Ronaldo talking of a new era, different tactics and even a different language, alluding to Jesus’s predecessor Roberto Martínez, this all felt rather run of the mill.

Rúben Neves, another player in Saudi, replacing João Neves in Portugal’s three-man midfield was the only change from their World Cup last-16 exit by Spain in Dallas.

Ronaldo finished with 27 touches, the fewest of any of Portugal’s outfield starters, and looked to the heavens after fluffing the best of the hosts’ chances to extend their lead four minutes into the second half.

View image in fullscreen Cristiano Ronaldo sends a shot wide on a night when good fortune in front of goal eluded him. Photograph: Miguel Lemos/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty Images

Neves put in a delicious cross from the right flank but Ronaldo, unmarked and alone with his thoughts in the six-yard box, shanked the ball over off his left shin. Sunday’s visit to Norway is his next opportunity to edge towards his 1,000 goals target. “I took him out 25 minutes before the end, because I thought it was important to have a fresh player on the pitch,” Jesus said. “I knew that Cris could stay a little longer, five or 10 minutes, but I was going to take him out anyway, I had planned it.” In a previous answer, he added: “Some players who are important were not up to their quality.”

Jesus, who twice managed Benfica and spent three years here in charge of Sporting, knows all about Ronaldo, having spent last season coaching him at Al-Nassr and defended the striker on the eve of this game, describing him as a symbol of Portugal. It is hard to disagree on that front. Ronaldo-mania is omnipresent in Lisbon, chiefly inside the official Portugal stores in Praça da Figueira, the city’s downtown, where you can buy CR7-branded briefs, face masks, action figures, lanyards, Lego, and even a Ronaldo boxset celebrating his time at Sporting.

Bellamy accepted Wales would suffer against a starting XI boasting five Champions League winners and three Ballon d’Or nominees, but began confidently. Bellamy does not have the same quality at his disposal, with Harry Wilson, Wales’s best performer in recent years, and Karl Darlow, these days the undisputed No 1, among those absent through injury. A harmless Ben Cabango header was Wales’s sole effort at goal in the first half and they did not trouble Diogo Costa. “He practically didn’t have to touch the ball,” Jesus said of his goalkeeper.

Ronaldo spurned four decent chances in the first half alone, the best of which was from about 12 yards and left him scuffing his boots in frustration. Then, after a predictably excitable buildup, there was a free-kick flighted into Wales’s yellow wall. He should have done better when Fernandes presented him with his first opening amid huge cheers from the locals, but his touch was rusty and the ball bobbled off his left foot, and he later volleyed wide from an awkward angle.

Wales were valiant. Jay Dasilva was excellent at left-back. Ben Davies, a Wales centurion and always a dependable performer for his country, marshalled the defence on his second appearance of the season, his only minutes for Tottenham coming against a Charlton B team in the Carabao Cup. Ward’s sole appearance was in the same competition for Wrexham six weeks ago.

Portugal racked up 23 shots but recorded only five on target and Wales will take plenty of confidence from this slender defeat. “I’m fully aware of who we were playing and what their value is,” Bellamy said, claiming the value of Portugal’s squad totals £1.4bn. “But the positive I’m coming away with is: I think there’s more [to come from us]. I’m beyond proud. We showed a big heart.”

Sports.title: Raphinha: ‘In my head I was leaving Barça, but a few small words can change you’
Sports.content:
For once, Raphael Dias Belloli puts the brakes on. The man who seems to be in perpetual motion, a footballer forever on fast forward, pauses, goes quiet for a moment and then, softly, utters something that says so much: “I think maybe people saw in me something I didn’t realise was there.” He did not know he was a leader, but he likes it. He did not know he was a captain, but according to his manager he is the “perfect captain”. And he did not know he was a No 9 either, but right now he is the best No 9 there is. In Barcelona or anywhere.

There was a time when Raphinha did not know whether he would be in Barcelona, when, feeling unwanted, he had accepted it was over, but this week he extended his contract to 2030. He will be 33 then: he would like to retire here and they would like him to retire here, too, a legend built on empathy and affection. “This is the best decision the club has made,” said Hansi Flick, the head coach Raphinha says changed his life. Sometimes you cannot get what you want so you have to settle for the best.

The first word Raphinha uses when training has finished and the tape starts rolling at Sant Joan Despí, when he is addressed as the world’s top No 9, is “false”. It comes with a smile; turns out there is nothing false about this 9. Seven games into the league season, the man filling in at centre-forward has scored 12 goals, plus two in the Champions League. The scorers leading the way in Europe’s other top leagues are five behind. No one in Barcelona’s history has started a season like this. And, no, Raphinha says, he has never played there before: “Even as a kid I wasn’t a 9.”

As if it is even about the goals. There may be no one as enjoyable to watch as Raphinha; no one as admirable or important either. The touch at speed is astonishing and there is a wild intensity about everything he does, only it is not wild, he says; it is worked upon, the entire system depending on him. The press defines Barcelona’s identity and it is, Raphinha says, “mechanised”. No, he is not going to reveal how but it begins with him. “As captain, he goes and everyone follows,” Flick says. “We always start with the No 9 and he has that incredible hunger and intensity, the mentality and attitude we need.”

Yet this is not what Raphinha or anyone expected. This summer Robert Lewandowski, Ferran Torres and Marcus Rashford departed, having contributed 38 league goals between them last season. They were supposed to be replaced by Julián Álvarez but Atlético Madrid refused to sell, leaving Barcelona with no striker. “There was a moment of need,” Raphinha says. “There was no No 9 for the [friendly] against Basel, so I played there.”

Raphinha backs Lamine Yamal to win Ballon d’Or – video

It was not supposed to be permanent, although Flick suspected it might be and was warming to the idea: Barcelona had not given up on Álvarez yet and the coach considered other solutions, including Anthony Gordon. This was better. Raphinha did not score but Barça got five.

“In pre-season we did a few tests: the manager liked what he saw and after Basel he told me a bit about his idea,” Raphinha says. “The adaptation came over the last two years, getting used to coming inside, closer to goal. But we tested [me as] an actual No 9 and it went well. There’s the occasional detail that has to be explained, but I’m OK. Before Elche [on the opening day], he asked if I was comfortable there or wanted to go back to my position. I said it was fine, see how it goes, we can always change back.”

Raphinha scored two against Elche, one against Athletic, two against Rayo and another at Valencia. Against Racing there was a hat-trick and another against Sevilla: right foot, left foot, header. Raphinha showed his old qualities and new, less expected ones: the movement, timing and clinical finishing of a classic No 9, efficiency to go with the intensity. Only one La Liga player has a better shot conversion rate. Against Feyenoord came two more.

View image in fullscreen Raphinha (right) is joined by Lamine Yamal – the player he says he is a ‘big brother to’ – after scoring during the Champions League match against Feyenoord. Photograph: Judit Cartiel/Uefa/Getty Images

Nor is it just about him. The point of Raphinha is that it is not even about him. Only once this season has he not scored, and against Levante he created the first two, then handed over the penalty for Lamine Yamal to add the third. Barcelona have scored five, two, five, five, five, four, seven and three, respectively in winning their first eight games.

Flick had done it again. “I always have and always will say that he changed my mentality, changed me as a person,” Raphinha says.

By 2024, Raphinha was convinced he had no future at Barcelona. His numbers were good: 10 goals and 12 assists in his first season, 10 goals and 13 assists in his second. But Lamine Yamal was emerging and, more importantly, Raphinha did not feel backed, completing 90 minutes seven times in 60 games under Xavi Hernández. It had not escaped his attention that Barcelona thought about selling him; it had not escaped anyone’s attention that they wanted to buy Nico Williams, publicly keen to reunite the pair that tore up the Euros.

Barcelona failed twice, and were all the better for it. A Photoshopped image of Williams in his No 11 shirt on social media hurt, Raphinha admitted. But Flick had arrived and if there is something even more powerful than the desire to prove people wrong, it is the desire to prove people right.

View image in fullscreen Raphinha fires in his team’s fourth goal in the 5-2 win against Rayo Vallecano. Photograph: David Ramos/Getty Images

“In my head, I knew I was leaving,” Raphinha says. “That was [mentally] done, that’s the truth. I was in Brazil and Flick called. He said come talk to him before taking a final decision. I met him and he said he trusted in me, that I was going to be important, that the team[’s play] would be good for me. In a moment like that, a few small words can change you. I felt a lot of faith in me. He gave me the confidence to play my football. I got an idea into my head: give everything, your life, regardless of the personal moment you’re in.”

Love won out, even if Raphinha is swift to add: “If you get results people are going to love you; if not, they’re not.” Feeling supported and valued changed everything. His success is a human story, his qualities human ones. He led Barcelona to the league. Flying in from the left, Raphinha scored 34 goals and provided 26 assists in 57 games. Another title followed in 2025-26 and although injuries reduced his contribution, there were 21 goals and eight assists in 33, Flick’s faith gratefully repaid.

His teammates’ faith, too. The dressing room had voted Raphinha as a club captain, third in line. He had not expected it and was genuinely touched. There was something in that moment, in the realisation of how they felt about him, how much they believed in him, that was transformative. Now Flick has named him his first choice.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen A jubilant Raphinha with the trophy after winning the Spanish Super Cup against Real Madrid. Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images

That moment brings pause, thought. “When I saw people had voted for me, it was like a switch had been flipped, a shift in mindset,” he says. “People could see something in me I didn’t realise was there, and that’s changed me. Before being captain, I didn’t know how much I would like it. Having that responsibility has also changed my mentality, helped me. I never thought I’d like being Barcelona captain so much. You feel you matter. It’s an honour. It’s not just wearing the armband.”

He is a natural, as pure a captain as there has been since Carles Puyol – even if he did need to be told. It is there in the relentless example he sets: Raphinha has sprinted the second-furthest distance in La Liga and Gradient Sports has measured only three players with more final-third pressures per 30 minutes out of possession. Raphinha says: “I talk less than most captains but I know people are watching. They think: ‘If this guy’s running like an animal, I have to follow.’. If you talk too much and then don’t do what you have to, people aren’t going to listen.”

Yet what teammates saw in him went deeper, to his very being. Leadership is there in the empathy, kindness and understanding too, in Raphinha returning the support that was good for him, an approach at once collective and individual. He says he can see when Lamine Yamal is drifting from games and how to reconnect him, every celebration shared with the teenager. A clip went round recently in which he quietly tells Gordon not to be afraid. And no clip was more powerful, more eloquent, than the moment when Flick sat on the bench, alone, lost in his thoughts and Raphinha consoled him, drawing him out of his dark place, roles reversed.

View image in fullscreen Fermín López, Raphinha, Lamine Yamal and Anthony Gordon celebrate their team’s third goal against Valencia. Photograph: David Ramos/Getty Images

“The coach-player relationship is the most important in football,” Raphinha says. “From the moment [Flick] arrived, we could talk to him about anything – and anything is anything. That time, I saw him, head down. At first, I didn’t really understand why. I asked what was wrong. He said he felt the team wasn’t playing well. From what I remember, I told him it was OK, we’d won and we would play well again. I prefer a thousand times to win playing badly than lose playing well. Win games, confidence and the football comes.

“What kind of leader [I am] depends on the moment. If I have to be slightly tougher, I can. But I prefer nicer moments, jokes. The last two years have been spectacular so I haven’t had to be the pesado [pain in the arse] often. I know that annoys people but someone has to do it sometimes.”

With a squad like this, especially? Four of Barcelona’s first team were born in 2007. “Buah!” Raphinha says, laughing. “That hurts: it shows I’m closer to the end than starting out at 18, 19, like them. But I’m in spectacular physical shape so [retirement] is some way off. It’s very easy with them. There are young players but they’re very responsible about their career, their lives. Once in a while, you have to [be paternal] because they’re kids. But they understand. If they get told off, they know it’s for their own good. I’ll tell them.”

View image in fullscreen Raphinha, pictured at the Barcelona training complex, is thriving in the role of captain. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

Is there something of the father figure in him with Lamine Yamal in particular? “No, no,” Raphinha jumps in. “Big brother, that’s better.” And Lamine Yamal is the star who should win the Ballon d’Or, he says: for his “individual numbers, collective titles, and the magic on the pitch, charisma. There’s no doubt. For me, he has to take the prize, no matter what. Even if I wasn’t Lamine’s teammate, for what he does, the numbers, the titles – and I think titles are important – he’s the candidate. One of one. Of three trophies, he won two with Barcelona. He won the World Cup with Spain.”

Only the Champions League escaped them; for two years Barcelona have come close, and it is their obsession now. “The semi-final against Inter [in 2025] hurt the most,” Raphinha says. “Against Atlético [in the quarter-final in 2026] we could have gone through, we could talk about things that could have gone differently, decisions. But against Inter, we had one foot in the final and to lose that way was hard. We’re a young team – that’s not an excuse – and sometimes you lack the maturity to manage key moments. This season we’re more mature, better prepared. If we carry on like this, with this mentality, we can compete for it all. We have everything.”

Starting from the front with the captain, the leader and the No 9.

Sports.title: Gakpo denies Klopp perfect start as Xavi’s Netherlands rescue draw against Germany
Sports.content:
At least Germany can be sure it will not be dull. Jürgen Klopp had predicted his debut as head coach could be wild, a trait he would accept as long as his team were lively enough. Both transpired in a frayed, pinball-like game whose lack of quality could be forgiven on account of its entertainment levels. The Netherlands more than merited a brilliant late equaliser from Cody Gakpo and by the time those present had drawn breath it felt appropriate that, for all the talk of new dawns, everyone finished back where they had started.

World domination is a far-off prospect for both of these flailing giants on such scrappy, frenetic evidence. But at least those with a stake in this famous old fixture, largely shorn of the spite and spit that defined it of old, could come away feeling something. Restoring those essential sensations of joy, pain and meaning sits at the very top of Klopp’s priorities. Germany looked raw and scattergun for long periods, reined in only by their lack of technical aptitude, but there were signs of an energy that had long been missing.

Nonetheless it was the more understated Xavi, making his own bow in charge of the hosts, who could punch the air in added time after Gakpo volleyed in a wonderful outside-of-the-boot cross from the substitute Ruben van Bommel. It so happens that the 22-year-old Van Bommel is son of the 79-times capped Mark; his grandfather is the former Netherlands manager Bert van Marwijk. An enthusiastic if largely toothless performance from Xavi’s crop was a reminder that the stardust of Van Bommel senior’s day is largely absent now; the equaliser’s conception, though, left lingering promise that the past can birth a brighter future.

“In a parallel world, if someone said you’d get a draw in Holland you’d take that,” Klopp said. “I feel we lost two points because of the time we conceded. But I’m fine with tonight, not more.” His approach to squad management across this four-game Nations League run had been to unveil a sprawling 44-player squad, a handful only passingly familiar even to some seasoned Bundesliga watchers, that would be split between assignments. His plans, and perhaps those of two club managers he must keep onside, were derailed by concerning injuries to Jamal Musiala and Kai Havertz.

The former felt his thigh in the warm-up, Nadiem Amiri taking his place in the starting lineup; Havertz was similarly afflicted early on, departing on the half-hour, and the pair were due to have MRI scans before returning home. “I hope we get the diagnosis tonight, I hope it’s nothing serious,” said Klopp, who expected the pair to at least miss Sunday’s match against Greece.

His team had begun with the intensity demanded before riding their luck, Virgil van Dijk unfortunate not to put one over his old boss when his glancing header was ruled out for a soft foul by Brian Brobbey on Marc-André ter Stegen. The Netherlands were further aggrieved when, with Brobbey lying on the floor near halfway requiring treatment, Joshua Kimmich elected to play on and set in train the move that opened Klopp’s account. The debutant right-back Philipp Treu crossed for Karim Adeyemi to attempt a close-range shot and, from the rebound, Felix Nmecha swept in.

View image in fullscreen Felix Nmecha finds the back of the net from close range to give Germany the lead. Photograph: Dean Mouhtaropoulos/Getty Images

Van Dijk led impassioned home protests, which turned into scuffles between the sides on the far touchline, but no laws had been broken. Germany should have doubled their lead when Adeyemi spooned Nathaniel Brown’s pass horribly high, Klopp reduced to grim laughter at the side, but Xavi’s players took charge thereafter.

“The second half is the way we must play,” Xavi said. “We want to show this ambition, passion and desire.”
