Ter Stegen, playing at his new Ajax home, frustrated his old Barcelona manager with commendable saves on numerous occasions while looking consistently jittery under set pieces. He should have finally been beaten when Max Meerdink, on for the stricken Brobbey, somehow diverted Denzel Dumfries’s centre wide from a matter of feet.

Germany were brisk but bereft of control in a scruffy but beguiling second period; much of that could be put down to their new broom but it will surely have irked Klopp that the substitute Serge Gnabry, one of his more experienced call-ups, had presented the ball carelessly to Van Bommel before the leveller.

“To develop a way of football you need more than two days,” Klopp said. “We only scratched the surface. We have to go deeper.” For better or worse, this taster was enough to promise a compelling ride ahead.

Sports.title: Israel’s Saied Abu Farchi sent off for gun gesture celebration in defeat by Austria
Sports.content:
Israel’s forward Saied Abu Farchi was ⁠sent off for celebrating his goal against Austria in ⁠his side’s 3-1 ​Nations League defeat on Thursday by using the corner ⁠flag to simulate a gun.

Abu Farchi headed home in the 55th ⁠minute to bring Israel level after ​Austria had ‌taken the lead ‌through a Romano Schmid penalty before ‌half-time at the Raiffeisen Arena in Linz.

The 20-year-old ran to the corner flag, grabbed it and made a gun-firing gesture during his celebration.

View image in fullscreen Saied Abu Farchi after scoring his side’s equaliser against Austria. Photograph: Georg Hochmuth/APA/AFP/Getty Images

The ‌referee had booked Abu Farchi four minutes earlier and showed ​him a second yellow card for the celebration, leaving Israel with 10 players.

Austria regained ⁠the lead in the 90th minute through ​Phillipp ​Mwene, who scored via Paul ​Wanner’s cross. ‌Sasa Kalajdzic ​added ​a third in stoppage time with a close-range finish.

The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away at Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina. The buildup had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which the Ireland manager, Heimir Hallgrímsson, had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly. The home side saw two shots cleared off the line before the Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhín Kelleher clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson’s side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland, who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday, showed plenty of spirit as they dug in for the second half, but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when the Kosovo captain, Vedat Muriqi, bundled the ball in from close range.

In a Group A4 match, Norway’s ‌Erling Haaland struck twice, including a 74th-minute winner, to edge his team past Denmark 3-2 in Oslo and earn their first competitive win over their opponents.

“It tasted sweet. It feels great to beat our neighbours,” the captain, Martin Ødegaard, said. “There is a lot we could have done better, but ​even when we were put under pressure, we found a way back and responded.”

View image in fullscreen Erling Haaland scores to put Norway 2-0 ahead against Denmark Photograph: Ulrik Pedersen/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

The Danes had powered back from a two-goal deficit and levelled the game on the hour after first-half goals from Oscar Bobb and Haaland had put the hosts 2-0 up. Norway were also left with 10 men in stoppage time after David Møller Wolfe was sent off following a second booking.

There was drama in Belgrade where visitors Greece came from a goal down to snatch a 2-1 victory over Serbia thanks to Tasos Douvikas’s winner deep in stoppage time. Malta came from behind to beat Andorra 2-1 in their League D clash, while Lithuania won 2-0 in Lichtenstein.

Sports.title: James Garner keen to live up to ‘mini-Valverde’ tag after late England call
Sports.content:
“It’s a very good comparison,” James Garner says, and he is not kidding. It came from Thomas Tuchel in March after the England manager had watched the Everton midfielder impress on his international debut against Uruguay. He was up against Federico Valverde and Tuchel went big with his praise. Garner was a “mini Valverde”, he said after the 1-1 draw at Wembley.

It was surely too much, despite the prefix that Tuchel attached, yet it was possible to see where he was coming from. Like Valverde, Garner wants to operate in central midfield but he can play at right-back or on the wing. And like Valverde, who they called El Pajarito – or the Little Bird – when he was a kid, Garner can sometimes fly a bit under the radar.

Is Valverde the most underrated player in the game? The more the question is asked, the more the point is lost but there is certainly something there. “You wouldn’t really call him a household name, would you?” Garner says of the Real Madrid player. “But players who have played the game – they know how good he is. I watch a lot of football. I watch all the Champions League games and he always stands out. So yeah, I would go as far as saying that he’s underrated. In my opinion, he’s one of the best midfielders in the world.”

The pros know. And within the game, there is a burgeoning appreciation of Garner, who located such outstanding form at Everton from the turn of the year that he won his first England call-up and was considered unlucky to miss out on the World Cup squad. In the end, Tuchel went with Jordan Henderson and Kobbie Mainoo as the midfield back-ups to Declan Rice and Elliot Anderson. Henderson played six minutes as a substitute during the tournament; Mainoo not at all.

“It was a tough phone call [from Tuchel] because you don’t know whether it’s a yes or a no,” Garner says. “He just said that he could only take a certain amount of players and I’ve missed out this time. I respect his decision and it just makes you hungrier.”

View image in fullscreen James Garner impressed on debut against Uruguay but missed out on the World Cup. Photograph: Alex Davidson/The FA/Getty Images

The 25-year-old is back in the squad for the upcoming Nations League fixtures, albeit as a late call-up after the withdrawals of Rice and Mainoo. Henderson was not picked on fitness grounds. Tuchel recalled Alex Scott and Myles Lewis-Skelly in his original selection and continues to overlook Adam Wharton. Anderson stands as the most established midfielder as Tuchel prepares for the visit of Spain to Wembley on Saturday night. Thereafter, England play Czechia and Croatia away before returning to Wembley to face Czechia.

Garner flew to Bodrum in Turkey on Sunday night for a holiday with his partner and he had just put the key in the hotel room door when he got the call from the Football Association. He flew home on Monday before reporting to St George’s Park on Tuesday. “It was a very short holiday,” he says with a smile. “I’m more than happy to be here now.”

Tuchel also gave a late call to Morgan Gibbs-White, who had just got to Dubai for a family holiday. The Nottingham Forest attacking midfielder made a lighthearted TikTok video in which he and his fiancee mimed Gotta Go My Own Way from High School Musical 2 as he packed up and headed back. Was Garner tempted to do something similar? “No. That’s not me,” he replies.

Garner is no-nonsense. He is laidback company but there is a toughness to him on the pitch, a warrior spirit to go with the intelligence of his game, the technique and range of his passing. Growing up in the Manchester United academy, he played as a centre-half until the age of 15 and his boyhood hero feels appropriate.

“I’ve never actually said this but I used to love Nemanja Vidic,” he says. “I used to love the No 15 [which Vidic wore] and things like that. Then you grow up a little bit more, I became a midfielder and I used to love Lampard, Scholes and Gerrard.”

Garner made the move into midfield with United at a junior tournament. “It was the Nike Cup and our midfielder got injured in the first game,” Garner says. “I’ve always been half-decent with the ball at my feet so they thought: ‘We’ll push him into midfield.’ I had a really good tournament and it just went from there. Albeit when I was with England under-16s and under-17s, I played centre-back.”

He is a student of the game. “I watch all matches and also, as mad as it sounds, I played Fifa for so long,” he says. “I’ve been so indulged in football since I was a kid. My brother is five years older than me, he played and I’ve always been around football. I was lucky enough to come through United’s academy, which is one of the best academies in the world, and I learned so much from a lot of good coaches. I’ve just always had that tactical awareness and maybe that helps me playing different positions.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Garner could not see a first-team pathway at United. They loaned him to Watford for six months, then Forest for 18 months. The writing was on the wall for him in the summer of 2022 when United bolstered their midfield with the signings of Casemiro and Christian Eriksen. His move to Everton for a bargain £9m still rankles with a section of the United support.

View image in fullscreen James Garner has no regrets over leaving Manchester United and joining Everton. Photograph: Gary Oakley/Everton FC/Getty Images

“It was the perfect thing for me to do – 1,000%,” Garner says. “I’ve never been shy of going into a more uncomfortable place, changing scenery or anything like that. I went on loan. I moved down to London and Nottingham. It was about playing games and Everton was the perfect choice. I didn’t want to fizzle into the background and just sit on the bench. I wanted to go to a team where I felt like I had a chance to fight for my position.

“Do I have any regrets about leaving United? No, not really. I am a big believer that everything happens for a reason. Had I stayed I wouldn’t have been where I am today so I am more than happy that I left.”

Garner made a statement on the international stage when he starred for the England under-21s in their European Championship triumph of 2023. He was named in the team of the tournament – as a right-back, which was where he played in the final when England beat Spain 1-0. He hopes to make another against the same nation.

“Spain have got the Ballon d’Or winner in their midfield [Rodri] so to play against someone like that is the ultimate test,” Garner says. “You want to go against the best and see how you fare.”

Sports.title: Former England player Andy Carroll reveals he was sexually assaulted in 2021
Sports.content:
The former England forward Andy Carroll has revealed in his autobiography he was sexually assaulted by a man in 2021. The 37-year-old included the details in his book, Owning It. As a victim of sexual assault, Carroll was automatically granted anonymity.

Carroll revealed the incident took place at his home during a second spell at Newcastle. The offender – a friend of his former partner, who was staying away at the time – was later jailed for three years, with Carroll having testified in court.

The former Liverpool and West Ham striker, who is now a player/co-owner of the National League South club Dagenham & Redbridge, said the incident happened when he was sleeping. He then threw the man out of the house, then knocked him unconscious when he attempted to get back inside.

“I was sexually assaulted, there I said it. Scary to even think about and only a few people knew about it before now,” wrote Carroll, who had decided to include the incident in his book “at the very last minute” after discussing it with his partner, Lou Teasdale.

“Me and Lou spent a lot of time discussing whether to mention it in this book or not. I avoided my publisher for so long that they probably suspected I got cold feet.

“Scary to talk about but it’s made [me] the person I am today as much as any of the good stuff. And if me talking about it helps just one person then good, it will have been worth it.”

Carroll said testifying in court, where the attacker was found guilty of sexual offences and placed on the sex offenders register, was “humiliating and embarrassing and absolutely horrendous”.

The 37-year-old said: “What happened to me affected every facet of my life. I’d think about it every day, making it difficult to focus on anything else, including football … The trauma of what happened to me hasn’t gone away.”

Sports.title: My bad TV history qualifies me to discuss Disney’s women’s football coverage | Max Rushden
Sports.content:
Disclaimer: I have made a lot of bad TV programmes. I have done quite a few below-average radio shows. Podcasts, there are millions of them – some might say too many – and I’ve done my fair share that won’t go down in history. In between those, I’ve hopefully done some pretty good ones – it’s not for me to say.

I have had good ideas and the odd great one that didn’t make it to air (attention the full-size unreferenced post-Keys and Gray elephant in the Soccer AM studio). I’ve had more awful ones. I’ve hosted shows where I’ve had almost complete editorial control, and ones where I could have been replaced by a performing monkey.

I’ve had to host TV shows at every possible height – sitting on a sofa, on a normal chair, on a normal chair behind a desk, on a bar stool in a pub, on a bar stool not in a pub, and standing up when there was somewhere comfortable to sit just out of shot. I complained a lot, but standing did actually work, Murray.

The point being, I have some experience when it comes to reviewing the opening night of the Disney+ coverage of the Women’s Champions League. The Hangout was hosted by Alex Scott with her fellow former England international Lianne Sanderson, the content creators Tyra Mills and Alex Bailess, and quite inexplicably a golden retriever called Barley Boy, who at the time of writing has 82,000 more Instagram followers than I have – I must work on my reels.

The show included a quiz about Italy, including guess the Italian name for football and what pasta the reporter in Milan is cooking. There’s an incredible still image of the panel staring at a load of farfalle on a big screen normally reserved for team lineups or key match incidents.

The immediate reaction was a mix of bewilderment and fury from seasoned lovers of the women’s game. Kathryn Batte wrote an understandable critique for the Telegraph. The broadcaster Flo Lloyd-Hughes posted on X: “Disney’s new UWCL coverage is the closest we’ve seen to CBBC football (derogatory). I wouldn’t be surprised if we see someone gunged for making a wrong prediction or perhaps Raven will make a cameo. Keep stopping to remind myself this isn’t a dream.”

Consistent with all the criticism is the truth that the men’s Champions League would never be covered in the same way. It is perhaps interesting to ask how the team arrived at the concept. Why replace former pros with content creators, why replace tactical analysis with asking what’s the biggest city in Italy? Why a dog?

The broadcaster Marva Kreel perfectly articulated one of the issues in her own X post: “I think a lot of the problem with the debates in women’s football broadcasting over analysis and punditry v content creation and gimmicky fun, is that in men’s football you can get both – and in different shows. In women’s football you get one show, and so they try to do it all.”

It’s a fair point. I’ve mainly hosted the show before the show – where a dog running around wouldn’t be regarded as a crime against the game. In fact hosting live football is significantly more straightforward than interviewing an indie band about their difficult second album or trying to come up with a three-hour radio show in the middle of the international break. The show Disney tried to make on Wednesday is technically much harder than Super Sunday – but that doesn’t mean it was the right call.

I can understand the thinking. I imagine the bosses told the producers they want to bring in a younger audience. I have been told this before. Exactly how to do that is impossible to work out. Should I stop making references to Jossy’s Giants and Aswad? And Disney could probably argue that most of the criticism didn’t come from young people. It came from people who expect the game to be covered in a certain way.

(From left) Former England international Lianne Sanderson, content creators Alex Bailess and Tyra Mills, and golden retriever Barley Boy. Photograph: Disney+

Disney may be being cynical – people are talking and writing about it. The hardcore will watch anyway. Had they produced more traditional coverage, no one would have said anything. And sometimes you have to try something different. I wouldn’t want to be too critical; Disney may give me a gig one day.

Major broadcasters have less money to make the same amount of stuff – and have had a battle over the past 20 years to work out how to harness social media. I saw it at Sky, where a Facebook livestream filmed on an iPhone in the green room would get as many views as the show itself with the costs of studio/lighting/sound/producers etc.

As a middle-aged man – whose wife accuses him of being a “boomer” – I really dislike the phrase “content creator”; perhaps I’m nervous that eventually they’ll take all my jobs. From what I saw, Bailess and Mills came across as very personable and fun – which was clearly the brief – and you can’t criticise anyone for taking a job. And they bring a following with them – quite how many followers lead to subscriptions is a different question.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

I feel for Scott, who perpetually finds herself in the middle of some sort of culture war. You are entitled to regard her as the greatest or worst broadcaster of her generation – or somewhere in between – as you are with me or anyone else. I know many listeners certainly feel the latter about my abilities.

I found the discourse around the end of Football Focus pretty troubling – people suggesting the show went woke and lost its way when she was appointed. It’s much more accurate to accuse me of turning Soccer AM woke, with my clarinet, lefty snowflake opinions and inability to flirt on live television. But then I’m not a woman and I’m white; generally people just accuse me of turning it shit.

But back to the Hangout. I imagine Scott didn’t suggest having a dog in the studio or having guess the pasta. Perhaps she has a lot of editorial control – I genuinely don’t know. But sometimes as a host you have to do what you’re told and do it with conviction.

The reality of live football coverage is that people are watching because they want to watch the game. If people want comedy, they’ll watch Curb Your Enthusiasm. If Liverpool are playing Real Madrid, the fans will watch it – and either enjoy or endure the coverage. But what you can do as a broadcaster is make it as compelling as possible, and there are different ways of being a good host or pundit.

Live football coverage hasn’t changed dramatically in 50 years. Welcome, team news, managers, bit of tactics or player focus, throw to commentators. Half-time: what did you make of that? Full time: what did you make of that?

The dog did not return for the second night of coverage. I know it would have been a strange and difficult day for everyone involved. They made a show, people didn’t like it and they had to go again the next night. Do you double down, screw the haters, or try to subtly move towards a more traditional setup? It seemed on Wednesday they went for the latter.

You can’t magic up an audience, but you can make people feel like you respect the game, you can do it in an entertaining way without introducing animals, and people will come back and watch you again.

Sports.title: UK Football Police Unit accused of ‘bringing Hillsborough’ into alcohol debate
Sports.content:
English football’s leading fans’ group has criticised the UK Football Policing Unit for “bringing Hillsborough into the debate” around drinking in sight of the pitch.

Talk of changing the law to allow fans to drink at their seat or in the stands has resurfaced after Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said the rules were outdated and discriminatory and should be scrapped.

The Football Supporters’ Association (FSA) immediately backed his call but the UKFPU urged caution, stating: “Following a number of football-related tragedies, changes in legislation were implemented after the Taylor Report for good reason and we are currently in the longest ever period without a significant football-related disaster.”

The UKFPU added it would be “incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence”.

“The UKFPU would welcome a meeting with the prime minister to discuss his views and explain the challenges these proposed changes would bring to policing and the safety of staff and fans at football games.

“Other sports simply don’t see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour. It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games.”

The Taylor Report referenced by the UKFPU was commissioned in the wake of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster, which resulted in the deaths of 97 Liverpool fans.

The FSA published a thread on its X account setting out its position on drinking in the stands, which began: “Arguably the most important point is that the UK Football Policing Unit’s comments bringing Hillsborough into this debate have to be corrected. The disaster was not caused by alcohol. Full stop. Fans were ‘unlawfully killed and a catalogue of failings by police and the ambulance services contributed to their deaths’.”

A spokesperson for the UKFPU said: “It was not our intention to link the issue of alcohol with the Hillsborough tragedy. The laws around alcohol, which we acknowledge were first introduced in 1985, are one of a range of measures in addition to the subsequent Taylor Report recommendations that have contributed to making football much safer for fans in this country.”

Burnham’s comments have sparked social media debate in which differing views have been expressed by match-going fans.

The FSA’s post on Thursday added: “It’s unfair to criminalise fans for having a pint – especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league. We are fundamentally sceptical of any law which is only targeted at football supporters.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“That doesn’t mean every club should be forced to serve alcohol to every seat! A club should have the choice to do what is right for its fans. Consultation is critical, some stadiums or stands might not be suitable (eg family areas) whereas it might be popular elsewhere.

“Ultimately, we think clubs, in liaison with their supporters, should be able to determine what is best for themselves, rather than relying on legislation which is decades old and was written through the prism of viewing all football fans as potential hooligans.”

The Sporting Events (Control of Alcohol) Act 1985 prohibits drinking in sight of the pitch in England and Wales in the top five men’s leagues.

Burnham said on Wednesday: “I don’t think it’s fair for football fans to be singled out in that way and I made that point. I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different. And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done, perhaps on a trial basis.

“But I’m not going to back away from what’s been a long-held view of mine. I don’t see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently from others.”

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo's night of frustration: Portugal star, 41, has goal ruled out, misses HUGE chance and is subbed off in narrow win over Wales
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo's night of frustration: Portugal star, 41, has goal ruled out, misses HUGE chance and is subbed off in narrow win over Wales

Cristiano Ronaldo endured a frustrating return to Lisbon as the veteran forward missed a golden chance and had a goal disallowed before being substituted in Portugal's 1-0 win over Wales.

Ronaldo, 41, had admitted in the build-up to the Nations League tie that he had considered retiring from international football after Portugal's World Cup exit in the summer.

The star has instead opted to continue his international career and captained defending Nations League winners Portugal in Lisbon, where he initially made his name 24 years ago.

While Ronaldo led the line in Portugal's first match under new coach Jorge Jesus, his Al-Nassr team-mate Joao Felix scored the opening goal with a deflected effort in the 22nd minute.

Ronaldo went close to doubling Portugal's advantage in the early stages of the second half.

After pulling away from Wales' defenders, Ronaldo looked set to provide the finishing touch to a Ruben Neves cross from six yards out.

Cristiano Ronaldo endured a frustrating night in front of goal as Portugal overcame Wales

Ronaldo, 41, missed a golden chance at the start of the second half before finding the back of the net to seemingly double Portugal's lead

The star was ultimately left frustated when his effort was ruled out by VAR for offside

Ronaldo, however, only proved able to steer a left-footed volley over the bar and ultimately found himself lying frustrated in the goalmouth.

His moment then appeared to have arrived in the 58th minute as Ronaldo ran onto a through pass before finishing past Wales' goalkeeper Danny Ward.

Ronaldo ran away to the corner flag and performed his iconic celebration, only for his joy to be dampened by a VAR check.

Portugal fans jeered and Ronaldo waved his arm in frustration when the goal was ultimately ruled out for offside, with the forward having made his run too early beyond the last defender.

His frustrating night came to an end in the 67th minute when he was substituted to a standing ovation, with Goncalo Ramos coming on in his place.

Portugal, who had missed several openings to extend their lead, survived a scare when a Brennan Johnson shot hit the woodwork before Lewis Koumas' follow-up was blocked.

The hosts would hold on to secure a narrow victory on Jesus' first game in the dugout.

Post-match, Jesus explained his decision to substitute Ronaldo, stating that he needed a fresh forward to press from the front.

Ronaldo was substituted to a standing ovation in the second half on his return to Lisbon

Portugal boss Jorge Jesus claimed he needed a fresh attacker to press up front

'That's what the game dictated, there were 25 minutes left and I needed to have at least one player who was fresh to press the build-up play,' Jesus said.

'I might not have had, technically, in offensive terms, the quality that Cris has to appear and hold the ball, but I knew that Goncalo [Ramos] would provide defensive speed right in our first defensive line, which is important.

'That's pretty much what I did, also because technically he didn't have that many plays.

'But anyway, I'm satisfied with the team.'

Sports.title: Chaos in the Football League as international call-ups force postponement of matches involving THREE lowest-ranked sides - and key target is missed
Sports.content:
Tighter rules imposed to minimise lower league postponements during international breaks have missed the target with more games off than at this time last year, including those featuring the three lowest ranked teams in the EFL. The League One programme has been ravaged with 16 of the next 24 fixtures off to accommodate national team call-ups. Five games in League Two are also postponed over the next two weekends, including Port Vale against Northampton, who are ranked 90th and 91st. It all seems self-defeating with complaints forever swirling around congested fixture lists and at a time when clubs could feast on greater exposure and bigger crowds without Premier League and Championship action. New criteria were brought in this season enabling clubs to apply for a postponement if they expected at least three players to be on duty for senior, Under-21, Under-20 or Under-19 internationals but only if those players had appeared before the 75th minute in 50 per cent of league games or four of the last five first-team games. This is more stringent than last season, when the limit was also three players but with the qualification rules applied only upon the U21, U20 and U19 – not the seniors – and if players started in 25 per cent of league games or in three of the last five first-team games. The League Two match between Northampton and Port Vale, who lie 22nd and 23rd in the table, is one of several postponed in the EFL due to international call-ups There is a slightly different protocol for goalkeepers, with clubs allowed to request a postponement if both the first and second choice goalkeepers are called up. League One leaders Bradford City are without two goalkeepers with regular number one Jon McCracken in the Scotland squad and Zac Hadi called up by Iraq U23s but Cameron Dawson, McCracken's deputy, is available. Bradford have confirmed their game at Reading will go ahead on Saturday, October 3 but the home game against Barnsley on Saturday has been called off by the visitors, who have Patrick Kelly with Northern Ireland, Tyrese Noslin with Curacao, Jonathan Bland with Wales U21s and Makenzie Kirk with Northern Ireland U21s. Reading's opponents Wycombe will also be without their number one 'keeper Conor Hazard, who is with Northern Ireland. The prospect of two games against teams with deputies in goal may explain some of the thinking behind Reading boss Leam Richardson's decision to play on despite three call-ups from his own squad - Charlie Savage for Wales, Andy Rinomhota for Zimbabwe and Jeriel Dorsett for Montserrat. 'Football is a squad game, and we have confidence in the players available to us, while keeping the fixture in place also helps us avoid adding another game to an already busy schedule,' said Richardson. 'It's better for the supporters too. Saturday afternoon is the ideal time to play football whenever circumstances allow, so we were pleased to keep this one in place.' It is not one dimensional. Some clubs want to play on for their own reasons and like the idea of a break for different reasons. Reading will play on despite having international call-ups and could take advantage of their next two opponents missing their first choice goalkeepers With seven on international duty, five of them first team regulars, it is difficult to see how Luton could be expected to play. This season's changes were made with an eye towards the congested schedules and in the hope of keeping more EFL fixtures on where possible. On a financial level, few clubs in the third tier like to lose Saturday afternoon games which are generally better attended and more lucrative than rearranged evening dates in midweek. But there is an inevitable balance to strike with all managers under pressure to win and reluctant to take the risk with some of their better players unavailable and possibly making selections and substitution decisions with the qualification rules in mind. Crawley Town, rock bottom of League Two, are not playing because of call-ups for winger Dion Pereira with Antigua and Barbuda, left-back Jonny Russell with Northern Ireland Under-21s and goalkeeper Nicholas Michalski with England U20s. Michalski, 19, on loan from Blackburn has been first choice for Crawley since veteran former Arsenal keeper Vito Mannone, 38, was injured in August. In last year's September international break eight of the 12 League One fixtures went ahead with a full set in League Two. In the October break last year there were seven of 12 League One games on and only one game off in League Two. There are different reasons in play. Former Premier League clubs Leicester City and Sheffield Wednesday are in League One this season, with bigger academies and appeal for talented youngsters on loan from the top-flight looking for experience. There is an increase in lower-league players searching out international football via ancestral links. And, for the first time, this year's international break is extended to cover two weekends featuring more games and bigger squads.

Sports.title: How Jurgen Klopp fared on his return: Fresh squad approach pays off and why he will already empathise with club managers as Germany are saved by technology he wants to scrap!
Sports.content:
Jurgen Klopp missed out on his first win as Germany manager with Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo scoring the stoppage-time volley which denied him. It was a fine finish from Gakpo and an equally exquisite cross from Ruben van Bommel after Serge Gnabry had given away the ball in the build-up. That ensured the Netherlands, now managed by Barcelona and Spain legend Xavi, avoided losing in Amsterdam. A draw was the deserved result at the end of what turned into a nasty Nations League clash. The tackles were flying in, though there were two apparent muscular injuries which will have a pair of Premier League managers concerned. Kai Havertz of Arsenal and Brian Brobbey of Sunderland – both of whom have started every league game for their clubs this season – needed substituting. It was while the latter was down injured that Germany controversially scored their opener. While in charge of Liverpool, Klopp used to find internationals stressful to watch for the very reason of injuries, and so he will have empathy for Mikel Arteta and Regis Le Bris now. Here is what we learned from this showdown between these two heavyweights. Jurgen Klopp was denied victory in his first match as head coach of the German national team His former Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo equalised late on as the Dutch earned a 1-1 draw TWO PREM STRIKERS INJURED Arsenal and Sunderland still have time – more than two weeks until their next Premier League fixtures with Leeds and Brighton respectively – but the sight of their strikers having to be substituted here will have sparked immediate fears back in England as one followed after the other. First, Havertz had to be substituted after 30 minutes. He had been on the receiving end of an ugly foul by Quinten Timber – on another day, VAR might have punished the midfielder whose brother, Jurrien, plays for Arsenal – but that did not seem to be the reason for Havertz’s withdrawal. It was a few minutes after Timber's challenge that Havertz dropped down, lifting up his shorts to show his strapped left thigh which appeared to be the source of his discomfort. Then, Brobbey likewise needed substituting after 35 minutes, with the Sunderland striker grabbing his right hamstring and immediately asking to be replaced. Arsenal forward Kai Havertz was forced off with an apparent thigh problem in the first half Brian Brobbey gave Sunderland cause for concern after suffering a hamstring injury DUTCH ANGER AT GERMAN OPENER MISPLACED It was while Brobbey was down injured that Germany scored their first goal of the Klopp era – and it left the Netherlands incandescent at their opponents for not kicking the ball out of play. Nadiem Amiri thought about it. The Germany midfielder had possession in the final third but rather than roll it away for a throw-in, he passed to his captain, Joshua Kimmich, to see what he wanted to do. Kimmich played on and from that very attack, Felix Nmecha scored to make it 1-0. Denzel Dumfries took the greatest exception to what he perceived as a lack of sportsmanship, chasing the Germany players as they ran to the corner flag to celebrate. Yet it was a perfectly legal opener despite the Netherlands’ complaints. Xavi’s main gripe with this goal should be how his side left Germany’s right wing entirely empty. Felix Nmecha scored Germany's goal after they continued to play while Brobbey was down The Netherlands were furious with Germany over what they viewed as a lack of sportsmanship VAR SAVES KLOPP AND DENIES XAVI When Klopp departed Liverpool in May 2024, he used his final pre-match press conference to tell us what he really thought of video assistant referees meddling in matches. ‘I would vote for scrapping VAR,’ he said before beating Wolverhampton Wanderers 2-0 in an Anfield farewell. Yet that very technology saved Klopp here, some 858 days on from the last time he stood on a touchline as a manager. Good job, too, because Germany’s defending for the set-piece from which the Netherlands thought they had opened the scoring was rather embarrassing. It was 0-0 at the time and came from a corner taken by Tijjani Reijnders. If anyone should know how dangerous Virgil van Dijk is in the air, it is Klopp, and yet Liverpool's central defender was uncontested. Germany were prioritising zonal marking inside their six-yard box. They placed nobody on the 6ft 5in bloke who scored a fair few headers under Klopp at Liverpool. Van Dijk just drifted forwards, headed in, and celebrated. However, VAR, desperate to get involved, sent the referee to his pitch-side monitor because it was thought Brobbey was blocking Marc-Andre Ter Stegen. The goal was disallowed, and the next time the Netherlands had a corner, Van Dijk found himself being man-marked. Virgl van Dijk had been denied the first goal of the match when Brobbey was adjudged by VAR to have interfered with Marc-Andre Ter Stegen from an offside position A NEW ERA UNDER KLOPP Unlike other managers, Klopp picked 44 players for Germany’s four Nations League fixtures, with half involved versus the Netherlands and Greece this week and the other half reserved for Serbia and Greece next week. Only goalkeeper Finn Dahmen of Augsburg is in both camps. It smacked of a desire to identify new, fresh, hungry talents. Both squads for this international break carried an average age between 24 and 25, and included 16 uncapped players, and it was in the spirit of giving opportunities that Philipp Treu won his first cap for Germany as a starter. Right back has been a priority position for Klopp, who would rather not use Kimmich there like his predecessor, Julian Nagelsmann. Treu is a 25-year-old for Freiburg and largely held his own as the Netherlands pushed for their second-half leveller until the bitter end. Germany relied on a series of saves from Ter Stegen while Mexx Meerdink, who replaced Brobbey, should have equalised when he missed the gaping goal. In Meerdink’s defence, he was stretching to meet the ball when it was blasted into the six-yard box. Gakpo eventually ensured this ended in a draw after Van Bommel’s classy cross with the outside of his boot, denying Klopp but giving Xavi cause to celebrate.

Sports.title: Premier League SPEED-GUN: 22.3mph Bradley Barcola beats Man United star to become the league's fastest footballer in a rapid top 20 ranking - but which Spurs player is the SLOWEST outfielder?
Sports.content:
Premier League SPEED-GUN: 22.3mph Bradley Barcola beats Man United star to become the league's fastest footballer in a rapid top 20 ranking - but which Spurs player is the SLOWEST outfielder?

Liverpool winger Bradley Barcola has been clocked as the fastest Premier League player in the top 20 speed rankings after five games.

Barcola, 24, joined the Reds in August for £123million from Paris Saint-Germain, where not only did he win two Champions League titles, but he also had a reputation for being rather speedy.

And in the latest top speed rankings on FotMob, he has been crowned king of the speedsters, clocking a rather rapid 22.3mph (35.9km/h) on the speed gun.

The sprint came during his Liverpool debut against Ipswich Town, which his side won 2-0, at the beginning of the month, where he was given heaps of space by the Tractor Boys to get those wheels turning.

However, in his two Premier League appearances that have followed – both starts – he has failed to hit the same heights in the speed department, while also struggling to find his feet in front of goal.

At the other end of the scale, the league's slowest outfielder is Tottenham defender Tosin Adarabioyo.

Bradley Barcola (right) recorded the fastest speed of the Premier League season so far in Liverpool's win over Ipswich earlier this month

Barcola has clocked a faster top speed than both Bryan Mbeumo (left) and Pedro Neto (right)

The centre-back, who signed from rivals Chelsea in the summer, has been clocked no quicker than 13.3mph (21.4km/h).

Back at the top of the pile, Barcola – yet to register a goal or assist for the Reds – has beaten out Manchester United's Bryan Mbeumo to the title.

The United winger just missed out on top spot, having clocked a marginally slower pace of 22mph (35.4km/h).

Behind Mbeumo there is a four-way tie for third, with the quartet of rapid stars clocking a marginally slower time than the Cameroonian.

Fulham's Gonzalo Garcia, Coventry City full-back Milan van Ewijk, Pedro Neto of Chelsea and Hull City's Robinio Vaz all recorded a top speed of 21.9mph (35.3km/h).

Slightly slower than them is Newcastle winger Jacob Murphy, who, despite his smaller role in the current Magpies team under Matthias Jaissle, has managed to clock 21.87mph (35.2km/h).

Bournemouth's Brazilian wonderkid Rayan has been lauded for his first year in English football, terrorising defences from the right-hand side.

A big part of the winger's game is his pace down the flank, and he clocked a speed just a pinch slower than Murphy, with 21.8 mph (35.1km/h) to his name.

PL speed rankings after five games Bradley Barcola (Liverpool) — 22.3 mph Bryan Mbeumo (Manchester United) — 22.0 mph Gonzalo García (Fulham) — 21.9 mph Milan van Ewijk (Coventry City) — 21.9 mph Pedro Neto (Chelsea) — 21.9 mph Robinio Vaz (Hull City) — 21.9 mph Jacob Murphy (Newcastle) — 21.9 mph Kristoffer Ajer (Brentford) — 21.8 mph Matias Fernandez-Pardo (Newcastle United) — 21.8 mph Rayan (Bournemouth) — 21.8 mph Ian Maatsen (Aston Villa) — 21.7 mph Anthony Elanga (Newcastle United) — 21.7 mph Reinildo (Sunderland) — 21.7 mph Alexander Isak (Liverpool) — 21.6 mph Cristhian Mosquera (Arsenal) — 21.6 mph Víctor Munoz (Liverpool) — 21.6 mph Bazoumana Toure (Newcastle United) — 21.6 mph Joe Rodon (Leeds United) — 21.6 mph Antonee Robinson (Fulham) — 21.5 mph Erling Haaland (Manchester City) — 21.5 mph

Tottenham's Tosin Adarabioyo is the Premier League's slowest player this season

One of the big shocks is that Anthony Elanga, who many deem one of the fastest stars in Europe, sits in a lowly 12th, despite his rapid start to the campaign prior to injury.

His 21.68mph (34.9km/h) is comfortably slower than his top speed of 22.58mph (36.35km/h) from last season, which would have rocketed him to the top of this list.

Alexander Isak has been criticised for losing a yard of pace since his record £125m move to Liverpool last summer, but he makes the top 20 in 14th, with a top speed just 0.1mph slower than former team-mate Elanga.

What he seems to have regained this campaign, however, is his clinical touch. The Swede has had his best ever start to a Premier League season, with four goals from just five games – including his winner against Bournemouth on Sunday.

Five slowest PL outfield players after five games Tosin Adarabioyo (Chelsea) — 13.3 mph Matt Targett (Hull City) — 14.0 mph Joe Gelhardt (Hull City) — 14.7 mph Michael Svoboda (Brighton & Hove Albion) — 14.7 mph Nicolas Domínguez (Nottingham Forest) — 15.0 mph

His Golden Boot rival Erling Haaland is known for his frightening pace, but he has only just squeezed into the top 20 through a six-way tie for 19th.

The Norwegian striker's top speed of 21.5mph (34.6km/h) has been matched by Fulham's roadrunner Antonee Robinson, Hull City's Mohamed Belloumi, Liverpool's impressive summer signing Jeremy Jacquet, fellow defender Josh Acheampong of Chelsea, and last but not least, Leeds' Dominic Calvert-Lewin.

But what Haaland can't be matched for is his ability to score goals, as he once again leads the scoring charts ahead of Isak.

The Manchester City man has netted five goals in as many games, in turn firing Enzo Maresca's side to the top of the tree at the international break with a 100 per cent win record.

Sports.title: PREMIER LEAGUE REPORT CARD - PART TWO: Man City's formidable start under Enzo Maresca, how Hull have shocked the league and Spurs and Man United struggle - last 10 sides GRADED
Sports.content:
The beginning of the new Premier League season has been scintillating to say the least with fans going through every possible emotion during the opening five gameweeks. While Manchester City and Arsenal being in the top two at this early stage is no great surprise, the league has had its fair share of unpredictability, with Spurs being bottom and Manchester United failing to take advantage of their kind start on paper. The newly promoted sides all look to pose a decent threat to the weaker sides – especially Hull, who have lost just once so far. The extended international break gives us time to take stock and review how clubs have got on. Daily Mail Sport has already graded the first ten teams – now it is the time for a verdict on the rest. Hull City Position: 8th. Points: 8 The first team to receive their grade in part two are the roaring Tigers, who have been electric upon their return to the Premier League. Many wrote this Hull team off before a ball was even kicked, deeming the squad too weak and the manager too inexperienced to have any chance of staying up. But after a ten-year hiatus from the Premier League, Jakirovic's men have looked more like European hopefuls rather than relegation fodder so far. They made a perfect start to the campaign by beating Manchester United and have kept up steady form since, seeing off fellow newcomers Coventry away and earning creditable draws against Chelsea and Aston Villa. Hull have found success through solidity and ruthless finishing – they were also the last side this season to concede a goal – and have outperformed their xG in every one of their wins this season. Defeat at Newcastle remains their only blip so far and, while it will be tough for Hull to maintain their early form and retain their top-flight status, they are already proving their doubters wrong. Grade: A Hull continue to surprise with the newly-promoted side losing only one of their opening five Ipswich Town Position: 11th. Points: 6 Another newly promoted team are up next. Ipswich Town have made a swift return to the Premier League at the first time of asking after relegation in 2024/25 - and look better equipped this time around. Under Gary O'Neil – sacked by Wolves after losing to his current club in late 2024 – they have made a promising start to their campaign as they bid to avoid dropping back into the Championship. Ipswich sit comfortably in 11th place at the first break of the season after two impressive victories over two sides that may also be battling for survival, Sunderland and Crystal Palace. Defeats at Old Trafford and at home to Liverpool were to be expected and are not the games O'Neil and his progressive, attacking side will be judged on come what May. If they maintain this level they have every chance of staying up. Grade: B+ Rolling over the competition: The Tractor boys are loving life back in the big leagues Leeds United Position: 5th. Points: 9 Yet another surprise package this season are Leeds, who have looked a huge threat so far this season. Dominic Calvert-Lewin's three goals in the first five matches have helped propel Daniel Farke's unbeaten side into the early European places. This has been no fluke either – Leeds have been playing some of the best football in the division with a five-man midfield that has the capacity to dominate proceedings. An impressive demonstration of their style came in a 4-1 rout of Newcastle, with three goals coming without reply in the first half. The season is still at a very, very early stage but Farke's start, coupled with the smart business done in the transfer window, will have fans dreaming of more than a relegation battle and perhaps an outside push for a European place. Leeds will return from the international break to the toughest of tests, a lunchtime kick-off at Arsenal. Most will assume the Gunners will end their unbeaten run but don't bet against an upset at the Emirates. Grade: A Daniel Farke has experienced some tough seasons in the Premier League before but now could have something special brewing at Elland Road Liverpool Position: 6th. Points: 9 Mixed results early on may have left supporters wondering where to stand on Andoni Iraola's start to life at Anfield. Following a dismal defence of their Premier League crown last season, leading to the sacking of Arne Slot, Iraola has arrived with fresh ideas and a new plan – which even he has admitted is tricky for his expensive band of stars. After the departure of Mo Salah in the summer, there are now only three players from Jurgen Klopp's legendary Premier League and Champions league winning side and finding replacements have been an expensive and largely unsuccessful process for Liverpool so far. But, after the issues of the 2025-26 campaign, Iraola has managed to get a tune out of some Liverpool's big money recruits. Alexander Isak is finally firing after returning from a nasty injury, Alexis Mac Allister is back to his best despite his contract dispute and Cody Gakpo has transformed his game. These improvements have helped Liverpool to remain unbeaten in the first five but draws with Forest, Newcastle and Fulham will be a worry. They have also been left defensively exposed in midfield at times and are yet to see a return of investment from £116million Florian Wirtz. Iraola will only grow into the role but, as the schedule gets tighter and tougher tests await, Liverpool will be hoping that doesn't take too long. Grade: B Alexander Isak is back in the goals and unbeaten Liverpool will hope Iraola can get this team of superstars finally ticking Manchester City Position: 1st. Points: 15 The only 100 per cent side so far are of course the perennial title challengers, Manchester City. City have adapted marvellously to life under Enzo Maresca. Worryingly for the rest, the former Chelsea boss appears to have picked up from where Pep Guardiola left off in the club's first season in a decade without the Spaniard at the helm. Erling Haaland has begun another campaign in splendid form, sitting at the top of the goalscoring charts with five in five games, and will hope his goals can bring the title back to the Etihad after two years, the longest it has been away from City since Guardiola's arrival in 2016. As always the owners splashed the cash in the summer, spending £321million to build a new midfield in the wake of legends Bernardo Silva, Ilkay Gundogan and Rodri all leaving. The investment already seems to be paying off. Elliot Anderson has started to look very accomplished at the base of Maresca's double pivot in midfield, the young Ayyoub Bouaddi has been impressively comfortable in a new league and Enzo Fernandez has been magnificent following his move from Chelsea. Arsenal will have a tough job on their hands stopping this City juggernaut from rolling towards what would be a ninth Premier League title but considering the start both teams have had we can be excited for another close and chaotic title race. Grade: A Manchester City are already firing under Maresca with five wins from five leaving them top Manchester United Position: 12th. Points: 5 From the blue half of Manchester to the red – and completely differing fortunes for United, who have endured a woeful start to the campaign. A kind start to the season, featuring games against two newly-promoted sides, has not yielded the results Michael Carrick, the club and the fans would have wanted or expected. The Red Devils got off to the worst possible start with defeat at Hull and haven't fully recovered since. They managed to respond the following week with an emphatic 5-2 win over Ipswich but that remains their only league victory so far this season. Carrick was trusted with the permanent role in the summer after an excellent end to last season but teams already seem to have worked his style out. Opponents appear to have got wise to his counter-attacking style and his players have struggled to break down opponents, while failing to keep clean sheets. Many feel the club's recruitment team left Carrick short in the summer window and the Red Devils are feeling the effects now. Unless these underlying issues with tactics and personnel are sorted, United are in danger of slipping back down the table and starting the process of a 'rebuild' all over again. Grade: D Manchester United have made a poor start to a season that had promised so much Newcastle United: Position: 9th. Points: 8 After a summer of being gutted Matthias Jaissle has done remarkably well to steady the ship at St James' Park. The Magpies had a testing transfer window losing not only Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimaraes but also their long-term manager Eddie Howe and have incredibly rolled with the punches perhaps looking even better as a result. Young German coach Matthias Jaissle has come in and instilled the same style of play that Jurgen Klopp and Thomas Tuchel found so much success with in England and is taking Newcastle into a new era. Of course they have not been perfect on Tyneside but considering what some Geordies feared I think they will be pleased with the steady progress they have made in the first month. The Magpies did take a real wing clipping against Leeds losing 4-1 away at Elland road but that aside results have been steady. They have had drawn two all twice at home and managed wins against Spurs and Hull, being the first side this season to pick up three points against the Tigers and appear to score in bunches with their goals coming within less than ten minutes of each other in both their wins. Grade: B Geordies will be extremely pleased with their start to season after a rough summer and look forward to the Premier League returning more than most Nottingham Forest Position: 13th. Points: 5 Oliver Glasner was tasked with being the man to provide stability to Nottingham Forest after the club churned through four managers last season, which began with Nuno Espirito Santo's acrimonious departure. Glasner's side are yet to truly get going so far this campaign, something that might concern their ambitious owner Evangelos Marinakis. Concerningly, Forest have failed to score in their three home matches against Leeds, Tottenham and Coventry, losing two of them. The 1-0 defeat to newly promoted Coventry – who had lost their opening four matches without scoring – will have worried fans heading into the extended international break. Forest's sole league win came away against midlands rivals Aston Villa, with Igor Jesus's late goal giving them their highlight of the campaign to date. Grade: C Forest will need to pick up regular points quickly to avoid slipping further down the table after the international break Sunderland Position: 14th. Points: 4 The Black Cats have the tricky task of backing up their stunning campaign last season after their promotion back to the top flight, which ended in Europa League qualification. Few are expecting them to kick on this campaign, with a drop off considered more likely due to having to balance European football with their domestic endeavours. Sunderland have only managed one win so far against a struggling Fulham side, but have also had to face both Manchester City and Arsenal in the first month. They performed well in both but ultimately suffered defeats, despite Brian Brobbey's hat-trick at the Etihad. Regis Le Bris's men will be frustrated to have slipped up in their season opener away at Ipswich where they lost late on to the hands of their former player, Jack Clarke. Four points may be seen as a disappointing return to date, with the fixture list only going to become more congested and the squad stretched after the international break. Grade: C+ Sunderland have been unlucky thus far but must begin winning again soon if they are to avoid the common second season relegation Tottenham Hotspur Position: 20th. Points: 2 After back-to-back 17th placed finishes, Tottenham's heavy summer spending prompted hope they could lift themselves out of the crisis state the club has been in. Yet Tottenham find themselves propping up the table after five games with Roberto De Zerbi's side still without a win in the league. Spurs have only managed two goals all season and are sat rudderless at the bottom of the table Most pundits believe Tottenham have too much quality to get involved in another relegation scrap, but their start to the season has been extremely worrying. Tottenham have proved unable so far to resolve their disastrous home record that has plagued them over the past two seasons. De Zerbi's side have been beaten by Newcastle and Aston Villa – who both underwent drastic summer changes as well – and also drew with Everton in front of their home fans. The club's ownership has so far yet to see the return on the more than £300million spent on new arrivals this summer, after they reacted to the scare of just surviving on the final day of last season. A major improvement in results after the international break is needed to lift the mood and ensure Tottenham are not facing a third consecutive season of struggle at the wrong end of the table. Grade: F

Sports.title: Phil Mickelson's legendary caddie lays bare the eyewatering financial cost that fans don't realize... and how much the golf stars tip after a tournament
Sports.content:
Phil Mickelson's legendary caddie lays bare the eyewatering financial cost that fans don't realize... and how much the golf stars tip after a tournament

Legendary former PGA Tour caddie Jim 'Bones' Mackay has pulled back the curtain on the financial realities of the role.

Mackay was best known for being at Phil Mickelson's side for all but one of his major championship wins as well as 41 PGA Tour victories.

He was hired by Mickelson when he turned pro in 1992 and carried his bag until 2017, winning the Masters three times as well as The Open and the PGA Championship.

Mackay later came out of retirement for a three-year stint caddying for Justin Thomas on the PGA Tour, but now works as an on-course reporter for NBC Sports.

And he has shed light on the not-so-glamorous realities of being a caddie on tour, revealing it costs around $40,000-50,000 a year simply covering the price of travel, hotels and other day-to-day costs.

The role also comes without any contract security, operating on a 'week to week' basis.

Jim 'Bones' Mackay is one of the PGA Tour's most legendary caddies after decades on the bag

Mackay was by Phil Mickelson's side for almost his entire career including five of his majors

'When I talk to people about caddying, one of the things that surprises them is the caddies pay for all their own expenses. So it costs [about] $40,000-50,000 a year to do what caddies do,' Mackay told Front Office Sports.

'There are no contracts in terms of the ability of a caddie to stay with a player [long-term]. You're literally week to week with those guys.

'Though you'll have caddies that sometimes spend 5, 10, 15 years with a player. And I think that the public might be a little surprised by how much input, in some cases, caddies have with the players.

'I mean, you know, as great a player as Scottie Scheffler is, and he's also got a world-class caddie in Ted Scott - he does very little on the golf course without kind of running it by Ted. So they're one heck of a team, as many player-caddie duos are on the PGA.'

Given they are not salaried employees, PGA Tour caddies usually make a base pay rate that can range from $1,500 to $3,000, then get a percentage of player earnings.

The percentage golfers tip on their earnings can vary, with a standard of 10 percent if the player wins, then around seven and eight percent if they finish highly.

However, with golfers needing to cover their own extensive costs, that number falls to around five percent if they finish poorly, and the caddie often gets nothing aside from their base rate if their player misses the cut and also goes home empty handed.

Mackay's star player Mickelson has earned an eyewatering amount over the course of his career, racking in $81,053,932 in official PGA Tour earnings - not including the $24,770,928 he made from majors.

Mackay has shed light on the cost caddies face that most golf fans do not even realize

Mackay is now an on-course analyst for NBC Sports during their PGA Tour TV coverage

Add in his lucrative $12,130,826 LIV Golf earnings later in his career after splitting from Mackay, and he has total career earnings of $117,955,685, per Spotrac.

With Mackay on his bag for much of that time, the caddie took home millions himself over the years.

But that lucrative reality is not the case for many caddies on tour, particularly for players grinding to make the cut each week rather than regularly winning tournaments.

Sports.title: NFL fans fume at 'no fun league' after 49ers star is handed huge fine for alcohol-themed celebration... as he insists: 'I don't even drink beer'
Sports.content:
NFL fans fume at 'no fun league' after 49ers star is handed huge fine for alcohol-themed celebration... as he insists: 'I don't even drink beer'

Furious NFL fans have ripped into league chiefs after San Francisco 49ers star Kyle Juszczyk was handed a $14,926 fine for his touchdown celebration on Sunday.

After scoring in their 35-13 win over the Dolphins, Juszczyk performed his trademark celebration by tilting his head back and pretending to drink a liquid.

However, the NFL have since handed him a hefty financial penalty for engaging in an 'offensive demonstration' while on the field.

'Your imitation of chugging a beer constituted an offensive demonstration and could reasonably be construed as being in poor taste,' the league said.

They added that further offenses will result in an escalation of disciplinary action, up to and including suspension.

Juszczyk - who boasts the nickname 'Juice' - has already appealed the fine, as per ESPN's Adam Schefter, and claimed: 'I don't even drink beer'.

Furious NFL fans have ripped into league chiefs after San Francisco 49ers star Kyle Juszczyk was handed a $14,926 fine for this touchdown celebration on Sunday

The 49ers star has already appealed the fine and claimed: 'I don't even drink beer!'

He also took to social media to confirm the news, writing: 'Can't make this stuff up'.

Fans noted that the 49ers star has used the celebration throughout his career and that this was the first time that the NFL had taken issue with it.

Juszczyk has spent a decade in the Bay Area after arriving from the Baltimore Ravens as a free agent back in 2017, establishing himself as an eight-time Pro Bowl selection.

It didn't take long for fans to voice their frustrations with the league on social media.

Former NFL star JJ Watt led the way, writing: 'I’m just going to go out on a limb here… For a guy whose nickname is Juice, could it not be “reasonably construed” that he is drinking… stay with me here… Juice?'

Another fan added: 'This is DUMB. What if he was drinking water? They literally sell beer in the stadiums'.

'Some of the NFLs main sponsors are beer companies. I’m getting sick of this. This leagues soft and they know it,' another disgruntled fan wrote online.

He was not the only player to find himself in hot water with the league office for an imaginary drink over the weekend, either.

Juszczyk was among a number of NFL stars to be handed a fine following the weekend action

Indianapolis Colts offensive lineman Matt Goncalves was hit with an $8,847 fine on Sunday night after pretending to pop the cap off a football and drink from it following a Tyler Warren touchdown against the Kansas City Chiefs.

The fines arrive amid a growing frustration from players over the league's clampdown on celebrations to start the 2026 season.

Cincinnati Bengals wide receiver duo Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins are also subject to fines from league chiefs over their new signature routine, which unfurls into a first-down signal in tribute to Dwayne 'The Rock' Johnson's iconic 'People's Elbow'.

Chase voiced his frustration with the league on Thursday, urging stars to band together with the NFL Players Association to push back against the strict enforcement.

'They're just stopping the fun,' Chase said. 'It is what it is.'

Sports.title: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua £150m fight is finally CONFIRMED - in Cardiff at 2am on a Friday night in December - and Netflix reveal price it will cost to watch
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua's long-awaited fight with Tyson Fury has finally been confirmed for December 11 at Cardiff’s Principality Stadium – and it will save Joshua around £7.5million in tax. It is understood each man will pocket around £75m for arguably the biggest bout to be staged on British soil after Joshua’s team, led by Eddie Hearn, succeeded in forcing the promotion’s Saudi backers to scrap plans to stage the showdown in New York. Hearn initially pushed for Wembley Stadium, but the combination of a roof over the Principality Stadium and the Welsh government’s willingness to bend their late-night curfew swung the fight towards Cardiff. The ring walk is expected to take place around 2am to suit a US-based audience, in line with the demands of Netflix, which will broadcast the heavyweight showdown. Although the delivery of the fight in Wales will be positioned as a victory for British fight fans, pragmatism around tax was also a key consideration in Hearn’s argument against Madison Square Garden in New York. As Daily Mail Sport revealed earlier this month, the two fighters would have been taxed around 30 per cent of their purses in America, compared to 20 per cent in the UK, with Joshua particularly unhappy about the prospect of an extra £7.5m being added to his bill. The two-time world champion instead demanded that his contract be honoured, which stipulated a British-based fight. Boxing supremo Turki Alalshikh said: 'Back in April, I said that any announcement would come from me. I can now confirm that Fury Vs Joshua will be coming to the UK, as I promised British boxing fans. 'The time for talking is over. Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua. Years in the making. One night to settle it. December 11th. LIVE on Netflix.' Netflix today confirmed the fight would be available 'at no additional cost' to subscribers. Their general membership pricing starts at £7.99 a month in the UK. Bookmaker Betfair make Fury the early favourite to win, pricing him at 8/15. Joshua is priced at 13/8. Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua has been announced for Friday, December 11 The roots of Joshua-Fury stretch back more than a decade, to when both men were emerging as Britain's leading heavyweight prospects Joshua tweeted: 'I am inspiring a generation', alongside an emoji of the British flag. His promoter Eddie Hearn, who fought relentlessly to keep the fight in the UK, wrote: 'WE DID IT. Forever indebted to the U.K. public for their support of Anthony Joshua. We couldn’t have got this over the line without you.' Fury's name appearing first on the card for the Battle of Britain will be an early win for the Gypsy King in his constant PR war with Joshua. The pair had originally been pencilled in to fight on November 20 at Madison Square Garden in New York, but a determined push from Joshua and Hearn saw the contracts re-negotiated to bring the fight back to British soil. Hearn had been adamant that British fans deserved the opportunity to watch two of the country's biggest sporting stars go head-to-head at home, and fought hard to make that happen. Fury, too, wanted the fight in the UK, but had been prepared to accept a move to America because of his concerns that the bout could once again slip away. Now those fears, after ten years of frustration, have been put to bed. The fight will take place in Cardiff, with the later-than-usual start time expected to mean ring walks at around 2am UK time as organisers attempt to satisfy the American audience watching on Netflix. Wembley had been the preferred venue for the showdown, but the major stumbling block was securing the necessary late-night permit. With Netflix and Turki Alalshikh keen for the event to cater to viewers in the United States, organisers required a start time significantly later than would normally be permitted at Wembley. Cardiff, however, was able to secure the required permit - clearing the final obstacle to bringing the fight back to Britain. Cardiff's Principality Stadium has come out on top to host the fight after weeks of negotiations

Your browser does not support iframes.

The scale of the occasion is already being felt in the Welsh capital, with hotels in Cardiff now understood to be sold out as supporters scramble to secure accommodation for one of the biggest fights in British boxing. For Joshua, the move represents the culmination of a push to ensure the fight was staged in the UK. The former two-times world champion and Hearn had been clear that, after years of watching British heavyweight stars travel overseas for major fights, Joshua-Fury belonged in front of their home crowd. Fury was willing to compromise on the location if necessary, however, with his priority being to finally get the fight over the line. The roots of Joshua-Fury stretch back more than a decade, to when both men were emerging as Britain's leading heavyweight prospects. Joshua won Olympic gold at London 2012 before turning professional, while Fury had already made his professional debut in 2008 and was building an unbeaten record of his own. For years, the prospect of the two eventually sharing a ring became one of British boxing's great hypothetical match-ups. Fury's stunning victory over Wladimir Klitschko in 2015 elevated him to the summit of the heavyweight division, while Joshua was rapidly closing in on world-title status himself. FURY VS JOSHUA - BIG FIGHT ODDS Fury to win - 8/15 Draw - 16/1 Joshua to win- 13/8 Victory method: Tyson Fury by Points or Decision - 16/5 Fury by TKO/KO/DQ - 13/10 Anthony Joshua by Dec/Tech Dec - 15/2 Joshua TKO/KO/DQ - 13/5 Fight to go the distance: Yes - 13/8 No - 4/9 Odds courtesy of Betfair Joshua claimed the IBF heavyweight title by stopping Charles Martin in 2016 before adding the WBA and IBO belts to his collection. By 2017, Joshua-Fury had evolved from a fantasy fight into a genuine target. But the negotiations repeatedly broke down. The closest it came to fruition was in 2021, when the two camps appeared to be on the brink of agreeing a two-fight deal. The proposed showdown was publicly discussed and appeared to be edging towards reality, only for Fury to become contractually obligated to face Deontay Wilder after an arbitration ruling. That fight ultimately took place, with Fury beating Wilder for a third time, while Joshua embarked on his own defining chapter against Oleksandr Usyk. Joshua lost his WBA, IBF and WBO titles to Usyk in 2021 before suffering a second defeat to the Ukrainian in their 2022 rematch. Once again, Joshua-Fury seemed to drift further away. Then came another tantalising opportunity. Negotiations accelerated in late 2022, with both camps discussing a potential December showdown, but the fight again failed to materialise. Fury moved on to other opponents while Joshua began rebuilding his career following the two defeats by Usyk. The emergence of Alalshikh and the rapid expansion of Saudi Arabia's influence over boxing created a fresh route to making the fight. And this time, the years of disappointment are finally over. The contracts have been signed. Joshua-Fury is no longer a fight being negotiated, teased or promised. It will take place in Cardiff on December 11.

Sports.title: Anthony Gordon raises theory over England drop-outs and makes Ballon d'Or claim
Sports.content:
Anthony Gordon raises theory over England drop-outs and makes Ballon d'Or claim

England have seen five players drop out of Thomas Tuchel's squad due to injury, and Anthony Gordon has a theory as to why those who play in the Premier League are more susceptible to knocks

View 2 Images Anthony Gordon has given his thoughts (Image: Beanyman Sports)

Anthony Gordon says England’s core of Premier League footballers has to deal with more physical intensity than their international counterparts. There have been a handful of drop-outs from Thomas Tuchel’s latest squad and there have long been questions over whether England players are on the verge of burnout when they head to summer tournaments.

‌



And Gordon, now playing for Barcelona in La Liga, reckons there are special demands on those playing their trade in the Premier League. He said: “In England, every game is as hard as the next.

‌



“Playing Arsenal is the same as playing a newly promoted side. That’s the difficulty of the Premier League. Every game is so intense. Everyone can win a game.

‌



“Hull were unbeaten until they played Newcastle. I think for the English players playing in the Premier League, it can be a lot tougher on the body than it can be playing elsewhere.”

‌



Harry Kane certainly seems to have benefited from what many see as the less strenuous demands of the Bundesliga and is a hot favourite to win the Ballon d’Or this year. Gordon sees it as a straight fight between the England captain and Lamine Yamal, his team-mate at Barcelona.

But the 25-year-old former Newcastle and Everton attacker has his eyes on eventually claiming the sport’s most prestigious individual prize. Gordon said: “Absolutely. I’ve always dreamt of that since I was a kid. I’ve never had a limit on what I can do in life.

“I understand that the people who are there at some point were not there. Everyone is on their own journey to get there. I believe anyone can achieve anything if they put their mind to it.

‌



“They just need a lot of luck. They need a lot of things to go their way. I’m trying to do everything I can to be the best player I can be. And hopefully I get a lot of luck and then we’ll see.”

Can Anthony Gordon win the Ballon d'Or one day? Have your say in the comments section.

View 2 Images Lamine Yamal is now Anthony Gordon's team-mate (Image: Pablo Rodriguez/Quality Sport Images/Getty Images)

‌



And Gordon is probably chronicling his ambitions in the diary he keeps. “I like to write things down,” he explained. “It always makes it more clear. I always write things down. I kind of like it because in years to come I can look back on it and pass it on to my kids.”

And the most difficult entry he had to write came after the World Cup semi-final defeat in the summer. Gordon put England ahead but was then substituted and watched his team-mates surrender the lead in the last few minutes.

He said: “I did not know what to write. I wrote down just pure emotion. It was a good few pages, I will tell you that.”

Sports.title: Cody Gakpo denies Jurgen Klopp victory on return in controversial Germany vs Netherlands draw
Sports.content:
Cody Gakpo denies Jurgen Klopp victory on return in controversial Germany vs Netherlands draw

NETHERLANDS 1-1 GERMANY: Former Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp looked to be on the way to a perfect start to life with his nation only for a late Cody Gakpo goal to see a share of the spoils

View 3 Images Jurgen Klopp made his managerial return against the Netherlands (Image: Getty Images)

Jurgen Klopp's return to the dugout was never going to be quiet was it? The former Liverpool manager took to the touchline for the first time since his Anfield exit and was denied a dream start as the Netherlands equalised late on against Germany.

‌



Klopp's ex-Liverpool captain Virgil van Dijk thought he had given his former boss a nightmare start to life in his new job after heading home from a corner. But VAR intervened to cancel the goal.

‌



Klopp could eventually celebrate himself though, with Felix Nmecha controversially giving Die Manschaaft the lead in Amsterdam following an off-the-ball incident involving Brian Brobbey and Jonathan Tah.

‌



Heading into the final stages, there was still time for the fiery affair to throw up another dramatic twist as Cody Gakpo volleyed home.

Germany's intent against their bitter rivals was clear from the start, with Klopp's brand of 'heavy metal' football seeing Brentford's Kevin Schade fire in a dangerous cross within the opening few seconds.

The hosts eventually found their feet and in-form Brobbey tangled with Tah as he attempted to charge into the box, albeit neither the referee nor VAR thought the incident was worthy of a penalty. There were then further appeals following an apparent handball by the defender but again, the referee was unmoved.

The Netherlands did eventually have the ball in the net. After scoring from a number of corners under Klopp at Anfield, his former captain Van Dijk got free of his marker to head home.

‌



After being all smiles with Klopp ahead of the game, his mood very quickly changed after seeing VAR intervene and chalk the goal off for Brobbey's apparent foul on goalkeeper Marc-Andre ter Stegen earlier in the move.

View 3 Images Virgil van Dijk thought he had given his country the lead (Image: Getty Images)

There was then even more controversy ahead of Germany's opening goal. Brobbey got in another tangle with Tah on the halfway line and seemingly picked up an injury.

‌



He signalled for a substitution and it appeared as though Germany would allow him to receive treatment as they slowed the game down.

But they surprisingly upped the tempo, played through their hosts and scored through Nmecha, which triggered an angry brawl between both sets of players.

View 3 Images It was an ill-tempered affair in Amsterdam (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Germany should have doubled their lead shortly after through Barcelona's Karim Adeyemi but he somehow fired over when faced with an empty net. In true Klopp fashion, the Germany boss gave an amusing reaction to the miss before applauding his players.

Mexx Meerdink was also guilty of spurning a few wonderful effort for the hosts - the striker firing wide in front of an unguarded net, while he also hit the post.

The ill-tempered tone of the evening continued with a crunching challenge from Nadiem Amiri that had both teams squaring off again.

Article continues below

And there was time for even more drama, with another of Klopp's former stars Gakpo finding acres of space to fire home in the late stages as he latched on to Ruben van Bommel's stunning cross.
