World.title: Bond yields surge to fresh two-decade highs, but oil prices are buffeted by Iran headlines
World.content:
Key U.S. Treasury yields surged to fresh two-decade highs Thursday as the price of oil jumped to as high as $108 per barrel.

The yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond soared as high as 5.47%, a level not seen in 22 years.

After having posted its biggest one-day rise since April 2025, the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury bond continued advancing Thursday. In early trading, it climbed as high as 5.18%. That remains its highest since 2007.

Because of the influence the 10-year yield has over consumer borrowing rates, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate jumped to 7.37% on Thursday, its highest since May 2024.

Meanwhile, oil prices jumped again overnight after a mediated U.S. dialogue with Iran at the United Nations General Assembly produced no tangible evidence of any progress toward ending the seven-month war.

Much of the day’s gains in oil were reversed shortly after midday ET after Reuters reported that U.S. and Iranian negotiators are exploring a phased path out of the war. The path reportedly involves Tehran’s reopening the Strait of Hormuz, according to Reuters’ multiple unnamed sources.

NBC News has not confirmed the Reuters report.

The reversal was short-lived, however, and international Brent crude oil continued to rise and closed higher by 3.4%, at $106.60. U.S. crude oil ended the day higher by 2.6%, at $94.61 per barrel.

Since the start of the year, both Brent and West Texas Intermediary crude are up more than 65%.

The rising oil prices have continued to push commercial diesel fuel prices to records. On Thursday, the national average price for diesel was $6.51, effectively unchanged from a day earlier but up 73% since the Iran war began.

Likewise, the national average price of regular unleaded gas was 50% higher Thursday than it was when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February, at $4.48 per gallon.

Stocks fell in early trading, but like oil, they sharply reversed course on the Reuters report. The S&P 500 erased a drop of 0.5%, while the Nasdaq Composite erased a 0.9% slip. Both indexes closed flat.

A global sell-off

Around the world, the bond sell-off is roiling sovereign debt markets.

“The acceleration higher in US rates yesterday is being felt globally as to highlight for the umpteenth time that we’re all in this global bond boat together,” wrote Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at OnePoint BFG Wealth.

The yield on Japan’s 10-year bond rose to its highest level since 1996 on Thursday, while Germany’s 10-year bund notched its highest yield since 2009.

“As summer officially ends, macro data are still fairly solid in the US, as indicated by a 4%-type unemployment rate and 2%-ish growth,” wrote Bank of America’s global rates analysts.

“But the risks continue to pile up for anxious markets,” they added, pointing to ongoing trade wars, the energy supply shock, upcoming midterm elections and potential risks to the AI boom.

A major driver of the surge in bond yields this week was a report from S&P Global, released Wednesday morning, that found that while U.S. business activity accelerated in September, “firms’ input costs have meanwhile jumped in September at the steepest rate for four years, with fuel and transport costs spiking higher.”

That led investors and traders to ramp up their bets on Fed rate hikes.

Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams said the central bank still has more work to do to help bring down inflation.

It’s “likely that another rate hike may be appropriate by the end of the year,” Williams said Thursday in a speech in London.

Nonetheless, he said, the U.S. economy has demonstrated “remarkable resilience” in the face of “significant shocks” hitting it.

Another key official, Anna Paulson, president of the Philadelphia Fed, said Thursday that she, too, expects “some modest further tightening may be warranted.”

In central banker parlance, tightening refers to raising rates.

Bessent makes a move

The rise in bond yields has continued despite a series of measures taken — and warnings delivered — by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent this month.

“I am the house now,” Bessent said Sept. 8, “and you can bet against me if you want.”

Rates have also continued to surge despite a warning from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in early September. Finn Gomez / Getty Images file

At the time, Bessent was defending a Treasury Department intervention to help prop up the Japanese yen. The hope was that a stronger yen would relieve pressure on the Japanese government to sell U.S. Treasury bonds.

But it hasn’t entirely worked, and as of Thursday, the yen had again weakened to levels on par with its exchange rate against the U.S. dollar from early September.

Bessent has also intervened in the U.S. bond markets, buying back longer-dated Treasurys in an effort to keep their yields low.

In response to the department’s initial buyback this month, bond yields rose — exactly the opposite reaction from what the administration intended.

Bessent has brushed off the stumble, insisting that the U.S. bond market is still the “best performing” in the world and crediting President Donald Trump for it.

“If some of the Bloomberg Terminal bros are unhappy with what I’m doing, well, that’s too bad,” Bessent said in an interview Sept. 10.

The second round of Bessent’s buyback plan was conducted Thursday, when the Treasury bought back about $4 billion worth of 20- and 30-year bonds. As with the initial round, yields rose to their highest level of the session on the news — but the jump was far less notable than it had been a month ago.

“Mechanically, today’s operation went more smoothly,” said Brian Rehling, co-head of global fixed-income strategy at Wells Fargo. But “long-end yields are still being set by inflation, Fed expectations” and the volume of debt being issued.

“Today’s operation is unlikely to alter the trajectory of long-term interest rates, which we believe will continue to move higher until the market believes inflation is being brought under control,” he added.

“US Treasury Secretary ‘House’ Bessent seems to be demonstrating the house does not always win,” Paul Donovan, the chief economist at UBS Global Wealth Management, wrote Thursday morning.

CORRECTION (Sept. 24, 2026, 2:19 p.m. ET): A previous version of this article misstated Thursday’s national average price for diesel. It was $6.51, not $4.51.

World.title: These young quarterbacks were supposed to break out. Now they’re hurt.
World.content:
The New York Giants were one of the NFL’s pleasant surprises in Week 1, beginning the John Harbaugh era with an impressive win over the Dallas Cowboys thanks in large part to the play of second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart.

The Giants’ dreams of a turnaround season quickly hit a roadblock on Monday, however, as Dart became the latest upstart QB to be sidelined with an injury. And now Dart may miss the rest of the regular season after imaging on Tuesday revealed his knee was hurt worse than the team initially feared, according to multiple reports.

Only two weeks into the NFL season, several of the game’s young stars are seeing their seasons upended due to varying degrees of injuries.

Dart joined the Chicago Bears’ Caleb Williams and the Washington Commanders’ Jayden Daniels as signal callers who had to leave the field early in Week 2. That trio joined a list of sidelined quarterbacks that also includes the Minnesota Vikings’ Kyler Murray and the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks’ Sam Darnold.

All five of those players are former first-round draft picks — and all are under the age of 30.

Dart left in the first quarter of New York’s 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. On a third-and-8 pass attempt, Dart was sandwiched by multiple players as the pocket collapsed around him, and he took a substantial hit to his left knee from a Rams linebacker.

Dart limped off the field and was taken back to the locker room. After initially being ruled questionable to return, he was ruled out for good in the second half.

“He’s going to be OK,” Giants general manager Joe Schoen told ESPN’s Laura Rutledge during the “Monday Night Football” broadcast, adding that Dart would undergo X-rays at the stadium.

Dart’s hard-charging play style raised eyebrows during his rookie season, when he missed time due to a concussion but seemingly refused to tone down his aggressiveness when he returned.

Jaxson Dart lays on the field after being injured during the first quarter of a game against the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium on Monday. Logan Bowles / Getty Images

During the preseason, Dart even expressed confusion at why he so often is required to enter the blue medical tent on the sidelines.

“I really respect the rules, and the thought behind, you know, the NFL has of keeping players healthy and reviewing things,” Dart said in August after a big hit required he undergo a mandatory medical evaluation. “But at the same time, I’m still puzzled by just feeling like every time that I get hit, you know, I just find my way in there.”

Dart’s injury Monday, though, came on a relatively routine pass play, highlighting how no quarterback is ever truly safe.

The same can be said of the Commanders’ Daniels, who dislocated his left elbow while trying to regain his balance after he was tripped by one of his own lineman in a 37-20 loss to the Cowboys. Daniels, the 2024 Offensive Rookie of the Year, dislocated the same elbow last season, in which he appeared in only seven games due to multiple injuries.

“It sucks for him,” Washington coach Dan Quinn told reporters Monday. “I know how much these guys put into it. So, when there are setbacks like this, you just want to stand by them.”

A little before Daniels’ exit, the Bears’ Williams was carted off the field with a hamstring strain in a 9-3 loss to the Vikings. While Williams’ emotional exit from the game quickly became a social media meme, it also cut short what had been an exciting start to the season. Chicago was coming off a Week 1 in which it had scored 59 points.

“He’s right now working through every avenue that he’s got available to get back on track here. We’ll see what that looks like,” Bears coach Ben Johnson told reporters Monday.

Johnson added that Williams has an ability to recover quickly, and his injury is considered week-to-week.

While the Bears, Giants and the Commanders all lost after their starters went down, their seasons are far from over.

The Vikings lost Murray in Week 1 but still managed a 2-0 start to the season with Carson Wentz at the helm. And now Murray is expected to start in Week 3 after recovering from a concussion.

The Seahawks are also 2-0 with Drew Lock playing in place of Darnold, and even exploded for 31 points on Sunday. Darnold is expected to return to practice this week, though his starting status is up in the air.

For now, the Bears will turn to Tyler Bagent, the Giants to Jameis Winston, and the Commanders to Marcus Mariota as the three clubs try to keep their seasons afloat without their young leaders.

And Dart, Williams and Daniels — all three of whom have flashed potential to not only be great players but stewards for the league because of their exciting style of play — will have to wait a little longer to cement their star turns.

World.title: Error leads to backlog of tens of thousands of voter registration applications in Texas
World.content:
Texas officials sent tens of thousands of delayed voter registration applications to county election officials this week after discovering an error, sparking a scramble to process them weeks out from the midterms.

The Texas secretary of state’s office told election officials last week that a problem with the Department of Public Safety’s system had been uncovered: Certain incomplete voter registration applications that were missing some information were not sent on to election officials, potentially leaving Texans unregistered or with out-of-date voter files. The nonprofit news outlet Votebeat was the first to report the problem.

State officials started transmitting the records on Tuesday. It’s unclear how many voters were affected, but large counties have reported tens of thousands of registration applications and updates that election officials must process in the less than a month before early voting begins on Oct. 19. And more applications are sure to pour in ahead of the Oct. 5 deadline to register to vote in Texas.

The state’s fourth-most populous county, Bexar, received more than 45,000 voter registration forms from DPS, and the fifth-most populous, Travis County, received more than 35,000.

“While that number may seem high, the Elections team is already hard at work reviewing every application and will be extending hours to make sure all records are updated well before early voting begins,” Bexar County Elections Administrator Michele Carew said in a statement.

Chris McGinn, the executive director of the Texas Association of County Election Officials, said he expected populous urban areas will be hit hardest, because there are more voter registrations to process and people in cities tend to move more often.

“There’s going to be a lot of counties that are paying a lot of overtime,” he said, speaking in a press briefing organized by the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation and Research.

McGinn said some of the records may be duplicative — people may check the box to register to vote when they update their driver’s license, for instance — but still need time and attention from election officials.

Alicia Pierce, a spokesperson for the Texas secretary of state’s office, said a voter who does not appear on the state’s rolls but believes they registered to vote can cast a provisional ballot, and election officials can later search DPS records.

Texas is hosting several competitive statewide elections this fall. Democratic state Rep. James Talarico is facing off against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton for a U.S. Senate seat. And Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa is challenging GOP Gov. Greg Abbott.

In a statement, Talarico called the error “unacceptable” and urged Texans to check their voter registration online.

“Less than two weeks before the voter registration deadline, thousands of Texans are now in the dark about their voter registration status — even more aren’t aware of this error at all,” Talarico said. “This is what a broken, corrupt political system looks like: Texans follow the rules, register to vote before the deadline, and still risk losing their God-given right to the ballot box because their government failed to do its job.”

McGinn said voters might be better off calling their local registrar’s office. Texas’ online system has reportedly had problems this year, with some registrations inaccurately showing up as inactive.

World.title: If Trump bans U.S. diesel exports, global prices will go even higher, experts say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump has said he's considering a ban on diesel exports to improve gas prices for Americans, a move experts say would only push an already-strained global market —further raising diesel prices in Canada and abroad.

During a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at a UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump said he's called for a diesel export ban.

"I've said, 'Let's not send out the diesel.' We make a lot of diesel. That could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline," said Trump, whose fellow Republicans are facing pressure over gas prices going into November's midterm elections.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who was on hand, said Washington is examining "whether it's feasible … and whether a full or partial ban would work."

And yet a White House official on Thursday denied a Politico report that the U.S. is actively preparing a 90-day ban of diesel exports, and U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said no one is considering a total ban.

The idea is being floated amid already record-breaking diesel prices, driven up by the conflicts in Iran and Ukraine. The price of diesel in Canada has been above $2 per litre for the last 12 weeks, and was sitting at $2.66 a litre on Thursday, more than a dollar higher than this time last year.

In the U.S., diesel prices have shot higher than $6.50 US a gallon, according to the American Automobile Association. Last year around this time, it averaged $3.69 US.

Experts agree that a U.S. ban on diesel exports would only throw the global market into further disarray.

"This seems like a fairly hare-brained policy idea that kind of misses the mark on what the real challenges are right now," Joe Calnan, the Calgary-based vice-president of energy at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute, told CBC News.

The U.S. exports around 1.5 million barrels per day of diesel, predominantly to Latin America and Western Europe, he said, and taking that out of the market suddenly would have the ripple effect of driving up prices across the board.

A report from U.K.-based analytics group Wood Mackenzie said Europe would be particularly vulnerable as its share of U.S. diesel exports has been on the rise, surging to 50 per cent in September compared to a 30 per cent average in 2025.

How it could impact Canada

A global price hike would include Canada, exacerbating ongoing problems, Calnan said.

Diesel powers the trucks that ship food and goods across the country, and the tractors that harvest our food.

WATCH | Farmers feeling the pinch: High diesel prices mean an expensive harvest for P.E.I. farmers | Duration closed caption 1:57 The price of diesel continues to climb and farmers on the Island are feeling it. They're getting hit particularly hard now as their machines roll through the fall harvest. CBC's Connor Lamont explains.

With farmers now in the middle of harvest season, the current price difference is already being felt. One Ontario farmer said earlier this month that the cost to fill his combine has jumped by $1,000 per refuel.

Calnan notes diesel is also used for power generation in Canada's far north, and for home heating in the Maritimes, meaning a potential diesel price hike could be felt more broadly in those regions.

"There will be impacts at the pump for diesel, [and] for those sorts of consumers," Calnan said.

And yet, a U.S. export ban wouldn't mean a shortage of diesel in Canada, experts say — Canada produces much more diesel than it imports. In 2024, the country exported 10.8 billion litres.

"We export almost two times more than we import, so Canada could get by without U.S. exports very easily," said Carol Montreuil, vice president at the Canadian Fuels Association.

"Pricing wise, it would be a different story."

Record-high prices

The war with Iran is one of the main factors lifting diesel prices. Before the U.S., together with Israel, initiated hostilities in February, the Strait of Hormuz handled around 125 commercial vessels a day, accounting for roughly 20 per cent of the world's crude oil and liquefied natural gas supply.

Ships have finally started moving through the strait again in recent weeks after months of closure, but it's still a trickle, with just 10 vessels transiting on Wednesday according to shipping data.

Vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on Aug. 31. A trickle of ships are moving through the strait now, but oil shipping is nowhere near the strait's usual capacity. (Stringer/File Photo/Reuters)

Conflict between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis near the Red Sea's Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another key supply route, is also adding supply stress.

Meanwhile, Russia, one of the biggest diesel exporters, has also extended a ban on diesel exports multiple times amid its ongoing war with Ukraine.

Because of these conflicts, an estimated seven million barrels a day of refining capacity is out of reach, Montreuil said.

"When you think of the world functioning on about 100 million barrels a day, removing seven million barrels per day, or around seven per cent of refining capacity, is a huge impact, and that impact is being felt on prices."

Although keeping all U.S. diesel within the country would temporarily aid in gas prices for Americans, experts say it would eventually drive up their costs.

Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at Gas Buddy, says diesel prices in the U.S. may go lower at first.

But then refineries in the U.S. would have to slow down production to avoid creating a diesel surplus once none was being exported. And with more diesel being redirected into storage, refineries would likely have to cut down on crude oil processing as well to make sure inventories don't go over capacity, ultimately impacting prices of regular gasoline.

"It would send a very chilling signal to U.S. refineries that the government is going to dictate what you can and what you can't do in terms of your supply," he said.

World.title: Thélyson Orélien's debut novel was shortlisted for prestigious prizes. Then the allegations started pouring in
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Quebec-based author is at the centre of an artificial intelligence scandal shaking the French literary world and raising questions around how the industry should be using AI — and its detection tools.

Breakthrough star Thélyson Orélien, a Canadian-Haitian poet and author, has been accused of writing his debut novel using generative AI, which he vehemently denies. The scandal comes as C’était ça ou mourir is being considered for various prestigious awards.

The allegation first surfaced Monday – the same day Orélien won the Prix du roman Fnac – on the anonymous X account "Balance ton Claude," which claims to expose AI slop.

The account claims to have analyzed several excerpts from the book using the AI-detector tool Pangram, which found the text was “100 per cent” AI.

CBC News replicated the Pangram experiment with different excerpts of the book, which led to the same result.

Speaking to franceinfo Wednesday, the president of the Académie Goncourt, which shortlisted Orélien for an award, said the latter wouldn’t be disqualified unless “irrefutable evidence” were to surface.

“The academy is taking the time to consider the various factors involved in this case before making a decision that will preserve both the integrity of the prize it awards and that of its work,” Claudel Philippe told CBC in a statement Thursday.

The executive director of Writers’ Trust of Canada, David Leonard, says the question of how trustworthy these AI-detection tools are is an issue the entire industry is grappling with. For now, the organization, which recognizes local writers, relies on self-declarations made by the authors.

But it’s exploring its options, he says.

“It's a very fast-moving issue,” Leonard said. “We don't want to be in a situation where we're getting false positives, nor do we want to be in a situation where we're using a tool that is not effective.”

On Thursday afternoon, Orélien's Montreal-based publishing house, Éditions du Boréal, announced it was suspending its press tour for the author, who is currently in France gearing up for award season.

"We unreservedly condemn the hateful messages and personal attacks of recent days and call on everyone to exercise restraint," it wrote in a statement.

It adds that its decision is to preserve Orélien's well-being and that the book, which was published in the spring, remains available.

WATCH | Allegations of plagiarism surface against Quebec-based author: Award-winning Quebec author accused of using AI for bestselling book | Duration closed caption 2:25 In recent months, Thélyson Orélien became a sensation for his debut novel C'était ça ou mourir, which follows a teacher escaping gang violence in Haiti’s Port-au-Prince. After the book won a prestigious award on Monday, an anonymous X account accused Orélien of using AI to write it, which he vehemently denies. Since then, other allegations of plagiarism have surfaced against the author.

What happened?

C'était ça ou mourir, which translates to "It was either that or die" tells the story of a man who undertakes a perilous journey across the Americas to escape gang violence in Haiti’s Port-au-Prince.

Orélien has previously said his own experience of leaving Haiti following the 2010 earthquake and stories of other migrants he met in Montreal helped shape the novel.

In a statement Tuesday evening, he attempted to soothe the scrutiny of his heavy use of metaphors and similes in the book, which many have pointed to as tells that AI was involved in the writing process.

"I come from a Haitian and Caribbean literary tradition in which poetry, imagery, repetition, and rhythm carry a living voice," Orélien said in the statement written in French and released by Éditions du Boréal.

"One might debate my style, but treating its techniques as evidence of artificial intelligence has nothing to do with literary criticism," he said.

In the same statement, Éditions du Boréal affirmed its support for the author, saying Orélien's manuscript was drafted several years ago and evolved over multiple exchanges with his editor.

However, new allegations have cast doubt on Orélien's credibility beyond the fiction-writing sphere.

Copies of the novel C'était ça ou mourir, which translates to "It was either that or die," by Thélyson Orélien are displayed on a bookstore table in Paris on Sept. 23, 2026. The quote highlighted on the cover underlines the strength of the text. (Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images)

Allegations of plagiarism

On Wednesday, the Quebec newspaper La Presse uncovered multiple instances of possible plagiarism in Orélion’s columns across different publications dating back to 2012. Radio-Canada's Décrypteurs has since verified those findings.

Orélien has not addressed the compounding scandal.

Speaking to Radio-Canada’s Tout un matin Thursday morning, La Presse’s vice-president of information, François Cardinal said he read the book – stopping short of calling it “incredible” – and at no point suspected the involvement of AI.

“We’ll never have a definitive answer on AI one way or the other. We can’t prove beyond all doubt that AI was used. And we can’t prove that AI wasn’t used,” he said.

But given the plagiarism allegations, he said the publication will likely not consider Orélien for future columns.

In an update Thursday morning, Éditions du Boréal said it was taking stock of the newest and "very serious" plagiarism allegations.

Thursday afternoon, the literary festival Salon du livre in the Eastern Townships announced it was dropping Orélien as its guest of honour.

A few hours later, Éditions du Boréal announced its suspension of Orélien's press tour.

In its latest statement, it continued to defend its editorial process, adding that despite its best efforts to produce a "definitive answer" as to whether the book was written by AI, the publishing house says it is simply "impossible at this stage to confirm or deny the allegations."

"The fact remains that the novel has reached tens of thousands of readers across the French-speaking world, as well as numerous international publishers," reads the statement. "In the absence of serious, tangible evidence, it is not for us to decide whether it has the right to exist."

Tools detect AI, not ideas

For Florent Michelot, a Concordia professor who researches AI in education, Orélien’s ordeal raises a key question: Have we entered an era where the final product is no longer enough when judging someone’s work?

“I didn’t read the book, but maybe [Orélien] developed very complex personalities for his characters, maybe he developed a wonderful atmosphere … and the AI only helped to write the sentences,” he said.

Michelot says he's personally tested Pangram, the AI-detector tool, and like many other experts who have spoken out since the controversy broke, he says the tool is "amazing."

Basically, the tool identifies patterns based on probability, he explains. If every word in an excerpt is statistically the most likely word to follow the one before it, then AI was most likely involved in the writing, according to the tool.

So, as more people lean on AI for things like research, spellcheck and translations, Michelot wonders if the creative process will begin to gain more value over the finished product.

A screengrab of AI-detection tool Pangram's analysis after CBC presented it with an excerpt from Thélyson Orélien's novel C'était ça ou mourir. (Cassandra Yanez-Leyton/CBC)

Humans reading humans

For French literature professor Emeline Pierre, who teaches at the Université de Montréal, the controversy has created a sense of unease, she says. The questions of why Orélien was targeted and why now are central to how she's digesting the situation.

Regardless, she puts in doubt the reliability of AI-detecting tools. As for the repetitions and metaphors in Orélien's text, she says they are characteristic of writing styles in the Caribbean.

"Once again, we see the journey of a Black person who makes their mark. And when that person perhaps goes too far — garners too much recognition — it seems to me that they eventually become a source of discomfort," she said.

She says the attention the controversy has garnered harkens back to the case of Jason Arday, a Cambridge professor who gained prominence after becoming the university's youngest professor in 2023 at age 37.

He was found dead inside his apartment after becoming the focus of a plagiarism scandal.

Pierre worries about the effect the Orélien story will have on emerging young Black writers, adding that the speed with which scandals seem to close in on their subject when they’re Black is worrisome.

Orélien left Haiti for Quebec after the 2010 earthquake. According to La Presse, a Quebec-based publication for which he's written a few columns, he lives between Montreal and Ottawa. (Joel Saget /AFP via Getty Images)

The executive director of the Writers' Trust of Canada says despite the controversy and AI’s seemingly growing writing proficiency, it’s not the future of literature itself he’s worried about, but the viability of writing as a career.

He says many authors support themselves by taking on other types of writing jobs and those are being eliminated by AI.

“So these tools are making it much more difficult for writers to make a living,” he said.

“We'll continue to write literature, and people wanting to read human-authored works will continue to want to read human-authored works.”

World.title: CEO who posted about wearing 'Lake America' sweatshirts to Halifax is no longer CEO
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Michigan tourist who recently went viral over a Facebook photo where she and three family members appeared to be wearing "Lake America" sweatshirts has parted ways with her employer.

Jane Smith, the former CEO of Family First Credit Union in Saginaw, is no longer employed there, according to a statement posted on Wednesday to the company's website.

"We are reaching out to inform you that Jane Smith is no longer an employee of Family First Credit Union, effective immediately," reads the statement addressed to "Family First Credit Union Members and Community" and signed by the chair of the board of directors.

The statement continues to say that chief operations officer Jason Acosta is now serving as interim CEO. It does not provide any further information about why Smith is no longer employed, or whether the decision to leave the company was hers.

CBC News has reached out to Smith, Acosta and the credit union's marketing team, and not yet heard back. But the company apologized in a statement posted to the Family First Credit Union Facebook page on Wednesday.

"We sincerely apologize for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused our members and community," the post reads.

"We understand that members of our community may hold different perspectives about this decision. Our responsibility is to act in the best interest of the Credit Union, uphold the trust of our members and continue putting our community first."

A screen grab of an Instagram post by Breaking News Canada from Sept. 13 shows the since-deleted Facebook post by Jane Smith that went viral. (@breakingnews.ca/Instagram)

'Like our sweatshirts?'

The news comes in the wake of the backlash over a photo Smith had posted to Facebook on her way to Halifax, in which she and three family members pose wearing "Lake America" sweatshirts that Smith later said were AI-generated.

"Like our sweatshirts? Not sure Canada will," said the Sept. 11 photo originally posted by Smith, and later shared by her sister, followed by "lol lol."

Judging by the reaction online, just weeks after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America" amid the trade war between the two countries, Canadians were not lol-ing.

In a previous interview with ABC12 News in Michigan, Smith said the image was AI-generated and meant to be a joke.

WATCH | Republican mayor rejects Lake Ontario name change: Republican mayor rejects Trump's Lake Ontario name change | Duration closed caption 5:09 Robert Corradino is the Republican mayor of Oswego, N.Y., a city on the southeastern shore of Lake Ontario. He says the body of water is central to his community's identity and the city's decision not to follow U.S. President Donald Trump's directive to rename the lake 'Lake America' is one his constituents 'overwhelmingly' support.

"We weren't trying to make a political statement," Smith told the news outlet.

"However, we were, you know, kind of poking fun at the fact that, you know, one of the Great Lakes's names were getting changed."

She further explained that the sweatshirts weren't real, saying she ran a photo of them through ChatGPT to add the "Lake America" gear, then posted it to her private Facebook page with an AI label.

When they arrived in Halifax, it was her sister who reposted it publicly, added the comment and didn't include the AI warning, Smith said.

"We never had actual sweatshirts. We never wore sweatshirts."

There's been ongoing backlash over Trump's proposed name-change on both sides of the border. Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canadians will call it Lake Ontario "now and always." In the U.S., three members of Congress have introduced a bill aimed at stopping Trump's renaming, titled "Hands off our Great Lakes."

World.title: Fat Bear Week is back. And this year, it's all about the mamas
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Interview with naturalist Mike Fitz: As It Happens 6:21 Mamas and their cubs join Fat Bear Week contest for 1st time

For the first time, Fat Bear Week includes big, beautiful mommas and their big, beautiful babies.

The annual brackets-style contest, run by Alaska's Katmai National Park and Preserve, is a celebration of the park's beefiest brown bears, who gorge on salmon from the Brooks River in order to pack on as many pounds as possible ahead of their winter hibernation.

"This year, we saw more bear families at the river than ever before," Alaska naturalist Mike Fitz told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal.

"So this year we are featuring five mother bears and their cubs in Fat Bear Week to try to tell some of those stories, because the health and size of a cub is a direct reflection of a mother's effort."

Fat Bear Week competitor Bear 910 is the daughter of former champion, Beadnose. (C. Loberg/Fat Bear Week)

Fat Bear Week started in 2014 and has since surged in popularity, inspiring similar initiatives, like Fat Marmot Week in Colorado.

More than 1.7 million votes were cast last year and the team expects to exceed that number this year, says Fitz, a former Katmai National Park ranger who now works as the resident naturalist for Explore.org, which helps run the contest.

The contest features 16 bears or bear families facing off in a single-elimination, bracket-style tournament.

And thanks to a particularly plentiful salmon run, the competition is fierce.

Chunk defends his crown

The bear to beat is Chunk, a.k.a. Bear 32, a crowd favourite with several victories under his belt. He won last year's competition after reaching a whopping 1,200s pounds while nursing a broken jaw.

But Fitz says there are a few up-and-comers to watch this year, including Bear 151, a.k.a. Walker.

"He's never won, but he's just a light bulb of a bear," Fitz said. "Every year, he just gets super pudgy. If I was to use another adjective for him, I would call him a pear-shaped."

When Backpack was an injured adolescent, rangers at Alaska's Katmai National Park and Preserve didn't think he would survive. Now he's fully grown and a major competitor in Fat Bear Week. (Explore.org)

There's also Bear 89, a.k.a., Backpack, who survived a severe limp during his adolescence to become the brawny beast he is today.

"He was the first bear that taught me how tough and resilient bears are, even at a young age," Fitz said.

Meet the mamas

But enough about the boys.

The fatter a bear gets during the summer and fall, the better their chance of surviving the long, cold winter. That's doubly important for females, says Fitz.

"A mother bear goes into the den with fat reserves not only to survive that hibernation period for herself, but also for her cubs," he said.

A female bear may mate in early summer, but the fertilized embryos don't implant until she's hibernating in her den come November.

"If you don't go into the den with enough body fat reserves, then the mother is not going to give birth," he said. "So the fact that we saw so many cubs return to Brooks River this year means that a lot of female bears in 2025 went into the den healthy."

Bear 806 has two cubs, one of whom is adopted. Despite her generosity in taking in another bear's offspring, she also killed and partially ate a different bear cub this summer. (T. Carmack/Fat Bear Week)

To celebrate that success, this year's bracket features five mother bears and their cubs.

There's Bear 132 and her three cubs, one of whom became lost for several frantic days in June, only to be reunited with its family.

There's also Bear 284, a.k.a. Electra, a mother of two who, according to her online bio, is known for her "curious and bold" personality, and Bear 610, described as "a small statured bear with a disproportionately large ability to overcome hardship."

Bear 806 is repping blended families with her biological cub and her adopted son, Biggie. Despite being generous enough to take in another bear's lost baby, she also killed and partially ate another bear cub in July who swam too close to her family.

Last, but not least, is Bear 901, who "readily achieves a level of fatness above that of many other bears," along with her sole surviving baby, one of the biggest cubs on the river.

Protecting salmon = protecting bears

Fitz says the Katmai bears' success is the product of Alaskans' dedication to protecting sockeye salmon, especially in the pristine waters of Bristol Bay, which is home to what he calls "one of the last great salmon runs on Earth."

But while Bristol Bay has seen record salmon runs over the last decade, he says the same is not true for all Alaska salmon.

The bears of Katmai are successful because of an abundant salmon run in the region. (Guy Runco/Katmai Conservancy/The Associated Press)

"Many are struggling, likely due to the effects of climate change and how it is impacting ocean food webs. Even though sockeye in Bristol Bay are doing well, we can't assume that will be the case in the future, especially if we continue to burn fossil fuels and force the climate to warm further or allow mining to happen," he said.

"Fat Bear Week offers us an opportunity to see the benefits that large, healthy salmon runs bring to ecosystems."

World.title: Alberta separation group releases report touting affordable transition to independence
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An independence organization is the latest group to try to price out what it might cost should Alberta decide in the future to become a sovereign nation.

The Alberta Transition Council (ATC) released a budget and costing plan this week which estimates about $5 billion in one-time expenses, while predicting that an independent Alberta would have a potential budget surplus of between $22.2 to $32.1 billion each year.

“This is affordable, this is doable and actually well within the means that Alberta has today. So our view is we can become independent, we can operate as an independent country and we can be successful financially,” said Dennis Kalma, the principal author of the ATC financial reports, in an interview with CBC News.

Having between $22 billion to $32 billion left over every year is money that could be used for different priorities, Kalma said, such as lowering taxes, paying down debt, building savings, or service and infrastructure improvements.

“Canada is a bigger organization. It's not known for its efficiency and a smaller country could do some simplification,” said Kalma.

ATC's figures vary drastically from a similar report by academics at the University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy.

A former treasury board senior manager called the ATC financials “magic” for ignoring hundreds of billions of dollars in costs, while also not detailing potential cuts in financial supports to seniors, low-income Albertans, and parents.

The ATC is the same group that previously released a 214-page “transition plan,” laying out a range of regulations and institutions that would need to transition to Alberta’s control from Ottawa.

Lawyer Keith Wilson, who leads the Alberta Transition Council and is also a leader with the independence group Let Alberta Decide, said the important point is not simply whether the books balance.

“It is whether there could be meaningful financial room left after Alberta pays for the services and responsibilities of a country,” Wilson said in a news release.

Pro-unity and pro-independence flags dot a patch of grass in Airdrie, Alta. (Mantai Chow/CBC)

‘Magic a prevailing theme’

This is the latest in a long line of reports trying to envision what would need to happen and what it would cost if Alberta residents decide to leave Canada.

Last week, the University of Calgary School of Public Policy estimated that the cost of establishing a new country would range between $50 billion and $170 billion over a five-year period and would be highly unpredictable over the long-term.

Former Treasury Board senior manager Lennie Kaplan also contributed a projection to a report from the Canada West Foundation, a Calgary-based think-tank. Kaplan estimated setting up an independent Alberta would cost more than $200 billion, with ongoing costs of more than $50 billion annually.

After reviewing the ATC’s reports, Kaplan described “magic as a prevailing theme,” since it should not be assumed that by virtue of Alberta becoming independent it can grow its way out of deficit and debt.

“Uncertainties and risks are treated as things to negotiate later on after separation,” said Kaplan in an email. The ATC “does not model output, employment or trade, and it makes no claim about the size of the economy in any future year.”

In addition, the reports do not cost continued access to trade agreements, among other issues, said Kaplan, which will “need to be reconciled by the ATC.”

Debt, service cuts and military

The biggest omission, experts say, is the ATC anticipating that an independent Alberta would not inherit its share of the federal debt.

In contrast, the U of C report forecast Alberta's debt would balloon as it takes on a portion of Canada's federal debt, rising to between $324 billion and $442.3 billion — requiring the province to spend billions more than it currently does on paying that debt's interest.

The ATC explained the federal debt was omitted since no settlement has been negotiated and the outcome cannot be known in advance.

For Trevor Tombe, an economics professor and contributor to the U of C’s report, the ATC’s decision to not account for any debt whatsoever being taken on by an independent Alberta, is “not a realistic scenario to contemplate.”

In addition, the ATC does not adhere to military spending to align Alberta with the international commitment of two per cent of GDP and does not include spending on First Nations and Métis programs.

The ATC also lists considerable savings "after replacing everything Canada does” currently for Alberta, however Tombe said those figures envision “a scale of services that are far lower than what currently exists,” and there is only leftover cash because of cuts.

For instance, the federal government provides individual benefits to seniors and low income individuals. There are other supports such as the Canada Child Benefit and grants to individuals and businesses.

The ATC proposes paying for the existing federal Old Age Security program by including it in a new Alberta Pension Plan, as opposed to covering the cost in an annual budget, as the federal government currently does.

“That's an unsustainable strategy,” said Tombe, unless taxes or worker contribution rates were increased.

“Those are big ticket items and largely accounts for the gap between their numbers and what we had from the School of Public Policy,” he said.

World.title: Netanyahu rejects genocide allegations in Gaza after mass walkout at his UN speech
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu delivered a high-stakes speech in New York Thursday, where many UN delegates walked out in protest, after which Netanyahu called them ‘moral cowards.’ Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas addressed the assembly in a pre-recorded message — he and other top Palestinian officials were denied U.S. visas.

Allegations of Israeli genocide in Gaza are not only false but "the biggest lie of the century," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told world leaders Thursday in a defiant speech that asserted his nation's right to wage war against Iran — and was not heard by scores of delegates who trooped out before he started speaking.

Netanyahu, his voice rising in emphasis, said attacking Iran "was one of the easiest decisions [he's] ever had to make" and denounced as "moral cowards" a mass of delegates who walked out of the UN General Assembly when he took the podium to speak.

"In defending itself, Israel is also also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall," Netanyahu said. "In fact, I want you to know that many of their leaders even thank us privately for taking out Iran's nukes."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) at UN headquarters in New York City on Thursday. (Mike Segar/Reuters)

When Netanyahu walked to the rostrum, a mix of cheers, boos and mass walkouts erupted. Scores of delegates marched out and most of the visible seats sat empty afterward.

"If there are any other moral cowards who have not yet left the hall, please do so now," Netanyahu said.

The Palestinian Mission to the UN had said in a message to many of the 193 UN member nations to bring as many staff as possible to the assembly hall and "collectively walk out of the assembly" once the Israeli prime minister is announced.

"This will send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end," the message said.

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly via pre-recorded video in New York City on Thursday, hours before Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took the stage to address world leaders in person. (Mike Segar/Reuters)

His remarks — which at times sounded like a stump speech as Israel gears up for elections — came after a week filled with speeches by world leaders accusing Israel of genocide and war crimes in Gaza.'

Israel rejects allegations that it committed genocide and war crimes and that it is illegally occupying Palestinian territory. All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law, but the Israeli government insists they are legal.

Netanyahu, who is prone to using visual aids during his General Assembly speeches, at one point held up a pager while reminding the audience of Sept. 17, 2024, when Israel remotely detonated thousands of pagers that had been distributed to the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group in Lebanon. The pager attack wounded more than 3,000 people and killed 12, including two children.

He reminded the assembly of the scale of the Oct. 7, 2023, attack in which Hamas militants killed about 1,200 people, according to Israeli tallies. "This is equal to 40,000 innocent Americans slaughtered in less than 24 hours," he said, or 16 times the death count on the 9/11 attacks that left nearly 3,000 people dead in New York.

Netanyahu thanked U.S. President Donald Trump for taking decisive action against Iran, and he insisted Israel would prevail: "We will continue to win because we have no other choice."

Abbas denied visa

Earlier Thursday, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas addressed the world leaders in a pre-recorded video from his office in Ramallah after the U.S. denied him and other top Palestinian officials visas to attend the gathering for the second year in a row.

"The Palestinian people face one of the most dangerous times in its history," Abbas said, citing long-term military occupation in the West Bank and the war in Gaza. Israel, he said, "has targeted all of the basic necessities of life."

As Abbas spoke, the Israeli delegation's seats in the General Assembly hall sat vacant.

In his speech, Abbas once again implored the international community to take more vigorous action and speak out more loudly against Israel.

"How much longer will some states continue to remain silent against Israel or supply it with the weapons it uses against our people? The world has witnessed the tremendous cost in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank," Abbas said. "What is the international community waiting for in order to protect the Palestinian people?"

Though negotiations have not taken place for years, Abbas urged the international community to push for a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Netanyahu has said no Palestinian state will be established while he is Israel's leader and has argued that the Palestinian Authority is not a partner for peace.

WATCH | A plan to remove Palestinians: Israel set to oust Palestinians from Gaza if U.S. signs off, defence minister says | Duration closed caption 2:06 Israel's Defence Minister says his country is ready to remove Palestinians from Gaza if the U.S. approves, a plan described as ethnic cleansing. Israel Katz said 'there is no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration.'

The international community has backed Trump's plan for a group of apolitical administrators to govern Gaza under the Board of Peace. But Abbas said the territory could not remain politically separate from the West Bank and East Jerusalem for the long term.

He said the Gaza Strip, East Jerusalem and the West Bank needed to be governed by "one state, one government, one law and one legitimate entity authorized to bear arms."

Abbas recorded the video on Wednesday.

Since 2005, the now-90-year-old Abbas has led the Palestinian Authority, which is the internationally recognized representative of the Palestinian people. But his support among Palestinians has withered during years of corruption and the sometimes-violent advance of Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.

Under Abbas, Palestine has been recognized as a country by a majority of UN member states. But on the ground in the West Bank, the mostly symbolic moves have not affected Israel's decades-long military occupation. Throughout the war in Gaza, Abbas and the authority have been largely sidelined from negotiations over its future in favour of a transition process shepherded by the U.S.-backed Board of Peace.

The Palestinian Authority was created under a series of peace agreements with Israel in the 1990s and administers semi-autonomous areas of the West Bank, while relying heavily on foreign aid.

It was ousted from Gaza after Hamas won parliamentary elections in 2006 and violently seized control. Abbas was elected to what was supposed to be a four-year term in 2005. The authority has not held presidential or legislative elections since 2006.

Israel captured the West Bank and East Jerusalem in the 1967 war, and the Palestinians want both as part of their future state. The Palestinians and much of the international community view the settlements as illegal and as an obstacle to creating a viable, contiguous Palestinian state.
