The Attack in Santo Domingo Este

In the early hours of Monday 21 September 2026, several people entered the home of merengue singer Julián Oro Duro and his wife, Zeneida Socorro Castillo, in the Brisa Oriental VI sector, near the San Isidro motorway in Santo Domingo Este. Zeneida was killed inside the house; according to an initial medico-legal report cited by Dominican media, she suffered craniofacial trauma and a stab wound to the left side of her neck.

Oro Duro, 58, was attacked when he returned home in the small hours. Two men beat him and stole cash, jewellery and a mobile phone, the Policía Nacional said in its preliminary account. The singer survived and was rushed to the Hospital General de la Plaza de la Salud, where he remains under medical care.

The exact circumstances of Zeneida Castillo’s death are still under investigation. El Espectador, reporting the case on 24 September, noted that what initially looked like a violent home robbery has acquired “new elements” that investigators are now analysing.

From Robbery Inquiry to Inner-Circle Case

The investigation took an unexpected turn when the Policía Nacional identified suspects with connections to the artist and his close circle. Four men are in custody: Phillips Michael Tejeda Vásquez, Juan Carlos Hernández García, known as ‘Peña’, Kevin Dariel Germán Troncoso, nicknamed ‘Yandel’, and Lawrence Mark Liranzo Marcos, alias ‘Chiquito’, aged 18, who was arrested under a judicial order.

The detail that has gripped the country is how close the suspects allegedly were to the family. According to the authorities, Tejeda Vásquez had worked on properties belonging to the singer and had accompanied him to various artistic engagements. Police spokesman Diego Pesqueira, presenting the preliminary reconstruction, said Zeneida had apparently been in contact with some of those involved before the crime — and had even offered them food and coffee.

Investigators have not publicly assigned specific roles to each detainee, and it remains unclear whether the murder was the planned outcome of the intrusion or a robbery that escalated. The theft of cash, jewellery and a phone was confirmed by police, but the presence of people trusted by the family has shifted the focus of the case.

A Merengue Scene in Mourning

Julián Oro Duro — the stage name of Gilberto Julián Sarante Perdomo — is a well-known figure in merengue típico, the traditional accordion-driven strand of the Dominican Republic’s national music. News of the attack prompted an outpouring of grief across the country’s entertainment world, with fellow musicians and fans gathering at the funeral home where Zeneida Castillo was laid out, Diario Libre reported.

The killing has also landed in the middle of a national debate about violent crime in the Dominican Republic, where high-profile cases quickly become tests of the government’s security policy. A murder inside a celebrity couple’s home — allegedly involving people the victims knew — has amplified that pressure.

The President’s Response

President Luis Abinader addressed the case publicly on 22 September, expressing solidarity with the artist and issuing a blunt warning to those responsible: “Les va a ir peor” — “things will go worse for you”. The presidential intervention underlines the political weight of the case.

For the authorities, the investigation is now a showcase. With four suspects in custody within days of the crime, the police are signalling speed; the court proceedings to come will determine whether the inner-circle theory holds.

What We Could Not Confirm

As of 24 September we could not confirm a motive beyond the confirmed theft, nor the specific role of each of the four detainees; the authorities have not said whether they believe one of them wielded the weapon. The full medico-legal report has not been published, only initial findings cited in Dominican media. It is also unconfirmed whether investigators suspect a mastermind beyond those already in custody, and the condition of Julián Oro Duro is known only as “receiving medical care”. We will update this article as the police and courts release more.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened to Julián Oro Duro and his wife?

In the early hours of 21 September 2026, intruders entered the couple’s home in Brisa Oriental VI, Santo Domingo Este. Zeneida Socorro Castillo was murdered inside the house; the singer was beaten and robbed of cash, jewellery and a phone when he returned home, but survived and is being treated in hospital.

Who has been detained in the Zeneida Castillo murder case?

Four men are in custody: Phillips Michael Tejeda Vásquez, Juan Carlos Hernández García (‘Peña’), Kevin Dariel Germán Troncoso (‘Yandel’) and Lawrence Mark Liranzo Marcos (‘Chiquito’, 18). According to the Policía Nacional, they had ties to the singer’s circle; Tejeda Vásquez had worked on his properties and accompanied him to performances.

Is merengue singer Julián Oro Duro alive?

Yes. Julián Oro Duro, 58, survived the attack on 21 September 2026 and was taken to the Hospital General de la Plaza de la Salud in Santo Domingo, where he is receiving medical care. President Luis Abinader has publicly expressed solidarity with him and warned those responsible that “things will go worse for you”.

World.title: Colombia Severs Diplomatic Relations with Iran Over Terrorism Links
World.content:
Politics: Colombia

Key Facts —Rupture. Colombia formally broke diplomatic relations with the Islamic Republic of Iran effective 19 September 2026, the Foreign Ministry announced in a statement reported by Caracol Radio on 24 September. —Reasons. The ministry cited human rights violations, alleged Iranian links to international terrorist and narcoterrorist groups, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and obstruction of UN nuclear inspectors. —Limits. The measure does not end consular relations with Tehran; consular services continue. —Regional pattern. Colombia is the second South American country to cut ties with Iran within weeks: Peru did so on 1 September 2026, also citing the Strait of Hormuz. —Context. The decision fits President Abelardo De la Espriella’s foreign-policy reset since his 7 August inauguration: restored ties with Israel, a pledged embassy move to Jerusalem and a clear alignment with Washington.

Colombia has formally severed diplomatic relations with Iran, accusing Tehran of links to terrorist and narcoterrorist groups, blocking the Strait of Hormuz and obstructing UN nuclear inspectors — the second such rupture in South America this month.

The Capitolio Nacional in Bogotá, seat of Colombia’s Congress. (Photo: The Rio Times)

What the Foreign Ministry Announced

Colombia’s Foreign Ministry (Cancillería) announced that the government formally broke diplomatic relations with the Islamic Republic of Iran as of 19 September 2026, Caracol Radio reported on 24 September, citing the ministry’s official statement.

“The events described deteriorated Colombia’s trust in the Government of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” the statement said. The ministry framed the move as an act of national sovereignty that, in its words, “will protect the borders, reject any form of external interference and promote the defence of citizens and Colombia’s interests before the international community”.

The timing is notable: the announcement became public on the same day that Vice-President José Manuel Restrepo addressed the UN General Assembly in New York on behalf of President Abelardo De la Espriella, who has pledged not to travel abroad during his term. Caracol noted that Iran is in conflict with the United States and Israel, the two allies at the centre of the new Colombian government’s foreign policy.

The Reasons Cited by Bogotá

The Cancillería listed four grounds for the rupture. First, human rights violations attributed to the Iranian government. Second, alleged links between Tehran and international terrorist groups as well as what the statement called narcoterrorist groups — a charge of particular weight in Colombia, where drug-trafficking organisations dominate the security agenda.

Third, the statement cited the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf chokepoint through which a substantial share of the world’s oil passes and which has been at the centre of Iran’s confrontation with the United States this year. Fourth, Bogotá accused the Iranian authorities of obstructing the work of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the UN body tasked with verifying the scope of Iran’s nuclear programme.

The statement did not name specific groups or incidents behind the narcoterrorism allegation, nor did it detail any concrete case involving Colombian territory.

What Changes — and What Does Not

The rupture applies to diplomatic relations: embassies and formal state-to-state political ties. The Foreign Ministry made one limit explicit — the measure does not mean a break in consular relations with Tehran, so consular services continue. Bilateral trade between Colombia and Iran is minimal, making the decision above all a political and symbolic signal.

Symbolically, however, the step is significant. It aligns Colombia openly with the United States and Israel in their confrontation with Tehran and continues the rapid unravelling of the diplomatic network built under former president Gustavo Petro, who had opened channels of cooperation with Iran on energy and technology.

A Regional Pattern: Peru Went First

Colombia is not alone. On 1 September 2026, Peru announced it was breaking diplomatic relations with Iran, citing restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz and what its government described as democratic backsliding in the Islamic Republic, El Comercio and Infobae reported at the time.

Two South American governments cutting ties with Tehran within a single month marks a striking shift in a region where Iran had spent years cultivating alliances — most visibly with Venezuela, and under Petro with Colombia itself. The coordinated flavour of the justifications, both centred on Hormuz, suggests alignment with Washington’s framing of the Iran conflict.

Part of De la Espriella’s Foreign-Policy Reset

Since taking office on 7 August 2026, President Abelardo De la Espriella has moved at unusual speed to reverse Petro-era diplomacy. His government restored full relations with Israel, pledged to move the Colombian embassy to Jerusalem, withdrew Colombia’s support for South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice, and recognised both Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara and Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, France 24 and El País reported.

The new administration also announced the closure of 14 embassies and 15 consulates and the rupture of relations with Cuba and Nicaragua, arguing that resources should be redirected to security. The Iran decision extends that logic: Foreign Minister Omar Bula has described the new Cancillería’s doctrine as modernisation, professionalisation and austerity, with a clear pro-Western alignment.

What We Could Not Confirm

As of Thursday evening we could not confirm the specific evidence behind the narcoterrorism allegation — the ministry’s statement names no group or incident. We have seen no official Iranian response to the Colombian decision, and it was not possible to verify whether 19 September marks the date of formal notification to Tehran or an internal decision. The practical consequences for the small Colombian-Iranian commercial relationship also remain undocumented. We will update this article if Tehran responds or the Cancillería publishes the full statement.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Colombia break diplomatic relations with Iran?

Colombia’s Foreign Ministry cited four reasons in its statement: human rights violations in Iran, alleged links between the Iranian government and international terrorist and narcoterrorist groups, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran’s obstruction of International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspections of its nuclear programme. The rupture took effect on 19 September 2026.

Does the rupture end consular services between Colombia and Iran?

No. The Colombian Foreign Ministry stated explicitly that the measure does not break consular relations with Tehran. Consular services therefore continue despite the end of diplomatic ties, and the practical impact is limited because bilateral trade is minimal.

Which other Latin American country recently cut ties with Iran?

Peru. On 1 September 2026 the Peruvian government announced it was breaking diplomatic relations with the Islamic Republic of Iran, citing restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz and democratic backsliding, according to El Comercio and Infobae. Colombia is the second South American country to do so this month.

World.title: Ghana’s Mahama Backs Global Push to End US Cuba Embargo
World.content:
Ghana · GEOPOLITICS

Key Facts — What happened Ghana, in West Africa, joined calls to end the US embargo on Cuba when President Mahama spoke on 1 September.

— The setting He spoke in Belgrade, Serbia, at a meeting marking 65 years since the Non-Aligned Movement’s founding conference there.

— The history The US embargo began in 1960, was widened by President Kennedy in 1962, and was written into law in 1996.

— The repeat Mahama repeated the call at the UN General Assembly in New York on Thursday, 24 September.

— The catch Washington has tightened pressure on Cuba in 2026, and only the US Congress can lift the embargo.

Ghana’s President John Mahama has renewed his country’s call to lift the US Cuba embargo. He casts the decades-old restrictions as a breach of sovereign equality and international law.

Mahama renews Ghana’s call to lift the Cuba embargo

In Belgrade, Serbia, on 1 September 2026, Mahama called for an end to the US economic, commercial and financial embargo on Cuba. He was addressing a meeting marking 65 years of the Non-Aligned Movement, and said unilateral coercive measures weaken the multilateral system.

A familiar call from the Global South

Mahama’s intervention in Belgrade placed Ghana firmly within a bloc of developing nations that has long challenged United States sanctions policy. The Non-Aligned Movement, founded in Belgrade in 1961 by states avoiding both Cold War blocs, remains a platform against great-power pressure.

Ghana’s position is consistent with its long-standing diplomatic ties with Cuba. The two countries have maintained friendly relations for decades, rooted in shared histories of anti-colonial struggle and South-South cooperation.

The embargo restricts US trade, investment and financial dealings with Cuba, and began in 1960 after Havana nationalised US-owned property. President Kennedy widened it in February 1962, and the Helms-Burton Act of 1996 wrote it into US law.

The US Cuba embargo and the great-power contest

The UN General Assembly has voted to call for an end to the embargo almost every year since 1992. Havana, backed by many developing states, calls it a blockade that punishes ordinary citizens rather than governments.

Washington treats the embargo as a central lever on Cuba’s communist government. Since January 2026, the Trump administration has added a de facto fuel blockade and new sanctions, most recently in September.

Mahama’s stance places Ghana in direct opposition to that United States position. It also signals Ghana’s broader alignment with Global South blocs that are increasingly vocal about reshaping the rules of international economic engagement.

Repeating the message at the United Nations

Mahama repeated the call at the UN General Assembly in New York on Thursday, 24 September. “Ghana reiterates its call for the immediate lifting of the decades-long economic, commercial, and financial embargo imposed on Cuba,” he said.

He also said the world must support Cuba’s “new Economic and Social Programme,” the Cuban government’s 2026 economic plan. Measures that inflict “collective economic hardship on ordinary citizens” run counter to human dignity and international law, he added.

Repeating the call just over three weeks later shows Ghana treats the issue as a priority, not a one-off gesture. The approach mirrors how African and Caribbean states use multilateral forums to press Washington on Cuba.

What Ghana gains and what it risks

Backing Cuba costs Ghana little diplomatically within Africa, where many governments share similar views on United States sanctions. It also reinforces Ghana’s credentials among Non-Aligned and developing nations that value solidarity against external pressure.

The risk is more subtle. Ghana maintains significant economic and security ties with Western partners, and openly opposing a core United States policy can complicate those relationships.

Mahama appears to be calculating that the benefits of Global South leadership outweigh any friction with Washington. The approach fits a broader pattern of African leaders seeking greater autonomy in a multipolar world.

The regional read-through for West Africa

Ghana’s stance reflects a wider mood in West Africa, where several governments are reassessing ties with traditional Western partners. Many African states see the Cuba embargo as a Cold War relic, and the issue carries symbolic weight.

For investors watching the region, the signal is clear: African governments increasingly take public positions that diverge from Washington. This does not mean a wholesale break with the West, but it does mean a more assertive foreign policy posture.

The Belgrade meeting, attended by more than 30 delegations, shows the Non-Aligned Movement still offers a stage for such statements. As great-power competition intensifies, smaller states are seeking collective weight in forums where their votes count equally.

What to watch next

The next test is the General Assembly’s annual embargo vote, usually held in late October or early November. In October 2025, 165 countries backed the resolution, seven opposed it and 12 abstained.

That was down from 187 in 2024, after US lobbying persuaded Argentina, Paraguay, Hungary and others to vote no. Washington shows no sign of easing, and only the US Congress can lift the embargo.

For now, Mahama has placed Ghana at the centre of a debate on sovereignty, economic justice and the multilateral system. The story fits a broader pattern covered in Africa: The New Scramble, as African nations assert themselves in a changing global order.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Mahama say about the US Cuba embargo? In Belgrade on 1 September, he called for an end to the embargo and said unilateral coercive measures weaken the multilateral system. At the UN on 24 September, he urged “the immediate lifting” of the embargo. When did the United States embargo on Cuba begin? The embargo began in 1960 after Cuba nationalised US-owned property following its 1959 revolution. President Kennedy widened it in February 1962, and a 1996 law means only Congress can lift it. Where did Mahama make his call to lift the embargo? He made it in Belgrade, Serbia, on 1 September 2026, at a meeting marking 65 years of the Non-Aligned Movement. He repeated it at the UN General Assembly in New York on 24 September. Why is Ghana taking a position on Cuba at all? Ghana co-founded the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961 and has kept friendly ties with Cuba for decades, rooted in anti-colonial struggle. Mahama frames the embargo as a question of sovereign equality and international law, not a bilateral dispute.

World.title: Kenya’s President Ruto Tells UN That Africa Wants Investment, Not Aid
World.content:
Kenya · GEOPOLITICS

Key Facts — What happened President Ruto of Kenya, East Africa’s commercial hub, told the UN on 23 September that Africa wants investment, not aid.

— The numbers Ruto cited more than US$4 trillion held by African pension funds, insurers, sovereign wealth funds and banks.

— The refinery He showcased a planned Lamu refinery, costing about US$16 billion, able to process 700,000 barrels a day.

— The fund Kenya’s presidency says its National Infrastructure Fund aims to raise up to US$40 billion without new public debt.

— What is still open Groundbreaking is planned for 30 September; the fund’s US$40 billion is a target, not money raised.

Kenya’s President William Ruto used the UN General Assembly to make the case for Africa investment not aid. “Africa does not come to plead,” he told world leaders in New York.

Ruto’s UN pitch: Africa wants investment, not aid

Ruto addressed the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, 23 September 2026. He pitched Africa as a destination for investment, not an aid case, with minerals, markets, energy and food to offer.

A direct message in New York

A central thread of Ruto’s speech was a reframing. He argued that Africa should no longer be treated as a recipient of aid but as a partner.

He urged Africa to process more of its minerals, crops and fuel at home instead of exporting raw materials. Africa’s resources, he said, “must become the beginning of African industry.”

The Kenyan leader framed this as a matter of economic logic, not charity. On borrowing costs, he said: “Capital must price risk; it must not price prejudice.”

The money already inside Africa

Ruto put a concrete figure on the opportunity. He cited more than US$4 trillion held by African pension funds, insurers, sovereign wealth funds, banks and other institutions.

That number is central to what his office calls an Africa-financing-Africa approach. At a New York finance roundtable on 21 September, he said the problem is the rules deciding where that capital may go.

In the speech he urged development banks to expand guarantees, risk-sharing and long-term lending in local currencies. He also noted that 46 developing countries now spend more on interest than on health or education.

Two flagship projects on the table

Ruto used his week in New York to showcase two large-scale plans. The first is a refinery at Lamu, on Kenya’s coast, backed by Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote.

Ruto put its cost at about US$16 billion and its capacity at 700,000 barrels of oil a day. Other published estimates range from US$15 billion to US$17 billion, and groundbreaking is set for 30 September.

The second is the National Infrastructure Fund, a state vehicle that Ruto signed into law in March 2026. Kenya’s presidency says it is designed to raise up to US$40 billion from investors without adding public debt.

Both projects fit the same theme: using African savings and partnerships to build assets that generate returns, rather than waiting for grants.

Beyond economics: UN reform and leverage

Ruto tied the investment pitch to a broader geopolitical argument. He repeated Africa’s demand for a permanent place on the UN Security Council, where five powers hold vetoes.

“The equality proclaimed in this Assembly ends at the doors of the Security Council,” he said. At a multilateralism summit Kenya co-hosted on 21 September, he said Africa faces neither east nor west, but forward.

This is where the story connects to the wider contest for African resources and influence covered in Africa: The New Scramble. Minerals, energy and infrastructure are now bargaining chips in a multipolar world.

What Kenya wants from the trip

Kenyan officials said the visit aimed to attract partnerships in energy, infrastructure, manufacturing, health, agriculture and technology. The delegation was not simply delivering a speech; it was shopping for deals.

The pitch is that Kenya can serve as a hub for investors who want access to the East African market. The Lamu refinery and the infrastructure fund are the visible anchors of that offer.

Ruto’s message is that Africa is not asking for sympathy. It is asking for capital on fair terms, and it wants to put more of its own savings to work.

What to watch next

The test of Ruto’s Africa investment not aid pitch is whether the rhetoric turns into signed agreements. The first marker is the Lamu groundbreaking set for 30 September.

The broader question is whether global lenders and rating agencies adjust how they price African risk. Ruto has made that rule change a central demand, not a side note.

For now, the speech has set a clear tone. Africa wants a seat at the table, a share of the value chain, and fair treatment for its capital.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did William Ruto say at the UN General Assembly in 2026? Ruto told the 81st UN General Assembly on 23 September 2026 that Africa wants investment, not aid. “Africa does not come to plead,” he said, presenting the continent as a partner for shared prosperity. How much money does Ruto say Africa already has in savings? He cited more than US$4 trillion held by African pension funds, insurers, sovereign wealth funds, banks and other institutions. He wants more of it channelled into infrastructure, manufacturing and energy. What projects did Ruto promote in New York? He promoted an East African refinery at Lamu, which he put at about US$16 billion. He also backed Kenya’s National Infrastructure Fund, which his office says aims to raise up to US$40 billion without new public debt. What is the East African refinery Ruto proposed? It is a planned refinery at Lamu, on Kenya’s coast, designed to process about 700,000 barrels of oil a day. Ruto put the cost at about US$16 billion, and the groundbreaking is set for 30 September.

World.title: Nigeria Cuts Late Tax Interest to Central Bank Rate Plus 1 Point
World.content:
Nigeria · FINANCE

Key Facts — The context Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, overhauled its tax laws in 2025 to raise more revenue outside oil.

— What happened From 1 October 2026, late naira tax payments carry interest at the central bank’s policy rate plus 1 percentage point.

— The benchmark The Central Bank of Nigeria cut that rate to 23 percent from 26.5 percent on 22 September 2026.

— The catch The old 5-point spread is gone, but the 10 percent late-payment penalty stays and a Treasury bill floor applies.

— The numbers Foreign-currency arrears are charged at SOFR, the main US dollar overnight benchmark, plus 6 percentage points.

— What comes next The Nigeria Revenue Service must publish each month’s rate by the third business day, with interest accruing daily.

Nigeria is cutting its late tax interest spread from 1 October 2026 and adding a floor tied to government borrowing costs. What defaulters pay will still track the central bank’s benchmark rate.

Tax defaulters to pay market-linked interest under a new federal government order

From 1 October 2026, late tax payments in Nigeria will carry interest at the central bank’s policy rate plus 1 percentage point. The change cuts the old spread of 5 percentage points and leaves the 10 percent late-payment penalty in place.

What the new late tax interest order changes

Taiwo Oyedele, Nigeria’s Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy since April 2026, issued the order. It rests on Section 65 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025, which took effect on 1 January 2026.

It binds the Nigeria Revenue Service, the federal tax agency that replaced the Federal Inland Revenue Service in January. State tax authorities and the tax authority of Abuja’s Federal Capital Territory must apply the same standard.

For naira debts, the rate cannot fall below the yield on 364-day Treasury bills, the government’s one-year borrowing cost. Foreign-currency arrears are charged at the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR), a US dollar benchmark, plus 6 percentage points.

The Nigeria Revenue Service must publish the applicable rate on its website by the third business day of each month. Interest accrues daily as simple interest, from the due date until payment, with no compounding.

Why the timing matters for taxpayers

The Central Bank of Nigeria cut its Monetary Policy Rate to 23 percent from 26.5 percent on 22 September 2026. The new regime starts just over a week later, so the cut lowers the naira benchmark from day one.

Under the old formula, a defaulter paid the benchmark rate plus 5 percentage points. Under the new rule, the spread falls to 1 percentage point, a saving even before the rate cut.

The Treasury bill floor means the effective rate cannot fall below what the state pays on one-year debt. With one-year bill yields well below the 24 percent the formula now gives, the floor does not bite for now.

The revenue push behind the rule

Nigeria has been tightening tax administration to raise non-oil revenue. President Bola Tinubu signed four tax reform laws in June 2025, and the new regime took effect on 1 January 2026.

By linking interest on arrears to market rates, the government treats unpaid tax more like credit. A business that delays paying tax is in effect borrowing from the state, and the formula prices that more transparently.

The 10 percent late-payment penalty remains on top of the interest charge. A defaulter therefore still faces a fixed penalty plus a market-linked interest cost, which makes prompt payment the cheaper option.

Who gains and who loses

Taxpayers with naira arrears gain from the lower spread, especially after the central bank’s cut to 23 percent. The drop from a 5-point to a 1-point spread is a direct saving, unless the Treasury bill floor binds.

Holders of foreign-currency tax arrears face a different calculation. SOFR plus 6 points may cost more or less than before, depending on dollar rates, but the applicable rate is now explicit.

State and Federal Capital Territory tax authorities gain a uniform standard, which should reduce disputes over interest. The Nigeria Revenue Service’s monthly publication duty also makes the system easier to audit.

The regional and global read-through

Across West Africa, governments are trying to broaden tax bases and rely less on commodity exports. Linking late-payment interest to market rates makes Nigeria’s enforcement more predictable for investors and lenders.

The approach has precedents elsewhere. Britain’s tax authority, for example, charges late-payment interest at the Bank of England base rate plus 4 percentage points.

As Africa’s most populous country tightens its fiscal machinery, the shift is part of a wider contest for revenue and credibility. The pattern is visible across the continent, as covered in Africa: The New Scramble.

What to watch next

The first test comes in early October 2026, when the Nigeria Revenue Service publishes its first monthly rate. That figure will set the baseline for late payments across federal, state and Federal Capital Territory authorities.

Watch whether the central bank keeps cutting, which would further lower the cost of naira arrears. Also watch one-year bill yields, since the floor would bite only if they rose above the policy rate plus 1 point.

Interest that accrued before 1 October stays under the old rules, while interest from that date follows the new formula. The order also replaces a 2017 notice on interest on unpaid taxes.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the new late tax interest rate in Nigeria from October 2026? Late naira tax payments from 1 October 2026 carry interest at the central bank’s Monetary Policy Rate plus 1 percentage point. The rate cannot fall below the 364-day Treasury bill yield. Does the 10 percent late-payment penalty still apply under the new rule? Yes. The existing 10 percent late-payment penalty remains unchanged and applies on top of the new market-linked interest charge. How are foreign-currency tax arrears treated under the new order? Foreign-currency arrears are charged at the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR), a US dollar benchmark, plus 6 percentage points. Interest is calculated daily as simple interest. How will taxpayers know which interest rate applies each month? The Nigeria Revenue Service must publish the applicable rate on its website by the third business day of each month. Interest then accrues daily without compounding, so the amount owed follows from the published rate and days outstanding.

World.title: Brent Crude Tops US$106 as Iran Warns War Could Spread to Indian Ocean
World.content:
Pan-African · MARKETS

Key Facts — The context The U.S. and Israel went to war with Iran in February 2026, disrupting oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

— What happened Front-month November Brent futures settled at US$106.60 on Thursday, Sept. 24, up 3.4% on the day.

— The warning Yahya Rahim Safavi, an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, said new attacks could spread the war to the Indian Ocean.

— The price driver Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis fired missiles at Saudi Arabia, lifting Brent above US$108 at the session high.

— Why it matters Brent is the benchmark for more than three-quarters of internationally traded crude, so shipping risk quickly reaches African fuel bills.

— What is still open It is unclear whether reported U.S.-Iran talks on a phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz will produce a deal.

Brent crude tops US$106 as Iran warns the war could spread to the Indian Ocean. The threat widens the risk for shipping routes that link Gulf oil, East Africa and Asia.

Brent crude tops US$106 as Iran warns war could spread to Indian Ocean

Brent crude rose above US$106 a barrel on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. An adviser to Iran’s supreme leader warned the war could reach the Indian Ocean, and Yemen’s Houthis fired missiles at Saudi Arabia.

Iran’s warning and the oil market

The warning came from Yahya Rahim Safavi, a military adviser to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. The former Revolutionary Guards commander spoke in a video released by Iran’s Fars news agency.

Safavi said the conflict had already spread from the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea. In response to further attacks, he said, the front could expand to “the Indian Ocean and perhaps beyond.”

Front-month November Brent futures settled at US$106.60 a barrel, up US$3.52 or 3.4%, Reuters reported. West Texas Intermediate (WTI), the U.S. benchmark, settled at US$94.61, up 2.7%.

Both benchmarks had been up about 5% at their session highs after the Houthi missile attack on Saudi Arabia. They eased after reports that U.S. and Iranian negotiators were exploring a phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent had settled even higher, at US$108.75, on Sept. 15, after drone attacks shut Saudi Arabia’s main pipeline to the Red Sea. Its wartime peak came on April 30, when it briefly touched US$126.41, the highest in four years.

Why the Indian Ocean matters for Africa

The Indian Ocean is not an abstract geography for African economies. Its shipping lanes connect Gulf crude to East African ports, South Asia and the wider Asia-bound trade corridor.

The Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea are already flashpoints in this war. Adding the Indian Ocean would widen the risk zone for fuel importers from Kenya to Mozambique.

Each time Brent crude tops US$100, import bills rise quickly for African refiners and fuel distributors. Exporters such as Nigeria and Angola earn more, though higher crude prices also lift the cost of any refined fuel they import.

No breakthrough yet at the United Nations

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian blamed the United States and Israel for global instability in his UN General Assembly speech on Wednesday. U.S.-Iran talks on the sidelines in New York showed little sign of progress by Thursday.

Later on Thursday, reports that negotiators were exploring a phased reopening of Hormuz trimmed oil’s gains. The reports described talks, not an agreement.

Without a diplomatic off-ramp, the oil market stays exposed to headline risk. Statements from Tehran, Washington or Tel Aviv can move prices by several dollars in a single session.

For investors and professionals watching African markets, the signal is clear. Energy costs are now tied to a conflict whose geography could expand, and the usual assumptions about shipping security no longer hold.

The great-power contest and energy flows

The current escalation fits a broader pattern of competition over maritime chokepoints and energy flows. Control of Hormuz, the Red Sea and possibly the Indian Ocean is central to how great powers project influence.

This is the same logic that drives the new scramble for African resources and routes. The Rio Times has tracked this shift in its pillar on Africa: The New Scramble, where energy security and critical minerals intersect.

For African governments, the lesson is uncomfortable. When distant powers fight over shipping lanes, African economies absorb the cost through fuel prices, freight rates and inflation.

Who gains and who loses

Oil-exporting African states may see a short-term revenue boost from higher Brent prices. Nigeria, Angola, Libya and Algeria price their crude against Dated Brent, the physical benchmark, so a sustained rise lifts export earnings.

Oil-importing African economies face the opposite pressure. Higher crude prices widen current-account deficits, weaken currencies and push up the cost of transport, electricity and food distribution.

The net effect across the continent is uneven. Some treasuries gain, many households lose, and the divergence between exporters and importers widens with every dollar added to the benchmark.

What to watch next

The immediate question is whether the United States or Israel strikes Iran again, which Safavi said could widen the war. His warning was conditional, but the market has already begun to price the risk.

The reported talks on a phased Hormuz reopening are the main diplomatic test. A deal could pull Brent back below US$100, where it closed on Sept. 22, while new strikes could push it higher.

For African importers, hedging fuel exposure where possible is the obvious defence. For exporters, the windfall is real but fragile, because a wider war would disrupt the lanes that carry their crude.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Brent crude rise above US$106 on Sept. 24, 2026? Brent rose mainly after Yemen’s Houthis fired missiles at Saudi Arabia, reviving supply fears. The same day, an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader warned new attacks could spread the war to the Indian Ocean. How does the Indian Ocean warning affect African economies? The Indian Ocean carries shipping lanes linking Gulf crude to East Africa and Asia. A wider war would raise fuel import costs for African importers while lifting revenue for exporters such as Nigeria and Angola. What was the previous high for Brent during this conflict? Brent briefly touched US$126.41 on April 30, 2026, its highest in four years. It moved back above US$100 in September and settled at US$108.75 on Sept. 15 after a Saudi pipeline shutdown. Why does a Brent price move matter for African importers? Brent is the benchmark for more than three-quarters of internationally traded crude. Shipping risk in the Gulf, the Red Sea or the Indian Ocean therefore reaches African pump and freight prices quickly.

World.title: Scramble On for Kenya’s Mrima Hill Rare Earths and Niobium
World.content:
Kenya · MINING

Key Facts — What happened Kenya, on Africa’s east coast, opened a tender in March 2026 for Mrima Hill, a rare earth and niobium deposit.

— The numbers The widely cited US$62.4 billion is a 2013 in-ground estimate by former licence holder Cortec, not a deal price.

— The catch Kenya’s 2022 mapping found thorium, a radioactive element, at the site, and no feasibility study has been published.

— Who is involved Kenya’s mining ministry says six bidders are shortlisted, two of them American; Critical Metals Corp says it is a finalist.

— What comes next Kenya has announced no award date, and Washington has pledged processing help without naming financing or a dollar amount.

Mrima Hill rare earths and niobium in Kenya’s Kwale County have drawn six shortlisted bidders. Washington has pledged to help Kenya process its minerals at home, as it competes with China for supply.

Nairobi, Kenya’s capital. The Mrima Hill deposit lies on the southern coast, near Mombasa.

Kenya’s Mrima Hill deposit lies about 65 kilometres southwest of Mombasa, the country’s main Indian Ocean port. Six bidders are shortlisted to develop it, including two from the United States, a senior mining official said on 9 September.

What sits under Mrima Hill

Kenya’s 2022 geological mapping identified five elements at the site: niobium, the rare earths yttrium and lanthanum, strontium and thorium. Niobium strengthens steel and aerospace alloys, and rare earths are used in electronics, magnets and defence equipment.

The best-known figure, US$62.4 billion, is Cortec Mining Kenya’s 2013 estimate of the rare earths’ in-ground value. Kenya revoked the licence of Cortec, a unit of Pacific Wildcat Resources, that same year.

An in-ground value multiplies estimated tonnes by prices and ignores mining and processing costs, so it is not a deal price. Kenyan reports on the 2026 tender cite other figures, such as US$64 billion, but none rests on a published feasibility study.

Thorium is a radioactive element. Its presence raises processing and permitting sensitivity for any future operator.

The tender timeline and the field

Hassan Joho, Kenya’s mining minister (cabinet secretary), opened the tender with a gazette notice on 27 March 2026. The notice invited expressions of interest and asked bidders to commit to processing the minerals inside Kenya.

Critical Metals Corp, listed on New York’s Nasdaq exchange, said in July 2026 that its consortium was one of three finalists. Australia’s RareX also said in July that it had been shortlisted.

In September, Principal Secretary Harry Kimtai, the mining ministry’s top civil servant, put the shortlist at six. The two counts have not been publicly reconciled.

Kenya has not published a feasibility study or any signed investment terms. That leaves the true commercial value of Mrima Hill unproven.

Washington enters the race

On 9 September, Frank Garcia, the State Department’s top official for Africa, said Washington would help Kenya build a minerals processing industry. Speaking to the American Chamber of Commerce in Nairobi, he rejected a model based only on exporting raw ore.

Garcia named no company, financing instrument, timetable or dollar commitment. That leaves the size and shape of American support open.

On 21 September, President William Ruto met Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the UN General Assembly in New York. The State Department said they discussed critical minerals and openings for US firms to add value in Kenya.

Why local processing matters

Kenyan officials have been clear that raw mineral exports are not the goal. They want processing capacity built inside Kenya, which would capture more value and create industrial jobs.

That position aligns with a wider African push to move beyond extraction. It also complicates the tender, because processing rare earths and niobium is technically demanding and capital-intensive.

Thorium adds another layer. Any processing route must handle radioactive material safely, which raises costs and regulatory hurdles.

The great-power angle

Mrima Hill sits inside the wider contest for critical minerals that now shapes diplomacy across Africa. Washington’s backing for Kenya’s processing plans fits its push to build supply chains outside China.

China dominates global rare earth processing, and the United States has been trying to build alternative supply chains. Kenya’s coastal deposit offers one potential piece of that puzzle.

The tender is therefore about more than geology. It tests whether Kenya can turn a contested, long-dormant deposit into a working industrial asset.

For readers tracking the new scramble for African minerals, this story fits the pattern covered in Africa: The New Scramble.

What to watch next

Kenya has not announced a final award date for the Mrima Hill tender. The next milestone would be the naming of a preferred bidder.

Opposition leader Rigathi Gachagua, a former deputy president, alleged that Ruto’s New York trip aimed to seal a deal with US firms. Mining minister Hassan Joho said in early September that no mining licence had been issued for the site.

The Centre for Litigation Trust, a lobby group, wants the Kwale High Court to halt a preliminary Kenya-US deal on the site. The court has deferred that request until it rules on the Attorney-General’s objection to its jurisdiction.

Investors should watch for any published feasibility study, because that would replace the old 2013 estimate with a defensible project value. Until then, the US$62.4 billion number should be treated as historical context, not a deal figure.

The thorium question will also matter. Any credible winning bid must explain how it will handle radioactive material safely and win local permits.

Frequently Asked Questions

What minerals are found at Mrima Hill in Kenya? Mrima Hill rare earths include yttrium and lanthanum, according to Kenya’s 2022 geological mapping, which also found niobium, strontium and radioactive thorium. Niobium strengthens steel, while rare earths are used in electronics, magnets and defence equipment. How many companies are still bidding for Mrima Hill? Mining Principal Secretary Harry Kimtai said on 9 September 2026 that six bidders are shortlisted, including two from the United States. Critical Metals Corp said in July that it was one of three finalists. Is the US$62.4 billion Mrima Hill figure a real deal value? No. It is a 2013 estimate of in-ground value by Cortec Mining Kenya, the former licence holder, not a deal price. Why does thorium matter at Mrima Hill? Kenya’s 2022 geological mapping identified thorium, a radioactive element, at the site. Any winning bidder must show how it will handle radioactive material safely and secure local permits.

World.title: Kenyan Contractors Sue the State Over Tax Breaks for Chinese Firms
World.content:
Kenya · BUSINESS

Key Facts — What happened Kenyan contractors have asked the High Court to force publication of tax breaks granted to Chinese-built projects since 2008.

— The projects The petition cites the Standard Gauge Railway, Nairobi Expressway, Thika Superhighway and Lamu Port, all built by Chinese firms.

— The legal claim Petitioners say tax and duty breaks were granted without published legal notices, breaching constitutional rules on public finance.

— The tax ruling In 2024, a tax tribunal upheld a KSh1.05 billion (about US$8.1 million) tax assessment against China Communications Construction Company.

— The local content rule Since 2014, foreign contractors must subcontract or partner with Kenyan firms for at least 30 percent of contract value.

— The catch The Attorney-General argues the dispute is purely commercial and filed in the wrong court; no ruling has been reported.

Kenyan contractors have taken the state to court over Chinese tax breaks they call unpublished and unconstitutional. They say the breaks let foreign firms underbid them for infrastructure work.

Nairobi, Kenya’s capital, where the petition is before the High Court.

Kenyan contractors and truck owners want the High Court in Nairobi to force publication of tax breaks for Chinese-built projects. The petition covers tax exemptions, customs duty waivers and other concessions granted since 1 January 2008.

What the petition demands

The petitioners include the African Centre for Corrective and Preventive Action (ACCPA), an advocacy group, and an association of small businesses. Two lifting and haulage companies, Swan Movers Lifters Limited and Universal Lifters Limited, are also petitioners.

The case, reported by Kenyan media in August 2026, is before the High Court at the Milimani Law Courts in Nairobi. The petitioners want the government to publish every legal notice, gazette notice or directive that granted such concessions.

They argue that concessions granted without published legal notices breach constitutional rules on access to information, public finance and taxation. They want such arrangements declared unconstitutional, null and void.

They also want the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA), the national tax collector, to audit all vehicles and machinery imported duty-free since 2008. Another order sought would bar agencies from awarding contracts priced on tax advantages that Kenyan firms cannot get.

The petition names four flagship projects: the Mombasa-Nairobi Standard Gauge Railway, the Nairobi Expressway, the Thika Superhighway and Lamu Port. Chinese firms built all four, and Chinese loans or investment financed the railway, the expressway and part of the Thika road.

The money at stake

The petitioners cite reports by the Auditor-General, Kenya’s public audit watchdog, on revenue lost to tax exemptions. Those reports, they say, put the loss at KSh41.2 billion (about US$318 million) in the 2023/24 financial year.

Dollar figures in this article use 129.5 shillings per US dollar, the open.er-api.com rate on 24 September 2026.

A separate tax case shows how the KRA pursues Chinese contractors. On 9 August 2024, the Tax Appeals Tribunal, a specialist tax court, dismissed an appeal by China Communications Construction Company (CCCC).

It upheld a KRA assessment of KSh1,047,557,661 (about US$8.1 million) in value added tax and corporation tax for 2016 to 2022. The tribunal found the company took part in an elaborate scheme to avoid tax, using invoices from shell companies.

That case concerned tax avoidance, not exemptions, so it is separate from the petition. It still matters because CCCC, a Chinese state-owned group, owns China Road and Bridge Corporation, which built the railway and the expressway.

Why local contractors are frustrated

The petitioners say foreign contractors import trucks and heavy machinery duty-free for a project, then keep using them in Kenya afterwards. ACCPA executive director John Maingi Macharia said the machines are neither re-exported nor properly audited.

Local firms buying similar equipment pay import duty, an import declaration fee and a railway development levy. The petitioners say this makes a truck at least 51 percent more expensive for a local operator.

They put the overall cost gap at 25 to 35 percent, enough for foreign rivals to underbid Kenyan firms. Some members now face insolvency after losing contracts and defaulting on equipment loans, they say.

Macharia said Japanese contractors received exemptions through a published 2021 gazette notice, unlike Chinese contractors on the four named projects.

Kenya has tried to protect local firms before. Since 2014, National Construction Authority rules have required foreign contractors to share at least 30 percent of contract value with Kenyan firms.

The petitioners say many affected firms held back from suing for fear of being blacklisted from government tenders.

The wider tax waiver debate

The petition lands amid long-running scrutiny of tax waivers for foreign companies in Kenya. In 2023, parliament’s finance committee questioned a KSh1.92 billion (about US$14.8 million) tax waiver linked to Chinese technology firm Huawei.

The Treasury granted that waiver in July 2022, covering withholding tax on payments to Huawei for laying fibre-optic cable. The new petition carries that scrutiny into infrastructure, where the projects involved are far larger.

The petition also covers “any related project” beyond the four it names. A ruling for the petitioners could therefore reach well beyond the railway, the expressway, the Thika road and Lamu.

China’s infrastructure footprint under pressure

Chinese state-owned contractors have built many of Kenya’s flagship infrastructure projects, from the Standard Gauge Railway to the Nairobi Expressway. That work is part of a wider Chinese push that has reshaped how African roads, ports and railways are financed and built.

The Kenya case fits into a pattern of rising scrutiny of Chinese lending and contracting across the continent. Governments that once welcomed Chinese capital are now asking harder questions about the terms attached to it.

For investors watching East Africa, the petition tests whether unpublished Chinese tax breaks can survive in court. The outcome could change how future infrastructure deals are structured in Kenya and beyond.

The wider contest over infrastructure finance in Africa is a central theme of Africa: The New Scramble.

What to watch next

The Attorney-General, the government’s chief legal adviser, has opposed the petition. The office argues the dispute is “purely commercial” and belongs outside the High Court’s Constitutional and Human Rights Division.

No ruling has been reported, and the case is next due in court on 6 October. If the court sides with the petitioners, the state would have to publish the full record of concessions granted since 2008.

Chinese contractors and the agencies that hire them will be watching, since existing concessions could be quashed. The court’s answer could reset the rules for future infrastructure deals in Kenya.

The core question is simple: should Kenyan taxpayers know what tax benefits the state gives foreign contractors?

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Kenyan contractors’ petition about? The petitioners want the government to publish all tax exemptions and customs duty waivers granted to Chinese-financed projects since 1 January 2008. They argue Chinese tax breaks granted without published legal notices are unconstitutional. Which projects are named in the petition? The petition names the Standard Gauge Railway, the Nairobi Expressway, the Thika Superhighway and Lamu Port. Chinese firms built all four. What was the tax tribunal ruling against CCCC? On 9 August 2024, the Tax Appeals Tribunal dismissed CCCC’s appeal and upheld a KRA assessment of KSh1,047,557,661 (about US$8.1 million). The case concerned tax avoidance, not exemptions. What happens if the court rules for the contractors? The state would have to publish the legal basis for concessions granted to Chinese-financed projects since 2008. Concessions granted without that authority could be declared unconstitutional and quashed.

World.title: Atlantic Reaches Late September Without a Hurricane for the First Time Since 1914
World.content:
The Atlantic Ocean has reached late September without producing a single hurricane, something that has not happened in 112 years. As of this morning, the U.S. National Hurricane Center was tracking Tropical Storm Fay southwest of the Azores and a disturbance south of the Cabo Verde Islands. Neither had reached hurricane strength, and no hurricane has formed in the Atlantic this season.

The last season to go this deep into September without a hurricane was 1914, and that season never produced one at all. In records dating to 1851, only 1907 and 1914 finished without a hurricane. Both predate satellite tracking, so some storms from that era may have gone undetected.

The 2026 season has produced six named storms, Arthur, Bertha, Cristobal, Dolly, Edouard and Fay. None reached hurricane strength, which requires sustained winds of 119 km/h (74 mph). That is far below a typical year as the first Atlantic hurricane usually forms by Aug. 11, and by this point the basin would normally have produced about 10 named storms, four hurricanes and two major hurricanes, based on 1991–2020 averages.

The storms that did form were weak and short-lived. Accumulated cyclone energy, a measure that combines the strength and duration of every storm in a season, stood at 6.2 on Sept. 22, about 93% below normal for the date, according to the hurricane center. The main reason is El Niño. The warming of the equatorial Pacific strengthens upper-level winds over the Atlantic and Caribbean, and that wind shear tears developing storms apart before they can organize and intensify.

Forecasters expected a quiet year. In its August update, the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration gave a 75% chance of a below-normal season, with seven to 13 named storms and two to six hurricanes. The season is not over. It officially runs until Nov. 30, and late September and October have historically produced dangerous storms, especially in the Gulf and along the U.S. East Coast.

Here in Costa Rica, the same El Niño is having a very different effect. The National Meteorological Institute has declared a meteorological drought across the Pacific slope and Central Valley, where rainfall is running up to 37% below normal and community water systems in 74 communities are rationing water.

Costa Rica rarely takes a direct hit from Atlantic hurricanes. Storms passing through the Caribbean have more often affected the country indirectly by pulling heavy rain across it, as Tropical Storm Nate did in 2017. The eastern Pacific has been far more active. Hurricane Polo regained Category 5 strength off Mexico’s Pacific coast with sustained winds of 260 km/h (162 mph), and the hurricane center was also issuing advisories today on Hurricane Odaly but neither storm is expected to affect Costa Rica.

If the Atlantic stays quiet through the end of November, 2026 would become only the third season on record without a hurricane.

World.title: Water Rationing Hits 74 Communities as El Niño Dries Out Costa Rica’s Pacific Side
World.content:
If you live on Costa Rica’s northern Pacific side, your tap may already be running on a schedule. Community water systems in 74 communities are rationing water because their springs and wells are losing flow, and some have dried up completely. The cuts are concentrated in five areas.

These are the Nicoya Peninsula and the coastal plains just north of it, the dry lowlands of central Guanacaste, the hills around Lake Arenal, the Gulf of Nicoya coast around Puntarenas, and the foothills where the western Central Valley drops toward the Pacific. Thirty-two community water boards have reported rationing, affecting about 6,525 connections, according to the national confederation that represents the country’s community water systems.

Emel Rodríguez Paniagua, the confederation’s vice president, separately put the number of systems rationing in Guanacaste at 23, with some communities now relying on tanker trucks and donated water. The cause is El Niño and rainfall on the Pacific slope and in the Central Valley is running as much as 37% below normal, and the National Meteorological Institute has declared a meteorological drought across the entire Pacific slope, the Central Valley and the western part of the northern zone.

This is not the usual dry-season squeeze. September is normally one of the wettest months in Guanacaste, when rivers rise, wells refill and pastures turn green ahead of the dry months. This year, streams are dry and some wells are running low in the middle of the rainy season. Ranchers are already feeling it. The Guanacaste ranchers’ federation reports cattle deaths from lack of feed in several parts of the province, and its executive director, José Chaves Ballestero, said midyear hay production has fallen between 50% and 70%.

The bigger worry is what comes next. The current El Niño is exceptionally strong, with August ocean temperatures in the equatorial Pacific exceeding those recorded in August 1997 and 2015, and the institute says the conditions could last at least until January 2027. That means much of the Pacific side may head into the dry season with its water sources already depleted.

If your water is being rationed, you will probably store some at home. Do it carefully, because stored water can make you sick. Use only clean containers with lids that are made for drinking water. Buckets, drums or tanks that once held other liquids, or that sit open, let bacteria and other contaminants into the water, according to the Costa Rican Association of Chemists. Keep your storage covered and clean.

Be sure of where your water comes from. Water from a source that hasn’t been checked, such as an untested well or a neighbor’s hose, can carry germs even when it looks clear. Watch for changes. If your water changes color, smell or taste, stop drinking it and report it to your local water board.

Find out your rationing schedule. Community water systems set their own hours, so ask your local board when service will be cut and plan your storage around it. Use less wherever you can. Heat drives consumption up, as people shower more often and run fans and air conditioning longer, and that also shows up on your electricity bill.

The larger utilities are watching closely as the national water utility, AyA, says some of its sources are already below normal for this time of year. In Heredia, the public utility company ESPH has issued a green alert but says the effects remain manageable for now, because it can switch to wells when surface sources drop.

The opposite problem is hitting the Caribbean. Rainfall there and across much of the northern zone is running up to 42% above normal, and in Sarapiquí, Guápiles and parts of Limón, saturated soils have flooded pastures and damaged some bridges and rural roads.

The two sides of the country face very different recoveries. Water systems damaged by flooding usually bounce back once rivers drop and repairs are made, Rodríguez said. A community that depends on a spring or well that is losing flow has no such fix, which is why the coming dry season is the main concern for the Pacific side.

World.title: Shyne backs Darrell Bradley for UDP leader and says Panton cannot unify party
World.content:
Shyne backs Darrell Bradley for UDP leader and says Panton cannot unify party

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Former United Democratic Party leader Moses “Shyne” Barrow has thrown his support behind former Belize City Mayor Darrell Bradley as a potential future leader of the UDP, while launching a sharp attack on the leadership of Tracy Taegar Panton.

In a strongly worded Facebook post on Thursday, Barrow declared: “READ THE ROOM! DARRELL BRADLEY FOR UDP LEADER!”

Barrow claimed Panton has failed to unify the UDP and pointed to resignations and internal dissatisfaction as evidence of continuing problems within the party. Those assertions represent Barrow’s assessment of the current state of the UDP.

The former party leader said he is prepared to support Bradley to become UDP leader and eventually seek the office of Prime Minister.

The intervention comes as Bradley himself has publicly signalled that he is open to leading the UDP if the position becomes vacant. In a recent interview, Bradley said he considers himself an option for the party, while stressing that he is not currently campaigning against Panton and remains in communication with both Panton and Barrow.

Barrow also called for changes to the UDP Constitution that would allow Bradley to seek the leadership.

Bradley previously served two terms as Belize City Mayor and later as President of the Senate.

Barrow’s latest intervention adds another public voice to the ongoing debate over the UDP’s direction and leadership.

World.title: NTUCB rejects Briceño’s response to 11 demands; ‘Actions will increase until will of the people achieved’
World.content:
NTUCB rejects Briceño’s response to 11 demands; ‘Actions will increase until will of the people achieved’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The National Trade Union Congress of Belize (NTUCB) has formally rejected Prime Minister John Briceño’s response to its 11 demands, saying none of the demands were met as submitted and announcing that it is preparing “activities and actions” in the coming days.

“These will increase in effectiveness and resolve until all 11 demands and the will of the people are achieved”, the Union cryptically said.

In a letter dated September 24, NTUCB General Secretary Timothy Dami said the Prime Minister’s September 15 response came 18 days after the union’s deadline and failed to address several matters, including the Vocational-Technical salary scale, two back-pay matters affecting Belize National Teachers’ Union members, and a timeline for filling the vacant Ombudsman post.

The union umbrella body also challenged Briceño’s assertion that unions have representation on the Belize Telemedia Limited (BTL) board through the Social Security Board. NTUCB argued that the seat is not specifically designated for a union or worker representative and maintained that Government could establish tripartite representation at BTL through its own appointments without requiring legislative changes.

Briceño had earlier rejected several of NTUCB’s major proposals, including its demand for the removal of BTL Chairman Markhelm Lizarraga and three other directors, restructuring of the Public Utilities Commission, and halting the Revenue Authority Bill. Government instead pointed to BTL’s record profits, the statutory independence of the PUC and the importance it attaches to the revenue-authority reform. Government also indicated that whistleblower legislation had been shared with social partners, campaign-finance proposals were being developed, and work was underway toward filling the Ombudsman vacancy.

NTUCB’s original August submission called for, among other things, tripartite representation at BTL, changes to the PUC, whistleblower and campaign-finance legislation, enforcement of civil-asset-recovery legislation, filling the Ombudsman vacancy and support for the Public Service Union’s position on the Revenue Authority Bill. It also contained specific salary, back-pay and education-related demands from member unions.

In Thursday’s letter, NTUCB said the Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry and Belize Network of NGOs share its concerns on several of the core governance issues, including BTL representation, the PUC, whistleblower protection, campaign-finance reform, civil-asset recovery, the Ombudsman’s Office and the Revenue Authority Bill. The groups have previously acted collectively as part of Belize’s social partners on governance concerns surrounding BTL.

“None of our 11 demands were met as submitted,” NTUCB stated, adding that it had not even received a date and time for a meeting to work through the outstanding issues. The Congress said its council has met to consider Government’s response and has also met with the Joint Social Partners.

NTUCB said the actions now being prepared will increase “in effectiveness and resolve” until its 11 demands are addressed.

World.title: International News: U.S. issues security alert over armed shutdown in Colombia
World.content:
International News: U.S. issues security alert over armed shutdown in Colombia

By Zoila Palma: The United States has issued a security alert for Santa Marta and surrounding areas in Colombia’s Magdalena and La Guajira departments following a 72-hour transportation blockade, curfew and shutdown of civilian activities imposed by an illegal armed group.

The U.S. Embassy in Colombia said the restrictions were imposed by the Autodefensas Conquistadoras de la Sierra Nevada (ACSN), also known as Los Pachencas, following a Colombian security operation against the organization. Authorities have deployed additional Army and police forces across the region.

The embassy reported numerous incidents, including vehicle burnings, intimidation of businesses, shootings and disruptions to public transportation and civilian movement. The group reportedly imposed the shutdown after Colombian security forces killed 13 of its members, including one of its top commanders, during a military operation earlier this week.

The U.S. Embassy advised American citizens to avoid demonstrations and areas with increased security activity, monitor local media and follow instructions from Colombian authorities.

World.title: Corozal schools receive 100 refurbished computers, ITVET gets VR welding systems
World.content:
Corozal schools receive 100 refurbished computers, ITVET gets VR welding systems

By Zoila Palma: Students at 5 primary schools in the Corozal District are benefiting from 100 refurbished desktop computers donated through a partnership between the Ministry of Investment and Transparent BPO.

St. Paul’s Anglican, Church of Christ, Christiline Gill, Assemblies of God, and Corozal Nazarene Primary Schools each received 20 desktop computers. The equipment is transforming classrooms into digital learning spaces and providing students with greater opportunities to develop essential computer skills.

In addition to the computer donation, the Investment Policy and Compliance Unit within the Ministry has equipped Corozal ITVET with four MIG Welding Virtual Reality Training Systems.

The advanced systems will allow students to train in a simulated environment, giving them practical opportunities to sharpen their welding skills using modern technology.

World.title: Father asks court to spare son jail after son allegedly pushes him down and kicks him for warning him about ‘bad area’; son shows up with neck stab wound after violent clash
World.content:
Father asks court to spare son jail after son allegedly pushes him down and kicks him for warning him about ‘bad area’; son shows up with neck stab wound after violent clash

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man walked free from a common assault charge after his father told the court he never wanted his son prosecuted and only sought police intervention to calm him down following a violent family dispute.

Stephen Barrington Flowers Jr., also known as “Fats,” appeared before the Chief Magistrate charged with common assault upon his father, Stephen Barrington Flowers Sr., following an incident on Gabourel Lane near the Belize Red Cross.

Flowers Jr. pleaded not guilty at his arraignment, while his father told the court he did not want any further action taken against his son.

“I nuh wah nothing because I nuh wah he go dah jail,” Flowers Sr. told the court.

The father explained that he had only wanted police to intervene and take his son into custody temporarily so he could calm down, but said he never intended to press charges against him.

The dispute reportedly began after Flowers Sr. warned his son about spending time in a particular area. According to the father, he was across from the Red Cross at around 7:30 a.m. on September 21 when he saw his son and warned him not to go to the Mansion area. He alleged that when he approached Flowers Jr., his son became violent, pushed him to the ground and kicked him about the body.

Both men, however, emerged from the confrontation with visible injuries. Flowers Jr. was seen in court with a large cut to the left side of his neck, while his father had an injury to his right index finger. Both father and son admitted they had been drinking and were under the influence at the time of the altercation.

Flowers Jr. apologized to his father in court and said he should have listened to him, acknowledging that his father had only been looking out for his best interest and safety.

Flowers Jr. also complained that police had refused to sign his medico-legal form after the incident, despite him suffering injuries.

With Flowers Sr. maintaining that he wanted no court action against his son, the Chief Magistrate dismissed the common assault charge and Flowers Jr. was free to leave.

World.title: Prime Minister delivers keynote address at 12th International Forum on African-Caribbean Leadership
World.content:
Prime Minister delivers keynote address at 12th International Forum on African-Caribbean Leadership

By Zoila Palma: Today, during the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister John Briceño delivered the keynote address at the 12th International Forum on African-Caribbean Leadership.

The event was held under the theme “The Global African Alliance: Reimagining Solidarity, Sovereignty & South-South Cooperation.”

The Prime Minister highlighted Belize’s unique position as a Caribbean and Central American nation and called for stronger Africa-Caribbean cooperation in trade and investment, climate resilience and development finance, technology, health, education, and skills development.

During the forum, Prime Minister Briceño was presented with the Distinguished Leadership Award for Economic Resilience and Regional Integration.

World.title: International News: US reopens major Mexican cattle port as Screwworm concerns ease
World.content:
International News: US reopens major Mexican cattle port as Screwworm concerns ease

By Zoila Palma: The United States plans to reopen its largest livestock inspection port along the US-Mexico border today allowing Mexican cattle imports to resume as officials ease restrictions imposed over concerns about New World screwworm.

The US Department of Agriculture said trade will resume at Santa Teresa, New Mexico, following a review of the situation.

While screwworm cases in Mexico have continued to rise, US officials say infestations have remained relatively contained, with two active cases currently reported in the United States.

The reopening is not expected to immediately reduce record-high US beef prices, Reuters report.

Experts say it could take five to eight months for imported Mexican cattle to reach slaughter weight, while US cattle supplies remain tight following years of drought and declining herd sizes.

World.title: Restoring trust: Taiwan’s rightful place in the free world
World.content:
Restoring trust: Taiwan’s rightful place in the free world

The views expressed in this article are those of the author and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

By Dr. Lin Chia-lung – Minister of Foreign Affairs; ROC (Taiwan): The rules-based international order is under growing strain as authoritarian states seek to weaken its safeguards and reshape international rule to serve their own interests. Even the fundamental principles of peaceful settlement of disputes and prohibition against the threat or use of force, which are enshrined in the United Nations Charter, have been openly challenged and flagrantly flaunted.

Today, the international community stands at a critical juncture. Either we act together to uphold justice, defend the rule of law, and maintain peace and security, or we watch the world order steadily crumble away, taking freedom, self-determination, and democracy with it.

There are few places where this choice is more starkly presented than in the first island chain of the Indo-Pacific. The region’s security has come under growing pressure from China, which continues to deploy gray-zone tactics—including military intimidation, cyber intrusions, and economic coercion—in an attempt to unilaterally reshape the existing rules and norms.

Standing on the front line of defense of freedom and democracy, Taiwan will continue to firmly uphold the status quo. However, preserving peace and stability in the region is not just in Taiwan’s interests. It is a shared concern of the international community.

The Taiwan Strait is one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes and a major artery for international supply chains. Its significance to global security and prosperity is reflected in statements from the G7 and other summits and ministerial-level meetings between Japan, the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, and other countries. They make up a growing chorus of voices worldwide that underline the importance of cross-strait peace and stability.

The integrity of the rules-based order is also being undermined by China’s deliberate misrepresentation of UN General Assembly Resolution 2758. Adopted in 1971, the resolution covers the question of China’s representation at the UN. The text does not mention Taiwan, determine its political status, or address its participation in the UN system. Yet China has conspired to conflate UNGA 2758 with the so-called “one China principle” and use the resolution to block Taiwan’s participation in the UN and other international organizations. If left unchecked, this distortion could set a dangerous legal precedent and serve as a pretext for future military action across the Taiwan Strait.

Despite its exclusion from the UN, Taiwan is determined to act as a force for good. The strengths that Taiwan possesses in advanced manufacturing, disaster preparedness, and public health could contribute to the international community in many ways.

Taiwan has pursued an integrated and value-added foreign policy based on strengthening democratic alliances, promoting collective security, and building economic resilience. Working with like-minded partners, Taiwan advances democracy, human rights, and freedom worldwide. As a leader in semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and technology, Taiwan is committed to building supply chains that are secure, resilient, and free from dependence on authoritarian regimes.

Through its Diplomatic Allies Prosperity Project, Taiwan fosters coprosperity with its partners. Taiwan contributes its expertise and resources to technology-driven projects in cooperation with its diplomatic allies to address development challenges and enhance local capacities. Concrete examples include collaboration on an integrated healthcare information system with Paraguay, the construction of a strategic oil reserve facility in Eswatini, and collaboration with Palau National Hospital on smart healthcare. These initiatives have strengthened data management and efficiency, bolstered energy security, fostered industrial growth, and advanced sustainable development.

Khalilur Rahman, President-elect of the upcoming 81st UN General Assembly, has made restoring trust and managing institutional transformation the overarching themes of his presidency. Taiwan shares these objectives and stands ready to help realize them.

Restoring confidence in the UN must begin with treating every member of the international community in a fair and just way. Transformation cannot be complete while a constructive and trustworthy member remains unjustly excluded.

We are calling on the international community to uphold the principles of inclusiveness, leaving no one behind, settling disputes peacefully, and neither threatening nor using force. These imperatives underpin the rules-based international order and should be applied consistently and without exception.

The free world needs Taiwan—and a stronger, more credible United Nations needs Taiwan’s meaningful participation. Working hand in hand with Taiwan will strengthen collective security, enhance economic and technological resilience, and build our shared capacity to withstand authoritarian pressure. Ensuring Taiwan’s meaningful participation in the United Nations is therefore essential to building a more inclusive, secure, resilient, and rules-based international order.

World.title: ‘I did not trip’: Dr Gabrielle Henry speaks on terrifying fall in new interview
World.content:
Miss Universe Jamaica 2025 Dr Gabrielle Henry .

Former Miss Universe Jamaica Dr Gabrielle Henry says moments before her serious and traumatic fall during the Miss Universe 2025 competition, she had simply been following instructions given to her by organisers.

“I stopped when I was told to stop, I looked at the cameras and then when I was instructed to go I turned to the left, which I was instructed to do,” she told Good Morning America (GMA), recalling the November 19, 2025 incident publicly for the first time, almost a year later.

At home, the video of her tumble generated shock and concern for the pageant queen, with Jamaicans offering prayers and well wishes.

The fall upended Henry’s life, shattering her dreams of representing Jamaica, she explained.

Henry’s disappointment was shared by her countrymen and was compounded by a series of prior shocks, including the Reggae Boyz’ failure to qualify for the World Cup and the passage of Hurricane Melissa.
