World.title: Jürgen Klopp starts Germany job with shaky Netherlands draw
World.content:
A late Netherlands goal denied Jürgen Klopp a win in his first match as Germany coach. The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund boss has big ambitions, but the game showed he's going to need more time to achieve them.

It looked, until the final moments, as though Germany would somehow hold on and grant Jürgen Klopp a victory in his first game as Germany coach.

"It felt mostly good," Klopp told German broadcaster RTL after the match, with his voice strained after a typically energetic display on the sidelines. "That was really exhausting for both teams today." He added that he naturally wanted a win but that he can "live with the point, too."

In the end, an injury time Cody Gakpo goal meant Klopp and his team had to settle for a 1-1 draw in their Nations League opener against the Netherlands. While the timing of the equalizer will sting, Germany was second best for much of the contest, which turned a ill-tempered at times. Nevertheless, Klopp was upbeat.

"I was very, very, very satisfied with many of the individual performances," he said, before admitting that "we can play better football and create more chances — that's for sure."

Gakpo plays his club football for Liverpool, where Klopp coached for more than eight years. So too does Dutch captain Virgil van Dijk, who thought he'd opened the scoring for the hosts early on, only to see his headed goal ruled out. A close-range finish from Lukas Nmecha then gave Germany the lead but not control of the game.

New faces, new coach, not yet new Germany

While there were a few patches of attacking play that resembled the kind of high-intensity, exhilarating football that Klopp produced at Liverpool and, before that, at Borussia Dortmund, Germany looked shaky at the back and were thankful for some wasteful Dutch finishing.

It is, though, difficult to judge much at this early stage. Klopp replaced Julian Nagelsmann after another poor World Cup showing from Germany and, after naming two different squads for the four Nations Leagues games in an extended international period, is still assessing how to make the most of what he has. Three players — Younes Ebnoutalib, Yannik Engelhardt and Philipp Treu — made debuts on Thursday, and more are likely follow over the next three games.

"I won't promise anything [in terms of trophies]. What I can promise is that we will definitely give it a try," he told reporters ahead of the game. "There's an impression that we have less quality than other countries. When things aren't working, you take a closer look and try to bring about changes. That's what we're working on now."

After Germany lost Kai Havertz to injury in the first half, having already had to change to starting XI after Jamal Musiala pulled out of the match in the warmup, the team was left without much of their attacking experience and class.

Klopp's record should buy him time

But Klopp won't panic. His methods, both tactically and emotionally, will take time to bear fruit. At Liverpool, it took nearly five years to win a trophy; at Dortmund, it took three.

"When the system isn't yet in place and the processes aren't yet established, then something like this happens," he said about Wednesday's performance. "I was very pleased with the passion, the intensity, but we can definitely play better."

Usually, waiting for success would not be acceptable for German national team fans. But after repeated recent failures, and with Klopp a popular figure, he has more credit in that bank than his predecessor, Julian Nagelsmann. The last coach to win a World Cup for Germany, Joachim Löw, said he will need it.

Jürgen Klopp has combined experienced internationals and newcomers in his first squads Image: Christian Schulze/nordphoto/picture alliance

"It is crucial now to give him the necessary time and space to implement his ideas," he told the Münchner Merkur/tz newspaper. "Jürgen stands for energy, intensity and a strong bond between the team and the fans. But even for him, not everything will work from one day to the next. After a disappointing World Cup, it takes trust, patience and a team that once again plays for Germany with great conviction."

Klopp calls for German unity, seeks Greece win

Klopp has already tried to unite the country behind the team. On the touchline in Amsterdam, he ran through his familiar repertoire of fist bumps, beaming smiles and growls at officials in a cap emblazoned with the words "one of 83 million" on it.

The headgear has already become a familiar sight. It's a reference to Germany's population and the 59-year-old has also referenced the importance of his team, and their flag, as a symbol of nationhood at a time when the far-right AfD (Alternative for Germany) are making substantial electoral gains.

"I'd like to reclaim the flag for myself — or for us," Klopp said. "I want us to always wave it in a way that makes no one think: 'What's wrong with you?' But, rather, that people simply get the feeling that you're happy and understand how lucky you are to have been born, raised or moved to this wonderful country."

While Klopp's charisma makes such a lofty ambition seem somewhat feasible, he's also pragmatic enough to know that for the German national team to be universally loved, it needs to win. Augsburg on Saturday, against Greece in the Nations League, would be a good place to start.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

World.title: UNGA: Gaza dominates agenda as Abbas, Netanyahu speak
World.content:
Skip next section Fiji calls for cheaper financial transfers for remittances, saying 'they are not aid'

Fiji's president pressed for climate finance for small island states and international action on global sea level rise Image: Frank Franklin II/AP Photo/picture alliance

Fijian President Ratu Naiqama Tawakecolati Lalabalavu addressed the chamber on behalf of one of the low-lying island nations at severe risk from climate change on Thursday.

He said that many of the UN's sustainable development goals remained off track with 2030 approaching and said that aid and financial assistance often did a poor job of reaching remote islands exposed to more natural disasters than average. But then he called for a wider financial system that would better enable Fijians to help themselves.

"There is one measure of delivery that reaches Fijian households directly," he said. "Remittances are now Fiji's third-largest source of foreign exchange."

Lalabalavu said these funds paid for school fees, rebuilt homes after cyclones and sustained families between harvests.

"Your excellencies, they are not aid. They are earnings of Fijians abroad, sent home. Yet Pacific corridors remain among the most expensive in the world through which to send money."

He noted how the chamber had in May committed to work to keep such transfer costs below 3% and to eliminate corridors costing more than 5% — he said that Pacific countries like Fiji wanted this to be "treated as an obligation and not an aspiration."

"Labor mobility must also not become a one-way transfer of the people that we have trained," the president said. "Fiji does not begrudge any Fijian the chance to build a life abroad. We ask only that those recruit our nurses, our teachers invest in the systems that recruited them."

Lalabalavu also alluded to Fiji recently declaring a national HIV emergencyand said that organized crime and drug trafficking was exacerbating this problem. He said that as a small impoverished country, Fiji had three requests for the international community:

"That treatment and diagnostics reach small states at prices we can pay. That the Global Fund and UNAIDS be resources at a level that does not force triage between regions, and that our partners treat Pacific narcotics interdiction as the shared security interest it is."

World.title: Three-way battle for power in world chess: Who will be elected FIDE president in Samarkand?
World.content:
The era of Russian presidents is coming to an end at the World Chess Federation (FIDE). Two Germans and one Kazakh are up for election. Among the issues at play are money, Kremlin influence, and unanswered questions.

"Gens una sumus" ("We are one family") is the motto of the World Chess Federation (FIDE). Yet when officials from some 200 countries gather for their congress in Samarkand on Saturday, September 26, it is not likely to feel like a joyous family reunion.

A new FIDE president is to be elected in Uzbekistan, and a three-way, politically charged race for the post has erupted, with the outcome uncertain. It has been clear since July that the incumbent FIDE president, Arkady Dvorkovich, would not be standing for re-election. The European Union had placed the former Russian deputy prime minister on its sanctions list due to his support for Russia's war of aggression in Ukraine.

Three entrepreneurs vying for the top job

The candidates standing for election are Kazakh billionaire Timur Turlov and two Germans: investor Jan Henric Buettner and entrepreneur Wadim Rosenstein, who is running as the official candidate of the German Chess Federation (DSB).

For the first time in over 30 years, FIDE will not be led by a Russian. Nevertheless, the three contenders repeatedly face two questions: What are their ties to Russia? And where do the millions come from that FIDE uses to finance itself and its competitions? For the Kremlin, chess remains a component of Russia's soft power, and little happens within FIDE without financial backers linked to Russia.

Jan Henric Buettner: The Formula 1 model

Buettner is arguably the best positioned to answer these questions. A native of Hamburg, he has made a name for himself in the chess world through his collaboration with former world champion Magnus Carlsen. The 62-year-old German has no known ties to Moscow that would require explanation. On the contrary: "We are the only team with no connection to Russia," Malcolm Pein — Buettner's candidate for vice president — told DW.

Jan Henric Buettner (3rd from left) is championing "Freestyle" chess alongside former world champion Magnus Carlsen (2nd from left). Image: Gregor Fischer/dpa/picture alliance

Buettner and his running mate say they intend to reduce reliance on Russian financial backers and make chess commercially successful. Buettner plans to distribute 20% of FIDE's revenue to chess federations worldwide. The former AOL executive looks to Formula 1 motor racing as his model – a vision likely considered too radical by many officials in the chess world. Consequently, Buettner is seen as having only an outside chance of winning.

Timur Turlov: The establishment candidate

The favorite to become FIDE's new president is Timur Turlov. Born in Moscow, he became a Kazakh citizen in 2022 and is one of the wealthiest men in the Central Asian nation. The entrepreneur is considered a close associate of outgoing President Dvorkovich and, by extension, a member of the FIDE establishment. Regarding finances, too, the status quo is likely to remain unchanged under the 38-year-old; after all, Turlov's publicly traded financial firm, Freedom Holding Corp., has been FIDE's main sponsor for many years.

The prospect of Turlov potentially holding the dual roles of FIDE president and major financial backer does not sit well with everyone in the chess community. Furthermore, Freedom Holding Corp. and its CEO are currently on Ukraine's sanctions list. Ukrainian authorities accuse Turlov's company of helping to finance Russia's war of aggression. Press reports also suggest that the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has taken an interest in Turlov's financial firm.

Report: Hamburger Sparkasse closes account

In the spring of 2026, Turlov acquired the Hamburg-based chess software company Chessbase. Shortly thereafter, the German chess news website perlenvombodensee.de reported that the company's principal bank, Hamburger Sparkasse, had closed the Chessbase business account.

Timur Turlov of Kazakhstan is considered the favorite in the race for the FIDE presidency Image: Sergei Fadeichev/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

Chessbase declined to comment on the matter. Hamburger Sparkasse also did not address the specific case but told DW: "If a business relationship falls under currently existing sanctions – for example, against countries such as Russia, Belarus, or Iran – this may unfortunately result in us being unable to continue specific business relationships."

DW approached Timur Turlov for comment but had received no response by time of publication.

The position of Volodymyr Kovalchuk, vice president of the Ukrainian Chess Federation is clear.

"If Turlov wins the FIDE election and poses a threat to Ukraine's security, then we will push for him to be sanctioned by the EU as well," Kovalchuk told DW.

However, there are now signs of a rapprochement between Turlov and the Ukrainians: Turlov is currently advocating for a Ukrainian official to be elected as a vice president on the FIDE board.

Wadim Rosenstein: Many outstanding questions

The third figure in the mix, Wadim Rosenstein, is also facing intense scrutiny in Ukraine.

"It is absolutely clear that we will not support such a candidate and, should he be elected, will also propose him for sanctions," Kovalchuk said.

Rosenstein was born in 1990 in what is now Ukraine and moved to Germany at the age of nine. In the autumn of 2022, the entrepreneur and amateur chess player began organizing elaborate chess events.

Questions have dogged him ever since, with his business activities and connections to Russia being the primary focus of this scrutiny. According to Rosenstein, the companies within his Düsseldorf-based "WR Group" operate in various sectors, ranging from toilet paper trading and real estate to industrial logistics. Until 2022, a key focus was supporting German companies in regions including Ukraine and Russia, Rosenstein told DW a few months ago. However, he said he was no longer active in Russia; instead positioning himself "globally" across "70 countries," including Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkey.

DSB President Paul Meyer-Dunker supports Wadim Rosenstein's bid to become the next FIDE president Image: Sebastian Kahnert/dpa/picture alliance

The company in Russia

However, one of the Düsseldorf entrepreneur's remaining companies in Russia has enjoyed economic success in recent years. In July, Rosenstein told DW that these companies were active "only on paper."

It has since become clear that "WR RUS," at least, is anything but a paper tiger. The Moscow-based company has been owned by Rosenstein since 2021. Publicly available data show that "WR RUS's" profit grew from around €300,000 ($341,230) to €1.7 million ($1.93 million) between 2022 and 2025.

Furthermore, records confirm that Rosenstein's German companies – "WR Logistics" and "WR Certification" – collaborated with "WR RUS" through the end of 2023. Documents from "WR RUS" also show a dividend payment equivalent to around €30,000 for the year 2023, which apparently went to him and one of his German companies.

DW again approached Wadim Rosenstein for comment on these matters but received no response by the time of publication of this report.

High-priced players, upscale venues

Since 2022, millions have been poured into Rosenstein's elaborate chess events year after year. The list of Rosenstein's events is long: it includes a top-tier tournament featuring world number one Magnus Carlsen, the 2023 World Team Blitz and Rapid Chess Championship at the prestigious Rheinterrasse in Düsseldorf, and, most recently, the global "WR Women's Chess Tour." A premium venue in Stuttgart has been selected for the tour's finale in November – a location whose name the sponsor is likely to appreciate, Rosenstein Palace.

A grand setting for the WR Women’s Chess Tour 2026: Rosenstein Palace in Stuttgart. Image: Markus Mainka/picture alliance

The FIDE presidential campaign is also costly. On social media, Rosenstein presents himself aboard a private jet during an international campaign tour. According to the Frankfurter Allgemeine newspaper, a portion of the campaign costs is to be covered by Rosenstein's running mate for the vice-presidency – a wealthy real estate entrepreneur from Singapore.

Rosenstein has not disclosed the total cost of his numerous chess activities to date or the exact source of the funds. His company, "WR Logistics," is one of the main sponsors. Rosenstein told DW in July: "I have also used my own funds and brought on partners who trust me."

But who are these partners?

A sponsor that didn't exist

While Rosenstein was preparing his FIDE candidacy in April 2026, he introduced the Düsseldorf-based company "Glotech." He stated he was "proud to introduce our next partner." The sponsor is reportedly providing €250,000 for chess activities in Europe. According to Rosenstein, Glotech is "a true supporter of our vision."

However, according to Glotech Managing Director Evgeni Schukin, this support never existed: "There was no agreement, and we did not make such funds available."

A professional-looking certificate: According to "Glotech GmbH," there was no sponsorship agreement (the graphic, which has since been deleted, was published on Wadim Rosenstein's "X" account in April 2026). Image: X/@WadimRosenstein

Rosenstein is campaigning primarily on the pledge that FIDE would operate "professionally" under his leadership. On his official website, "WR 2026," he promises transparent and direct communication.

DW approached Rosenstein for comment on the financing of his chess activities, but he did not respond.

Political connections

With the support of the DSB and its president, Paul Meyer-Dunker, Rosenstein has succeeded in establishing himself as a serious challenger to the Turlov, the favorite within FIDE.

The 36-year-old also enjoys support from the world of German politics. In early September, Rosenstein met with Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann.

"Joachim Herrmann supports the candidacy of the German applicant Wadim Rosenstein," a subsequently issued statement read.

The Bavarian Interior Ministry told DW that this support related to the "sport-specific focus" of the bid but did not constitute "an assessment of Mr. Rosenstein's private or business activities, nor a prejudgment of any potential reviews by competent authorities."

Online debate cut short

The DSB only learned of the meeting between its FIDE candidate and the Bavarian interior minister after the fact. According to Meyer-Dunker, the DSB supports Rosenstein because he stands for "consistent professionalization" and "greater transparency" within the World Chess Federation. The DSB "has no information regarding Wadim Rosenstein's business activities beyond what has appeared in public reports," Meyer-Dunker said.

Rosenstein had an opportunity to address questions and explain his plans for FIDE's finances in early September. A US chess website had organized an online debate for the candidates. Rosenstein delivered the opening statement; he spoke for just under four minutes, then suddenly exclaimed: "See you in Samarkand!" before cutting the connection.

DW has approached Rosenstein several times to ask why he did not participate in the rest of the discussion regarding FIDE's future. There has been no response to this either.

Dasha Thyssen contributed to this article as a co-author. This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Ethiopia's military says it killed hundreds of TPLF rebels
World.content:
The TPLF fought against against the Ethiopian military from 2020 to 2022 in a conflict that saw hundreds of thousands of civilians killed. A resumption of fighting has sparked fears of another brutal war.

Fighting between Ethiopian troops and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) escalated on Thursday, threatening to shatter a fragile 2022 peace deal.

The renewed fighting first broke out in the Tigray Region in northern Ethiopia on Wednesday.

"We are in the situation of full-blown war now," TPLF vice president Amanuel Assefa told AFP news agency.

On Thursday, Ethiopia's military said it "launched a counter-offensive that inflicted heavy personnel and equipment losses on the TPLF."

The military said it killed 272 people among the Tigrayan rebels and wounded some 260 more. These figures could not be independently verified, and there was no breakdown given for soldiers and civilians.

Calls for deescelation

The African Union, the United Nations and other international observers have called for restraint and deescelation.

"I am disappointed to see the leadership of the TPLF, that the United States sanctioned earlier this year, make the poor decision to launch a large-scale offensive today," said Ervin J. Massinga, the US ambassador in Addis Ababa.

"Rejecting dialogue sponsored by the African Union under President Obasanjo and engaging in an unwinnable fight does nothing for the people," he added.

TPLF troops patrolled the regional capital Mekele on Wednesday Image: AFP

What led to the resumption in fighting?

The TPLF was Ethiopia's dominant political force from 1991 until 2018.

It governed with a coalition of other ethnic-based parties, but critics accused it of creating these parties as loyal opposition to sideline preexisting ethnic movements.

When Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed took office in 2018, he sidelined the TPFL in favor of a government not based on ethnic lines, dominated by his Prosperity Party.

Abiy's early foreign policy saw him repair relations with Ethiopia's former archrival Eritrea — efforts for which he was awarded the Noble Peace Prize in 2019.

But his later determination for landlocked Ethiopia to have access to a seaport was seen as provocative in Eritrea as well in Somalia.

Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The TPLF then launched a rebellion against Abiy in 2020, spiraling into a two-year war that saw some 500,000 killed due to violence, famine and the collapse of health services.

During that war, Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF.

Speaking at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, Ethiopian President Taye Atske Selassie Amde decried "the forces of destruction and mayhem" and "interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements."

Ethiopia's President Taye Atske Selassie Amde condemned the brewing conflict at the UN General Assembly Image: Seth Wenig/AP Photo/picture alliance

Conflict spreads to Amhara region

Fighting was also reported in the Amhara region in the Ethiopian highlands.

The AFP news agency received reports of fighting around the holy city of Lalibela, home to Ethiopia's ancient, UNESCO-listed rock-hewn churches.

Flights to the popular tourist destination were suspended on Thursday.

Why can't Ethiopia and Eritrea be friends? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The TPLF announced an alliance with Amhara's Fano militia, a former foe that has been waging its own insurgency in the region since 2023.

The Fano militia originally emerged as an opponent of TPFL rule and the two sides still have competing claims over land that was absorbed in to the Amhara region from the Tigray region after the last war.

"The only issue joining them is their opposition to Prosperity Party rule," said Kjetil Tronvoll, a professor of peace and conflict studies at Oslo New ⁠University College.

World.title: After several difficult years, economists now expect German economy to grow
World.content:
Germany's economy is growing again, but recovery remains on shaky ground. High government spending is keeping the economy afloat, while energy prices, a shortage of skilled workers and debt continue to weigh on it.

After several difficult years, the German economy has regained its footing. Leading economic research institutes now expect the economy to grow by 1.3% in 2026 and by 1.1% next year — significantly more than was forecast back in the spring.

As to the reasons behind this, economists have pointed first and foremost to the global economy. Despite the war in Iran, they say, the economy is proving surprisingly robust.

"This is benefiting the German export sector, and underlying this is also the global boom in artificial intelligence," said Oliver Holtemöller of the Leibniz Institute for Economic Research in Halle during the presentation of the latest report in Berlin.

Because of the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has cut off supplies from competitors, German companies have seen increased demand from abroad for petroleum and natural gas-based chemical products, for example.

In addition, the construction of AI data centers is driving demand for German companies. Some examples include machinery for energy production and services related to information and communication. Government spending on infrastructure and defense is also a significant driver of this upswing.

German industry shifts to defense production amid job losses To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, researchers believe it will not last. For 2028, the institutes expect growth of only 0.4%.

"The drivers of growth will continue to dwindle," said Stefan Kooths of the Kiel-based research institute IfW. High energy prices, a shortage of skilled workers, an aging population and years of low investment by many companies are slowing growth. The institutes therefore warned against misinterpreting the latest positive figures as the beginning of a new economic boom.

Upturn fueled by debt

In this situation, the federal government is also playing a decisive role. The coalition of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU)/Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) has decided to invest heavily in modernizing infrastructure and the Bundeswehr.

In the short term, this additional spending is also helping to generate business for companies and safeguard jobs. At the same time, investments in roads, railways, digital networks and military equipment should strengthen Germany's competitiveness.

Economic analysts agree that this spending has had a positive effect on the economy. The government has been an important engine of growth, especially at a time when consumers are tightening their belts and many companies are postponing investments. But this is also where economists are raising concerns. That's because the spending is financed through debt.

According to forecasts, the government deficit will rise from 4.1% of GDP this year to 4.7% in 2028. At the same time, the government's interest burden will grow. Future budgets will have to allocate an ever-larger share of funds to servicing debt.

"We have two major challenges: one is demographics, and the second is energy security and energy prices," said Holtemöller. In this context, he sharply criticized what the economists see as a lack of clarity regarding "the measures, reforms and regulatory framework" that Germany aims to use to phase out fossil fuels. They noted that a vision for how the energy transition could be carried out in accordance with the Climate Protection Act is "not even vaguely" outlined.

Is Germany's weak economy boosting the right-wing AfD? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

AfD's success scaring off skilled workers

Germany's greatest challenge remains the declining labor force. As the baby boomers enter retirement, the economy is losing millions of workers, and many industries are already complaining of labor shortages. There needs to be greater openness "to the immigration of skilled workers," said Holtemöller.

Referring to the electoral successes of the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) — a party that is, in part, right-wing extremist — Holtemöller cited studies indicating that "regions where populist parties are in power tend to have weaker economic growth than other regions." Openness, he emphasized, is the most important factor.

If immigration remains low, the average age of the population will only increase. This will drive up the cost of social security contributions, which in Germany are evenly split between employees and employers. On pension reform, economists are calling for doing away with the option to retire early after 45 years of contributions without any reduction in benefits. They argue that the debate about moving away from this policy is misguided.

What are the German government's pension, labor reforms? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany's economy in transition

While the government is mobilizing billions, the private sector's momentum is lacking in many places. Investors are being deterred "because they don't know what to expect or what the business landscape looks like here," Kooths explained.

"What companies need now are not new debates but decisions on economic policy," said Helena Melnikov, chief executive of the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry. "This can only be achieved through a decisive course of reform: cutting costs, reducing bureaucracy, streamlining procedures and modernizing infrastructure."

For many decades, Germany was a country with a strong industrial sector. But that sector continues to shrink, with about 15,000 industrial jobs lost every month. Particularly hard-hit are industries such as automotive, mechanical engineering and metals. At the same time, the past two years have seen the emergence of many startups in the fields of digitalization and AI.

But according to economists, these new companies lack support, particularly when it comes to financing. As a result, many are relocating to the US. "We're very good at things like development, patent applications and so on, but the problem is that the ideas developed here end up creating value elsewhere," noted Timo Wollmershäuser of the ifo Institute in Munich.

Volkswagen crisis: Emden plant closure impacts whole region To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

When asked what could further improve growth prospects in Germany, the researchers pointed to a catalog of reforms that was presented last spring. The proposals include, among other things, a cap on social security contributions and stronger work incentives for older workers. As for the energy transition, the institutes placed greater emphasis on price signals and advocate against taking national action on climate protection without other countries.

Notable criticism was directed at the fuel rebate scheduled to take effect on October 1. Researchers said it amounts to a blanket handout for which there is insufficient fiscal leeway.

The government cannot currently afford such expensive measures, and they are "also economically counterproductive," said Holtemöller of the Leibniz Institute. Cutting fuel taxes would "undermine efforts to reduce demand, which is precisely what is needed when energy supplies are tight."

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: CNN, MS NOW, Politico regain access to White House
World.content:
A federal judge has ordered President Trump to restore White House access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico after he banned the media outlets from the premises. Hours later, the media announced they had been granted access.

CNN, MSNBC, and Politico journalists were allowed back in the White House on Thursday, hours after a federal judge said US President Donald Trump must lift his ban on journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico accessing the White House.

The ruling came in response to a lawsuit filed by the news organizations contesting the ban, which was issued on September 18.

In his order, District Judge Tim Kelly said the ban was likely unconstitutional.

Kelly said his order must remain in place for 14 days.

"This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law," Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the outlets, said in a statement emailed to the AP news agency. "We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action."

On Thursday morning, journalists from three affected media outlets were initially denied access. However, later in the day, the media announced they had been granted access to the White House.

What did the judge say about the ban?

Kelly rejected the government's claim that national security concerns promoted the ban.

"The record lacks factual support for defendants’ contention that the revocation of plaintiffs' hard passes will ​in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation ​proceeds," he said.

He pointed out that Trump himself had initially cited only an "alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity" in reporting by the outlets as the reason for the ban.

At a Wednesday hearing, Kelly said two previous rulings from the US Court of Appeals for the ⁠District of ​Columbia Circuit had established that White House press passes can be revoked only after due process.

He said the banned news outlets did not appear to have been given a proper chance to contest the ban.

Kelly, who was nominated by Trump in 2017, ordered a CNN journalist’s access restored in a similar case in 2018.

The ban has led other media outlets, including DW, to take action in solidarity by suspending pooled coverage of Trump events.

Department of Justice support for ban

On Tuesday, the Justice Department had argued in a filing that access ⁠to the White House was a privilege, not ​an entitlement, and that the president had the authority to deny access news organizations.

The outlets, in turn, argued they were singled out because of the content of their coverage and called the ban a "blatant violation" of the First Amendment, which prevents government infringement on freedom of speech and freedom of the press in the United States.

World.title: Houthi advances in Yemen drive displacement, deepen humanitarian crisis
World.content:
With more than 132,000 people already displaced by the latest fighting and Houthi territorial gains, Yemen is on the brink of slipping back into a full-fledged humanitarian emergency. DW spoke with people on the ground.

Mohammed Musleh is still in shock. Following the Houthi capture of the port town of Mokha earlier in September, his family had to flee their home without time to pack.

"We have no idea what will happen now," the 46-year-old told DW. His wife, Muna, is also worried, as the family couldn't bring their personal identification documents. "The Houthis told us to leave, basically immediately. We had no time to take anything," she said.

For now, the family and their two young daughters are staying with relatives in Aden, the largest city controlled by the government in southern Yemen. "We tell our kids in the meantime that we hope to return home soon," the couple said.

Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of the Presidential Council, the leadership body of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, said that recent battlefield changes would not alter the government's goal of restoring state authority nationwide.

However, given the latest advances by the Iran-backed Houthis and their territorial gains in Yemen, a return of the Musleh family to their home in Mokha is unlikely for now.

Since late July, the Iran-backed Houthis have expanded their areas of control from the north and center of the country to much of Yemen's Red Sea coast, seizing territory from forces of the internationally recognized and Saudi-backed government. The conflict continues to escalate, along with an exchange of missile and drone attacks between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis are currently pushing further into the country toward the strategic Kahboub Mountains. The mountain range is significant as it overlooks areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key waterway that had been serving as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports amid Iran's blockade of the nearby Strait of Hormuz.

Staying at home or leaving Taiz?

The mountains are also only around 40 kilometers (25 miles) southwest of Taiz, which is under government control.

Yemeni government forces and Houthi forces are fight over control of the strategic Kahboub Mountains near Taiz Image: Marwan Abdullah Yahya Saeed Al-shabi/Anadolu/IMAGO

Fatima, a mother in Taiz, has been telling her children that the sounds of shelling are from fireworks. "We are scared and we are also worried as gas has already become unavailable and prices are rising. Merchants are no longer coming into Taiz," she told DW, asking not to publish her full name for fear of reprisal.

Rania and her children have also decided to stay at home in Taiz for now. "But we fear that if the Houthis tighten their grip on the city of Taiz, we will find ourselves under siege again," she said. She also doesn't want to use her first name, and vividly recalls the "suffocating blockade of 2015 and 2016, when the entry of food and goods was cut off."

During the previous war between the Iran-aligned Houthi group and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, which began in 2014 and largely ended with a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022, Houthi forces blocked most routes into the government-controlled city of Taiz for almost two years. The restrictions on food, medical supplies and humanitarian aid drove up prices and left people on the brink of famine.

Growing displacement numbers

The World Health Organization said this week that at least 674 people have been killed and 2,998 injured since fighting escalated in August. However, due to the ongoing clashes, the death tally may already be higher, as fighting is ongoing.

The conflict has also prompted mass displacement of more than 132,000 people, according to the International Organization for Migration. In recent days, more than 90,000 people found refuge in Aden, Lahj, Abyan and Al Dhale'e governorates and even in Marib, the UN refugee agency's Yemen representative Armen Yedgaryan said on Tuesday.

He also predicted that intensifying fighting could drive more mass displacement, with growing numbers of people expected to flee to Djibouti, Somalia and other countries, as well as within Yemen.

According to the IOM, at least 132,000 people have been displaced, and numbers are likely to grow in the coming period of the conflict Image: IOM Djibouti/AFP

"Conditions for displaced people are increasingly severe as they arrive at already congested displacement sites in urgent need of shelter, food, clean water, healthcare and protection, placing additional pressure on fragile services and infrastructure," he said.

Even before the latest escalation, more than 5.2 million people were internally displaced in Yemen, and the current fighting is deepening an already dire humanitarian crisis in the country, the UN refugee agency added.

Around 22 million people require humanitarian assistance, including internally displaced people and around 65,000 refugees and asylum-seekers, mainly from Somalia and Ethiopia.

Displaced Yemenis help other displaced Yemenis

"I was in the Al-Kud site, a camp for internally displaced people or IDPs, in Abyan governorate on Sunday," said Alison Bottomley, an advocacy adviser with the Norwegian Refugee Council in Yemen, adding that "317 families have arrived since the fighting began, increasing the number of people from 1,460 to 2,629 people."

However, there is no funding to support them. "These IDPs are surviving purely off the generosity of other IDP families."

She told DW that she met Mustapha, a man who was displaced from his hometown of Mawza seven years ago during the previous war in Yemen. He has been living at the IDP site ever since. "He told us he was hosting 22 families in his shelter, all people from his hometown in Mawza. Together, they share a single latrine. When I asked how they were all eating, he said they share one meal together every other day."

The UNHCR's Yemen operation is only 18% funded in 2026, leaving aid organizations without funds to respond to the latest escalation Image: REUTERS

Houthi leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, meanwhile, released a video message in which he told Yemenis in western and southern provinces that they are not the target.

However, Yemeni political analyst Hisham Al-Omeisy said these are empty words.

"The Houthis may measure this offensive in kilometers gained and territory seized, but Yemenis are measuring it in homes abandoned, families torn apart, and lives lost," he told DW.

"There is something profoundly cruel about pursuing military gains while ordinary Yemenis are once again being condemned to fear, hunger and displacement," Al-Omeisy said, adding that "the lines on the map may change, but the blood, grief and shattered lives behind those lines belong to real people. Yemen's civilians cannot continue to be treated as collateral damage in the Houthis' pursuit of power."

Edited by: Andreas Illmer

World.title: Nigeria, US agree to boost mining investment on sidelines of UN General Assembly
World.content:
On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Nigeria and the US inked a new mining deal. Nigeria is home to deposits of lithium, gold, tin, gemstones, iron ore and phosphate.

Nigeria and the US have agreed to "deepen" American investment in the West African country's mining sector.

The deal was signed on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York City, Nigeria's Minister for Solid Minerals Dele Alake announced on Thursday.

"This is an important step in strengthening Nigeria-US cooperation around our mineral resources, valued at about $700 billion (€796 billion)," Alake said.

"The framework covers geological data and exploration, mineral development and processing, infrastructure, and technical capacity,"he added.

'We want more local processing'

Although known for its vast oil reserves, Nigeria is also home to deposits of lithium, gold, tin, gemstones, iron ore and phosphate.

Lithium, in particular, is in high demand globally as an essential component in the batteries are powering the green energy transition.

Alake said the agreement, which was signed on Wednesday, would be used to identify viable projects. He hinted that local jobs could be created by onshoring the refining of minerals, which until now have largely been exported as ore.

Would you drink this? Nigeria’s toxic gold river To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Nigeria cannot remain a source of raw materials while others capture most of the value," Alake said. "We want more local processing, quality jobs, stronger skills and greater opportunities for Nigerian businesses."

However, these goals come as Nigeria's mining sector remains mired by safety concerns and environmental concerns.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

World.title: Netanyahu reta a una Asamblea de la ONU semivacía en protesta por su invasión de Gaza: “Acusarnos de genocidio es la mayor mentira del siglo”
World.content:
El primer ministro israelí, que se juega su futuro el próximo mes en las elecciones, lanza un mensaje de dureza frente a las críticas. Abbas denuncia una “limpieza étnica” contra los palestinos

Dos imágenes muestran con claridad el creciente aislamiento y crítica internacional que sufre el Israel de Benjamín Netanyahu. Dentro de la sede de la ONU, el primer ministro conservador ha sido recibido este jueves con abucheos y con la marcha de muchas delegaciones antes de que empezara a hablar. La Asamblea General semivacía era una metáfora potentísima. “Si hay otro cobarde que se quiera ir, por favor que se vaya ahora”, ha dicho él, desafiante, mientras miembros de su delegación gritaban: “Am Israel Jai” (El pueblo de Israel vive, en hebreo). Fuera del edificio, la policía detenía a un centenar de manifestantes, entre los que estaban la actriz Susan Sarandon y la candidata a congresista demócrata Darializa Ávila Chevalier, que protestaban contra la presencia de un mandatario al que acusan de cometer un genocidio en Gaza.

Precisamente esa acusación ha protagonizado uno de los momentos más calientes de una intervención dura, amenazante, en la que Netanyahu ha dejado claro que no piensa dar marcha atrás ni un milímetro. La idea de que su país, que nació con el trauma sin igual del exterminio nazi de más de seis millones de judíos en Europa durante la II Guerra Mundial, esté cometiendo un genocidio ahora es, según su gobernante, “la mayor mentira del siglo”.

Netanyahu fue más allá. No solo niega haber cometido ese crimen. Es que, además, asegura que tan solo se han defendido para evitar ser ellos las víctimas de un genocidio. “Esto es lo que los amigos de Hamás del [alcalde de Nueva York, Zohran] Mamdani nos habrían hecho si no lo hubiéramos frenado”. Esas acusaciones, ha dicho, tienen como consecuencia una creciente persecución de los judíos por todo el mundo. “Nos acuchillan por las calles”, ha asegurado.

Al margen de la opinión de Netanyahu, un creciente número de expertos y la mayor organización profesional de estudiosos del tema ―la Asociación Internacional de Académicos del Genocidio― consideran que el país ha cometido un genocidio, al actuar con la intención de destruir, total o parcialmente, a los palestinos. El político conservador no es investigado por este delito por el Tribunal Penal Internacional, sino por crímenes de guerra y contra la humanidad. En cambio, sí hay una causa abierta por genocidio contra Israel en el Tribunal Internacional de Justicia (de la ONU) por una denuncia de Suráfrica a la que se han sumado otros Estados.

03:05 Seis momentos del discurso de Netanyahu en la ONU El primer ministro israelí, Benjamín Netanyahu, en su intervención ante la Asamblea General, este jueves. Foto: LEV RADIN (EFE)

El primer ministro ha hablado ante la Asamblea General consciente de que el próximo mes se juega su futuro político. Las encuestas para las elecciones israelíes del próximo 27 de octubre muestran a los dos bloques, pro y anti-Netanyahu, muy igualados. En un mes, el mayor superviviente de la política israelí podría seguir al frente del país o tener que jubilarse, y enfrentarse quizás a distintos procesos judiciales.

En este contexto, ha lanzado un mensaje duro, combatiente, que giraba en torno a una idea: Israel no tiene otra opción que responder con toda la fuerza si quiere sobrevivir. “Vamos a ganar, no tenemos otra alternativa”, ha repetido. Esa impresión, considera, quedó más clara que nunca tras el 7 de octubre de 2023, que fue “el día más sombrío de la historia de Israel”, cuando Hamás “cometió la mayor masacre de judíos desde el Holocausto”.

Enemigos muertos y espíritu quebrado

Ha sacado pecho por que un país del tamaño del Estado de Nueva Jersey sea capaz de librar una guerra en siete frentes (Gaza, Cisjordania, Líbano, Irán, los hutíes de Yemen y las milicias chíies de Irak y Siria). Y se enorgullece de los resultados cosechados hasta ahora, con muchos de sus enemigos y su espíritu, quebrado: “Los terroristas que mataban israelíes y estadounidenses ya no están. Y los que quedan, están tratando de reorganizarse”.

Por eso, Netanyahu ve las acusaciones que le llegan del mundo exterior como ataques a Israel o al pueblo judío en general. La violencia de los colonos en Cisjordania, que un creciente número de países occidentales, liderados por el Reino Unido, se empiezan a tomar en serio con la imposición de sanciones a Israel, son para él una minucia. Los ha definido como “un puñado de delincuentes menores de edad”, en torno a 150 que a veces “encienden fuegos” y que han causado “a lo mejor dos o tres muertos” en lo que va de año. Netanyahu lo ha comparado con los “miles de ataques” palestinos contra “colonos pacíficos” y “honorables”.

“Los antisemitas del mundo quieren aterrorizar a nuestro pueblo”, ha afirmado. En esta cosmovisión en la que gran parte del planeta está en contra de ellos, Netanyahu ha tenido palabras de agradecimiento a un país, Estados Unidos, y a un hombre, Donald Trump, su mayor aliado, con el que el pasado febrero emprendió una guerra en Irán de incierto futuro: “Entendió que no podía dejar avanzar a los ayatolás fanáticos que gritan ‘muerte a Estados Unidos’. No fue un acto solo para protegerse, sino para salvar a la civilización”. El contraejemplo de Trump es el alcalde Nueva York, al que ha acusado de antisemitismo rampante: “A todos los que difunden mentiras sobre mi país y sobre nuestros valientes soldados, ya se encuentren en esta sala o en el despacho del alcalde antisemita de Nueva York, les digo lo siguiente: ¡Deberían avergonzarse!”.

El presidente palestino, Mahmud Abbas, en el vídeo con su mensaje para la Asamblea General de la ONU, este jueves. LEV RADIN (EFE)

Abbas: “Un plan colonial maligno”

Netanyahu ha hablado pocas horas después de que lo hiciera el presidente de la Autoridad Palestina, Mahmud Abbas. Pero este no lo ha hecho desde Nueva York, sino que se tuvo que conformar con mandar un vídeo. El Gobierno de Estados Unidos no le concedió un visado para entrar en el país argumentando que no había cumplido con sus acuerdos para buscar la paz, una decisión que va contra las normas de la ONU.

En su alocución, Abbas ha acusado a Israel de llevar a cabo una política de “discriminación racial, limpieza étnica y terrorismo” contra los palestinos, con el objetivo de que se marchen y quedarse con la tierra. “Lo que está sucediendo en Gaza, Cisjordania y Jerusalén no son incidentes aislados, sino un plan colonial maligno cuyo objetivo es hacer imposible la vida de los palestinos en su tierra, para obligarlos a dejarla. […] No permitan una nueva Nakba [la expulsión o huida de cientos de miles de palestinos entre 1947 y 1949], no permitan más masacres”, ha reclamado a la comunidad internacional.

Las críticas del líder palestino no se circunscriben a Israel, también ha pedido un examen de conciencia a los países que a su juicio se lavan las manos ante la tragedia que vive su pueblo: “¿Por cuánto tiempo más algunos Estados permanecerán en silencio sobre Israel o le seguirán suministrando armas que pueda usar contra nuestra gente?”.

“El mundo ha sido testigo de un tremendo costo para la franja de Gaza y Cisjordania. ¿Qué espera la comunidad internacional para proteger al pueblo palestino, garantizar su presencia en su tierra (…) e implementar la solución de dos Estados sobre una base de legitimidad internacional?”, se ha preguntado Abbas.

World.title: 10 experiencias en el Matarraña para sacarle todo el jugo a la comarca aragonesa en septiembre
World.content:
Pedalear por la vía verde de la Val de Zafán, caminar por el Solo Sculpture Trail, dormir en un antiguo molino de papel y más pistas en esta zona de la provincia de Teruel que es tierra de cañones y, sobre todo, de buitres

Wikipedia dice, todo el mundo repite —incluida la IA—, y será verdad mientras no se demuestre lo contrario, que el río mediterráneo mejor conservado del planeta es el Matarraña. Este afluente del Ebro, de casi 100 kilómetros de longitud, ha dado nombre a la comarca en la que Teruel se funde y confunde con Tarragona y Castellón, y ha labrado las rocas calizas de los Puertos de Beceite, donde nace, como si en vez de agua pura llevara carburo de silicio verde, abrasivo y cortante a más no poder. Aparte de fabulosos cañones y de pozas que piden a gritos bañarse hasta bien entrado el otoño, este rincón del noreste de la provincia de Teruel tiene muchas otras cosas que sorprenden al viajero.

La primera es que aquí no hablan como los demás turolenses, sino chapurriau, una variedad aragonesa del catalán cantarina y cadenciosa que, a los forasteros, salvo que sean de las provincias de al lado, les suena a valenciano. Matarraña —o Matarranya, como lo escriben también— es un no parar de sorpresas. Tomen nota de estas 10.

Más información 24 horas en Ayamonte, la ciudad de Huelva donde vivir uno de los mejores atardeceres de Europa

Penetrar en la comarca siguiendo a un tren loco

Por Matarraña pasó un tren hoy difícil de explicar, que iba de La Puebla de Híjar a Tortosa, del norte de Teruel al Bajo Ebro, y que pretendía llegar algún día hasta la orilla del mar. Un loco sueño ferroviario que duró 30 años (de 1941 a 1971) y que dejó este abrupto y solitario rincón del mapa aragonés lleno de puentes inútiles y de estaciones en mitad de ninguna parte.

Se esfumó el tren, pero su itinerario y su espíritu insensatos permanecen en la vía verde de la Val de Zafán. Una buena manera de hincarle el diente a la comarca es echarse a pedalear desde la que fue la estación de Valjunquera con las bicis y los guías de Senda. Salvo en un par de túneles, que no se ve nada, se va descubriendo un paisaje cada vez más ordenado de olivos y almendros y una luz cada vez más mediterránea. Hay una parada obligada en el alto viaducto que hay a 9,5 kilómetros del inicio, para saludar al río Matarraña. Al otro lado, en otra antigua estación, se halla el muy recomendable hotel La Parada del Compte.

Comer lo que comió Picasso

Pedaleando por una vía verde llana no es que se haga mucho ejercicio, pero hambre sí que se hace. Para calmarla, no hay mejor opción en toda la comarca que Fonda Alcalá. Ubicado en Calaceite, miembro de la Asociación Los Pueblos Más Bonitos de España, por esta casa de comidas algo más que centenaria —data de 1922— han pasado García Márquez, Álvaro Cunqueiro, Francesc Català Roca, Paco de Lucía, Serrat… No en este orden, lógicamente. El que no pasó, pero sí comió lo que aquí se hace, fue Picasso. Les perdius de Picasso, las perdices que le guisaron en esta casa y le llevaron enlatadas a Francia en 1967, y las judías blancas de Beceite con sardinas de cubo son dos platos legendarios, fundamentales. Pero el chef Ignacio Alcalá se inventa todos los días otros más excitantes y divertidos, que es lo que aprendió a hacer en las cocinas de Neichel y Can Roca.

Hacer senderismo en una galería de arte

He aquí sin duda lo más flipante de la comarca, naturaleza aparte: Solo Houses, una hermosa finca campestre de 200 hectáreas en el municipio de Cretas, donde llevan 13 años materializándose como naves alienígenas casas alucinantes de arquitectos de vanguardia que se pueden alquilar desde 850 euros por noche y donde pronto lo hará un hotel de habitaciones circulares exentas, con vistas al bosque diseñado por Smiljan Radić, Premio Pritzker 2026. Obviamente, alojarse aquí es solo para amantes de la arquitectura y gente con pasta.

Una mujer pasea entre esculturas del Solo Sculpture Trail, en la localidad de Cretas. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

El resto debe contentarse con ver los ovnis de lejos, paseando entre las vides de la bodega Venta D’Aubert y las esculturas del Solo Sculpture Trail, un circuito creado por los propietarios de todo esto, los galeristas Christian Bourdais y Eva Albarrán, para exponer al aire libre y vender obras que tampoco parecen de este mundo. Se tarda hora y media en ver las 20 esculturas y solo cuesta cinco euros. También se puede visitar la bodega y catar cinco de sus vinos por 25.

La bodega Venta D’Aubert. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

Asomarse a la vecina Tarragona por un desfiladero

Si pasear por un sendero de pago entre esculturas carísimas parece algo pijo y rebuscado, en el pueblo de al lado, en Arnes, podemos hacerlo en un lugar verdaderamente salvaje, el desfiladero de Els Estrets, y bañarnos en las aguas inmaculadas del río que lo atraviesa —un afluente del río Algás, que a su vez lo es del Matarraña—, sin pagar un euro. Al llegar al aparcamiento donde arranca la senda, descubriremos estupefactos Les Gronses, unas formidables moles anaranjadas donde pululan escaladores, cabras monteses y buitres leonados.

El desfiladero de Els Estrets, en la vecina Terra Alta de Tarragona. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

Y nada más echarnos a andar, un cartel que dice: “Parc Natural dels Ports”. Estamos en Cataluña, concretamente en la Terra Alta de Tarragona. Otro cartel advierte que el baño solo está permitido en el Toll Blau (el charco azul). Allí veremos dos o tres humanos y, más adelante, si es que se dejan ver, alguna nutria y la libélula Macromia splendens, en peligro de extinción. Mucho más fácil de observar, libando en las lavandas, es la mariposa Cleopatra. El desfiladero se recorre, yendo y volviendo por camino evidente, en un par de horas.

Dormir en un antiguo molino de papel

Vistas desde el hotel La Fábrica de Solfa, en Beceite. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

Beceite, además de un bonito pueblo, con muchas de sus casas colgadas sobre el encañonado río Matarraña, es el campo base ideal para explorar la comarca, porque está cerca de su paraje más deseado —el Parrizal, donde nace aquél— y porque hay un hotelito familiar que es un hotelazo. La Fábrica de Solfa, que así se llama, fue un molino de papel: con la fuerza del río se trituraba ropa vieja y se obtenía la pasta necesaria. Ahora es una fábrica de actividades: todas las que se cuentan en este reportaje y algunas más. De amorosos cuidados que prodigan Javier y Alberto Moragrega a los que llegan exhaustos después de hacerlas. Y de ricos platos: el recapte de fesols de Beceite, el ternasco de Aragón, las texturas de té de roca y todo lo que se sirve en el restaurante Marca al Agua. Tampoco se desayuna mal, viendo a las nutrias jugar en el río saltarín. Lo único malo es que aparecen al rayar el sol, así que hay que madrugar.

Darse un baño de multitudes y otro en un ‘fish spa’ natural

A solo tres kilómetros de Beceite se encuentra el Parrizal (o Parrissal), el desfiladero que nadie que visita esta comarca deja de admirar y recorrer, a tal punto que hay que reservar online para evitar mayores aglomeraciones de las que ya se forman sobre las tablas de dos palmos de ancho que hay instaladas en las paredes verticales del cañón, a buena altura sobre las aguas impolutas del recién nacido Matarraña. Avanzar nadando por el propio río, que sería lo deseable para librarse del sudor propio y de los atascos, está prohibido.

Pasarelas en la senda del Parrizal. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

Donde sí está permitido mojarse y remojarse es en La Pesquera, en las pozas que forma el río Ulldemó, afluente del Matarraña, a tres kilómetros también de Beceite. Comparadas con las de otros ríos de montaña, estas aguas de hipnótico color verde jade son hasta cálidas. Y mucho más relajantes: metes los pies y acuden docenas de diminutos barbos y madrillas a limpiar tus células muertas. Esto es ictioterapia y La Pesquera, un fish spa natural, sin kimonos ni musiquillas new age.

Remar con el último sol en el pantano de Pena

Kayak al atardecer en el pantano de Pena. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

A la misma distancia de Beceite que el Parrizal y La Pesquera, está el pantano de Pena, uno de los más antiguos de Teruel (de 1930) y el único de la cuenca del Matarraña. Si hubiera muchos pantanos, no sería el río mediterráneo mejor conservado del mundo. Ir allí a navegar en kayak al atardecer es una de las actividades que recomienda y organiza La Fábrica de Solfa. Desde el hotel se llega con una bici eléctrica en un cuarto de hora y, después de rodear el embalse en media más, se embarca y se rema hasta el centro para admirar cómo el penúltimo sol se duplica en la cabecera y el agua se vuelve de oro. Girando luego el kayak en redondo y apuntando con la proa hacia el noreste, se ve cómo los últimos rayos iluminan la Caixa, una cumbre que a los matarrañeses les parece que tiene forma de caja de caudales y por eso la llaman así. Si remando y girando se vuelca accidentalmente, o adrede para refrescarse, no pasa nada: aquí está permitido el baño.

Asistir al banquete de 500 aves carroñeras

José Ramón Moragrega entre buitres en el Observatorio de Aves Mas de Bunyol. ANDRÉS CAMPOS

En la sierra de Arca, donde está la Caixa, anidan multitud de buitres leonados. No es solo que allí hay cortados rocosos idóneos para ellos. Es que al pie de la montaña, en una masía de Valderrobres, vive José Ramón Moragrega, que lleva más de 30 años alimentándolos. Todos los días, Buitreman —así le llaman— sale a las 9.15 con una carretilla llena de pulmones de cerdo y la vuelca ante una muchedumbre expectante de estas enormes carroñeras. Hasta 500 de ellas se reúnen para compartir de muy malos modos este desayuno, formando una monumental tremolina de polvo, chillidos e iracundos aleteos. Todo puede verse y fotografiarse en el Observatorio de Aves Mas de Bunyol, una masía que es también un formidable hide, con grandes ventanales orientados a los cuatro vientos para no perderse nada, desde el momento en que Buitreman vuelca la carretilla y se aparta a toda velocidad de sus pequeños de picos afilados como cuchillos —por eso va con casco, porque más de una vez ha salido descalabrado—, hasta cuando aparecen los alimoches para disputarse las migajas de la tragantona.

Al despedirse de los visitantes, Moragrega les confía casi entre lágrimas su delicado estado de salud y que sus niños pueden quedarse pronto sin desayuno si alguna entidad pública o privada no asume la gestión del observatorio, que es también alojamiento rural. Es un negocio rentable, asegura.

Vuelta a las rocas huesudas del Masmut

Muchos buitres leonados que desayunan en Mas de Bunyol pasan el resto del día haciendo la digestión en las Rocas del Masmut, en Peñarroya de Tastavins, donde hay una importante colonia de ellos. El PR TE-157, uno de los Senderos Turísticos de Aragón, bien mantenido y señalizado, invita a rodear este manojo de peñas anaranjadas de más de 100 metros de altura, similares a los Mallos de Riglos, cuyo nombre se cree que viene de los masmuda, una tribu bereber que quizá estuviera asentada aquí cuando España era musulmana.

Es una ruta circular de poco más de tres horas, cuatro si el senderista se desvía a los tres kilómetros para subir al mirador del Masmut. Situado a 500 metros de las rocas y a similar altura, es un buen lugar para verlas como las ven los buitres, asomando como las falanges de un gigante muerto y enterrado bajo la costra caliza del Matarraña.

Un pícnic regenerativo para despedirse del Matarraña

La última sorpresa de esta ruta llena de ellas la puede dar Tel·lúric, una masía centenaria del municipio de Ráfels cuyos nuevos propietarios no es que respeten la tradición agrícola de los masos, de estas catedrales civiles del campo matarrañés, es que van un paso más allá. O un paso más acá, porque trabajan la tierra con tal cuidado que no solo no se agota, sino que se regenera. Los olivos, los almendros y las viñas que atiende Sorin Dragoman no son soldados invasores de ejércitos cuadriculados, sino pacíficos hermanos de los pinos, las carrascas, el tomillo, el romero, el té de roca y el poleo.

Con todo lo que aquí se produce (vinos, aceite y almendras con certificación ecológica y de agricultura regenerativa) dispuesto sobre un mantel a cuadros, y también con las carnes a la brasa que salen sin parar de la cocina, se organizan unos pícnics delante de la masía que son una manera estupenda de despedirse del Matarraña. El águila culebrera sobrevuela los cultivos de Tel·lúric sin sospechar que son cosa de humanos.

World.title: Fifth West Nile virus death confirmed as number of cases rises
World.content:
A fifth person has died after contracting the West Nile virus since the turn of the year, while the number of confirmed infections has increased to 44.

The public health agency RIVM said another 16 patients had been detected since the last update a week ago. The agency has stressed there is no risk of a pandemic because the virus cannot be transmitted from person to person.

Doctors, vets, virologists and other specialists are monitoring the spread of the disease and deciding if extra precautionary measures need to be taken.

The virus, which is transmitted by mosquitos, causes no symptoms in 80% of people who contract it. but West Nile fever leads to neurological problems in around 1% of cases and in exceptional cases it can be fatal.

Following the death of a hospital patient in Utrecht, the RIVM said last month that the virus was now circulating in the Dutch mosquito population. Previous deaths had been limited to people who were infected while travelling abroad.

Around half the infections reported to the RIVM this year have been in Zuid-Holland province, with other cases in Utrecht, Noord-Holland and Noord-Brabant, Gelderland and Overijssel.

West Nile virus can also be contracted by other species such as birds and horses, but they cannot transmit the infection to humans. The RIVM has recorded 136 positive tests in horses and 171 in birds so far this year.

World.title: Meta takes down Dutch satirist’s film made with Meta glasses
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Instagram removed a video by Roel Maalderink in which the satirical journalist films himself asking the employees of parent company Meta how they feel about the controversial camera glasses.

In the short video, which can still be seen on Alphabet-owned YouTube, Maalderink dons the so-called “pervert glasses” and quizzes staff after instructing the device to start recording.

The gadgets, the most popular version of which is sold by Meta, look like normal glasses but allow users to film and take photos covertly.

The employees, all of whom have their features blurred and are unrecognisable, are not pleased about being recorded.

The video, made together with digital rights organisation Bits of Freedom, was removed from Instagram over what Meta said was “bullying and harassment”.

“I’ve been making satirical videos about everything for 10 years now: Gaza, Ukraine, refugees,” Maalderink said in a statement. He added that this was the first time he had had a video taken down.

Bits of Freedom said that this behaviour shows the company’s power. “Meta determines what becomes publicly discussable and how the debate unfolds. Apparently, there’s no room for criticism directed at Meta itself,” the organisation said.

Earlier this week, Dutch privacy watchdog AP warned that sharing images made with camera glasses violates GDPR rules unless permission is given by everyone in the image.

World.title: Ships on IJssel restricted to one-way traffic as drought lingers
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Highways agency Rijkswaterstaat has imposed a one-way system on the IJssel river in the east of the country because of falling river levels.

From Friday morning barges and boats travelling from Arnhem to Zutphen will have to take a detour of up to 300km.

Rijkswaterstaat said the water channel in the river was too shallow to allow ships to pass each other.

The summer drought has brought the flow in the major Dutch rivers down to unprecedented levels, with the Rhine down to 600 cubic metres a second at Lobith, the point where it enters the Netherlands from Germany.

Koninklijke Binnnenvaart Nederland, which represents inland waterway users, said it was a further blow for a sector that had already been forced to adopt limits on its activities.

Spokesman Andries de Weerd told NOS: “We’ve been taking half or even one-third loads, and now we’re having take the long route round, so unfortunately the costs are going to go up a little.”

Railtrack operator ProRail has announced there will be no trains to or from Amsterdam central station on Saturday, October 3 due to maintenance works.

The timetable on Sunday, October 4 and Monday, October 5 will also be significantly altered. International trains to and from Germany will terminate at Utrecht.

The work is part of ongoing renovations at the capital’s main train station. Currently it services around 200,000 travelers per day, one of the busiest in the country. That number is expected to grow to 275,000 per day.

Platforms are being widened and staircases are being added to accommodate the increase.

ProRail advises anyone traveling to Amsterdam to check the NS travel planner.

World.title: Repairs to A15 motorway bridge will cost hauliers €600k a day
World.content:
The partial closure of a motorway bridge in Rotterdam for repairs is expected to cost the transport sector at least €600,000 a day because of longer journeys.

The bridge, which carries traffic on the A15 to the Maasvlakte, was closed a week ago on safety grounds after inspectors found cracks in the main beam.

Traffic will be restricted to the hard shoulder during emergency repairs, which are expected to last six to eight weeks. The bridge carries 36,500 vehicles a day, including 15,500 heavy goods vehicles.

On the first day of the works, September 17, a 12km tailback built up behind the bridge, adding an hour to the journey.

Transport en Logistiek Nederland (TLN), which represents the sector, surveyed its members on the impact of the closure and found that they expect journeys to take an extra 15 to 60 minutes.

Every 30-minute delay costs €600,000 when projected across an entire day’s traffic, TLN calculated.

“The longer the disruption lasts, the faster the damage adds up,” said TLN chair Elisabeth Post. “Especially if the old bridge eventually has to be removed entirely, which will reduce capacity further.”

The road and rail bridges were last renovated in 2021, ahead of plans to replace them entirely after 2030.

The state of infrastructure in the Netherlands is becoming a growing problem. The Merwedebrug, which takes traffic on the A27, was closed to lorries and coaches in July, at a cost of €1.5 million a day, while the A28 at Nijkerk was shut for 48 hours at the start of September after inspectors found sand and gravel holding up the base supports had been eroded.

The government announced an extra investment of €1.5 billion in next year’s budget to spend on maintaining roads, railways and waterways, but the full cost of the maintenance backlog is estimate to run into the tens of millions.

World.title: Gelderland to impose nitrogen limits on farms despite BBB split
World.content:
Gelderland has become the first province to restrict farming in “buffer zones” around nature reserves to bring down nitrogen compound emissions.

The provincial assembly voted to draw a 500-metre cordon around the Veluwe and three other vulnerable areas, in anticipation of nationwide restrictions that the government is drawing up.

New livestock farms and extensions to existing ones will be banned within the buffer zones from this year.

Other limitations will be phased in over the next 10 years, including a ban on synthetic fertiliser, restrictions on gas consumption and an obligation to make cattle sheds more energy efficient.

The plans have divided the parties in the agricultural province, which has the highest levels of ammonia pollution in the Netherlands.

They were drawn up by Ans Mol, executive member for the farmers’ party BBB, who said that doing nothing would mean “very big risks” for the sector. But seven of the BBB’s 12 assembly members voted against the plan.

Farmers’ protests

Coalition partners VVD, CDA, ChristenUnie and the SGP all backed the measures, which were also supported by the opposition parties GroenLinks, PvdA and D66.

Farmers picketed the provincial assembly building in Arnhem at the weekend to protest against nitrogen restrictions, arguing that they were not supported by evidence and deprived farmers of a future.

The provincial plans have been announced while the government in The Hague is still drawing up its own schedule of measures to bring down nitrogen pollution so that major housebuilding and infrastructure projects can go ahead.

Chris Backes, professor of environmental law at Utrecht University, has warned that some provinces will have to bring in their own measures to prevent the government using the “emergency brake” of a 5% to 10% reduction in heads of cattle.

Farmers are also facing legal action from environmental campaign groups such as Mobilisation for the Environment (MOB), which has petitioned regional courts to cancel the licences for 130 farm businesses.

All construction projects have to obtain a nature permit which shows they comply with environmental regulations, including European limits on nitrogen compound emissions around Natura-2000 conservation areas.

World.title: Jetten warns Trump of “jeopardising” relations over ICC
World.content:
Prime minister Rob Jetten has said the Dutch are pulling out all of the diplomatic stops to prevent further sanctions against the International Criminal Court in The Hague, warning American president Donald Trump against further escalations.

”My message to President Trump is very clear: don’t do it. Do not further jeopardise the relationship between Europe and the US by imposing new sanctions on the ICC,” Jetten told journalists in New York.

The prime minister is set to address the United Nations later today.

The Wall Street Journal, Reuters and the Associated Press have all reported in recent days that the United States is planning to escalate its fight with the ICC and sanction the institution as a whole as part of its campaign to dismantle the court “brick by brick”.

The White House has already sanctioned 13 staff members, including court president, Japanese Judge Tomoko Akane, over the investigation into alleged Israeli war crimes in Gaza.

As the court’s host state, the Netherlands is obliged to provide assistance such as cooperation with security, facilitating visas and transporting defendants and witnesses.

A number of opposition parties in the Netherlands feel the government is not doing enough to protect the institution. MP Kati Piri of Pro told public broadcaster NOS that the cabinet has adopted a “super weak” stance so far.

In a letter to parliament earlier this month, foreign affairs minister Tom Berendsen said the Dutch had been regularly meeting with the court and other countries to discuss the situation, writing that “Dutch efforts have contributed to the court’s ability … to continue the vast majority of its operations unimpeded thus far.”

World.title: House price growth slows to 3.3%, transactions fall
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

House prices increased by 3.3% in August, continuing a slowdown that began at the start of 2025.

The latest monthly update by the statistics agency CBS showed prices fell by 0.1% from July to August. The number of transactions was also down by 2.9% compared to a year ago.

House price growth peaked at 11.5% in January 2025 as the market recovered from a brief slump in 2023, but since then the rate has declined steadily.

The average price paid for a house, excluding newbuild properties, increased to €503,523, having passed the half-million mark in July. On average prices are now 17.8% higher than the last peak in July 2022.
