World.title: Why children often get sick after starting nursery?
World.content:
For many families, the first months of nursery can feel like a cycle of runny noses, coughs, and missed days. Children who were rarely ill before may suddenly seem to be sick all the time, leaving parents wondering whether something is wrong.

Written by: Dorottya Fekete

Medical reviewer: Dr. Veronika Boros, Pediatrician, FirstMed Budapest

In most cases, this pattern doesn’t signal a serious health problem. Starting nursery or preschool means spending more time around other children and encountering viruses that the child may not have met before. The frequent minor infections that follow each other are a common part of early childhood.

For families arriving from abroad and beginning life in Budapest, there can also be an added challenge: knowing what is considered normal, when to keep a child home, and when medical advice is warranted. Dr. Veronika Boros, a pediatrician at FirstMed, explains what parents should know.

Children often get sick after starting nursery. (Source: Getty Images)

The first nursery year can mean a lot of illnesses

Toddlers have many opportunities to exchange viruses when they spend time together in a group. They play closely, share toys, and are still developing everyday hygiene habits such as covering coughs and washing their hands properly.

As a result, the beginning of nursery or kindergarten often brings more respiratory infections than parents were used to seeing before. One cold may seem to end just as another begins during the autumn and winter months.

Starting nursery means children suddenly spend much more time around other children and meet viruses they have never encountered before. (Source: Getty Images Signature)

This does not necessarily mean that a child’s immune system is weak. Exposure to common infections is part of normal childhood development, and the frequency of illness often becomes less disruptive as children get older and encounter fewer unfamiliar viruses.

It can nevertheless be difficult for parents to judge where normal childhood illness ends and a problem begins. The overall picture matters, including how the child behaves between illnesses, whether they recover as expected, and whether symptoms are becoming more severe or persistent.

A child’s wellbeing is part of the adjustment

Starting nursery is more than an increase in exposure to germs. It is also a major change in a young child’s everyday life.

New company, different routines, and many new experiences to process. Some children settle quickly, while others need considerably more time to feel comfortable. The adjustment itself can be tiring and stressful, mostly during the first weeks.

For parents, familiar routines can help make the transition easier. Consistent sleep and mealtimes, reassurance, and enough rest can support a child as they adapt to their new environment.

If a child remains very distressed about nursery or seems to be struggling with the transition for a prolonged period, parents can raise this with their pediatrician. A pediatrician can help consider the child’s overall wellbeing and advise whether any additional support may be appropriate.

If you missed it – Men’s health screening in Budapest: A guide for expats

What can parents do between one cold and the next?

There is no way to prevent every infection a child encounters at nursery, but everyday habits can reduce the spread of illness and support general health.

Applying everyday hygiene practices, adequate sleep, and a varied, balanced diet can reduce the spread of infections and support recovery. Routine childhood vaccinations protect against a range of serious infections.

Handwashing: This is one of the simplest preventive measures. Encourage children to wash their hands regularly, primarily before eating and after using the bathroom or arriving home from nursery. Parents can reinforce the habit by making handwashing part of the family’s routine.

Adequate sleep and a varied, balanced diet: These are also important aspects of caring for a growing child. When a child is unwell, rest and fluids become vital.

Vaccination is another significant part of prevention. Routine childhood vaccinations protect against a range of serious infections, while seasonal influenza vaccination can help reduce the risk of flu. Families should discuss their child’s vaccination needs with a healthcare professional. FirstMed provides information about influenza vaccination and other preventive care for children.

It is also worth following the nursery’s illness rules. Keeping a sick child at home gives them time to recover and reduces the chance of passing an infection to classmates and staff.

One common misconception is that antibiotics are needed whenever a child has a cold. Most ordinary colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics do not treat viral infections. A pediatrician can help determine when medication may be appropriate and when supportive care is better.

When is it time to call the pediatrician?

Frequent minor illnesses in little children after starting nursery do not automatically require a medical appointment. However, some symptoms deserve professional attention, especially when a child appears significantly unwell or is not recovering as expected.

Parents should seek medical advice if a child has a high or persistent fever, difficulty breathing, signs of dehydration, or symptoms that are not improving. An unusually sleepy child who is difficult to wake, significantly less active than usual, or generally appears much more unwell than expected should also be assessed.

The same applies when parents are simply concerned that something is different from their child’s usual pattern. Parents do not need to work out the diagnosis themselves before contacting a pediatrician.

For international families in Budapest, FirstMed provides English-speaking pediatric care at its clinic in Hattyú utca, near Széll Kálmán tér. Pediatrician Dr. Veronika Boros is among the doctors caring for children and families at the clinic. Parents can seek advice even when they are unsure exactly what is causing their child’s symptoms.

Questions parents often ask about nursery illnesses

Is it really normal for a child to be ill so often after nursery starts?

It can be. The first months of group childcare often involve frequent minor infections because children encounter viruses they haven’t been exposed to before. This pattern does not automatically indicate an underlying health problem. What matters is how severe the illnesses are, how well the child recovers, and whether they remain well between episodes.

How many colds should a young child have?

There is no single number that applies to every child. Young children in group childcare can have repeated respiratory infections, particularly during the first nursery year. The frequency may look quite high when one infection follows closely after another. If illnesses are unusually severe, prolonged, or accompanied by other concerning symptoms, a pediatrician can assess the individual child.

Should my child stay home from nursery when they are ill?

A child who is unwell generally needs time to rest and recover at home, and staying home also helps reduce transmission to other children and staff. The appropriate return-to-nursery point depends on the illness, the child’s condition, and the nursery’s rules. If you’re unsure, ask your pediatrician for guidance.

How do I know when a cold needs medical attention?

A typical mild cold can often be managed with rest, fluids, and observation. Seek medical advice if symptoms are severe or persistent, the child has difficulty breathing, has a significant fever, shows signs of dehydration, or isn’t improving. You may also consult a pediatrician if your child seems unusually unwell or if your instincts tell you something is not right.

The bigger picture

The first nursery year can be exhausting for parents who feel they are constantly dealing with another cold. In many cases, however, frequent minor illnesses are part of a child’s adjustment to group childcare, not evidence that something is seriously wrong.

Keeping expectations realistic can help. Children will get sick, mainly when they first enter a group setting, and parents cannot prevent every infection. Good daily habits, appropriate vaccinations, enough rest, and knowing when to seek medical advice can make the period easier to navigate.

If you would like to explore the topic in more detail, FirstMed’s full guide covers childhood illness after starting nursery and provides further information for parents in Budapest.

Medical disclaimer: This content is for informational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Please consult a qualified healthcare professional.

World.title: Investment in Hungary: the next question is not where capital comes from, but how long it stays
World.content:
Hungary has spent years building a position within Europe’s manufacturing and investment landscape. New factories, logistics projects and international companies have expanded the country’s industrial base and strengthened its links with wider European supply chains. But attracting capital is only the first part of the equation. The more difficult question is whether that capital has enough reasons to remain, expand and support the next stage of economic activity.

Written by Abdulla Saeed Alhebsi (A.S. Alhebsi)

For investors making decisions over several years rather than several quarters, the quality of an investment destination is measured by more than the initial cost of entering a market. They look at infrastructure, logistics, access to skilled workers, the reliability of institutions, the ability to expand operations and the predictability of the environment in which a project will operate.

This distinction matters because long-term capital behaves differently from short-term capital. A short-term investor can react quickly to changing conditions. A company building a factory, logistics network or research operation cannot move its assets with the same speed. Once capital is committed to physical infrastructure, the quality and continuity of the surrounding environment become part of the investment itself.

Hungary already provides useful examples of this dynamic.

Consider Debrecen. BMW’s investment there is not simply a factory project. The company developed a major manufacturing site dedicated to electric vehicles, while related activities have expanded around the investment. This illustrates how an initial manufacturing commitment can generate additional economic activity when the surrounding ecosystem is capable of supporting it.

A similar lesson can be seen in southern Hungary. METRANS is developing an intermodal rail and road terminal in Szeged, strengthening connections between manufacturers in the region and wider European transport networks. The importance of such infrastructure is not simply the value of the terminal itself. It is the additional connectivity it can provide to companies making longer-term decisions about production and distribution.

These examples point to a broader principle: investors do not assess an industrial project in isolation. They assess the system around it.

That system includes roads and railways, energy and telecommunications, customs procedures, suppliers, education and workforce development, financial services and the capacity to respond when conditions change. A company may enter because of an attractive initial opportunity, but its decision to expand depends increasingly on whether the wider system continues to work.

If you missed it: CATL launches trial operations at Debrecen battery factory

This is where institutional clarity becomes important

Global investors managing long-term capital increasingly operate in an environment where infrastructure needs are growing while traditional sources of financing face constraints. BlackRock has highlighted the growing role of private capital in financing infrastructure and other long-duration assets. Its discussion of infrastructure and private markets reflects a broader shift in the investment landscape.

The World Bank Group has made a related point from a development perspective. Its Private Sector Investment Lab identifies regulatory certainty, guarantees, foreign-exchange solutions, new investment structures and additional equity capital among the areas that can help mobilise private investment. The underlying issue is straightforward: capital is more willing to commit for longer periods when investors can understand the rules, identify the risks and assess how those risks can be managed.

For Hungary, this creates an opportunity as well as a responsibility.

The opportunity is to move beyond competing primarily for individual projects and strengthen the conditions that encourage companies already operating in the country to deepen their commitments. A new factory may create jobs and exports, but the larger economic value can come when that factory becomes the anchor for suppliers, research, logistics, training, business services and further investment.

The responsibility is to recognise that long-term investors are not only evaluating today’s conditions. They are evaluating the conditions they expect to face five, ten or twenty years from now.

That changes the way investment policy should be viewed.

Instead of asking only, “How much capital can Hungary attract this year?” policymakers and business leaders can also ask, “What makes an investor want to reinvest here after the first project is complete?”

The second question is harder, but it is also more revealing.

A company that builds a plant and later adds a research centre, service operation or additional production line is making a different statement from a company that completes one project and looks elsewhere for its next investment. Reinvestment can therefore be viewed as a practical indicator of how investors experience the business environment over time.

The same logic applies to infrastructure. A logistics terminal is valuable not only because of its own capacity, but because it can reduce friction for manufacturers and connect them more efficiently to markets. A skilled workforce is valuable not only because it fills today’s vacancies, but because it gives companies greater confidence that they can expand tomorrow. Institutional clarity works in the same way: its value is not always visible in a single transaction, but it can influence whether companies are prepared to make the next one.

Hungary’s recent investment activity shows that the country can attract substantial international capital across manufacturing, automotive, electronics and business services. The next stage is therefore less about proving that Hungary can attract capital and more about strengthening the conditions under which capital can become embedded in the economy.

That requires looking at investment as a long-term relationship rather than a single transaction.

For investors, the question is not simply where money can be placed. It is where money can continue to operate effectively as markets, technologies and supply chains change.

For Hungary, the strategic question is correspondingly clear: can the country make today’s investment decisions become tomorrow’s reinvestment decisions?

What’s next? Who gets the house? Property inheritance in Hungary for international owners

The answer will depend not on one incentive, one factory or one announcement, but on the continued performance of the system surrounding every investment.

Capital may arrive because of an opportunity. It stays when the environment continues to make expansion, adaptation and long-term planning possible.

That is the difference between attracting investment and building an investment ecosystem.

Sources

BlackRock — “2025 Larry Fink Annual Chairman’s Letter”

World Bank Group — “Private Sector Investment Lab”

Hungarian Investment Promotion Agency — “BMW Plant Inaugurated in Debrecen”

Hungarian Investment Promotion Agency — “METRANS to construct third terminal in Hungary”

World.title: Bosnia Dismisses Two Soldiers for Glorifying Ratko Mladic
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp



Bosnia’s Defence Minister Zukan Helez at a military ceremony in Sarajevo, December 2023. Photo: EPA/FEHIM DEMIR.

Bosnia’s Defence Minister Zukan Helez on Thursday officially signed the dismissal papers of two soldiers following an internal probe into “ethno-nationalist misconduct” within the Armed Forces.

The two were part of a broader group of 37 military personnel Helez reported to the Prosecutor’s Office of Bosnia and Herzegovina this month for activities that glorified the late Bosnian Serb warlord Ratko Mladic.

Mladic died last month in a UN jail in The Netherlands, aged 84, while serving a prison sentence for genocide and other wartime crimes, and was buried with military honours in Belgrade, Serbia.

“While I am the Minister of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there will be absolutely no tolerance for the glorification of war criminals within the Armed Forces,” Helez stated, following the dismissals.

“Our military must remain an institution of ultimate trust for every single citizen – an organisation that firmly respects victims, legal frameworks, and the values of long-term peace,” he added.

Out of the 37 initial complaints about the glorification of Mladic by servicemen, ten cases have been qualified as criminal offences and forwarded to state prosecutors along with supporting evidence.

The remaining cases have been redirected to the judiciary to determine whether deeper criminal responsibility exists under domestic laws.

Under Bosnia’s criminal code, the public denial of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes established by binding international and domestic courts is illegal. Guilty verdicts incur a prison sentence of up to five years.

World.title: Kosovo Marks Banjska Attack Anniversary as Main Suspects Remain Free
World.content:
Kosovo President Albulena Haxhiu lays a foundation stone commemorating Kosovo Albanian policeman Afrim Bunjaku who was killed in the Banjska attack, September 24, 2026. Photo: BIRN/Florinda Kelmendi

Marking the third anniversary of the attack by Serb gunmen on Banjska in the north of Kosovo, family members, colleagues and political leaders gathered in the village on Thursday to commemorate the police officer who was killed there in 2023.

A foundation stone for a memorial to the policeman, Afrim Bunjaku, was laid. However, the main suspects, including the Kosovo Serb politician who took responsibility for the attack, Milan Radoicic, remain out of reach to Kosovo’s justice system.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti wrote on Facebook that “three criminals were killed during the operation that day, three have been in prison since then, and all the others will eventually face justice in our country”.

Kurti referred to the Serb gunmen as a “paramilitary terrorist group” and adding that the attack was “organised, directed, and financed by Belgrade and led by the arch-criminal Milan Radoicic”.

Minister of Interior Xhelal Svecla wrote on Facebook that Bunjaku made the ultimate sacrifice, saying that the Kosovo police had showed extraordinary professionalism that day.

“Three years ago, our Republic faced the largest terrorist attack in post-war Kosovo, organised and supported in every aspect by Serbia’s state apparatus,” Svecla wrote.

“In defence of legality, constitutionality and the safety of our citizens, Sergeant Afrim Bunjaku fell in the line of duty that day. Our Republic defended its territory, citizens, and constitutional order, triumphing over Serbia’s terrorism,” he added.

In April, the Pristina Basic Court convicted three Kosovo Serbs of terrorism and “serious acts against the constitutional order and security of Kosovo” by participating in the attack in September 2023.

Blagoje Spasojevic, 33, and Vladimir Tolic, 40, who were arrested in military fatigues at the scene, were sentenced to life in prison. A third suspect, Dusan Maksimovic, 29, who was seized the next day, was sentenced to 30 years in prison.

Announcing the verdict, Judge Ngadhnjim Arrni said that at 1 a.m. on September 24, 2023, the three defendants were part of a “well trained” group of Serbs who brought weapons, military camouflage and equipment, aiming to destabilise the “basic political, constitutional, economic, and social structures of the Republic of Kosovo through a well-organised plan” and through the attempted secession of the majority ethnic Serb north of the country.

All three pleaded not guilty. However, during the closing statements, Spasojevic called his participation in the events “the biggest mistake of my life”.

On the day of the attack, dozens of armed Serbs ambushed a police patrol in Banjska. Bunjaku, 50, was killed and another police officer, Clirim Shaqiri, was wounded. Three gunmen were killed but reports say others were injured and treated in Serbia, their fates unknown.

In total, 44 individuals and one legal entity were named in the indictment. Forty-three of them, including Spasojevic, Tolic and Maksimovic, were charged with terrorism and serious acts against the constitutional order and security of Kosovo.

A legal entity, RAD d.o.o., and its owner, Radule Stevic, were charged with money-laundering, as was one of the other 43 – the alleged ringleader, local Serb powerbroker, businessman and politician Radoicic.

Radoicic, former deputy leader of the Serbian-backed Kosovo Serb party, Srpska Lista, is currently in Serbia. It is not known where the other suspects are.

Radoicic accepted responsibility for the attack. But Serbia, which does not recognise Kosovo’s independence, is unlikely to hand him over for trial.

According to the indictment, he had been financing a “structured terrorist group” since 2017, with the aim of “separating” four Serb-majority municipalities in northern Kosovo “to join them with the Republic of Serbia”.

The indictment said the attackers underwent training at the Pasuljanske Livade military training ground in central Serbia, just over 100 kilometres north of the Kosovo border, just days earlier, citing drone footage seized in Banjska.

It said that Serbia placed at the group’s disposal “all necessary” military infrastructure and logistics equipment “to commit the terrorist attack”.

In May 2026, a BIRN investigation traced the vehicles to a Belgrade-based car rental firm, Pent Rent, which is part of a network of businesses linked to two Kosovo Serbs – Zvonko Veselinovic and Radoicic. This network, which includes an electricity infrastructure firm owned by Pent Rent, has profited from a string of contracts with the Serbian state.

In October 2023, BIRN found that some of the mortar rounds and anti-tank rocket launchers used by the Serb attackers had passed through state maintenance centres in Serbia in 2018 and 2021, while ammunition included assault rifle rounds that match those made in 2022 by the Belom factory, a Serbian state arms producer.

World.title: Vote on Montenegrin Speaker’s Removal Over Mladic Condolences Blocked
World.content:
Montenegrin Parliament Speaker, Andrija Mandic. Photo: EPA-EFE/CATI CLADERA.

Montenegro’s parliament on Thursday did not debate a motion to dismiss Andrija Mandic of the right-wing New Serbian Democracy party as parliamentary speaker as previously planned, because there was no quorum to hold the session.

The trigger for the planned vote was the message of condolence that Mandic sent to the son of former Bosnian Serb military commander and genocide convict Ratko Mladic after his recent death.

The opposition Democratic Party of Socialists, DPS responded to the blocked vote by saying that it will submit the motion to dismiss Mandic again at the next plenary session.

The DPS also said that until a session is held at which lawmakers are allowed to vote on the dismissal of Mandic, it will not cooperate with the government or the parliamentary majority.

“We will not participate in a simulation of democracy … From today, this government is holding Montenegro’s political stability hostage,” DPS leader Danijel Zivkovic told a news conference in parliament.

“[Mandic] did not even allow a quorum to be established, so that it could be determined who was in the chamber, if anyone … And then there is the treatment of media representatives, who were not allowed to enter the chamber,” Zivkovic said.

There was already a heated atmosphere in parliament because Mandic did not allow the extraordinary session to be broadcast or the media to enter the plenary hall, prompting opposition lawmakers and some members of the ruling majority to leave the chamber.

Boris Mugosa, leader of the opposition European Alliance accused Mandic and the parties in the government allied to New Serbian Democracy of “brutally violating the constitution by preventing the session from being held”.

The DPS announcement that it will suspend cooperation with the government and the governing majority could complicate the closing of negotiating chapters on Montenegro’s path to the EU, as this also requires a constitutional amendment that needs a two-thirds majority in parliament.

The Europe Now Movement, part of the governing coalition, said it was “the democratic and constitutional right of every lawmaker to decide whether to take part in consideration of a particular agenda item”.

But it added: “At the same time, we view statements by some opposition figures that they will not vote for the constitutional amendments necessary to close the negotiating chapters as an attempt to seize power before the elections by using Montenegro’s European path as leverage.”

New Serbian Democracy was defiant however, painting the outcome as a victory for pro-EU, pro-Serbian politician Mandic ahead of the parliamentary elections, which must be held by June 2027.

“The score on the board is 3-0: three for Andrija Mandic, for a European future, and zero for those who want divisions,” New Serbian Democracy MP Dejan Djurovic told a press conference.

World.title: Albania’s Cannabis Traffic is No Longer Only One-Way
World.content:
Albanian authorities have intercepted three cannabis shipments from Canada over the last three months, seizing more than 230 kilograms.

At Tirana Airport in July, police found 46 kilos of cannabis in gelatine form in passenger luggage, just over two weeks after the first direct flight from Toronto landed in Tirana.

Authorities made the other two seizures at Durres Port in vehicles shipped from Canada.

In August, police found about 80 kilos hidden in a specially modified vehicle. In September, they found another 107.7 kilos behind wooden panels in a camper, packed in a container with two other vehicles.

A decade ago, this direction of trafficking would have seemed unlikely.

World.title: Magyar in Rome: Can the Church Maintain Its Influence in Hungary After Orban?
World.content:
Papal meeting aims

Magyar himself doesn’t seem too keen on confronting the Catholic Church. That’s perhaps unsurprising given his own Catholic background. “He graduated from the Piarist grammar school in Budapest, and his family has long been well-known in church circles,” religious affairs commentator Janos Reichert tells BIRN.

On the campaign trail Magyar was, on one occasion, photographed with a rosary around his wrist. He uses John Paul II’s dictum “Do Not Be Afraid” as his strap line on social media. And he’s been careful to incorporate visits to major Hungarian Catholic sites like the Archabbey of Panonnhalma and the Marian shrine at Mariapolcs into his public persona.

Both Magyar and his ministers have avoided directing harsh rhetoric toward the churches. Indeed, the government’s recent invitation to them to contribute formally to a public consultation on potential reform of Hungary’s abortion law sparked strong criticism from some human rights NGOs. According to Amnesty International Hungary, “It sends a very bad message” when “church leaders… sit at the same table during the same professional consultation as doctors and professional organisations representing women.”

Nonetheless, Tisza faces making some decisions that could entail difficult adjustments for the churches.

A new legal framework for church-state relations is currently being prepared. Details are unknown yet, but the poor condition of Hungary’s public finances, and perceptions that discretionary grants have been traded for political loyalty from the churches, make an overall cut in state support seem likely.

Separately, the public funding of schools operated by churches in Hungary is also a sensitive area. The number of church schools (of all denominations) doubled under Fidesz and pupils are resourced at a ratio of 3:1 per capita compared with peers in secular institutions. Those schools have long faced criticism for enabling Roma segregation because of the very low admission rates for Roma pupils.

The new education minister, Judit Lannert, has made clear her ambition to tackle both issues, stating in an interview in June her intention to remove the “unfair [funding] disparity between state and church institutions”. Lannert also said that church schools can “remain in operation if they admit Roma children alongside non-Roma children”.

Hungary and the Vatican may well wish to consult on this, given that the operation and funding of Catholic schools isn’t simply a matter of domestic law but also of a 1997 treaty with the Holy See.

In Laky’s view, however, while Magyar will want to reassure Pope Leo about Hungary’s reliability as a partner, another factor should also be remembered. “Magyar is very much a social-media politician,” he notes, before continuing “so every high-level meeting is a photo opportunity.”

An audience with the Pope “is about as valuable as these get”, he adds.

World.title: Serbian Authorities Ridicule Spyware Attack Allegations Before Elections
World.content:
In December, three days before New Year, Jelena Kontic was working on her phone, communicating with university colleagues, political activists and members of the public. It was during the peak of large-scale student-led protests in Serbia, and she was helping to build up a network of contacts for election monitoring.

Five months later, the MA student at the Faculty of Philology, University of Belgrade, received a ‘Threat Notification’ from Apple.

“Apple detected a targeted mercenary spyware attack against your iPhone,” the message read. “This attack is likely targeting you specifically because of who you are or what you do.”

Suddenly, Kontic said, her phone felt like “a ticking timebomb”.

And she was not the only target.

World.title: Albanian Spy Chief’s Arrest a Major Blow to NATO Member’s Reputation
World.content:
The arrest of Vlora Hyseni has dealt a serious blow to the integrity of the Albanian State Intelligence Service that she led and raised questions about the process that led to her appointment.

While MPs from the ruling Socialist Party said any wrongdoing by Hyseni was her own, the opposition framed her arrest on Tuesday morning as a matter of national security worthy of parliamentary debate.

Special organised crime and corruption prosecutors accuse Hyseni, 42, of disclosing state secrets and aiding a perpetrator, as part of a probe into the alleged rigging of public tenders issued by the National Agency for Information Society, AKSHI, which coordinates the development of state information systems and digitalisation procedures and runs the state public services portal, e-Albania.

Attending the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister Edi Rama announced Hyseni’s dismissal; President Bajram Begaj issued a decree to that effect on Tuesday evening.

World.title: Kosovo Court Orders MPs to Elect President by October 6
World.content:
A Kosovo parliament session, September 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Kosovo’s Constitutional Court on Wednesday ordered MPs to elect a new head of state by October 6 to avoid new snap elections – which would be the fourth parliamentary polls in two years.

The order comes ten days after the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, filed a complaint, alleging that parliament had exceeded the deadline for its inauguration.

“The 60-day deadline for the election of a President started on August 8 and will expire on October 6,” the court said.

The court rejected the PDK’s request to halt the work of parliament in the meantime and declare the vote on a new government unlawful. It declared parliament already inaugurated and ordered MPs to elect the fifth and final deputy speaker “as soon as possible”.

On September 14, the PDK complained to the court that the inauguration of parliament a day before had violated the rules, while one day later it asked the court to assess whether the parliamentary vote that re-elected Albin Kurti as Prime Minister was valid.

The PDK claims Kurti’s ruling Vetevendosje party violated the 30-day deadline to inaugurate parliament and that the assembly cannot be considered inaugurated until all five deputy speakers are elected.

Prior to this submission, the PDK withdrew its candidate for the post of deputy speaker, while four others were elected. The court has now ruled that parliament must elect the PDK candidate.

Kurti was re-elected Prime Minister by MPs at a session boycotted by the opposition parties. A narrow majority of 62 MPs out of 120 voted for Kurti’s new cabinet. Eight MPs from the Belgrade-backed Srpska Lista voted against.

If parliament fails to elect a new President by October 6, new elections will be called within 45 days.

In late August, Vetevendosje’s Kurti and the head of the Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, Lumir Abdixhiku, agreed on Bekim Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court judge and diplomat, for the President’s post.

But Sejdiu withdrew from the race on September 14, following disagreements within the LDK parliamentary group over his candidacy.

For a vote electing the President to be valid, at least 80 out of 120 MPs must be present in the chamber. If the first two rounds of voting fail, the third round requires only a simple majority of MPs to elect the President – but at least 80 of them still need to present in the chamber.

Kosovo has been without a President since April 4, when Vjosa Osmani’s five-year term ended. Parliament speaker Albulena Haxhiu from Vetevendosje is serving as Acting President.

Opposition parties had claimed that Vetevendosje may have been preparing the ground for snap elections to be held at the end of December, when many members of the Kosovo diaspora, which mostly supports Kurti, come back to Kosovo for the holidays. However, under the new ruling, any snap elections would have to be held by mid-November.

Perparim Gruda, an MP from the PDK, said that the court’s verdict shows that “the constitution cannot be adapted to the interests of the moment”.

“Vetevendosje could not shift the constitutional deadlines according to its political interest and push the country towards elections on December 27, as it intended,” Gruda said.

World.title: Here’s How the New Zagreb Pedestrian Zone Will Look
World.content:
September the 25th, 2026 – The brand new Zagreb pedestrian zone has been presented as part of European Mobility Week.

Zagreb’s city administration has emphasised that the presented solution retains hospitality terraces as an important part of the social life of the Lower Town, but provides for their uniform design and better integration into the public space. Poslovni reports that three years after the temporary arrangement of the pedestrian zone in Masarykova Street, the City of Zagreb has presented the project for its permanent and comprehensive arrangement that covers Masarykova and Teslina streets as well as parts of Preradovićeva and Gajeva up to Berislavićeva Street.

The project envisages uniform paving of the entire space, divided into a pedestrian zone and a calmed traffic zone between Republic of Croatia Square and Gundulićeva Street, as well as the formation of new public focal points at key intersections and points within the zone. Special emphasis has been placed on the greening of the space. The planting of around 50 new trees connected into a continuous tree line between the two arms of the Green Horseshoe is planned, along with additional green surfaces, urban furniture, drinking water fountains and spaces for rest. The project also includes new bicycle parking, zones for short-term stopping and delivery, as well as a series of measures that improve accessibility for persons with disabilities and the safety of all users of the space.

a unique and well connected pedestrian zone in the heart of zagreb

The conceptual design was prepared by the Institute for Spatial Planning of the City of Zagreb, and an extensive participatory process included citizens, residents, business users and experts of various profiles, it was announced on Thursday from the Office of Zagreb Mayor Tomislav Tomašević.

Zagreb Deputy Mayor Luka Korlaet said that by arranging the pedestrian zone they are creating a complete public space intended for safer and higher-quality pedestrian movement, staying, socialising and public events. It is especially important, he says, that they are connecting the existing pedestrian spaces and expanding the pedestrian zone on the northern arms of the Green Horseshoe, from Republic of Croatia Square to Zrinjevac. In this way they are creating a unique, connected and passable pedestrian whole in the very centre of Zagreb, Korlaet emphasised.

Director of the Institute for Spatial Planning Nikša Božić said that an interdisciplinary team of the Institute worked on the project, which brought together architects, landscape architects, traffic experts and other collaborators.

“It is particularly important to us that through the preparation of the conceptual design we built on the tradition of arranging public spaces that the Institute developed in previous decades, participating in projects such as the arrangement of Jurišićeva and Draškovićeva streets, the Stock Exchange Square and other important city locations,” Božić said.

what are the top priorities?

He noted that in preparing the solution the Institute took into account the collected views, proposals and needs of citizens as well as the results of expert analyses of the space and its development potentials.

The results of a survey fully completed by around 3,400 citizens showed that 88.4 percent of participants support the comprehensive arrangement of the space. The temporary arrangement was rated as positive or extremely positive by 76 percent of respondents, while 72 percent of them supported the expansion of the pedestrian zone to Teslina and Gajeva streets. As the most important priorities citizens highlighted more greenery, benches and spaces for staying, as well as better organisation of traffic and delivery.

World.title: Zagreb City Break, Remote-Worker Style – Why 90 Days Could Be All You Need
World.content:
September the 25th, 2026 – Zagreb is an up and coming city break, but it could be more than that thanks to the remote worker boom. Many talk about Croatia’s famed “digital nomad visa”, but 90 days and zero admin could be all you need.

Not every remote worker wants (or needs) a full digital nomad visa. For many professionals, the classic Croatian “temporary stay of digital nomads” route – with its income thresholds, documentation piles and multi-month planning – is overkill. If your passport already allows visa-free entry to the Schengen area, you can simply turn up and stay for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. That window is long enough to settle into a real routine, yet short enough to feel like an extended city break rather than a bureaucratic relocation. Zagreb is perfectly suited to this lighter approach.

the 90 day limit could be all you need

Unlike the coastline and the islands, which swing between peak-season summer intensity and winter quiet, Zagreb functions as a proper European capital all year. Trams run, cafes stay open, co-working spaces keep their regular hours, and the cultural calendar never really stops. You get the infrastructure of a serious city without the summer price spikes that hit Split or Dubrovnik.

Reliable high-speed internet is the baseline, not a luxury. The co-working scene is mature and varied – from community-focused hubs to quieter central spots – so you can choose between focused workdays and networking as the mood takes you. Plenty of remote workers simply rotate between a well-chosen apartment and a handful of cafes with strong Wi-Fi and power sockets; the cafe culture here is built for lingering.

a big-little city with plenty to offer

Outside working hours, the city rewards curiosity. Upper Town’s cobbled streets and the instantly recognisable St Mark’s Church, the Museum of Broken Relationships, Maksimir Park, Lake Jarun (Zagreb’s unofficial “sea”), and the open-air Dolac Market are all within very easy reach. In the evenings, the bar and restaurant scene is lively without being overwhelming. Weekends open the door to day trips – Plitvice Lakes, the hills around Samobor, or a quick train to Ljubljana – without the stress of long-haul logistics.

Cost of living remains noticeably lower than in most Western European capitals, so a three-month stay feels financially sustainable rather than extravagant.

you don’t need to be a digital nomad to… be a digital nomad

Croatia’s official digital nomad temporary stay is designed for longer periods (up to 18 months) and requires proof of remote work for a non-Croatian entity, health insurance, a clean criminal record, and a minimum income currently set at 2.5 times the average net salary – currently over €3,600 per month, or the equivalent in savings. Processing takes time and the paperwork is real.

The 90-day Schengen short stay, by contrast, asks far less of you if your nationality qualifies for visa-free entry. You arrive, register your accommodation as required, work remotely for your existing foreign employer or clients, and leave before the 90 days are up (or before you hit the 183-day tax-residency threshold if that matters to you). No special permit, no income threshold tied to Croatian averages, no multi-week application process. It is simply a long, productive city break with a laptop. Of course the usual rules apply: you cannot take local employment, and the days count toward your overall Schengen allowance. But for many remote professionals testing life in Croatia, or simply wanting a change of scenery without administrative drama and a baptism of fire from the Croatian bureaucratic machine, that is precisely the point.

who could this work best for?

This approach suits a whole cohort of people; those who already work remotely for a company or clients outside Croatia and hold a passport that allows 90 days visa-free in the Schengen zone, those who want a proper base rather than a series of hotel stays and those prefer a walkable, cafe-packed European city with four seasons and good transport links, and those who are curious about Croatia but not yet ready to commit to the full digital nomad process. It also works well as a trial run. Spend 60–90 days in Zagreb, get a feel for the rhythm, the food, the community and the climate, then decide whether a longer digital nomad stay or a return trip next year makes sense for you.

no visas, no paperwork, and full freedom

Book a furnished apartment or serviced flat with reliable internet rather than a short-term tourist rental if you can. Join a coworking space for at least a few days a week to meet people. Use the city’s excellent public transport and the green spaces to keep the work–life balance healthy. And treat the weekends as genuine exploration time – Zagreb rewards slow discovery more than checklist tourism.

In short, you do not need a special visa to work remotely from Croatia for three months. You just need a laptop, a passport that opens the Schengen door, and a city that actually works for everyday life. Zagreb quietly delivers on all three. For practical information on accommodation, events and getting around, the Zagreb Tourist Board is a good starting point. The rest is simply showing up and getting to work – and leisure.

World.title: Končar Showcases Croatian Manufacturing to the World in Berlin
World.content:
September the 25th, 2026 – Končar has showcased Croatian manufacturing to the world in Berlin, taking the most prominent positions at this year’s InnoTrans.

Končar’s striking visuals were visible in the most prominent positions right at the entrance to the space of the prestigious fair, and the scene at the very entrance to the exhibition area was spectacular, where Končar’s train, a top product of Croatian industry, was positioned in a more prominent place than giants such as Alstom and Stadler. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that after it was put into regular service on the Zagreb – Split route a week earlier in cooperation with the customer HŽ Passenger Transport, the second train from this series has now also been presented to the international public. With the global premiere of its latest solution for more modern, more comfortable and more sustainable passenger transport, Končar has once again confirmed that the knowledge, competences and technological solutions developed in Croatia compete on equal terms with the biggest names in the European railway industry.

croatia impresses visitors from around the world

The InnoTrans fair in Berlin once again brought together the world’s leading manufacturers, carriers, operators and experts from the fields of transport technology, railways, public transport and sustainable mobility. Among the most visited parts of the fair was the outdoor exhibition area with 3,500 metres of track, on which 130 exhibitors from 17 countries of the world exhibited a total of 113 vehicles, including the latest generations of trains, locomotives and vehicles with alternative propulsion systems. Precisely in such an international environment Končar is presenting technological solutions developed and produced in Croatia for the jubilee 10th time, confirming its position among the relevant European manufacturers of modern rail vehicles and advanced solutions for sustainable urban mobility.

berlin breaks records

All 42 exhibition halls in the Berlin Messe complex, with a total exhibition area of around 200 thousand square metres, are completely full. After two years ago it was the only one at InnoTrans to present a battery train, which then also became the first such product in commercial use in Europe and one of the first such products in the whole world, Končar has also displayed its new bimodal electro-diesel train at one of the most attractive positions on the outdoor exhibition area of the fair – on 75-metre-long tracks.

At the same time, the latest solutions for railway infrastructure, electrification, urban mobility and traffic digitalisation were presented on the spacious indoor area, further emphasising the ability of the domestic company to independently develop and deliver integrated technological solutions for the transport systems of the future.

“The presentation of our latest bimodal train at InnoTrans is confirmation that Končar today stands side by side with the leading European manufacturers of railway vehicles. It is a product of a new generation that confirms the strength of domestic knowledge, innovation and industrial competences and Končar’s ability to respond to the requirements of modern and sustainable railway transport. We believe that precisely with such projects we contribute to strengthening the competitiveness of the Croatian economy and positioning Croatia among the countries that actively participate in shaping the future of sustainable mobility in Europe,” emphasised Končar Management Board President Gordan Kolak.

One train, two sources of propulsion and no compromises – precisely this idea guided the development of the new Končar bimodal electro-diesel train that combines the advantages of electric and diesel traction and enables uninterrupted traffic on electrified and non-electrified sections of the railway network. Additional operational adaptability is provided by the possibility of controlling up to three coupled units from one driver’s cab, whereby the capacity of the train can be adapted to the actual transport needs. Accordingly, it is an innovation that represents a direct response to the need for more sustainable and more efficient railway transport on long routes that encompass both types of infrastructure, and is the result of many years of experience and independent development at Končar – Electric Vehicles.

With its presentation Končar rounds off a unique development portfolio of trains and, after electric, diesel-electric and battery trains, is introducing the fourth propulsion platform developed and produced in Croatia to the market. The new train is also one of the best references of the long and successful application of Croatian products in domestic railway transport. Namely, the model from the new generation that was put into service last week represents a total of the 70th train that Končar has delivered to HŽ Passenger Transport, which further confirms the joint orientation towards the modernisation of the domestic railway system.

a new era

“The new train for long-distance transport combines the development, design and production competences of the Končar Group. Thanks to the bimodal propulsion system it ensures a high level of reliability and quality of service on the entire network, while bringing passengers a higher standard of comfort through first class, a catering zone and full accessibility for persons with reduced mobility. It is a technologically advanced and operationally flexible solution that meets the requirements of modern railway transport and the long-term needs of sustainable mobility,” emphasised Josip Ninić, President of the Management Board of Končar – Electric Vehicles.

By developing advanced rail vehicles, digital platforms and integrated solutions for critical infrastructure, including railway and transport systems, Končar is increasingly entering a new era of electroenergetics and urban mobility and occupying the position of a serious European partner for the implementation of complex projects. In this way it not only confirms the technological strength of Croatian industry, but also actively contributes to positioning Croatia as a relevant participant in the European green and digital transition and one of the centres of development of the technologically most complex solutions in this part of Europe.

This year InnoTrans is celebrating its 30th anniversary – and, quite fittingly, the fair is recording new record figures. For the first time more than 3,170 exhibitors will participate, which is around 200 more than in 2024, which was also a record year. All 42 exhibition halls in the Berlin Messe complex, with a total exhibition area of around 200 thousand square metres, are completely full. The same applies to the outdoor exhibition area of InnoTrans of 20 thousand square metres, where this year 113 vehicles from 17 countries will be exhibited.

Of the approximately 130 exhibitors presenting themselves on the outdoor area, around 30 of them are participating in that segment for the first time. Therefore the event has great prospects of surpassing the record attendance of around 170 thousand visitors from 2024. That is a huge advance compared to the modest beginnings of what is today the world’s leading railway transport fair.

World.title: Exotic Indian Bananas Successfully Being Grown in Međimurje
World.content:
September the 25th, 2026 – Exotic Indian bananas are successfully being grown in Međimurje, seeing seeds turn into three thousand seedlings.

In the municipality of Štrigova, an area in the north of Međimurje known primarily for its vineyards, one of the largest plantations of Indian bananas in this part of Europe was planted a few years ago. Index reports that behind the project is the family of Ivan Žižek, who decided to grow this unusual fruit after learning that it tolerates low temperatures well and is not attacked by diseases, HRT reports.

3,000 seedlings

The Žižek family planted a plantation of Indian banana, also known as pawpaw (asimina), in the village of Banfi three years ago. Since the seedlings are expensive and they needed more than three thousand of them, they opted for a cheaper but slower route. “We obtained a larger quantity of fruit from Italy, manually extracted the seeds, processed them and put them to germinate. Luckily, everything germinated excellently so we grew the first rootstocks of asimina that way. After that I personally started grafting them,” Ivan explains.

The trees are not yet in full yield so for now the family is selling only fresh fruit. In a year or two they plan to start production of food and cosmetic products from that fruit. “A tree in full yield can give around 20 kilograms. We plan to place 20 to 30 percent on the market through retail chains, and the rest would go into the food industry – for craft breweries, jams, liqueurs and aromatic wines,” says Roman Mraz.

hail reduced the yield

This year’s plantation was also quite damaged by strong hail that hit the area in June. “Still, with some earlier varieties we noticed that the first fruit we tasted was of good quality and tasty inside,” Ivan emphasises.

The Indian banana plantation is not the only example of growing exotic crops in that area. Namely, next to the edge of the plantation of fruit that originates from North America, the Žižek family is also growing 16 pistachio trees, whose original homeland is the Middle East, and 65 feijoa bushes, a fruit species from South America.

World.title: Croatia Needs to Keep Investing in Nautical Tourism
World.content:
September the 24th, 2026 – Croatia must keep investing in its nautical tourism sector as 2.7 million overnight stays are recorded so far in 2026.

In the first eight months of this year, over 431,000 charter guests visited Croatia, who recorded more than 2.7 million overnight stays. Ana Blaskovic reports for Poslovni that Croatia must continue investing in nautical tourism in order to maintain competitiveness, while also resolving the issue of concessions that are expiring for individual marinas, it was said at the conference Nautical Tourism of Croatia 2030.

The country currently has 216 nautical tourism ports and other facilities for berthing and accommodating vessels, with almost 19 thousand berths. Minister of Maritime Affairs Oleg Butković emphasised that the key challenge remains seasonality, since the highest traffic and revenues are realised in July and August. The goal is to develop a year-round business model and additional content that would attract nautical tourists outside the main season as well.

According to his words, the Croatian Government should soon adopt decisions on the extension of concessions for individual existing concessionaires who have the documentation ready. The process, he said, is being prepared in cooperation with the ministries of tourism and finance and the European Commission. At the Croatian Chamber of Economy they emphasise that for further investments it is necessary to ensure legal certainty and a competitive business framework.

Concessionaires say they are ready to continue investing in marinas and charter, while the sector is at the same time being pressed by rising operating costs and a shortage of quality labour. The Ministry of Tourism and Sport highlights the green and digital transition as important directions of development.

World.title: Zoran Milanović Harshly Criticises “Out of Control” Croatian Prices
World.content:
September the 24th, 2026 – President Zoran Milanović has harshly criticised “out of control” Croatian prices, saying that time flies and things are getting “worse and worse”.

President Zoran Milanović is participating in the Lider conference Day of Big Plans, which is being held at the Westin hotel in Zagreb. Index reports that the conference discusses the macroeconomic and economic challenges and circumstances coming in 2027. “Time flies, and things are getting worse and worse. Not only in Croatia, but everywhere around us, things are slowly slipping out of control. The UN and the international system of collective security are being mocked by their biggest financiers,” Milanović said at the beginning, reports N1.

“the international order has ceased to exist”

“The international order has ceased to exist. Every sanction – a bilateral sanction – anyone’s, without UN verification is illegal. On the surface, the numbers have all advanced, GDP per capita, often a very deceptive piece of data about prosperity behind which great inequality is often hidden. Purchasing power parity is such that the differences aren’t too great in relation to some countries that we once looked at with envy,” the president stated.

“Average salaries aren’t small… However, what can be bought with that money? Croatian prices have completely spun out of control, we can only hope that things will start to eventually calm down,” he said. The worst thing, the president says, is that no one specific can be blamed for that situation, neither the governor, nor the finance minister, nor the prime minister, but one has to look at the surrounding countries, much larger than Croatia.

on the topic of europe

“The European Union and Europe as a continent have been in regression for the last hundred years, with flashes of progress that occurred after the great wars into which Europe dragged the whole world. Europe is in a cycle of shrinking into itself. Nothing that comes from Berlin or some other European metropolis should be taken either too seriously or not seriously,” Milanović said.

“Europe has some very serious problems with energy that it hasn’t managed to solve for decades already, but the moment that is said out loud, you are immediately labelled extreme left, extreme right, pro this, pro that, but that is not the way we can talk and plan, that is not a conversation at all,” the Croatian president clearly states. We have to build a nuclear power plant, Milanović said, adding that when one country attacks another, the whole world gets a bill to pay.

on america and iran

The president also commented on the situation between the USA and Iran. “It’s a symptom of the disease of large systems and large empires when people no longer want to sacrifice themselves for that system,” he stated.

“The European Union is not democratic and when I say that, I don’t necessarily mean that that makes it bad in itself, on;y that it is not democratic – people are appointed to the highest and most important positions by processes that are not democratic, and more and more people see and feel that and that is why more and more of them vote the way they vote,” Milanović warned.

World.title: “Revolutionary” New Croatian Road Toll System is, Of Course, Delayed
World.content:
September the 24th, 2026 – The so-called “revolutionary” new Croatian road toll system is delayed, which comes as a surprise to absolutely nobody.

Croatian Motorways still haven’t selected who will create the application and everything else needed for the upcoming Croatian road toll system. Poslovni reports that the project is worth around €160 million and we’re yet to have any idea when it will finally start functioning. All drivers on Croatian motorways should be able to drive without stopping and messing around with tolls and ENC’s as of March, but this “revolutionary” move has, of course, stalled. An unexpected problem has appeared in the development of the application into which every driver would have to enter their data and card details, reports klikni.hr.

Because of an appeal lodged by a company among whose owners is also a firm registered at the Commercial Court in Bjelovar, with its seat in Zdenci, Croatian Motorways have hit a roadblock (no pun intended). Portals with cameras are already being installed on the motorways, but the web portal, mobile app and integration data buses – that is, the part of the system with which drivers will directly interact – is still far from realisation. To make the irony greater, that part of the work is estimated at “only” €330,000 excluding VAT.

appeals, delays and issues – a true croatian saga

Let us recall, at the end of May Croatian Motorways awarded that job to a consortium of bidders consisting of the Zagreb companies Bos Projekt and Infinum and the British AMR CyberSecurity. The Zagreb company Abysalto appealed against the decision, and the State Commission for the Control of Public Procurement Procedures back at the end of July partially accepted its claims and annulled the selection decision.

HAC now has to re-evaluate the bids. According to data from the court register, Abysalto has three members of the company: the firm King ICT, Stipo Matić and the firm Novčić više. Matić is, at the same time, the president of the supervisory board of Abysalto. Novčić više is registered in the register of the Commercial Court in Bjelovar, and its seat is in Zdenci, a municipality in the east of Virovitica-Podravina County that had a mere 1,453 inhabitants when the last census was carried out. In the list of activities of that company, IT is not mentioned. It is registered, among other things, for the production of pellets, biomass and biogas, forest management, energy distribution and waste transport.

The sole founder of the company from Zdenci is King ICT, and the director is Stipo Matić, which means that the same owner appears in Abysalto both directly and through the company registered in Bjelovar. The share capital of Abysalto was increased in the middle of last year from €7,000 to €5.3 million, and in the same period part of the assets of the company Omega software was also transferred to the company.

the clock is ticking and time is running out

Time for the new Croatian road toll system of toll collection is rapidly running out. The development of the software and application takes six months, and the company responsible for implementation would like to start testing as early as January. The situation is all the more complex because even after HAC reselects the contractor a new appeal is possible, and with it further delays in the realisation of this job.

Transport Minister Oleg Butković despite the standstill claims that the system will start on time. “We’re sticking to that deadline, everything is proceeding at its own pace,” Butković said rather vaguely. From Croatian Motorways they state that all activities are being carried out according to the legal deadline, but they do not deny that it is a complex project in which the appeal deadlines in public procurement procedures must also be respected.

World.title: As Many as 40% of Croatian Retirees at Risk of Poverty
World.content:
September the 24th, 2026 – Another horrendous statistic for the country as as many as 40% of Croatian retirees are formally at risk of falling into poverty.

Just over the border in neighbouring Slovenia, 27 percent of retirees over the age of 65 are at risk of poverty, and in Norway, just nine percent are in the same category, the report states. Poslovni reports the shameful statistic that around 40 percent of Croatian retirees over the age of 65 live at risk of poverty, according to recent Eurostat data. Only Latvia and Lithuania have a higher share, while the European Union average is 19 percent.

Melita Čičak, acting director of the Pension System Directorate, warned in an interview for Dnevnik Nova TV about the difference in the length of working service between Croatia and other countries.

“All of these countries that are ahead on this list have significantly longer service; for example, in Slovenia the average service is 38.9 years, while in Croatia it’s 32 years,” she said. According to the data presented, the average pension in Croatia has risen by 113 percent since 2016 and now amounts to €764. That is laughable given that the staggering rise in the cost of living is burdening everyone, particularly retirees, who allocate a large part of their income to their most basic needs.

“Inflation always hits retirees first. We know that they’re unfortunately a social category and that they spend the largest part on healthcare, utilities, on medicines,” said economist Petar Vušković. The report also warns about the rise in heating and fuel prices, which further pressures retirees. Speaking about people remaining for a longer time in the world of work, Čičak concluded: “We haven’t yet decided to raise the age for acquiring the right to a pension like other countries, but through other mechanisms we encourage longer remaining in the world of work.”

World.title: Trans activists accuse state gender committee of bias and obstruction
World.content:
Trans activists in Estonia have accused the state gender reassignment committee of obstruction and bias, and are demanding that the committee's chair be removed.

ETV show "Pealtnägija" heard both sides of the heated dispute; the gender reassignment committee (Riiklikku soovahetuskomisjon) says its critics represent a small but vocal minority.

Appearing in the "Pealtnägija" segment which aired this week were Karmen Ott, 22, and Stephanie-Emma Zorianska, 27, both from Harju County, and Sona Kravtšenko, 26, from Ida-Viru County. All three were born as boys but had felt since childhood that this gender assignment was not right for them.

The upbringing for all three and the struggles with gender identity which accompanied this could each make for a long story of its own, "Pealtnägija" reported, but suffice to say that Stephanie, who was born into challenging circumstances and grew up in a foster family, "came out" at around the age of 15; Karmen told her parents two years ago, while Sona, whose family is devout Jehovah's Witnesses, only revealed her identity to her family last summer.

All three appeared on "Pealtnägija" under their own names and were going public for the first time, with all its associated risks. These were particularly great for Sona. Not only has her mother not accepted that the person she calls her son in fact identifies as a trans woman, but the segment will likely be the first time many in the Jehovah's Witness congregation the family belongs to will have heard about the situation.

More than that, in giving the interview, Sona says she risks being shunned by the Jehovah's Witnesses, a socially conservative sect, and even of her mother no longer speaking to her. "I do hope she will, but that risk is very real. The possibility that I'll be thrown out of my home and no one will speak to me anymore is also a very real risk."

However, the reason Sona, Karmen and Stephanie are publicly sharing their journeys is much bigger than even these personal struggles, they say – and go all the way to the committee itself.

"I think this entire process, the way it works in Estonia, is so drawn out. It is long, it is humiliating, it weighs on people who are already having a hard time, because we are a minority in Estonia. And it is clear that the whole point of this committee is not to help people, but to fob them off and waste time and simply hide them away somewhere," Stephanie said.

To understand these accusations, a detour into history is needed. While during the Soviet era such issues were taboo or even punishable as a criminal offense, just before the turn of the millennium and a few years after Estonia had restored its independence, a medical expert committee on gender reassignment was established under the auspices of the Ministry of Social Affairs. This would investigate whether to permit a person to change their gender in terms of officialdom – for instance Estonian ID codes start with a "3" if the holder is male and "4" if female, if born in the 20th century; those born from 2000 onwards similarly have a "5" (male) or "6" (female) at the start of their ID code.

Initially, the rules set up required genetic testing to prove that a person was transgender, a document signed by the minister authorizing the start of medical intervention and, finally, if desired, another appearance before the commission to change the first digit of one's personal identification code.

The committee's work was suspended for a year in 2021, and its chair also changed. The rules were then also streamlined: A psychiatrist's diagnosis that the person is transgender and one meeting with the committee have since then been sufficient to decide this; also that decision is signed off on by the committee chair rather than the minister.

The committee consists of 11 doctors and other specialists. At least three, and usually four of these attend each and every meeting. The meetings are held on the premises of the West Tallinn Central Hospital.

According to the official statistics, the number of applications for gender transition has more than quadrupled in just the past five years: From 42 applications in 2020 to 177 last year. Compared with the situation 10 years ago, however, the committee's workload has increased tenfold during that time: A decade ago there were just nine recorded gender change applications.

The committee is chaired by long-serving gynecologist and fertility specialist Kai Haldre. According to Haldre, most applicants are young trans men, ie. women seeking to become men.

The rise was in line with trends elsewhere in the world, Haldre said. "We knew that in Western Europe and elsewhere there had been a sharp spike from around 2013-2015. Gender dysphoria among teenage girls had increased so sharply that wait lines suddenly appeared in many countries, and we were also told: You'll see, you'll end up with long waiting lists of several years," Haldre said.

There is no single explanation for why the increase has been so large. A separate question is how far social media has contributed to the rise in applications. Although the committee has upped the frequency of its meetings several times, it is still struggling with the volume of work. It has the capacity to meet with around 150 applicants a year, giving an average waiting time of two years. This very fact drew criticism from the gender equality commissioner in summer this year.

Karmen cited her own case, saying that in 2024 she realized she had to do something. "So what had happened was that I put my name down for the commission, sent a letter, and then they replied that my commission appointment should be sometime in 2027. That made me very disappointed in our health care system," she said. In the end, Karmen sought help from a foreign clinic which prescribed hormone therapy for her.

Formally speaking, the committee merely confirms the diagnosis of transsexualism which had been previously made by a psychiatrist, which carries the code F64.0 under the official classification, but in practice, in many respects, gender transition cannot be carried out in Estonia without it. For example, a doctor can prescribe the hormone therapy needed for gender reassignment independently, but confirmation from the committee is nevertheless generally required. In addition, without it the population register will not change a person's personal identification code from male to female or vice versa.

Karmen nevertheless got an available commission appointment unexpectedly this spring, as well as permission to begin treatment. Sona, however, was so disheartened by the lengthy wait time that she sought treatment on her own initiative too. Stephanie meanwhile had been turned down about a decade ago on the grounds she was still a minor then; she, too, has now been on the waiting list for a lengthy period of time.

"For some time I was writing to them every month, but the replies were along the lines of: 'look, we don't have time and we can't, and, essentially, stop writing to us'. You're sent running from one place to another, and then you realize that in their eyes you're not even a person at all. By law, these people are supposed to be the ones who help, but there is zero help from them. The whole process is humiliating," Stephanie said.

Added to the humiliation is the fact that Stephanie was attacked in the Mustamäe district of Tallinn last winter, due to her appearance. While traveling to work and having applied light makeup, she noticed a young man taking pictures of her on the bus. When Stephanie remarked that it was not pleasant to be taking pictures of people, she was violently assaulted, and suffered a broken tooth.

The investigation into the assault fizzled out, and no suspect was apprehended. In the wake of the attack, however, Karmen, Sona and Stephanie set up an initiative group with like-minded people, and at the start of summer sent the ministry an extremely extensive request for clarification; the content of this questionnaire sharply criticized the medical expert committee in its current guise, and, in a short period of time, garnered 400 signatures from transgender people and their supporters.

Karmen said the most troubling issue was that under the new regulation, the committee's only requirement is for gender identity issues, yet medical professionals have said the committee should green-light procedures such as hormone XXX therapy. "You don't need to go there for hormone therapy or any other medical procedures. In practice, however, nothing has changed, as doctors still require it. We know of one specific case where a doctor refused to prescribe hormone therapy to a patient out of fear that they could go to prison as a result," Karmen said.

In addition to the long waiting times, transgender people have charged the committee with humiliating transgender people by requiring a diagnosis which implies a psychiatric illness, basing its work on outdated scientific research and being ideologically biased.

Haldre's response was that patient groups tend to develop their own "mythologies." "I've sometimes said, half-jokingly, 'you know, I'll do anything you want, but bring me an article. Bring it and show me where the evidence base is'," Haldre said, adding that the core group, which consists primarily of young people, may not understand how the medicine works or the logic behind it.

Haldre, who has fought for women's abortion rights for decades, said the nucleus of the critics consists not only of young transgender people, but of people who often have complicated family backstories, not to mention strong views. For example, Stephanie bore a sign at this year's Tallinn Pride which effectively told the committee to go to hell. One anonymous letter from an activist, however, was so threatening that Haldre felt she had to contact the police.

Another source of frustration for activists is that since obtaining the necessary treatment via official channels takes years, many young people turn to foreign pharmaceutical intermediaries, or even run the risk of obtaining hormones on the black market.

At the same time, doctors say they never refuse to prescribe any medication simply out of small-mindedness.

"If medical intervention is needed, if an endocrinologist assumes such great responsibility, including, so to speak, with off-label drugs or medications which are not intended for this and have never been studied for it, then they need broader confirmation. That is also the case from the standpoint of medical ethics, not to mention surgery in this field," Haldre explained.

The same core group recently began calling themselves "Transrinne" ("Transfront"), which "Pealtnägija" said was a signal move. They have authored pages of analyses and appeals, suggesting that the committee and its chair are biased. Among other things, several activists secretly recorded their appointments with the committee, to demonstrate what they say are regressive and irrelevant questions being asked there. One of the clearer criticisms is that the committee does not follow World Health Organization (WHO) principles in determining whether someone is transgender. They also criticize Haldre for links to organizations that they consider transphobic.

What particularly offends those involved is that being transgender was historically speaking classified as a psychiatric disorder, and even to this day is classified under the code F64 in Estonia's system, denoting a disorder. Internationally, however, it is no longer considered a disorder – for instance in the U.S. gender identity disorder was struck off the American Psychiatric Association's diagnostic manual in 2013; WHO officially removed being transgender from its list of mental disorders at the start of 2022. According to Haldre, the classification issue in Estonia is an administrative one and not a regressive one.

"Pealtnägija" communicated with Haldre on a continual basis in preparation for its reportage, both by phone and in writing. Clearly disturbed by the accusations, Haldre repeatedly recalled that the committee's previous chair, Imre Rammul, had stepped down partly because of similar criticism. Social Affairs Minister Dr. Karmen Joller (Reform), who "Pealtnägija" asked for comment, also warned that doctors should not be attacked personally. "There are few competent specialists, and involving them is made more difficult by the fact that committee members have come under intense pressure," Joller said.

There is, however, one thing the parties agree on: that the regulations could be changed so that the committee would no longer have to consider whether or not to allow the first digit of a person's personal identification code to be changed. The gender equality commissioner, Christian Veske, said he supports this idea.

"To my mind, this is wholly problematic. A medical committee, as the name infers, should deal with health-related, medical procedures, as it were. To then give that medical committee an additional function, on which a transgender person's ability to bring their documents into line with their identity hinges, is a major issue for me, and I personally consider it unfair," Veske said.
