World.title: China Misses Basketball Medal in 2nd-Worst Asian Games Finish
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019050/China Misses Basketball Medal in 2nd-Worst Asian Games Finish
World.content:
China’s men’s basketball team has suffered its second-worst defeat in its history at the Asian Games, calling into question the coach’s abilities and the team’s training methods.

On Sunday, China lost 70-79 to Iran, two days after it lost 77-97 to Japan, host of this year’s Games, its second failure to reach the finals and its largest-margin loss in men’s basketball at the tournament. The country finished fourth, one place higher than at the 2014 Asian Games in Incheon — its worst result ever.

China has claimed eight Asian Games titles, with its most recent gold coming in 2018. Since then, China has failed to win the title.

Head coach Guo Shiqiang said the team fatigued toward the end of the tournament, noting that only nine players were available for rotation partway through the Games due to injuries. He also said the team’s younger players lacked major tournament experience and had struggled to play consistently, and that “the team had failed to execute its pregame tactical plans.”

China’s unusually long training and competition period this summer has been a focus of criticism. The team spent around 140 days in camp before the Games, domestic media reported. Internationally, teams typically spend only one to three weeks at training camps, widely considered to be intensive and demanding.

Criticism has also centered on Guo, 51, a former starting point guard for China’s national team who began coaching the team in 2006 and became head coach in 2009. After leaving the team to coach locally in 2010, he returned as head coach in 2024, and led China to a runner-up finish at the 2025 FIBA Asia Cup.

Critics have questioned Guo’s tactical approach. Against Iran, China’s defense focused heavily on protecting the net rather than the court’s three-point line, leaving space for their opponents to take jump shots and make three-pointers. The team also struggled to secure rebounds in both its matches against Iran and Japan.

Others criticized Guo’s offensive strategy, arguing that he relied too heavily on the backcourt, that players became isolated at crucial moments, and that his in-game player selection was overly conservative.

The defeats have prompted broader discussion about whether China’s traditional approach of requiring athletes to spend a large portion of the year in training camps can keep pace with changes in the sport, particularly the increasing emphasis on spacing, perimeter shooting, and shooting efficiency.

“Everyone on our team has worked extremely hard this summer,” Guo said in a post-game interview with domestic media. “Every member of the Chinese men’s basketball team has put in a tremendous amount of effort.” His comments sparked widespread backlash online, with many arguing that the team’s prolonged exhaustion from training camp caused the poor results.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.title: Three Sisters Cross China to See What Keeps Their Family Apart
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019040/Three Sisters Cross China to See What Keeps Their Family Apart
World.content:
YUNNAN, Southwest China – Growing up in a remote mountain village in Yunnan province near China’s southwestern border with Vietnam, Zhou Lifang had only ever seen clouds from below. In late July, on her first flight, the 16-year-old saw them from above.

“I thought clouds were transparent because (my) textbook said clouds are made of water vapor,” she tells Sixth Tone. “But I didn’t expect them to be like a white wall. The clouds you see from the ground are in pieces, but from the sky they are one big mass.”

Lifang and her 14-year-old twin sisters, Zhou Lixin and Zhou Liyi, were among 145 students from Yunnan taking part in “Mountain-Sea Bond,” a four-day program in Shanghai that included reunions with parents working in the city.

The sisters are among China’s “left-behind children,” who remain in their home communities while their parents migrate for work, often placed in the care of grandparents or other relatives. China had 9 million such children in 2022, according to the 2023 Rural Education Development Report.

Born in Kunming, Yunnan’s provincial capital, the sisters have lived for more than a decade with their grandparents in a village in Malipo, a county in the Wenshan Zhuang and Miao Autonomous Prefecture roughly 400 kilometers away by road. Their parents, Zhou Yuneng and Zhang Shunfen, now work in Shanghai, where Zhou drives for a ride-hailing service and Zhang sorts groceries at a supermarket warehouse.

Smartphones have long allowed Zhou and Zhang to remain involved in their daughters’ lives from afar. They check in, offer advice, and try to mediate fights between the sisters. But they can see and hear only what the girls choose to share, and cannot always persuade them to talk.

Asked how well she knows her daughters now, the mother says they all like drawing, then pauses. “Close to zero,” she admits. “I don’t really know what they like anymore.”

After more than a decade of parenting largely by phone, Zhou and Zhang would spend two weeks sharing a 20-square-meter room in Shanghai with their daughters, their longest stretch together since the girls went to live with their grandparents.

On her own

Before the sisters left early that morning, their grandmother, Kuang Tianzhen, 64, tucked 50 yuan ($7) into each girl’s pocket, twice their usual weekly allowance. Rumors of scams in their border village had made her uneasy about the journey.

“Where will you stay in Wenshan?” she asks, the prefecture’s seat. “This is all reliable, right?”

After the neighbor’s car carrying them disappeared from view, their grandfather, Zhou Shucheng, 72, sat brooding outside the house for at least half an hour, staring down the rain-soaked road and gently petting the tabby cat his granddaughters had adopted.

Four hours later, the sisters arrived at a hotel in Wenshan for a predeparture meeting with participants from surrounding villages and counties. They would spend the night there, then continue to Kunming the next day for the flight to Shanghai.

“Are you Zhou Lifang’s parents? Have your three children arrived yet?” a trip organizer asks over the phone.

“I am Zhou Lifang,” she replies. “We’re already here in the lobby.”

Lifang was the only child in the tour’s WeChat group; everyone else was a parent. She had followed instructions about when and where to meet and confirmed the arrangements for all three sisters.

Inside the hotel’s meeting hall, grandparents sit beside children waiting to register while organizers address the crowd from the stage.

Elders are heard asking “Where should I sign?” and “Do I fill this part in?” At the line marked “guardian,” some pause, unsure whether to write their own names or those of the children’s parents in Shanghai.

One grandmother checks her granddaughter’s schoolbag, rebraids her hair, and films her on her phone. When organizers ask the adults to leave, she goes downstairs, then turns back and slips inside again.

Lifang sat quietly on one side of a wide pillar, her twin sisters on the other. Unlike many of the children around them, the sisters had arrived without a grandparent.

The sisters began attending boarding school around age 6. When home, they helped with farm work and tended the family’s wood-burning stove. Before they had smartphones of their own, they called their parents using their grandmother’s phone or a public telephone at school.

At 12, Lifang went alone to a hospital near her school for a tuberculosis screening while her mother guided her through the process over a video call.

“Sometimes I felt pretty helpless,” she says. “I would ask adults passing by for help and follow their directions.” On other visits, her mother advised her to follow a classmate who knew the hospital better.

When the village prepared to allocate plots of collectively owned farmland, Lifang took the call and passed the information to her grandmother. During school vacations, she tidied the twins’ room and called her mother when she needed money or help handling her sisters.

Her grandfather divides farm work and allowances equally among the three girls. But when they argue, he tells Lifang, “You’re the older sister. You’re the eldest. You should give way to them.”

The twins usually side with each other against Lifang, and a stray remark can set off a fierce argument. From Shanghai, Zhang tells her, “If someone hits you, whether it’s your sisters or your schoolmates, you should hit them back.”

Lifang sometimes goes into a room and locks the door instead. “Then they can’t come in,” she says. “They’ll play a game, and after that, everything will be fine.”

She has repeatedly asked her parents for a room of her own. When she wants to be alone, she sometimes sits on a swing her father built on the rooftop. On a nearby window, smiling faces the sisters traced with their fingers years ago remain visible beneath layers of dust.

“Sometimes I wish I could be the younger sister, not the older one,” Lifang says.

Close to zero

When the twins moved to the village at 3, they sometimes cried for their mother. Their grandmother would carry one of them outside and point toward Kunming, along the road winding over the mountain.

“I’d hold her for a while and tell her that her mother was there,” Kuang recalls. “Then she’d stop crying. They’re good girls, easy to coax.”

Their father had tried to leave the twins in the village a year earlier. He drove them there when they were 2, but couldn’t bear to leave them and took them back to Kunming.

By 2015, private kindergarten in Kunming cost 1,800 yuan ($250) per child per month, meaning fees for all three would have consumed 5,400 yuan of the couple’s roughly 6,000-yuan monthly income.

The family was also hundreds of thousands of yuan in debt after rebuilding the village house and paying hospital bills for the grandfather and one of the twins, who had spent several weeks in neonatal intensive care with meningitis. Because the girls lacked local household registration, or hukou, enrolling them in Kunming’s public schools was difficult.

For the next decade, their parents remained in Kunming, making the six-hour drive to the village every month or two for a weekend or holiday.

Years of installing wood floors damaged both of Zhou’s knees. The work required him to squat and sometimes kneel. “After every shift, I would get off my scooter and walk stiff-legged,” he says. In 2025, chronic arthritis forced him out of construction, and the couple moved to Shanghai, approximately 2,500 kilometers away.

When the sisters missed their parents, Lifang says, they video-called them. “Mom and Dad would always say they only had a few more days of work and would be back to see us soon.”

Over time, however, the girls stopped asking when their parents would return for good. “They used to say, ‘Mom, I miss you,’” Zhang says. “Since I moved to Shanghai, I hardly ever hear that anymore.”

In 2023, the couple installed a camera at the gate of the village house, primarily for safety. It lets them check on the grandfather and see when the girls return from school. They chose not to install one in the girls’ bedroom.

“I just feel that girls, after all, need some privacy,” Zhang says.

The mother also bought her daughters smartphones with large screens to make video calls easier and placed few restrictions on how they used them.

“Kids today are different from us back then,” she says. “Digital devices aren’t just for studying anymore. They have access to so many things on their phones. I don’t restrict them too much.”

The twins often decline their parents’ calls or hang up after a few sentences. Sometimes, one answers while playing on the computer, points the phone’s camera at the ceiling, and keeps playing.

Asked why, one of the twins says, “Just because I don’t have the patience.”

Every time this happens, Zhang just smiles and rarely lets her temper show.

“I feel that if I push too hard, I lose the right to speak,” she says. “I’m afraid they’ll think, ‘You didn’t raise me. You weren’t there when I was small, and now you want to tell me what to do.’ So sometimes I can’t be too direct. I have to be careful how I put it.”

When Lifang and the twins argue, the parents try to settle their disputes by phone, usually scolding both sides. Each girl comes away believing that she alone has been blamed.

“That’s because of the distance and what a phone call can’t do,” the mother says. “If it were face to face, a few sentences would clear it up.”

Unlike the twins, Lifang video calls Zhang almost every day and has her saved in her phone as “Dear Mom.” But she seldom calls Zhou. “Dad is quite busy driving day and night, so I rarely call him,” Lifang says. “I’m afraid of interrupting his work. I feel like I’m not close to him because he’s too strict.”

Even with Zhang, much of Lifang’s life remains outside their conversations. At school, some classmates seek her out for tarot readings, calling her “Master Zhou.” Others mock the way she speaks, comparing it to barking, and give her insulting nicknames.

Lifang spends nearly every break between classes drawing. She draws when she feels happy, angry, or embarrassed, and says it helps her relax. She keeps one sketchbook, which she rarely shows others, for times when she feels low.

One drawing shows a figure with its arms crossed and an X over its mouth. In the background, Lifang has written, “What if speaking is also a fault?”

“All I can do is draw them as ugly monsters,” Lifang says.

She closes the sketchbook.

“There are some words I cannot show,” she says. “Cannot.”

In another sketchbook, Lifang has created Yumeng, a cheerful girl from the sea who grows increasingly troubled as she tries to save a city from destruction. “Why should I, who am already living such a miserable life, have to save others?” the character asks.

Lifang also has a circle of friends her parents know little about. She met them through a nonviolent multiplayer game she describes as “healing.” Unlike the competitive games her sisters prefer, it lets players explore different settings, build homes and farms together, and talk.

“Besides my best friend at school, they are the most important friends in my life,” Lifang says.

Before boarding the flight to Shanghai, Lifang sent them an update: “I’m boarding now, so I can’t reply to your messages. I’ll send you some amazing pictures later.”

Under one roof

Two days after reuniting privately with their parents, all three sisters stepped onto a stage in matching pale green T-shirts and brand-new canvas shoes their mother had prepared before their arrival. “Mountain-Sea Bond” organizers had chosen the family for a letter reading at the Aug. 1 reunion ceremony.

Standing between the twins, Lifang began reading, with Zhang beside her daughters and Zhou watching from the audience.

“Before, I never understood why you were always away and could not be with us,” she reads. “Only on this trip, after coming to Shanghai where you live and work, did I truly understand how hard you work and how much you have given.”

When Lifang finishes, the audience applauds, and Zhou begins to sob. As the sisters come down from the stage, he pulls the twins close and continues crying until his face turns red. The twins’ eyes fill with tears.

“You don’t see your children often,” he says after regaining his composure. “And then suddenly you realize they have grown up all at once.”

After the ceremony, the family go to Jing’an Joy City, a Shanghai mall the sisters had long wanted to visit for its anime shops. Lifang taught herself to draw manga and now takes commissions through an app from clients across China, earning several dozen yuan per drawing. She hopes to attend one of China’s leading art academies, though she usually tells adults she wants to become a civil servant like her older cousin.

The program ended that day, but the sisters remained in Shanghai for the rest of their two-week stay. All five shared a one-room, 20-square-meter unit with a private bathroom and an induction cooker in one corner.

Zhou and Zhang had moved there at the beginning of the year, hoping the girls might eventually join them in Shanghai. Before the trip, Lifang had assumed the move had made her parents’ lives easier.

“Now that Mom and Dad work in Shanghai, the conditions are better, and the work is a little easier,” she says.

Zhou no longer installs floors, but his ride-hailing shifts often last at least 12 hours. “If you work less, you can’t make enough,” he says. “You drive for 11 or 12 hours, come back, charge the car, make something to eat, then sleep. The next day, you get up and repeat it. That’s the job.”

Zhang works similar hours sorting groceries at a supermarket warehouse and has no regular weekends. Sometimes they go an entire day without seeing each other awake; one leaves breakfast behind before the other gets up.

During the visit, Zhou took another week off from driving, while Zhang continued working. The parents would not allow the girls to go out alone in an unfamiliar city.

Before leaving Yunnan, Lifang says, “I want to help my mom sort groceries at the supermarket warehouse.” In Shanghai, she often accompanied Zhang to work, while the twins remained in the apartment.

One night, Zhang returned late from work and began tidying the room. One of the twins ran over and hugged her.

“Mom, I feel like you’ve worked so hard,” Zhang recalls her saying. The girl then began to cry.

“I feel like she’s really growing up,” Zhang says.

Despite all five sharing one room, the sisters argued less during the visit. Disputes that had been difficult to settle over the phone rarely became as heated in person, Zhang says.

Even before his daughters arrived, Zhou had been considering returning to Yunnan after another year in Shanghai.

“Whatever happens, I should go back and do whatever work I can, as long as we are by their side,” he says.

But Zhou has taken no steps toward moving and cannot say what work he might find near the village. Its karst terrain leaves little room to expand farmland, and 796 of its 2,172 residents work elsewhere, according to a village official.

Zhou and Zhang each earn about 8,000 yuan ($1,120) a month in Shanghai, though Zhou can make more by taking fewer days off. Returning would mean giving up the income that had drawn them farther from their daughters.

During their stay in Shanghai, the sisters called their grandmother about once a week. One day at a café, a blue parrot perched on Lifang’s shoulder. She has long wanted one like it, and blue is her favorite color. Lifang immediately called Kuang on video.

“Grandma, look what’s on my shoulder,” Lifang says. “Isn’t it impressive?”

“Behave yourself,” Kuang replies. “Where are the twins?”

“They went with Mom to work.”

“When will you come back?” Kuang asks. “How are you getting home?”

“Dad says he’ll drive us back next weekend,” Lifang says. “My school starts early.”

Editor: Apurva.

The Shanghai Small and Medium-sized Enterprises Technology Talent Introduction Service Center has organized six such reunions since 2024. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.title: China Tells E-Commerce Apps to Stop Selling Loans
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019049/China Tells E-Commerce Apps to Stop Selling Loans
World.content:
As young Chinese increasingly borrow through food-delivery and e-commerce apps, Chinese payment institutions, apart from banks, will no longer be allowed to list financial products such as loans and credit services among payment options at checkout, according to a new national policy set to take effect later this month.

The new measures, announced in April by the People’s Bank of China and seven other government departments, will take effect on Sept. 30. The rules also require companies to clearly state when they are selling financial products and bar bundled “buy now, pay later” financial services as a default option at checkout.

Companies must also direct users to financial institutions’ own platforms to purchase credit products, rather than third-party platforms; provide prominent risk reminders that must be read before purchase; and must either provide an option for customers to turn off algorithmic recommendations or algorithms that do not take into account their personal characteristics. Only financial institutions and certain authorized accounts may market financial products online.

In recent years, platforms ranging from food delivery and e-commerce to video streaming and online travel have begun offering installment-payment options at checkout, making it easier for consumers to access credit without undergoing traditional bank credit assessment or acquiring a credit card.

These services are usually provided by the platforms themselves or through third-party financial institutions, and encourage users to access loans through default selections, prominent placement of credit options, or discounts tied to activating consumer-credit products.

Sixth Tone found that on Black Cat Complaint, a mediation service launched by tech company Sina, hundreds of thousands of customer complaints about such credit services have been lodged. Complaints ranged from credit services being activated without customers’ knowledge, difficulties canceling services, disputed interest charges, and aggressive debt collection and personal information leaks when payments were not met.

“The core purpose of the new rules is to draw a clear boundary between payment tools and credit and wealth-management products, while better protecting consumers’ rights to know and to choose,” Dong Ximiao, director of the Shanghai Institution for Finance & Development, told domestic media.

As of Friday, the topic had garnered more than 42 million views on microblogging platform Weibo, with many users expressing support for the policy.

On Tuesday, customer service representatives from e-commerce platforms including Alipay, Meituan, Douyin, and JD.com told domestic media that their per-month payment plans will remain available.

Several platforms have begun to clearly identify credit service providers and separate credit services from regular payment methods. For example, Alipay’s online consumer credit service Ant Credit Pay is now listed under a separate “Credit” section.

However, some platforms still place credit options alongside or above regular payment methods. A check by Sixth Tone on Monday found that when placing a food delivery order on Meituan and Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, credit-related options still appear alongside regular payment channels. Default selections and discounts encouraging their use also remained.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: iStock/VCG)

World.title: The risks in Marcos’ 2027 P7.2-trillion ‘people-centered’ spending bet
World.content:
With over a third of the budget pre-committed to debt burden and mandatory local government allotments, execution is everything

This P7.2 trillion 2027 record-breaking spending bet is billed by government as the “People-Centered Growth for an Inclusive and Resilient Future.” Essentially, this spending plan is about 6% higher than the national expenditure program (NEP) of 2026 and represents roughly 21.7% of the country’s projected gross domestic product (GDP).

More crucially, this spending plan is also financially crafted to serve as both a representative development blueprint and political statement of President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr.’s (PBBM) administration before the 2028 presidential elections.

But beneath the bold promises of social transformation of this record-breaking spending plan lies a complex fiscal matrix that balances ambitious social expenditures against a highly constrained financing environment.

As claimed, the Marcos administration’s allocation strategy explicitly prioritizes areas designed to directly impact the daily lives of the masses. Branded as a “people-centered” financial paradigm, the Social Services sector captures the lion’s share of the budget at P2.456 trillion.

Within this pillar, basic and higher education receive a combined budget allocation of P1.326 trillion, with “Basic Education” cornering an allotment of P976 billion or 13.55% of total budget. This massive investment is a response to both chronic classroom shortages and the need for structural educational reforms.

The healthcare system has an allocation of P358.8 billion funneled into the Department of Health (DOH), specialty hospitals, and the state insurance program, PhilHealth. Concurrently, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) is given P241.6 billion to sustain targeted cash transfers and social safety nets for vulnerable populations.

Beyond direct human development, public spending aimed at fueling long-term economic momentum got an allocation of P1.833 trillion. This includes a budget allocation of P1.467 trillion specifically earmarked for infrastructure investments, with P644 billion notably passing through the Department of Public Works and Highways.

A significant sub-allocation within public works is dedicated to climate resilience and flood control, a vital pivot following severe monsoon and storm disasters that triggered national corruption scandals over infrastructure integrity.

Food security is strengthened by investing P276.57 million into agriculture and land reform to protect consumers from unstable food prices.

Ironically, the proposed 2027 agricultural budget falls short of providing a meaningful incentive package. It remains highly inadequate given that the agri-food economy accounts for 33% of GDP and supports 38% of overall livelihoods, according to data from Oxford Economics.

Funding plan

While the spending side paints a picture of robust public investment, the source of financing reveals a narrower, more precarious fiscal landscape. The government anticipates generating P5.21 trillion in revenues for 2027. Unfortunately, this is P1.99 trillion (or 27.64%) short of what is needed to pay for the record-breaking budget.

This mismatch creates a projected P1.69-trillion fiscal deficit, which is about 5.1% of the country’s economic output or GDP. To bridge this gap and cover maturing obligations, the government is leaning heavily on a P3.3-trillion gross borrowing program.

The financing strategy of the budget is met with alarm from public finance experts and opposition lawmakers, noting that nearly a quarter of the entire spending program is effectively debt-funded. However, to tactically minimize exposure to global currency fluctuations and geopolitical shocks, the government is resorting to a conservative 72:28 borrowing mix. This means approximately 72% will be sourced domestically via Treasury bonds and bills, while the remaining 28% will come from international markets and foreign project loans.

While this domestic bias safeguards the state from external shocks, it means that the country’s cumulative outstanding debt is projected to spiral to a record P21.48 trillion by the end of 2027. Consequently, the mandatory payment of interest and principal or debt servicing has become a massive structural drag, consuming a staggering P1.14 trillion or 15.9% of the total budget, leaving the government with very tight discretionary fiscal room.

In summary, the 2027 budget is an ambitious attempt to accelerate economic growth while shielding ordinary citizens from global economic headwinds. Funding education, health, and climate infrastructure is undeniably the right path toward sustainable human capital development. However, the structural reality of the budget reminds us that populist, “people-centered” expenditure is only as sustainable as its financing.

With over a third of the budget pre-committed to debt burden and mandatory local government allotments, execution is everything. If the government fails to eliminate corruption in infrastructure procurement and cannot significantly boost tax revenues, the P7.2-trillion budget risks burying future generations under a mountain of debt rather than lifting them into prosperity.

The takeaway

The 2027 revenue framework of the budget is built on a set of core economic growth forecasts and macroeconomic assumptions that carry significant structural risks. The foundation of this multi-trillion-peso framework reveals a clear tension between optimistic state targets and a more fragile economic reality.

The government based its revenue targets on an assumed 5% to 6% GDP growth rate. While faster growth boosts tax collections, achieving this target faces major hurdles. The Congressional Policy and Budget Research Department (CPBRD) warns that the economy is on weaker footing due to low investment, shrinking household spending, and a late-2026 slowdown. If growth misses expectations, as it did in early 2026, revenues will drop, automatically widening the budget deficit.

Also, the structural design of the budget signals a shift toward slower fiscal consolidation. Rather than pursuing aggressive debt reduction, the administration is prioritizing short-term economic growth. This is evident in downgraded medium-term revenue expectations, which Fitch Ratings notes were lowered to 15.5% of GDP from the original 16.5% target outlined in the Medium-Term Fiscal Framework (MTFF).

Without major new tax measures, the government is relying on enhanced enforcement and digitization initiatives by the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) to boost annual collections by 8%. However, CPBRD data indicate that the overall national tax effort will likely flatten out at around 14.6% of GDP. This stagnation leaves the state highly vulnerable to revenue shortfalls if modernization efforts yield slow results.

Likewise, the entire revenue framework assumes that inflation will stabilize within a predictable target band, keeping consumer prices and interest rates steady. This stability remains highly vulnerable to both internal and external shocks. Lawmakers recognize that volatile global fuel prices, domestic agricultural disruptions, and geopolitical tensions, such as conflicts involving major global powers, could quickly upset these calculations. Continued inflationary pressures or a weaker Philippine peso present a dual risk: they erode domestic consumer spending, which is the primary driver of Philippine GDP, while simultaneously driving up the import costs of essential fuel and raw materials.

Finally, to bridge the widening gap between traditional tax collections and the P5.21-trillion goal, the framework relies heavily on non-tax revenues, specifically an aggressive P101.5-billion government asset privatization target.

Policy institutions like the Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) have raised concerns over this strategy, pointing out a lack of public clarity regarding which state assets will actually be sold. Furthermore, relying on lump-sum asset sales serves as a temporary fiscal band-aid. It offers a one-time cash injection that cannot sustainably fund recurring national debt servicing or mandatory state operations over the long term. – Rappler.com

World.title: Alex Eala suffers surprise Singapore Open exit as world No. 180 Russian scores shocker
World.content:
FRUSTRATED. Alex Eala in action for the Philippines at the 2026 Singapore Open.

The defeat marks the first time Alex Eala, currently the world No. 18, loses to a player ranked outside the top 100 since she broke into the top 50

MANILA, Philippines – Alex Eala used to be the one pulling off upsets, but on Thursday, September 24, she found herself on the receiving end.

Eala suffered a surprise exit from the Singapore Open after a stunning 4-6, 7-5, 6-3 defeat to world No. 180 Tatiana Prozorova of Russia in the round of 16 at Centre Court of the OCBC Arena on Thursday, September 24.

Seeded second, Eala looked poised to reach the quarterfinals after racing to a 4-2 lead in the second set, only to drop 11 of the final 15 games as Prozorova secured the biggest win of her career.

The loss marked the first time Eala, currently the world No. 18, lost to a player ranked outside the top 100 since she broke into the top 50 in November 2025.

Most of the fans who packed Centre Court expected Eala to cruise to the last eight, especially after she reached the third round of the US Open earlier this September.

And Prozorova’s track record hardly hinted at her capacity for a shocker as she was making her first appearance in the round of 16 of a WTA 500 tournament. She has also made a Grand Slam main draw just once.

The 22-year-old Russian, however, defied the odds.

“Wow, I just did it,” said Prozorova. “I just believed in myself ’til the end. I knew that she will fight. I will also fight ’til the end. That was what I did and it worked.”

Eala even grabbed a 3-2 lead in the deciding set after breaking Prozorova, but the Russian hit her stride and reeled off the next four games to earn the right to face China’s Wang Xinyu in the quarterfinals.

Prozorova fired 52 winners, including a forehand that sailed past Eala and wrapped up the marathon match in 3 hours and 9 minutes.

Coming off a two-week break after the US Open, Eala produced just 24 winners, although she tallied fewer unforced errors, 52-63.

Eala can shift her focus to the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, where she is expected to contend for the women’s singles crown following her bronze finish in the 2023 edition in Hangzhou, China.

With the likes of world No. 1 Elena Rybakina of Kazakhstan, No. 17 Naomi Osaka of Japan, and defending champion Zheng Qinwen of China skipping the continental showpiece, Eala enters the tournament as a leading contender for the gold medal. – Rappler.com

World.title: Unbeaten Gilas 3×3 teams reach Asian Games semis after contrasting wins
World.content:
DOWN BUT NOT OUT. Kacey dela Rosa in action for Gilas Women 3x3 in the 2026 Asian Games.

Gilas Women breeze past Singapore, while Gilas Men survive Chinese Taipei as they move within a win of giving the Philippines its first Asian Games medal in 3x3 basketball

MANILA, Philippines – Gilas Pilipinas’ 3×3 teams inched closer to Asian Games medals as the men’s and women’s squads both stayed unbeaten and advanced to the semifinals on Thursday, September 24.

Gilas Women continued their dominant ways after a swift 22-12 win over Singapore in the quarterfinals at the Kinjo Futo Station Square Venue in Nagoya, Japan.

Kennan Ka put up 7 points and 9 rebounds, while Amyah Espano delivered 7 points and 4 rebounds, including the two-pointer that sealed the win for the Filipinas with over two minutes to spare.

Singapore led 7-5 with seven minutes left before the Philippines rode on a finishing 17-5 run.

Kacey dela Rosa also shone with 6 points and 3 rebounds as Gilas Women preserved their perfect record after sweeping Group C with convincing wins over Mongolia, Macau, and Malaysia.

While their female counterparts cruised to the semifinals, Gilas Men survived a thriller, hacking out a 21-19 win over Chinese Taipei.

Luis Pablo churned out 6 points and 6 rebounds in the win that saw the Filipinos fight back from a 17-18 deficit with a little over a minute remaining.

Doy Dungo put the Philippines in the front seat with a gutsy two pointer, 19-18, but a technical free throw allowed the Taiwanese to pull level at 19-19.

Koji Buenaflor scored on a putback to regain the upper hand for Gilas Men before Pablo sealed the win with a drive to the hoop as Chinese Taipei bungled its attempt to steal the victory, missing three straight shots from beyond the arc.

Nic Cabañero topscored for the Philippines with 8 points, Dungo supplied 5 points and 3 rebounds, while Buenaflor added 2 points and 10 rebounds.

Like the women’s crew, Gilas Men kept their record spotless after beating Mongolia, Sri Lanka, and Kazakhstan in Group A.

Gilas Women tangle with Thailand, while Gilas Women battle South Korea in the semifinals on Friday, September 25.

A win by either team will secure the Philippines its first-ever Asian Games medal in 3×3 basketball. – Rappler.com

World.title: Tropical Storm Queenie expected to stay far from Philippine landmass
World.content:
While Tropical Storm Queenie (Surigae) won't directly affect the Philippines, its trough or extension could trigger scattered rain and thunderstorms

MANILA, Philippines – Tropical Storm Queenie (Surigae) is expected to remain far from land and will not have a direct effect on any part of the Philippines, although its trough or extension is causing some rain in portions of the country.

The tropical storm had entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) at 7 am on Thursday, September 24. It is the country’s 17th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for September.

As of 4 pm, Queenie was located 1,205 kilometers east of Northern Luzon, moving northwest at 25 kilometers per hour (km/h).

So far, it still has maximum sustained winds of 75 km/h and gustiness of up to 90 km/h. But it may intensify into a severe tropical storm on Friday, September 25, and into a typhoon by Sunday, September 27.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) expects Queenie to generally move west northwest until Friday, before turning north northeast by Sunday. Its exit from PAR could happen by Monday morning or early afternoon, September 28.

While Queenie won’t directly affect the country, its trough or extension could trigger scattered rain and thunderstorms in Mindanao, the Negros Island Region, Aklan, Iloilo, Guimaras, and Siquijor, as well as isolated rain showers or thunderstorms in the rest of the Visayas and Bicol, on Thursday evening.

Strong to gale-force gusts may also hit Davao Oriental, Davao Occidental, and Sarangani in the next two days, still due to the trough of the tropical storm.

Other parts of the country have generally fair weather, with just localized thunderstorms.

The southwest monsoon or habagat is already winding down. The transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan could start within the next couple of weeks, according to PAGASA Weather Specialist John Manalo. – Rappler.com

World.title: Gilas Women miss Asian Games semis after loss to Chinese Taipei
World.content:
DRIVE. Afril Bernardino in action for Gilas Women in the 2026 Asian Games.

Afril Bernardino leads all scorers, but her effort goes for naught as Gilas Women crash out of the Asian Games quarterfinals for the second time in a row

MANILA, Philippines – For the second straight Asian Games, Gilas Women missed out on a breakthrough final four appearance.

The Filipinas’ run ended at the hands of Chinese Taipei as they absorbed an 83-71 loss in the quarterfinals at the Aichi International Arena in Nagoya, Japan, on Thursday, September 24.

Veteran forward Afril Bernardino delivered a game-high 23 points to go with 7 rebounds and 2 steals, but her effort went for naught in the defeat that saw Gilas Women play catchup from almost start to finish.

Although the Philippines enjoyed a 5-0 start off a Bernardino three-pointer and a Camille Malagar bucket, the Taiwanese ended the opening quarter on a 15-4 run and never trailed the rest of the way.

Janine Pontejos added 12 points, Stefani Berberabe put up 12 points and 4 assists, while Kent Pastrana finished with 11 points, 4 rebounds, and 3 steals for the Filipinas, who suffered the same fate as their 2023 campaign.

In the 2023 edition in Hangzhou, China, Gilas Women also advanced to the quarterfinals but got clobbered by South Korea.

Gilas Women missed the usual production of naturalized player Elizabeth Means, who tallied just 4 points and 3 rebounds after averaging 15.7 points, 5.7 rebounds, and 3.7 steals in the group stage.

Young center Hsiao Yu-wen dominated for Chinese Taipei with a 14-point, 17-rebound double-double, while Huang Ling-chuan and Han Ya-en chimed in 13 and 11 points, respectively.

Bunched in Group B, Gilas Women compiled a 2-1 record after blowing out Kazakhstan, 86-58, and Hong Kong, 90-73, before they fell to 2023 runner-up Japan in an 89-67 loss.

The Scores

Chinese Taipei 83 – Hsiao 14, Huang L. 13, Han 11, Lin Y. 10, Peng H. 9, Chen 7, Peng S. 6, Huang H. 5, Cheng 5, Lin W. 3, Lin T. 0.

Philippines 71 – Bernardino 23, Pontejos 12, Berberabe 12, Pastrana 11, Means 4, Yam 4, Malagar 3, Pingol 2, Surada 0, Del Carmen 0, Joson 0, Clarin 0.

Quarters: 15-9, 42-34, 65-56, 83-71.

– Rappler.com

World.title: For Pope Leo, the risk of an AI apocalypse is a major concern
World.content:
VATICAN AND AI. Pope Leo looks on on the day of the weekly general audience in St. Peter's Square at the Vatican, on September 23, 2026.

Pope Leo has raised the possible dangers of AI development frequently throughout his 16-month-old papacy and first discussed the issue publicly on his third day in office

VATICAN CITY – The Vatican warned about the risk of an apocalypse spurred by artificial intelligence years before major American firms sounded the alarm at the United Nations Security Council on Wednesday, September 23 — a concern that Pope Leo is placing at the heart of his papacy.

Leo, who in May called on world leaders for global rules to oversee the industry, renewed his warnings about AI at a Vatican meeting on Thursday, September 24, and is expected to do so again on Friday, September 25, in a speech at the Paris headquarters of the UN’s culture and education body, UNESCO.

“This is not happening on day zero for the Holy See,” Rev. Paolo Benanti, a leading Vatican advisor on AI issues, told Reuters, referring to recent calls for a slowdown that have been endorsed by the CEOs of AI firms Anthropic, OpenAI and xAI, among others.

“The transformative power of AI…could produce a magnitude of societal changes that are very hard to predict,” said Benanti, an Italian academic who recently took part in the AI summit hosted by Britain’s King Charles.

The priest said he could not reveal details about the contents of the summit’s confidential discussions.

In a speech to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences on Thursday, Leo said AI can benefit humanity, but it has introduced “new dangers to security and international peace.” He urged global leaders to “govern wisely” in overseeing the technology.

Cardinal: The future of humanity is at stake

Leo, the first US-born pope, has raised the possible dangers of AI development frequently throughout his 16-month-old papacy and first discussed the issue publicly on his third day in office.

In his May appeal, released as his first major document, Leo warned that AI systems spread misinformation, prioritise ​conflict and could lead the world down a path of unending war.

Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican’s top diplomat, reiterated Leo’s call for international regulation of the industry at an event in Rome last week, warning that countries cannot “go it alone” on the technology.

“The future of humanity is really at stake here,” Parolin said. The world, he said, needs “everyone’s involvement in establishing some common rules that can genuinely govern this phenomenon.”

Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah spoke at the Vatican’s launch event for the Pope’s May document, known as an encyclical.

Asked if the Vatican is in ongoing dialogue with any AI firms, Benanti stressed the decentralized nature of the global church and said some discussions are being led by local bishops.

On September 16, the US bishops’ conference said it had created a new AI task force after several of its leaders met with executives that day.

“The dialogue focused on ways to keep any system of artificial intelligence at the service of humanity and the urgent need to address the real and present dangers such technology presents,” a statement said.

Leo warns about autonomous weapons

The Vatican began warning about the risks of AI in 2019, hosting two conferences that year on the possible dangers of the technology. The late pope Francis warned attendees at one of the events that misinformation spread by AI could spark a world war.

The Vatican also teamed with Microsoft MSFT.O, IBM IBM.N, the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization and the Italian government in 2020 to issue a call for AI development that “does not have as its sole goal greater profit or the gradual replacement of people in the workplace.”

Leo has urged oversight especially for the development of weapons systems, such as those being used in the Russia-Ukraine war. He said in his encyclical that such weapons have advanced “practically beyond any human ‌reach to govern them.”

The Vatican’s advocacy on the global stage against autonomous weaponry goes back decades, Benanti said, likening AI-powered drones to landmines that are indiscriminate with their targets.

The priest compared the Vatican’s warnings about the risks of AI to how popes have long called for nuclear disarmament.

“If nuclear weapons can destroy humanity … the manipulation of generative AI content in social spaces can destroy the capabilities of people to stay together as a society,” he said.

“Nuclear weapons have to be stocked inside facilities, and you can count and control them. AI is not this visible.” – Rappler.com

World.title: At least P5-billion gap seen for free tuition in SUCs, says budget sponsor
World.content:
DEMONSTRATION. Students of the Polytechnic University of the Philippines in Manila walk out of their classrooms to protest corruption in the government's infrastructure projects on October 10, 2025.

The budget shortfall may affect investments in computers, classrooms, laboratory equipment, engineering software, and research publication support, among others

MANILA, Philippines – The government has to plug P5.321 billion in funding deficiencies in the free higher education program for state universities and colleges (SUCs), a lawmaker said on Wednesday, September 23.

Pinoy Workers Representative Karl Legazpi reported the amount during the House plenary deliberations for the budget of SUCs next year.

Under the 2027 National Expenditure Program, the government will be allocating a total of P27.44 billion for the free college program across 113 SUCs in the country next year.

Legazpi, the budget sponsor for SUCs, said the funding deficiencies were P506 million for 2025, P2.048 billion for 2026, and P2.766 billion for 2027.

The budget shortfall may affect investments in computers, classrooms, laboratory equipment, engineering software, and research publication support, among others, according to Legazpi.

“Ang binigay na solusyon ng CHED (Commission on Higher Education), una would be to increase the tuition of our students and to cover for the deficiency from the DBM (Department of Budget and Management),” he said.

“Mayroon ngayong inaraal na formula kung ano ‘yong mainam na pagtaas para sa estudyante para hindi masaktan ang kanilang financial status,” he added.

(The proposed solution from CHED is first, to increase the tuition of our students and to cover for the deficiency from the DBM. A formula is being reviewed for a favorable increase for the students’ tuition without affecting their financial status.)

Higher tuition would then be the basis for computing government subsidies.

The government implements the free higher education program through Republic Act No. 10931 or the Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education Act (UAQTEA), which was passed into law in 2017.

In August, the DBM announced that it released P9.753 billion to CHED for funding deficiencies in the free tertiary education of 108 SUCs, covering arrears for academic years 2022 to 2025.

Legazpi said the budget went to faculty and institutional development, research, and other core functions of SUCs.

During a House appropriations committee hearing on August 28, CHED also said it is seeking an additional P29 billion to pay for the college tuition of all projected beneficiaries of UAQTEA programs.

Other financial grants under CHED include the Tertiary Education Subsidy and the Tulong Dunong Program.

Regularization of college teachers

Meanwhile, Legazpi said there are around 55,000 workers with job orders and contracts of service across SUCs. From this figure, around 26,000 employees have teaching positions.

ACT Teachers Representative Antonio Tinio urged CHED to create new plantilla items for them. He also pushed for an adjustment in the pay for Instructor I teachers, which remains at Salary Grade 12.

“Kailangan iwasto natin ang inhustisya na ‘to. Nag-commit ang CHED na kagyat haharapin ang DBM at Civil Service Commission. We expect that this will be acted upon soon,” Tinio said.

(We need to correct this injustice. The CHED committed to meet with the DBM and the Civil Service Commission. We expect that this will be acted upon soon.)

Lawmakers also pushed for the restoration of funding for maintenance and other operating expenses of some SUCs next year, saying that budget cuts could affect the salaries of contractual workers. – Rappler.com

World.title: Tokayev Expresses Condolences Over Deaths of Service Members in Caspian Sea
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has expressed his condolences to the families and relatives of service members who died in a tragic incident during military exercises in the Mangystau Region on Sept. 24.

Tokayev instructed the Government Commission to take all necessary measures to establish the circumstances of the incident and provide assistance to the families of those who died.

Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Defense reported that 19 service members were swept into the Caspian Sea during a naval exercise in the Mangystau Region on Sept. 24 amid deteriorating weather conditions and strong winds. Three service members were rescued, including one who was hospitalized, while nine others died. Search operations continued.

World.title: ADB Forecasts Resilient Growth in Asia-Pacific, Kazakhstan’s Outlook Unchanged
World.content:
ASTANA — Economic growth across developing Asia and the Pacific is expected to moderate to 5% in 2026 from 5.5% in 2025 before rising slightly to 5.1% in 2027, according to the Asian Development Bank’s latest outlook.

The ADB’s September 2026 outlook revised its 2026 regional growth forecast upward by 0.1 percentage points compared with its July projection. Strong investment, government support and growing technology exports linked to global artificial intelligence investment are expected to continue supporting economic activity. At the same time, geopolitical tensions and climate-related risks are putting pressure on food and energy prices.

The bank lowered its regional inflation forecast for 2026 to 4.2%, from 4.3% in July, citing price stabilization measures. However, the forecast for 2027 was raised slightly to 3.5%, compared with 3.4% previously in July. Both projections remain above the 3% inflation rate recorded in 2025.

ADB identified escalating conflicts and a strong El Niño as the main risks to the regional outlook. A prolonged or broader conflict in the Middle East, as well as an intensifying war in Ukraine, could keep global energy prices high and volatile. Meanwhile, El Niño, the periodic warming of sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, is expected to continue through the first quarter of 2027, potentially increasing energy demand and reducing agricultural production.

Kazakhstan growth forecast remains unchanged

Kazakhstan’s economic outlook remains unchanged from the ADB’s July forecast. The bank expects the country’s economy to grow by 4.8% in 2026 and 4.5% in 2027.

This projection is consistent with the ADB’s earlier assessment of Kazakhstan’s economic trajectory, which also forecast growth of 4.8% in 2026 and 4.5% in 2027 amid moderating oil production and continued government investment.

According to the report, growth will be supported by non-oil sectors and continued public investment. Manufacturing, construction and services are expected to contribute to economic activity despite disruptions in the oil sector. Off-budget financing and infrastructure spending are also projected to provide additional support.

The focus on non-oil sectors comes as Kazakhstan seeks to maintain economic momentum while reducing its reliance on hydrocarbons. Recent developments in construction, manufacturing, transport, trade and agriculture have also been highlighted as potential drivers of growth.

Inflation in Kazakhstan is forecast to gradually decline to 10.4% in 2026 and 9.5% in 2027, supported by earlier monetary tightening and prudential measures.

Across Central and West Asia, the ADB revised its growth forecasts downward by 0.1 percentage points for both 2026 and 2027, to 3.7% and 4.1%, respectively. The revision was attributed mainly to weaker-than-expected external demand, particularly in Türkiye.

Earlier ADB forecasts have likewise pointed to inflation and external economic conditions as key factors shaping Kazakhstan’s outlook. In July 2025, the bank raised its regional growth forecast while warning of increasing inflationary pressures in Kazakhstan and other Central Asian economies.

The ADB said developing Asia and the Pacific remain resilient despite growing economic and geopolitical risks. The bank emphasized the importance of measures to protect vulnerable populations from higher food and energy costs as governments navigate continued uncertainty.

World.title: Nine Servicemen Die in Incident During Caspian Sea Military Exercise
World.content:
ASTANA – Nine servicemen have died after 19 Kazakhstan Armed Forces personnel were swept into the Caspian Sea during a naval exercise in the Mangystau Region on Sept. 24 amid a sharp deterioration in weather conditions and strong winds, the Ministry of Defense reported.

Rescuers rescued three servicemen, including one who was hospitalized. Search operations for the remaining servicemen are underway.

The Government has established a commission to investigate the deaths, chaired by Deputy Prime Minister Kanat Bozumbayev. The commission includes the defense minister, Mangystau Region Akim Nurdaulet Kilybay and representatives of relevant ministries and agencies.

Units of the Naval Forces, the Ministry of Emergency Situations, aviation and other relevant services have been deployed to conduct search and rescue operations.

A commission from the Ministry of Defense, headed by Defense Minister Lieutenant General of Aviation Dauren Kossanov, has been urgently dispatched to establish the circumstances of the incident and coordinate the search and rescue efforts.

The Defense Ministry expressed its deep condolences to the families and relatives of the servicemen who died. The families will receive all necessary assistance and support.

The Prosecutor General’s Office has opened a criminal case into the deaths of the servicemen. An investigative team has been established, with officers from the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Ministry of Emergency Situations and the Prosecutor’s Office working at the site. Authorities have ordered necessary forensic examinations, and the investigation is under special control.

The Khazar Korgany-2026 exercise began on Sept. 22 in Kazakhstan’s sector of the Caspian Sea, involving more than 500 servicemen, Naval Forces vessels and boats, hydrographic vessels, Border Guard Service units and Air Defense Forces aviation.

World.title: Tokayev: Kazakhstan People’s Council to Strengthen State-Society Dialogue
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has called on the newly established Kazakhstan People’s Council to become a practical platform for dialogue between the state and society, saying its constitutional status opens new opportunities to address national and regional problems.

New platform for public dialogue

Speaking at the first session of the Kazakhstan People’s Council, Tokayev described its establishment as an important step in Kazakhstan’s ongoing political transformation. He said the new institution brings together representatives of different groups of society and is designed to strengthen public participation in state decision-making.

According to the President, the council is not an alternative to the Kurultai, Kazakhstan’s new legislative body, and must not interfere with its powers. Instead, the two institutions should maintain regular dialogue and coordinate their work, particularly when developing legislation that affects citizens’ interests, reported Akorda on Sept. 24.

The council includes representatives of ethnic and cultural associations, regional maslikhats and public councils, and civil society organizations. Tokayev said this composition would allow regional issues to be raised at the national level and establish a new system of interaction between the state and society.

He urged council members to avoid formalism and bureaucracy, maintain direct contact with citizens and address complex and pressing issues.

Economic and social progress

Tokayev highlighted Kazakhstan’s economic and social progress over the past seven years. GDP grew by 29% to $306 billion, while foreign exchange reserves and National Fund assets exceeded $138 billion. Kazakhstan attracted more than $162 billion in investment during this period, while small and medium-sized businesses accounted for more than 40% of the economy.

More than 20 million square meters of housing are built annually. Since 2019, 1,342 schools with capacity for more than one million students have been constructed. Life expectancy has reached 76 years, while more than 1,200 healthcare facilities have been opened.

More than 35,000 kilometers of roads have been built and repaired. Tokayev described these as record indicators in Kazakhstan’s history and said the country had entered the top 40 most competitive countries in the world.

Regional development and infrastructure

At the same time, Tokayev called for stronger public oversight of infrastructure projects and higher construction standards, citing concerns about the quality of some housing and roads.

He instructed the authorities to strengthen control over road construction, improve quality-assessment mechanisms and increase public oversight of infrastructure projects.

Tokayev also stressed the need to address Kazakhstan’s future workforce needs. By 2035, the country is expected to require 2.9 million specialists, including 1.8 million in skilled trades, notably in industry, construction, agriculture and IT.

Kazakhstan’s international role

Tokayev said Kazakhstan would continue to deepen international cooperation and attract investment, while promoting the country’s interests, history and culture internationally.

He said his goal was to position Kazakhstan on the global stage as a middle power and promote the country’s opportunities.

Concluding his address, Tokayev urged the People’s Council to remain closely connected with citizens and ensure that its work produces practical solutions to issues affecting the country and its people.

World.title: Astana Brings in Singapore’s Changi for New Airport Development
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is stepping up efforts to develop Astana as an international aviation hub and strengthen its transit potential through a new partnership with Singapore-based Changi Airports International (CAI), a global airport investor, manager and consultant.

The Astana akimat (administration), Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport and CAI, a subsidiary of Changi Airport Group (CAG), have signed a framework agreement to cooperate on the long-term development of Astana’s airport infrastructure, including the construction of a new airport and the further development of the existing international airport.

The agreement covers two main areas of cooperation. The first involves constructing a new airport in Astana, while the second focuses on developing Astana International Airport, including potential CAI participation in management, operations and maintenance (O&M), as well as other areas of its development, the Astana Akimat reported on Sept. 23.

The parties are currently working to agree on the partnership structure, project implementation terms and the necessary documentation.

Astana Deputy Akim (Mayor) Yevgeny Glotov, Deputy Minister of Transport Talgat Lastayev, and Changi Airports International Chief Executive Officer Eugene Gan signed the agreement.

About Changi Airport Group

Changi Airport Group is a Singaporean state-owned company that manages and develops the country’s airport infrastructure, including Singapore Changi Airport. CAG oversees airport operations, passenger and cargo traffic, commercial infrastructure, services and digital solutions.

In 2025, Changi Airport handled around 70 million passengers and more than 2 million tons of cargo, connecting Singapore with more than 170 cities worldwide. The airport has been named the World’s Best Airport 14 times at the Skytrax World Airport Awards, including in 2025 and 2026.

CAG conducts its international airport business through Changi Airports International, which has experience across more than 90 airports in over 35 countries.

The agreement comes amid a broader expansion of Kazakhstan-Singapore cooperation. During Singapore Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong’s visit to Kazakhstan in August, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev highlighted Singapore’s airport-development experience, while the two countries have also been strengthening ties in transport, investment, digitalization and technology.

The partnership has gained momentum in recent months, including the launch of a quantum technology center in Almaty and expanded air links between Kazakhstan and Singapore. The new airport agreement adds aviation infrastructure to the growing areas of bilateral cooperation.

World.title: Kazakhstan, China Push for Greater Middle Corridor Connectivity
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and China reaffirmed their commitment to expanding the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), or Middle Corridor, as a safe, efficient and competitive link between Asia and Europe during a high-level meeting in Beijing.

First Deputy Prime Minister Nurlybek Nalibayev made the remarks while participating in the Global Sustainable Transport Forum and a high-level meeting on the TITR during his working visit to Beijing on Sept. 23 at the invitation of Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang.

Nalibayev said Kazakhstan’s strategic goal is to become a major Eurasian transport and logistics hub by developing the East-West and North-South corridors, upgrading border and port infrastructure, and introducing modern multimodal transport services.

He identified the Middle Corridor as a key priority of Kazakhstan’s transport policy. He called for coordinated efforts to make the route safer, more efficient and predictable through competitive tariffs, streamlined procedures and common service standards, according to Kazinform.

China backs greater corridor capacity

China’s Vice Chairman of the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress Shohrat Zakir said Beijing attaches particular importance to the TITR and is ready to work with partners to increase its capacity and efficiency.

He proposed strengthening infrastructure connectivity, harmonizing cross-border transport and customs procedures, developing a digital platform for multimodal transportation and expanding financing and business opportunities along the route.

Azerbaijan’s Deputy Prime Minister Shahin Mustafayev also stressed the need for coordinated infrastructure development and removing bottlenecks, while Kyrgyz Deputy Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers Erlist Akunbekov highlighted the importance of improving transport access for landlocked Central Asian countries.

Kazakhstan-China cooperation

During the visit, Nalibayev held his first bilateral meeting with Ding Xuexiang, who co-chairs the Kazakhstan-China Cooperation Committee. The officials discussed expanding trade and economic ties, investment, agriculture, high technologies, interregional cooperation and transboundary rivers.

Nalibayev also met with executives of China Communications Construction Company (CCCC) and CITIC Group to discuss investment in Kazakhstan and joint infrastructure projects, the Prime Minister’s press service reported.

Before the forum, Nalibayev presented CITIC Group Chairman Xi Guohua with Kazakhstan’s Order of Dostyk (Friendship), second degree, on behalf of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. The award recognized his contribution to strengthening Kazakhstan-China relations and expanding trade and economic cooperation.

The Global Sustainable Transport Forum brought together around 1,000 representatives of governments, international organizations, diplomatic missions, businesses and expert communities.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Foreign Minister Expands Bilateral Ties at UN General Assembly
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has launched an active diplomatic agenda at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, with Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi holding talks with counterparts from several countries and discussing global peace, security and humanitarian law on Sept. 23 in New York.

Expanding bilateral partnerships

On the first day of the General Assembly’s High-Level Week in New York, Tileuberdi held talks with his counterparts from Hungary, Moldova, Poland, Slovenia, Ukraine and El Salvador, the ministry’s press service reported.

The discussions focused on bilateral cooperation, prospects for expanding political dialogue and trade and economic ties, as well as key international and regional topics.

Tileuberdi also met with UN Under-Secretary-General and UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) Executive Director Rebecca Grynspan, a candidate for UN Secretary-General, and UNESCO Director-General Khaled El-Enany. The meetings addressed ways to strengthen cooperation with UN institutions and improve the effectiveness of multilateral mechanisms.

Focus on peace and security

Tileuberdi also took part in a high-level discussion, Reaffirming the Promise of Peace: Using the Power We Have, which focused on conflict prevention and resolution, preventive diplomacy, mediation and strengthening partnerships within the international system.

Participants exchanged views on strengthening the UN’s role in maintaining international peace and security and using existing mechanisms more effectively to settle disputes peacefully.

New diplomatic relations

An important outcome of the first day was the establishment of diplomatic relations between Kazakhstan and the Central African Republic. The two countries’ foreign ministers signed a joint communiqué confirming their interest in developing bilateral ties and cooperation on international platforms.

Tileuberdi also participated in a working meeting of foreign ministers of the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) member states, where participants discussed priorities for cooperation between the CSTO and the UN.

Kazakhstan promotes compliance with Humanitarian Law

At a separate meeting with foreign ministers of the founding states of the Global Initiative to Strengthen Political Commitment to International Humanitarian Law (IHL) and International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) President Mirjana Spoljaric, Tileuberdi stressed that the effectiveness of international humanitarian law should be measured by its ability to protect civilians and medical and humanitarian personnel, safeguard critical civilian infrastructure and ensure the delivery of humanitarian assistance.

The meeting brought together the founding states – Kazakhstan, Brazil, China, France, Jordan and South Africa – to discuss preparations for the Humanity in War high-level conference, scheduled for Dec. 7 in Jordan.

Tileuberdi emphasized that international humanitarian law must be applied universally, consistently and in good faith, without selectivity or politicization.

Following the meeting, the founding states and the ICRC called on the international community to join the Initiative, strengthen compliance with international humanitarian law and ensure high-level participation at the upcoming conference in Jordan.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Switzerland Open Way For Up to 28 Weekly Passenger Flights
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Switzerland have expanded the legal framework for direct air connectivity, with the two countries signing a memorandum allowing designated airlines to operate up to 28 passenger flights per week, the Kazakh Civil Aviation Committee’s press service reported.

The memorandum was signed following negotiations between the aviation authorities of Kazakhstan and Switzerland in Astana on Sept. 23. The Kazakh delegation was led by Civil Aviation Committee Chair Saltanat Tompiyeva, while the Swiss delegation was headed by Laurent Noel, head of the negotiation division at the Swiss Federal Office of Civil Aviation (FOCA).

Representatives of Air Astana, SCAT, SWISS International Air Lines, Basel Airport, Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Embassy of Switzerland in Kazakhstan also took part in the talks.

The negotiations focused on prospects for developing direct air links and practical issues related to opening new routes between the two countries. The document also establishes a legal framework for cargo services without restrictions on flight frequencies or capacity. The two sides also agreed and initiated a draft air services agreement for subsequent signing. The agreement is expected to provide an updated legal basis for further development of air connectivity between Kazakhstan and Switzerland.

The Swiss side said it sees potential for expanding direct air links and is currently considering the launch of regular flights to Kazakhstan. The development of direct air connectivity is expected to create additional opportunities for tourism, trade and business cooperation between Kazakhstan and Switzerland.

New routes could also increase passenger and business flows between the two countries by providing more direct travel options for tourists, companies and other travelers. The memorandum and draft agreement create the regulatory conditions for airlines to consider new services, while the actual launch of regular routes will depend on decisions by the carriers involved.

World.title: ‘TRIPP project will move forward slowly’: US discusses regional connectivity agenda
World.content:
US discusses upcoming investments in the TRIPP project

Discussions in New York focused on the peace agenda between Armenia and Azerbaijan, as well as regional connectivity. The US administration organised an event titled “Prosperity through Peace: Investing in the Trans-Caspian Trade Route and the TRIPP Initiative”.

The “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP) is a road that will connect Azerbaijan with its autonomous exclave of Nakhchivan through Armenian territory. For several years, Yerevan and Baku failed to reach an agreement on the issue. Azerbaijan demanded a road that it called the “Zangezur Corridor”. Armenia’s authorities said they were ready to unblock all roads but rejected the term “corridor”, which implies that the country would lose control over the territory and, therefore, its sovereign rights. The two sides reached an agreement only on 8 August in Washington. They agreed that the road would remain under Armenia’s sovereign control, while the US would join the unblocking process as a business partner. The project therefore took the name “Trump Route”, after the mediator. The road will be about 43km long. TRIPP also includes plans to build railway lines, energy infrastructure and digital communications networks. The US views TRIPP as a multimodal corridor designed to expand connectivity along the East-West axis, linking the South Caucasus, Central Asia and the West.

The speakers included the foreign ministers of Armenia and Azerbaijan, as well as Brendan Hanrahan, head of the US State Department’s Bureau of European and Eurasian Affairs. US special envoy for peace missions Steve Witkoff, representatives of Georgia and Central Asian countries also took part in the discussion.

According to Radio Azatutyun (Radio Liberty), Witkoff emphasised that, according to various estimates, the TRIPP route could cut delivery times for certain goods by 2.5 to three weeks:

“Witkoff’s key message was that the project’s potential benefits could extend beyond the two countries. It could create a new East-West transport artery, speed up the movement of goods, expand access to Central Asian markets and strengthen the role of American companies in this strategically important region — Eurasia.”

The Trump administration sees the project as a kind of test of whether the political momentum generated by the Armenia-Azerbaijan peace process can translate into tangible commercial infrastructure.

The official Yerevan statement on the event was brief. It said the speakers had discussed progress in the region since the Washington summit on 8 August 2025. They also discussed investment in the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund. The fund aims to attract private investment in projects along the wider Trans-Caspian trade route, also known as the “Middle Corridor”.

Armenian officials have repeatedly said that the fund has an “indirect and secondary” connection to the TRIPP initiative itself. The TRIPP Development Company will be specifically responsible for developing and implementing the project. Initially, the US will own 74% of the company’s shares, while Armenia will hold 26%. After the 49-year term expires, Armenia’s share will rise to 49% if the partners extend their agreement for another 50 years.

“The section running through Armenia is not yet ready for construction”

The event in New York focused on moving the TRIPP initiative towards practical implementation. The discussion covered issues such as financing, the creation of institutional mechanisms and infrastructure planning.

“Progress in the next phase will be measured not so much by diplomatic statements as by feasibility studies, investment commitments and, ultimately, construction itself,” US representatives said.

As part of engineering and feasibility studies, experts are currently examining the proposed railway route, taking technical, environmental and social factors into account.

The studies are expected to be completed in late 2026 or early 2027. The next steps will involve selecting companies to participate in the project and assessing investment opportunities.

According to US participants in the discussion, however, the territory through which the railway will run is not yet ready for construction. At the same time, they stressed that the United States takes the initiative seriously, pointing to the work already underway to advance TRIPP. They also warned that the project would not be completed overnight.

“TRIPP will move forward slowly, given the project’s technical complexity and geopolitical sensitivity,” said Andrew D’Anieri, deputy director of the Eurasia Center at the Atlantic Council.

He said the process would require engineering studies, regulatory decisions, funding and tenders. Only then would the “technically complex construction” phase begin. Preliminary estimates suggest that building the railway itself would also take considerable time — at least 18 months from the start of construction.

Pashinyan: “TRIPP will open a new era for our country and economy”

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan is also in the United States. In New York, he took part in a panel discussion at the Concordia Summit, held on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

Speaking about the peace established between Armenia and Azerbaijan and the opportunities it has created, he stressed that efforts are now focused primarily on implementing TRIPP. The project, he said, would unlock the full potential of regional connectivity.

“It will open a new era for our country and economy,” the prime minister said.

Alongside TRIPP, the Armenian government also intends to implement its Crossroads of Peace initiative, which aims to fully reopen the country’s transport links.

The prime minister’s office said that Pashinyan had discussed the implementation of TRIPP and the reopening of regional transport links with the Turkish president during his visit to the United States the previous day.

US discusses upcoming investments in the TRIPP project

World.title: Georgian judge challenges in Constitutional Court law criminalising insults against public officials
World.content:
Georgia: judge challenges officials’ insult law

A judge at Kutaisi City Court in Georgia, Tsitsino Kikvadze, has asked the Constitutional Court to review the constitutionality of Article 173¹⁶ of the Administrative Offences Code.

Kikvadze says the provision, which establishes special administrative liability for insulting state and political officials and public servants, may violate freedom of expression.

The judge notes that such conduct is already covered by Article 166 of the Administrative Offences Code. But Article 173¹⁶ ties liability to a person’s official status and therefore provides for harsher penalties.

Under the contested provision, verbal insults, swearing, offensive remarks or other insulting acts directed at a state or political official, public or civil servant while they are performing their duties or in connection with their work are subject to administrative liability.

Since June, Georgia’s Interior Ministry has had a new department tasked with combating hate speech, including monitoring what people write and say in public places. Lawyers criticised the initiative at the time as an attempt to legalise censorship. On social media, the department was dubbed the “scrolling agency”.

Since then, dozens of people have been fined. Also, TV host Vakho Sanaia was sentenced to 14 days of administrative detention and activist Giorgi Akhobadze to one month, both over Facebook posts.

What arguments did the judge make in her constitutional petition?

The constitutional petition stems from a specific administrative case.

On June 23, 2026, a unit of the Interior Ministry’s Human Rights Protection Department filed an administrative offence complaint with Kutaisi City Court against citizen Irakli Kezevadze.

According to the complaint, Kezevadze verbally insulted Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze in a Facebook post on June 3. At the court hearing, he confirmed this and said he had been drunk.

Kezevadze also described his difficult social and family circumstances. He said his wife had died three years ago, he had no children, was unemployed and was caring for his sick mother.

Asked whether he continued to make similar comments on social media, he said he no longer did so and was “not engaged in such activities at all”.

Duplication

Judge Kikvadze argues that such conduct is already covered by Article 166 of the Administrative Offences Code. The purpose of that provision is to protect public order and the peace of all citizens. Article 173¹⁶, by contrast, provides special protection to a particular category of people — public officials — and makes liability dependent on their official status.

The two articles provide for different penalties

Article 166 provides for a fine of 500 to 3,000 lari (about $190-$1,100) or up to 20 days of administrative detention.

Article 173¹⁶ provides for a fine of 1,500 to 4,000 lari (about $600-$1,500), while administrative detention can last up to 45 days.

Harsher penalties for insulting public officials than private citizens

The judge also considers it problematic that Article 173¹⁶ does not allow for exemption from liability.
