World.title: Albanese laments 'breakdown' of global rules in major UN speech
World.content:
Anthony Albanese has lamented a "breakdown of international rules" in a UN speech naming climate change and AI as key global challenges, just two days after Donald Trump told the same forum that both concerns were a "hoax".

The prime minister's speech also doubled as a pitch for a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council, where Mr Albanese said Australia hoped to help safeguard international law.

"Clearly, the multilateral system we have all known and benefited from is under immense strain," he told the UN's annual general assembly summit.

"Australia supports the rules and institutions that underpin open trade and connectivity. That order, based on agreed rules and institutions, faces massive disruption."

AI and climate change were the key issues that demanded global cooperation, Mr Albanese said, despite the "breakdown of trust, civility and social cohesion" that was promoting conflict within and between countries.

He said climate change was already causing an increase in extreme weather and threatening the "very existence" of Australia's Pacific neighbours.

And he referenced yesterday's revelations that an AI agent had hacked Australian Medicare data when repeating his call for "action to shape artificial intelligence development rather than be passively shaped by it".

Many other leaders have made similar arguments about climate and AI from the UN rostrum this week. But both positions pit Australia against the US, which, under Mr Trump's leadership, has aggressively pushed back on calls for global action on either issue.

Mr Albanese delivered the speech in New York as Mr Trump hosted Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a state dinner at the White House.

During an earlier meeting, Mr Xi told Mr Trump that the superpower countries had a responsibility to "develop and manage AI for good".

But Mr Trump said while AI would be discussed during their three-day summit, he wanted to "leave it exactly where it is".

Australia has nominated for a seat on the Security Council in 2029-2030. Two non-permanent seats are available and Finland is the only other nominee.

If successful in its bid, Australia would use the position to "amplify the voices of small states and middle powers", Mr Albanese said.

"We understand the UN mission cannot be entrusted solely to the great powers or the biggest countries or even the loudest voices alone."

World.title: Retiring Dolphin lauded as one of NRL's toughest ahead of prelim final
World.content:
Ray Stone has claims to being the toughest man in the NRL.

Not that the Dolphins' warrior would care two hoots for the title as he nears retirement at the end of the 2026 season at the tender age of 29.

But there was a reason coach Kristian Woolf singled him out at last year's presentation night for playing the last six rounds with a broken hand and final 15 rounds with needles in both shoulders.

He had off-season shoulder surgery after pushing himself to play when the Dolphins had multiple forwards on the injured list.

Stone is one of those players who performs when busted. When fit and relatively injury-free, though, he is even more dangerous.

"There are a lot of tough men who play our game but he is in the top group," Woolf said.

"It is not just his toughness, it's his commitment to the team that I really admire.

"He is just a guy who refuses to let his teammates down. It doesn't matter if it is playing injured, he is making an effort on a kick-chase, getting into a tackle or a carry.

"I love his hit-ups off the kick-off. I get a kick out of watching those because he runs so hard. He is just committed to the team. That is what we are going to miss."

Stone has been linked to a boxing career but AAP understands he has obtained multiple tickets in trade areas and will only get in a ring if he sees fit. He can hold them up, as the saying goes.

Finals battle between an unstoppable force and an immovable object Brian To'o and Greg Marzhew have never met a rugby league problem they couldn't solve by running over it and now the two wrecking balls will go head-to-head with an NRL grand final berth on the line.

"It is probably based on family time for me," Stone said, when asked why he was calling time.

"The kids are getting a bit older and I am quite busy on weekends so I want to be a part of that."

Woolf wanted him on deck in 2027.

"I have spoken to him a number of times and asked if I could change his mind but he has got other things in life he wants to do," the coach said.

"I respect that about him. He knows what he wants. He has pushed himself through the pain."

Stone was the second player signed at the Dolphins after starting his NRL career at Parramatta, where he played 31 matches in five seasons. At the Dolphins, he has notched 81 games in four years.

Dolphins coach Kristian Woolf has tried his very best to convince Stone to play on next season.

"The reason I came up here was for opportunity," he said.

"I was in and out of first-grade at Parramatta where we had a strong team and I spoke to Wayne Bennett about coming here and he said I'd be more of a consistent first-grader."

The warhorse, who plays mostly off the bench, has scored eight tries for the Dolphins but, like an old-school footy player of the past, he doesn't smile after any.

"It's not something I stress about," Stone said, through gritted teeth.

"I like to leave all my celebrating until after the game when the boys have got the result."

The Dolphins have won 16 of their last 18 matches coming into Friday night's NRL preliminary final. (Getty Images: Matt King)

He's done plenty of that this year, with the Dolphins winning 16 of their last 18 matches ahead of the preliminary final against Sydney Roosters.

"This year I've been a lot healthier and the squad has too, which has definitely helped our middle rotation," Stone said.

"Last year, pretty much our whole starting pack was in rehab. The minutes have been distributed a lot more which has helped me stay healthy."

Woolf is just glad to have Stone in the team after he missed the early rounds with his shoulder recovery.

"We did miss him too. He is a small man in a big man's world who plays so tough," Woolf said.

"He is loved, respected and will be missed next year.

"He is going to leave a legacy that people don't realise. There are no discipline issues around Ray. He turns up and gets his job done every day of every week."

AAP

World.title: Ex-AFL star Mark Hutchings's partner dies after childbirth
World.content:
Former West Coast Eagles player Mark Hutchings says his partner Hannah has died two days after the birth of their daughter.

Hutchings revealed her death in a social media post late yesterday.

"It is with deep sadness that I share the sudden loss of my beautiful partner, Hannah," he wrote on Instagram.

"2 days following the birth of our daughter, Sofia.

"I am shattered."

Loading Instagram content

Hutchings said Hannah had been looking forward to motherhood.

"Her dream was to become a Mum, so it's been incredibly difficult to take," he wrote.

"Sofia and I love you and will miss you very much Hannah."

A one-club player, Hutchings played 120 AFL games for the Eagles, and was part of the 2018 team that won a premiership by defeating Collingwood in the grand final.

A host of AFL players and former West Coast teammates, including Jeremy McGovern, Jack Darling and Mitch Brown, left messages of support in the comment section on the Instagram post.

Mark Hutchings played 120 AFL games for the Eagles and was part of the 2018 premiership-winning team. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

"You'll be the best Dad for your beautiful daughter, we got you," retired ruckman Nic Naitanui said.

"Thinking of you mate. Sending all our love your way," Mark LeCras said.

In his social media post, Hutchings thanked his friends, family, former teammates and colleagues for their sympathy.

"Thank you for all of your messages of support, I can't always reply to them all but I do appreciate them," he wrote.

No further details about Hannah's death were provided.

World.title: Eight USS Abraham Lincoln sailors attempted suicide on extended deployment
World.content:
Eight sailors attempted suicide while deployed with the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier strike group, which spent a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea supporting the Iran war, according to the Navy's top civilian leader.

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao provided the information to US Senator Kirsten Gillibrand in a letter dated Tuesday, local time, after the New York Democrat inquired last month about the strike group's crew.

The Lincoln's extended deployment drew international attention following reports of crew stress and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products.

Eight attempts in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months is actually low, experts say. The Navy reported 356 suicide attempts across the service in 2024, while there were more than 1,500 attempts among all active-duty personnel that year, according to the latest annual report.

Doctor Harold Kudler, a former national lead for mental health services at the Department of Veterans Affairs and a retired VA psychiatrist, said the reported attempts were not the best measure for conditions on the Lincoln and its supporting destroyers, particularly with no additional details.

"But something happened to get those families upset. Something happened to raise concerns about the health and well-being of those troops," Dr Kudler said, referring to media reports that quoted sailors and their families.

"It reverberated through the military and reverberated across the country.

"So we need to understand what that was because we don't need that to happen again."

Dr. Kudler said it could be challenging for troops counting down the days of their deployment to have it extended, and the Lincoln could be a learning opportunity for the Navy.

"Let's really do a serious look at what lessons have been learned and what we can do in the future," he said, "to ensure that these kinds of deployments, if they are necessary, are easier on the service members and the families".

Acting Navy secretary defends conditions

Senator Gillibrand asked Acting Navy Secretary Cao several questions focused on ship conditions, including the availability of mental health support, healthy food, and hygiene.

The senator also asked if there were any suicides.

"There have been no suicides on board during this deployment," Mr Cao wrote in the letter, which was obtained by The Associated Press and reported earlier by CNN.

"Since the beginning of Lincoln's deployment, there have been a total of eight suicide attempts across the strike group — this number includes the Lincoln crew and Sailors from the carrier wing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers, and all embarked aviation squadrons."

The US Navy Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln set the US record for the longest time at sea without making a port call. (Reuters: Chalinee Thirasupa)

Mr Cao wrote that the carrier deployed with a psychologist, a clinical social worker, a counsellor, three behavioural health technicians and a therapy dog.

Mr Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced from two to one for a short time.

However, he wrote that four nutritionally balanced meals were served daily.

Mr Cao acknowledged delays in scheduled resupply shipments but said the Navy prioritised the delivery of hygiene products and established a rotation to streamline distribution to different squadrons.

He also acknowledged piping failures on the carrier early in its deployment as well as temporary issues with desalination units.

Trump downplayed ship condition reports

US President Donald Trump had downplayed reports about conditions on the Lincoln, which left its home port in San Diego in November, arrived in the Middle East in January in support of operations against Iran, and spent a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 260 days.

Destroyer USS Benfold stranded with 300 sailors for four days Sailors aboard the US Navy ship endured four days stranded in the Pacific, without power, amid serious questions about the quality of life aboard naval vessels.

The carrier and some of its supporting ships stopped in Thailand in early September on their way back home to California.

The Lincoln's commanding officer, Captain Dan Keeler, said then that the ship was heading home soon but may make further supply stops. He declined to say the exact date the strike group was expected back in the US.

Last month, Mr Trump called the nearly nine months at sea that the sailors endured a "good period of time" but added that "over the years, we've had them out there much longer".

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also said that conditions aboard the Lincoln were "completely misrepresented".

Senator slams 'deteriorating conditions'

Senator Gillibrand took aim at Trump and Hegseth in a statement released this week in response to Mr Cao's letter.

Senator Gillibrand asked the acting navy secretary about ship conditions, mental health support, food supplies and hygiene. (Reuter: Evelyn Hockstein)

"What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as 'fake news' turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members," she stated.

"Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect.

" That this administration can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members. "

Extended deployments of carriers wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment.

The Navy is enforcing a blockade on Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz, and the Trump administration has offered no clarity on how it intends to wind down the nearly seven-month-old war.

AP

World.title: New generation of students carries Tongan culture forward
World.content:
Si'i Kae Hā, meaning "small but significant" in Tongan, is the name of Robinvale Secondary College's Tongan dance group.

Last week, the group lived up to its name when 24 students travelled eight hours from the small town of Robinvale in Victoria's north-west to perform at the Cultivating Creative Cultures with Communities (4Cs) Showcase in Melbourne.

They were the first regional Victorian group to perform in the showcase in its 20-year history.

Robinvale College captains Ruby Hingano and Sione Heitonga have been part of Si'i Kae Hā since its inception. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

College captains Sione Heitonga and Ruby Hingano helped establish the dance group in 2023 as a way for students to connect with their culture and community.

Ruby, who is both Aboriginal and Tongan, said joining the group has helped her discover a side of her identity she did not grow up knowing.

"Starting this group let me connect with my Tongan side more and with more of my family too," she said.

Si'i Kae Hā performing their 4Cs Showcase set for their school during an assembly. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

Passing culture to the next generation

Robinvale College education support workers Lueni Kolofale and Samuel Fangatua, who have been a driving force behind the group, also grew up in Robinvale.

They were taught by Tongan elders who helped keep their culture alive.

Their school experience was filled with regular opportunities to perform at annual showcases, community events and travelling roadshows.

Robinvale College staff who have helped bring Si'i Kae Hā to life. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

When Ms Kolofale and Mr Fangatua returned as staff, many of those opportunities were gone.

The pair saw an opportunity to rebuild that connection, helping to pass cultural knowledge on to another generation.

Si'i Kae Hā girls dancing during the Robinvale College assembly. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

Mr Fangatua said the Si'i Kae Ha group had grown beyond just dance, with students' curiosity branching out to Tongan traditions, culture and language.

He said that connection had flowed into their education.

"They're not going to do well in their education if they don't know who they are," he said.

Students are expected to maintain their behaviour and schoolwork to take part in performances and trips.

Ms Kolofale said students had gradually learnt that representing their culture also meant living its values of respect and love.

One parent, Sela Tuiaki Ale, said she had seen that change in her own children.

Sela Tuiaki-Ale with her son Latu Masila and daughter Suliana Mafi. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

Her children were raised speaking English, as she and her partner were also born and raised in Australia.

She said the dance group had given them another way to learn about their Tongan heritage.

"They were born and raised here, so to see them still want to learn about our culture and live in it as well is really good," she said.

Her parents and grandparents had embraced the opportunity too, helping dress the students in traditional attire and watching them perform.

Ms Ale's family was one of many who had played a role in the group's success.

Tongan elder Lupe Taumoefolau helping the students prepare to perform. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

A community effort

In the lead-up to the 4Cs showcase, the community raised $10,000 to take the students to Melbourne.

Parents and Tongan elders helped create the traditional wear and teach the dances.

The significance of the journey was not lost on 4Cs director Latini Matautia-Ulugia.

"It really does take a lot of people to okay something like this," she said.

"The fact that the school said yes and gave them the opportunity to fundraise and then were supported by community, I thought that was really is something that should be shared."

Department of Education Regional Director Tip Kennedy attended to support the school, the first time a department representative had attended the event.

Sione said he was nervous in the lead-up to the night and had "prayed countless times", while Ruby said that despite the nerves, she was just excited to perform.

Si'i Kae Hā boys dancing for their school. (Lua Ikenasio)

Both said that once they hit the stage, they were filled with pride.

For their teachers, watching the students carry their culture onto a Melbourne stage was a moment of awe.

"When we got to the venue in Melbourne we were like … who do we think we are coming all this way, doing all of this? From little Robinvale?" Ms Kolofale said.

The group is already looking forward to returning next year.

For now, Si'i Kae Ha continues to give Robinvale students a way to carry their culture forward, thousands of kilometres from Tonga.

World.title: Customers say Qantas not being 'fair dinkum' on costly outback flights
World.content:
For anyone travelling to Queensland's "capital of the outback", a flight could cost more than an interstate or overseas trip.

John Elliott was "staggered" to discover earlier this month that a return flight between Brisbane and Longreach would cost $1,386, even though he booked five days in advance.

The cost of the two-and-a-half-hour flight was equivalent to a last-minute Qantas flight to Auckland and only $450 less than a last-minute budget flight to Singapore.

John Elliott wants airlines to prove that remote flights cost them as much as they say. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

"I think it stops a lot of people travelling. Basically, the only visitors that we get to western Queensland have to drive," Mr Elliott said.

Mr Elliott, who has formerly coordinated events in Winton, said he had seen expensive rural flights deter not just outback residents, but also potential holiday-makers and those bringing drawcard tourism events to the west.

He said "corporate Australia" was treating people in the bush "with a lack of respect".

"Whenever we had a big event, it was cheaper for us to charter an 80-seater jet and fly direct from Brisbane into Winton [than book a commercial flight]," he said.

"I just don't think Qantas are being fair dinkum at the moment."

Qantas is the only airline that services the route between Longreach and Brisbane.

Outback routes already subsidised

Of the more than 40 routes in regional Queensland, seven servicing 23 towns take airfare subsidies from the state government.

Maximum fares on these regulated routes are capped where demand is considered "too low" to be commercially viable.

Contracts currently held by Rex and Qantas are reviewed every five years, but the Department of Transport and Main Roads has delayed its decision by 12 months so it can "consider all the feedback" from 37 consultation sessions.

The larger Qantas 737 jets have double the number of seats, which can reduce the overall cost per passenger. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

It's not the only review underway: the Australian Productivity Commission is also inquiring into the cost of regional airfares, with a draft report due in November.

In its submission, Qantas said Dash 8-400 planes were the "most suitable" aircraft to service smaller or remote regional routes because they had "lower maintenance and operating costs" than the smaller Q200 and Q300.

But the carrier said the aircraft, which carried fewer than half the passengers of a standard commercial jet, were not as profitable due to the "economy of scale".

"On average, these services are more than twice as expensive to operate than Qantas 737s and about three times more expensive than Jetstar and Qantas international services on a per-passenger basis," the submission said.

Outback residents face sky-high airfares Outback residents are paying the price of an international ticket to travel to their nearest capital city.

The airline has been contacted for comment.

Central Queensland University aviation expert Steve Leib said the fleet of smaller planes used on rural routes tended to be older and more expensive to operate.

"The costs just continue to creep up as aircraft age … and those smaller aircraft with fewer seats are in less of a position to help you recover the revenue associated with that [maintenance]," Dr Leib said.

Shaun Radnedge is calling for more regional flights and more affordable fares. (Supplied: Murweh Shire )

Calls for airlines to 'justify' prices

Several councils in the south-west have been lobbying for a new contract with the government

Murweh Shire Mayor Shaun Radnedge said prices were not the only issue.

"Every plane is full at the moment. People are saying they can't access seats," he said.

"We have had health services actually had to postpone what they had planned here in Charleville because they could not get a seat."

Cr Radnedge said now the region would be "in limbo" for another year, before they could bring in more flights and more affordable fares.

He said the state government had not consulted with his shire about delaying the review.

John Elliott is concerned costly outback airfares are sending tourists to other towns or overseas. (ABC Western Qld: Maddelin McCosker)

Now living in Toowoomba, Mr Elliott said governments should force carriers to prove whether remote flights really cost them as much as they claimed.

"I think the federal government need to say to Qantas, 'You need to be fair dinkum, you need to be transparent,'" he said.

"You need to justify how you can charge that much for a flight that really doesn't equate to anything their operation does [else]where in Australia."

World.title: Macklemore announces 'Free Palestine' tour after being dumped from Ed Sheeran shows
World.content:
American rapper Macklemore, who was dropped as the opening act for Ed Sheeran over pro-Palestinian remarks, has announced he will headline his own "Free Palestine" concert tour that will start next month.

The tour will begin in Dublin, Paris and London, the rapper said in an Instagram post on Thursday, local time.

Ed Sheeran's tour chaos The withdrawal of a touring band and support acts for Ed Sheeran's Loops tour is a saga involving the removal of Macklemore from shows over pro-Palestinian comments. Here's how it's played out thus far.

US dates and additional performers will be announced later, he said, adding that proceeds would be donated to organisations that support the Palestinian people.

"Being apolitical during a genocide doesn't work anymore," Macklemore said.

"People are asking artists to show up, educate themselves and be in community. To use the stage for more than entertainment. To push back when the call for a free Palestine is met with attempts to silence it."

Israeli officials have strongly denied their actions in Gaza amount to genocide — despite being deemed so by a UN inquiry — and say they are justified as self-defence.

The Grammy-winning rapper had been due to perform at eight additional Sheeran shows when he was removed last month from the tour following his remarks at a show in New Jersey.

"A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine,'" he said on stage.

Macklemore said owners of stadiums where Sheeran was set to play had objected to those remarks.

Sheeran, an English-born singer-songwriter and one of the world's top-selling recording artists, said the decision to dump Macklemore came from tour organisers, not him, and that he tried to find a resolution.

Ed Sheeran has distanced himself from the Macklemore controversy, saying he was not behind the decision to drop the rapper. (Reuters: Kylie Cooper)

He apologised for his handling of the situation at a performance in Philadelphia and decried Israel's treatment of residents in Gaza as "unjustifiable".

Macklemore has been an outspoken critic of Israel's assault on Gaza and its occupation of the West Bank.

"If these last couple of weeks have shown us anything, it's that something has shifted over the last three years," Macklemore said on Thursday.

"There has been a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now.

"What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage.

"When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention."

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Man dies after being found with life-threatening injuries in Qld home
World.content:
Police have established two crime scenes in a regional Queensland town as part of an investigation into the "sudden" death of a man aged in his 80s.

Emergency services were called to a property on Ivan Street in Surat, 80 kilometres south of Roma and 450 kilometres west of Brisbane, at about 3:40pm on Thursday.

A Queensland Ambulance spokesperson said paramedics were initially called to a "medical episode" at the residential property.

When they arrived, they found a man with life-threatening injuries.

He was taken to the Surat Hospital, where he later died.

The Queensland Police Service (QPS) said two crime scenes had since been declared at a unit and at a nearby vehicle.

Police said the man's "sudden" death was being treated as suspicious and investigations were ongoing.

A QPS spokesperson said there was no ongoing threat to the public.

Anyone with information that could assist the investigation is being urged to contact police.

Surat has a population of about 400 people, according to the 2021 census.

World.title: Police officer killed in Redfern crash
World.content:
Updated PoliticsNSWTragedy Police officer killed in Redfern crash Jack Gramenz and Riley Walter Updated September 25, 2026 — 10:11am ,first published September 25, 2026 — 6:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A police officer has been killed and another hospitalised, as their shocked and devastated colleagues investigate an early morning crash in inner Sydney. The female constable was a passenger in a fully marked police vehicle travelling under lights and sirens along Gibbons Street, Redfern, when it crashed into a tree about 1.30am on Friday. She died instantly, police said. Police comfort one another after a female constable died in a crash in inner Sydney. TNV Wreckage of the NSW Police vehicle. Sam Mooy A male constable – the driver – has been taken to Royal Prince Alfred Hospital in a stable condition.



The officer killed in the crash, believed to be aged in her 20s, joined NSW Police less than two years ago. A photo of the crash scene taken from a nearby apartment complex. Facebook A critical incident has been declared. Sam Mooy She was based at Redfern police station – about 100 metres from the crash site – in her first posting after graduating from the force’s Goulburn academy. The female constable died instantly, police said. TNV



Officers were seen hugging and comforting each other at the scene on Friday morning. “It’s just a tragic day for all police in NSW where two young officers were doing their job as police across the state do 24/7,” Police Association of NSW president Kevin Morton said. In a statement, the union said officers across NSW were shocked at the death of their colleague. The car was travelling under lights and sirens when it crashed into a tree. Sam Mooy Premier Chris Minns said it was devastating news.



“My thoughts are with the family, friends and colleagues of the officer who has lost her life,” Minns said. “Every day our police officers put themselves in harm’s way to keep the rest of us safe, and today the entire NSW police family will be grieving. “I’m also thinking of the officer injured in the crash and everyone who responded to this terrible scene.” A male constable was also taken to hospital. TNV NSW Police Minister Yasmin Catley said police officers dedicate themselves to looking after others.



“Today the NSW Police family is mourning one of its own,” Catley said. “My heart is with her family, her loved ones and her colleagues on this dark day.” Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane said she was heartbroken. “She was out working while most of us were asleep, protecting the community,” Sloane said. “Our police put themselves in harm’s way every day to protect us. Today, we stand with them as they mourn one of their own.”



NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon returned early from annual leave on Friday and is expected to address the media at midday. A crime scene has been established, and a critical incident has been declared. Detectives have removed several bags of evidence from the crash site. The Law Enforcement Conduct Commission is monitoring the investigation. A report will be prepared for the coroner and an inquest will likely follow. Police at the scene in Redfern on Friday morning. Riley Walter The last time a NSW police officer died in an on-duty crash was in March 2016, when Sergeant Geoffrey Richardson, 43, crashed into a tree in the state’s Hunter region while responding to a pursuit of a suspected stolen car.



A large section of Gibbons Street remains closed from Lawson Street to Cleveland Street as crash investigators examine the scene. Regent Street is closed in both directions between Cleveland and Redfern Street. Bus routes are being diverted and motorists are advised to avoid the area as the police investigation is expected to take some time. More to come Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: ASX falls after shaky day on Wall Street
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX falls after shaky day on Wall Street Stan Choe Updated September 25, 2026 — 10:09am ,first published September 25, 2026 — 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has slid at the open after a shaky day of trading on Wall Street. The S&P/ASX 200 was 40.5 points, or 0.5 per cent, lower to 8661.5 in early trade. The ASX lost 0.7 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was weaker at US70.08¢. Yields once again were following the track of oil prices, which have been scattershot because of uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow crude oil to flow freely again from the Middle East. Bloomberg The S&P 500 finished nearly flat and edged down by less than 0.1 per cent following several turns between losses and gains. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 161 points, or 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite added less than 0.1 per cent. Stocks have slowed their rally since the S&P 500 climbed to the brink of its all-time high earlier this week as pressure from the bond market has cranked higher.



Related Article Opinion

Weight loss How McDonald’s is grappling with the Ozempic boom Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer The yield on the 10-year Treasury jumped to 5.20 per cent from 5.11 per cent late Wednesday and is back to where it was in 2007. High yields slow the overall economy by making it more expensive to borrow money, while also undercutting prices for stocks and other investments. Yields climbed through the morning, which pushed stocks downward, until they took a sudden turn lower in the midday hours. The 10-year yield dropped from nearly 5.17 per cent to less than 5.13 per cent in about 20 minutes before ultimately turning higher again. Yields once again were following the track of oil prices, which have been scattershot because of uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow crude oil to flow freely again from the Middle East. The price for a barrel of Brent crude in the most actively traded part of the market went from $US102 to roughly $US99 in a matter of minutes midday Thursday. It later rose to settle at $US100.22, up 2.1 per cent from the prior day.



It’s not just worries about expensive oil and inflation that have sent Treasury yields higher. The US economy continues to expand, which also supports yields. On Thursday, a report showed fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week and further strengthened expectations for the economy. Such numbers could convince the Federal Reserve that the economy can withstand more hikes to short-term interest rates. The Fed raised its main interest rate last week for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing the economy and removing some of the fuel for inflation. Traders now see better than a coin flip’s chance that the Fed could raise rates twice more by the end of the year, according to data from CME Group. So far, the solid overall economy has helped US companies continue to deliver strong growth in profits. That in turn has helped their stock prices remain relatively strong despite worries about war, inflation and tariffs.



“The headlines have turned more ominous, but the underlying drivers of growth remain intact,” strategists at Barclays wrote in a report. “As long as AI-related investment, US corporate profitability, and consumer spending continue to beat expectations, the economy and markets seem capable of absorbing tighter central banks and higher rates.” Stitch Fix became one of the latest US companies late Wednesday to report better quarterly results than analysts expected. But its stock nevertheless tumbled 21.6 per cent after it said “a more challenging consumer environment” could hold back its revenue growth this upcoming fiscal year. Related Article Opinion

World markets The Trump effect: Why cracks are widening in financial markets Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Darden Restaurants, the company behind Olive Garden and LongHorn Steakhouse, fell 3 per cent after reporting a profit for the latest quarter that matched analysts’ expectations. High yields in the bond market hurt prices for all kinds of stocks, and they often hit hardest on those seen as the most expensive. That puts the target on AI stocks, which soared for years in the frenzy around the technology.



Higher yields also make it more expensive for companies to borrow money to build AI data centers, which could slow their construction and restrain demand for AI chips. Nvidia slipped 0.4 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. On the winning side of Wall Street was Everpure. The data storage and management company’s stock jumped 11.2 per cent after it stood by its financial forecasts for this fiscal year and said it expects revenue growth to accelerate in the following one. All told, the S&P 500 fell 1.90 to 7,704.13 points. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 161.61 to 51,349.98, and the Nasdaq composite rose 3.34 to 26,939.37. In stock markets abroad, indexes fell modestly around much of the world. A drop of 1.2 per cent in Shanghai and gain of 0.8 per cent in Tokyo were two of the bigger moves.

World.title: ICAC Operation Rosny LIVE updates: Former Toplace lawyer Sharangan Maheswaran to continue evidence
World.content:
After watching Jean Nassif give his unhinged evidence to the corruption inquiry recently from his Beirut bolthole, the impression left was that the fugitive developer was certifiably crazy.

But receiving a surprise mention during Thursday’s evidence, supposedly as Nassif’s “enforcer”, was a genuinely crazy figure, one-time bikie gang enforcer “Crazy Dave” Lima, whose corporate entities have included Krazye and Mother Clucker.

Also known as Sofe Veiru Levi, “Crazy Dave” has a conviction for violence and was second-in-charge of a bikie gang known as Notorious. On one occasion, Crazy Dave’s parole was revoked after police discovered he’d met “The Executioner”, a martial arts fighter, at the Gypsy Lounge in Kings Cross.

World.title: Clowning world mourns Jolly Goodfellow, a performer in a class of his own
World.content:
CultureTheatrePerforming arts Clowning world mourns Jolly Goodfellow, a performer in a class of his own Jackie Dent September 25, 2026 — 8:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

He once performed for 53 hours straight without sleep and was perpetually dressed as a medieval jester. Now the clown world is mourning one of its legends: Jolly Goodfellow, the Australian fool known as Rumpel aka Rumpelstiltskin, who died in Los Angeles, aged 54. As tales of crying with laughter and links to his shows on YouTube are shared, a fundraiser has been set up to “pass the very final hat” around to “resolve, return, house (or re-house) his endless stashes of props, fabulous costumes, musical instruments, drawing and incredible documentation,” and eventually bring his cremated remains home to Australia. So far, just over $37,000 has been raised. The clown world is mourning Jolly Goodfellow, aka Rumpel. Last week, police found Rumpel dead in his prop-filled van, where he had been sleeping during the recent heatwave, his death attributed to natural causes. But the clock is ticking. His body remains with the coroner, and until the family gets a death certificate, his van stays impounded — racking up more fines to pay by the day. Rumpel was a mythical character in the global clowning scene, known to sleep in bushes, caravans and at the chai tent in pursuit of a life busking and at festivals. His unstructured, nonsensical shows were filled with slapstick, silly noises, rambling poetry and philosophical musings. On and off stage, he spoke in a high-pitched voice; some say he rarely dropped character. His motto? “Crikey!”



“He was an unsung genius,” said Mike Finch, former artistic director and co-CEO of Circus Oz, putting Rumpel’s mastery of his craft on a par with painters Vincent van Gogh or Frida Kahlo. “In the world of clown and street performance, he really was in a class of his own.” Rumpel was born Sean Goodfellow in 1972 in Adelaide to parents Roxley Halleday and Brian Goodfellow, who met as advertising artists. His family settled in Melbourne in 1976 and he moved from school to school as he often got in trouble for his hyperactivity and playing the fool in class. “No education system was really able to contain him,” recalls his older sister, Antonia Goodfellow. Prone to constantly changing his name and voice, he was exposed to clowning at a young age, when the siblings befriended a tightrope walker in Carlton Gardens while waiting to be picked up from primary school. The man strung his rope between two trees and taught the kids to walk it. He also rode a unicycle. “I think that was his [Rumpel’s] first real taste of meeting someone like that and experiencing those clowning and circus skills,” she said. He left school and after doing the rounds of alternative festivals in the 1990s – Adelaide Fringe, Maleny (16-hour show), Woodford, Confest – he headed to Europe, where over two decades he built a reputation for absurd marathon performances. He played in every country in Europe and got star treatment at festivals including Glastonbury. The only “proper” job he ever had was in 2006 and 2007 performing in Cirque du Soleil’s Beatles show Love in Las Vegas, although he was unhappy after his song, The Fool on the Hill, was allegedly cut because Yoko Ono felt the show had too many Paul McCartney songs.



Legends abound and his life off stage was as chaotic and adventurous as his shows. He often checked in at airports in full costume to reduce the weight of his suitcases, laden with rubber snakes, balls, spring shoes and noisemakers. He once landed at Heathrow, dressed as a jester, and when asked at customs if he had money for his stay, presented a bag of Australian coins. He was put straight back on a plane to Melbourne. En route to a festival in Austria, his friends accidentally left him behind at a service station, returning to find him in his undies holding a toothbrush. They hadn’t noticed he had got out of the truck to freshen up. Jolly Goodfellow the clown, aka Rumpel or Rumpelstiltskin. Rumpel has been described as sweet, brave, strange, gentle, humble, authentic, endearing, prolific, vulnerable, irritating, achingly funny, properly silly, from another dimension, allergic to cash, the kookiest of kooks, a child at heart, highly skilled at circus tricks, and always late for planes and parties. “He really was the performer’s performer,” said Annie Lee, a former partner, long-term friend and member of comedy trio the Kransky Sisters. Jolly — who changed his name from Sean by deed poll — was born with muscular dystrophy, a genetic condition his father also had. Around 2008, Rumpel was in a serious car crash on the way to Burning Man in the US, which Antonia thinks “flicked a switch” and triggered the disease. He settled in LA, clowning and working as an extra, before returning to Australia in 2019. Struggling with his health, he was restless, and in June this year returned to LA to get back into performing and sort out his props, which included a hurdy-gurdy and a Volkswagen Beetle painted like a ladybug. The death of the once-in-a-generation performer has shocked many, and a Facebook page dedicated to him is filled with an endless stream of funny, adoring anecdotes. One fan, who witnessed the end of his legendary 53-hour performance in Poland, said the world needs characters like him more than ever: “Undoing the serious matters of life if only for a moment, and making us approach reality with a smile and a good laugh. It was a crown that Rumpel wore like no other ... Jest In Peace, King of Clowns.”

World.title: Police officer killed in Redfern crash
World.content:
Updated PoliticsNSWTragedy Police officer killed in Redfern crash Jack Gramenz and Riley Walter Updated September 25, 2026 — 10:11am ,first published September 25, 2026 — 6:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A police officer has been killed and another hospitalised, as their shocked and devastated colleagues investigate an early morning crash in inner Sydney. The female constable was a passenger in a fully marked police vehicle travelling under lights and sirens along Gibbons Street, Redfern, when it crashed into a tree about 1.30am on Friday. She died instantly, police said. Police comfort one another after a female constable died in a crash in inner Sydney. TNV Wreckage of the NSW Police vehicle. Sam Mooy A male constable – the driver – has been taken to Royal Prince Alfred Hospital in a stable condition.



The officer killed in the crash, believed to be aged in her 20s, joined NSW Police less than two years ago. A photo of the crash scene taken from a nearby apartment complex. Facebook A critical incident has been declared. Sam Mooy She was based at Redfern police station – about 100 metres from the crash site – in her first posting after graduating from the force’s Goulburn academy. The female constable died instantly, police said. TNV



Officers were seen hugging and comforting each other at the scene on Friday morning. “It’s just a tragic day for all police in NSW where two young officers were doing their job as police across the state do 24/7,” Police Association of NSW president Kevin Morton said. In a statement, the union said officers across NSW were shocked at the death of their colleague. The car was travelling under lights and sirens when it crashed into a tree. Sam Mooy Premier Chris Minns said it was devastating news.



“My thoughts are with the family, friends and colleagues of the officer who has lost her life,” Minns said. “Every day our police officers put themselves in harm’s way to keep the rest of us safe, and today the entire NSW police family will be grieving. “I’m also thinking of the officer injured in the crash and everyone who responded to this terrible scene.” A male constable was also taken to hospital. TNV NSW Police Minister Yasmin Catley said police officers dedicate themselves to looking after others.



“Today the NSW Police family is mourning one of its own,” Catley said. “My heart is with her family, her loved ones and her colleagues on this dark day.” Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane said she was heartbroken. “She was out working while most of us were asleep, protecting the community,” Sloane said. “Our police put themselves in harm’s way every day to protect us. Today, we stand with them as they mourn one of their own.”



NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon returned early from annual leave on Friday and is expected to address the media at midday. A crime scene has been established, and a critical incident has been declared. Detectives have removed several bags of evidence from the crash site. The Law Enforcement Conduct Commission is monitoring the investigation. A report will be prepared for the coroner and an inquest will likely follow. Police at the scene in Redfern on Friday morning. Riley Walter The last time a NSW police officer died in an on-duty crash was in March 2016, when Sergeant Geoffrey Richardson, 43, crashed into a tree in the state’s Hunter region while responding to a pursuit of a suspected stolen car.



A large section of Gibbons Street remains closed from Lawson Street to Cleveland Street as crash investigators examine the scene. Regent Street is closed in both directions between Cleveland and Redfern Street. Bus routes are being diverted and motorists are advised to avoid the area as the police investigation is expected to take some time. More to come Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: ASX falls after shaky day on Wall Street
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX falls after shaky day on Wall Street Stan Choe Updated September 25, 2026 — 10:09am ,first published September 25, 2026 — 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has slid at the open after a shaky day of trading on Wall Street. The S&P/ASX 200 was 40.5 points, or 0.5 per cent, lower to 8661.5 in early trade. The ASX lost 0.7 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was weaker at US70.08¢. Yields once again were following the track of oil prices, which have been scattershot because of uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow crude oil to flow freely again from the Middle East. Bloomberg The S&P 500 finished nearly flat and edged down by less than 0.1 per cent following several turns between losses and gains. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 161 points, or 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite added less than 0.1 per cent. Stocks have slowed their rally since the S&P 500 climbed to the brink of its all-time high earlier this week as pressure from the bond market has cranked higher.



Related Article Opinion

Weight loss How McDonald’s is grappling with the Ozempic boom Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer The yield on the 10-year Treasury jumped to 5.20 per cent from 5.11 per cent late Wednesday and is back to where it was in 2007. High yields slow the overall economy by making it more expensive to borrow money, while also undercutting prices for stocks and other investments. Yields climbed through the morning, which pushed stocks downward, until they took a sudden turn lower in the midday hours. The 10-year yield dropped from nearly 5.17 per cent to less than 5.13 per cent in about 20 minutes before ultimately turning higher again. Yields once again were following the track of oil prices, which have been scattershot because of uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow crude oil to flow freely again from the Middle East. The price for a barrel of Brent crude in the most actively traded part of the market went from $US102 to roughly $US99 in a matter of minutes midday Thursday. It later rose to settle at $US100.22, up 2.1 per cent from the prior day.



It’s not just worries about expensive oil and inflation that have sent Treasury yields higher. The US economy continues to expand, which also supports yields. On Thursday, a report showed fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week and further strengthened expectations for the economy. Such numbers could convince the Federal Reserve that the economy can withstand more hikes to short-term interest rates. The Fed raised its main interest rate last week for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing the economy and removing some of the fuel for inflation. Traders now see better than a coin flip’s chance that the Fed could raise rates twice more by the end of the year, according to data from CME Group. So far, the solid overall economy has helped US companies continue to deliver strong growth in profits. That in turn has helped their stock prices remain relatively strong despite worries about war, inflation and tariffs.



“The headlines have turned more ominous, but the underlying drivers of growth remain intact,” strategists at Barclays wrote in a report. “As long as AI-related investment, US corporate profitability, and consumer spending continue to beat expectations, the economy and markets seem capable of absorbing tighter central banks and higher rates.” Stitch Fix became one of the latest US companies late Wednesday to report better quarterly results than analysts expected. But its stock nevertheless tumbled 21.6 per cent after it said “a more challenging consumer environment” could hold back its revenue growth this upcoming fiscal year. Related Article Opinion

World markets The Trump effect: Why cracks are widening in financial markets Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Darden Restaurants, the company behind Olive Garden and LongHorn Steakhouse, fell 3 per cent after reporting a profit for the latest quarter that matched analysts’ expectations. High yields in the bond market hurt prices for all kinds of stocks, and they often hit hardest on those seen as the most expensive. That puts the target on AI stocks, which soared for years in the frenzy around the technology.



Higher yields also make it more expensive for companies to borrow money to build AI data centers, which could slow their construction and restrain demand for AI chips. Nvidia slipped 0.4 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. On the winning side of Wall Street was Everpure. The data storage and management company’s stock jumped 11.2 per cent after it stood by its financial forecasts for this fiscal year and said it expects revenue growth to accelerate in the following one. All told, the S&P 500 fell 1.90 to 7,704.13 points. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 161.61 to 51,349.98, and the Nasdaq composite rose 3.34 to 26,939.37. In stock markets abroad, indexes fell modestly around much of the world. A drop of 1.2 per cent in Shanghai and gain of 0.8 per cent in Tokyo were two of the bigger moves.

World.title: Waitangi Tribunal finds Crown had no clear plan for Māori health after scrapping Te Aka Whai Ora
World.content:
The Waitangi Tribunal has found the Government had no clear alternative plan for Māori health when it scrapped Te Aka Whai Ora - the Māori Health Authority.

The second part of the Hautupua: Te Aka Whai Ora (Māori Health Authority) Priority Report was released on Friday, and examined the Crown's process for developing plans to address Māori health in place of a Māori health authority.

The Tribunal found the Crown:

failed to adequately inform Māori about its alternative plans

failed to recognise and respect tino rangatiratanga

failed to consult with Māori and be sufficiently informed about key elements of its plans

failed in its duty of active protection and Māori's right to self-determine what is best for Māori health

failed to properly engage with Māori about the Hauora Māori Strategy and Pae Ora Amendment Act.

It found these breaches had caused, and would continue to cause, short and long-term prejudice to Māori and repeated its previous finding that the Crown had shown "reckless disregard for the Crown-Māori relationship".

They recommend that a stand-alone Māori health authority be revisited.

'Significant lag' after Te Aka Whai Ora disestablished

Te Aka Whai Ora was scrapped as part of the Government's 100-day programme. The Pae Ora (Disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill was introduced under urgency in February 2024.

Then-Health Minister Dr Shane Reti said at the time the Government wanted to pursue "a different dream" for Māori health, with greater decision-making and care delivered closer to home and hapū.

However, the Tribunal said the Crown did not have a clear alternative plan in place when that happened.

It said the Crown's failure to develop one resulted in a "significant lag" between the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora and an alternative.

"For nearly 18 months the Crown repeatedly informed claimants, the Tribunal, and the public of its intention to develop alternative plans in lieu of Te Aka Whai Ora, but these intentions did not materialise and were not reflected in Crown action," the Tribunal said.

It found the delay was inconsistent with the principles of kāwanatanga and good government.

"The Crown failed during this period to take any meaningful action towards Māori health equity or to provide an alternative plan to Te Aka Whai Ora," it said.

The Tribunal found that inaction breached the principles of equity, active protection and options.

'No meaningful consultation'

The Tribunal said there was no meaningful consultation with Māori over key elements of what the Crown eventually described as its alternative plan.

"We see no evidence of meaningful engagement or consultation between the Crown and its Tiriti / Treaty partner," the Tribunal said.

It said the Crown's approach had "in many ways" deteriorated since the first stage of the inquiry.

The Tribunal found iwi-Māori partnership boards were approached after decisions had already been made. It described this as "more of a box-ticking exercise than any form of meaningful engagement with Māori".

It said the purpose of consultation was for the Crown to fully understand the impact of proposed legislation, policies and actions on Māori rights and interests.

"The Crown has failed to do that in this instance," it said.

The Tribunal found the Crown failed to adequately inform Māori about its alternative plans, saying it had told them the plans were forthcoming before later confirming the plans were already in place.

It found this breached the principle of good government.

The Tribunal said the Crown failed to properly engage with Māori about two key elements of the alternative plan: the Hauora Māori Strategy and changes to the Pae Ora Amendment Act.

'Double standard' over health system reviews

The Tribunal also criticised the Crown for what it described as a "double standard" in how it reviewed changes to the health system.

It found Te Aka Whai Ora was reviewed just 10 months after its establishment, while the Government said other system-wide changes in the health sector would need to operate for longer than a year before being reviewed.

"The Crown failed in its duty to follow its own laws, rules, and standards," the Tribunal said.

"This signals a double standard and is a breach of the Tiriti / Treaty principle of good government."

It said a regulatory impact statement for changes to the health system only partially met quality assurance requirements because of limited consultation. The Tribunal said this was despite its previous recommendation that the Crown should undertake proper regulatory impact analysis for matters affecting Māori health.

What was the Government's alternative plan?

The Crown initially told the Tribunal an alternative plan was being developed.

Over the course of the inquiry, it pointed to a range of health system settings and changes, including the roles of iwi-Māori partnership boards, the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee, the Ministry of Health and Health New Zealand.

It also identified the Government Policy Statement on Health, the New Zealand Health Plan and the Hauora Māori Strategy as key elements.

The Tribunal assessed these existing health system settings as the Crown's alternative plan. But it questioned whether those arrangements met the Crown's obligations as a Treaty partner.

Tribunal concerned about shift away from Māori-specific health policy

The Tribunal highlighted a Cabinet circular issued in September 2024 directing agencies to focus on "needs", rather than ethnicity.

It said the shift in language and policy approach was also reflected in health targets which focused on the total population rather than Māori-specific outcomes.

The Tribunal said evidence presented during the inquiry showed that the effects of this shift were "far from minimal".

It said a focus on the mainstream population ignored the particular health characteristics and needs of Māori. A shift away from Māori-specific approaches was a clear signal that "te Tiriti is not central in relation to policy development, service design or delivery," the report said.

Tribunal recommends revisiting standalone authority

The Tribunal recommended that the Crown:

commits to revisiting the option of a stand-alone Māori health authority

consults extensively with Māori and make informed decisions on matters concerning Māori health

bases all decision-making concerning Māori health, particularly measures addressing longstanding Māori inequities, on robust evidence and scientific knowledge.
