World.title: Auckland man used missing $20.1 million Lotto ticket as bookmark for almost two months
World.content:
A West Auckland man has discovered the Lotto ticket he had been using as a bookmark for almost two months is worth $20.1 million.

The man, who has chosen to remain anonymous, said the winning ticket had been sitting inside a book since July. He only found it when he picked the book back up, following a break from reading.

"I put the ticket straight into my wallet ready to check the next time I went to the shop," he said.

He knew Blockhouse Bay Postshop & Stationers had sold a winning ticket, but "didn't put two and two together". The ticket could easily have stayed on the bookshelf for months, he said.

After scanning the ticket at a self-check kiosk, he initially believed the "major prize" alert meant he had won "likely a few thousand dollars".

"It still didn't cross my mind that it would be $20m."

The Lotto operator "was more excited than me" about the win, he said.

"I think I was in shock."

He said he would share the news of his lottery win with close family in the near future, as he decides what to do next.

"I'm going to take things slow and really think about what to do with this money.

"I do want to go on an overseas trip, but that's the only plan so far."

In August, Lotto asked players to check their tickets after the prize went unclaimed for several weeks.

"We're so pleased the lucky winner found his ticket and checked it before we started the next stage of our search," Lotto NZ head of corporate communications Will Hine said.

"I can only imagine what it must have felt like to realise that his bookmark was worth $20.1m."

There's still one more unclaimed prize in Auckland - a $333,333 winning ticket was sold at Four Square St Heliers for the 27 June draw.

World.title: Ōrewa beach sauna facing deadline to move given reprieve
World.content:
Auckland Councillor John Watson, "in a kind of statement of defiance to my ongoing years", leapt in the sea after a hot sauna at Ōrewa beach last month in late winter.

"I'm still here ... It's really quite invigorating," Watson said.

"That's been one of the key things from people is there's a real health and mental wellbeing benefit to it," said Watson on Thursday.

But the sauna has been facing a deadline to move on by next Thursday from the council-owned campground despite 4000 people signing a petition backing it to stay there.

Auckland Council has now given it till 22 October.

Sauna Collective owner Cam MacKinnon is asking for 29 October, to take in Labour weekend and also come after a key local board meeting that will consider his new proposal about when and how the business uses the campground on 27 October.

The council gave his company advance notice as summer approaches on the basis the business cannot operate when sites are in high demand.

On Thursday, MacKinnon told RNZ, "They're definitely leaving me hanging."

Albany ward councillor Victoria Short. Supplied

"Like every day I have to let my guys who work for us, our firekeepers, who we care deeply about, [know] like, but 'Sorry, I don't have any more information'. And then they're having to answer all our regulars and our people who care about the sauna who ask them the same question."

On Thursday the council told RNZ it told MacKinnon last Friday he would get a short extension.

It emailed him late on Thursday saying he had till 22 October "to enable you to make alternative arrangements".

But any decision on future occupancy depended on how the council managed the impacts, after fielding complaints about smoke, smell and obstruction of beach views, and increased car and foot traffic from non-campground guests, it said.

MacKinnon has proposed a year-long trial of a new arrangement where he shuts down from December to Waitangi Day, pays more for the site and compensates campers nearby.

Albany ward councillor Victoria Short said MacKinnon was not being pushed out or treated unfairly.

"We're trying to work with him to come up with a solution for him to be somewhere else with this agreement that we've kind of had in place where he's going to be there during off-peak season and on peak season he has to find a new location," said Short.

They had to work "just to make sure that everything is kosher, especially when it comes to the safety and liability aspects".

MacKinnon runs two other mobile saunas though Ōrewa is his mainstay. He said Friday's meeting left him uncertain about its long-term future.

"We might be under the assumption that we might be able to come back but they definitely weren't indicating anything like that," he said.

"That's not a given, not at all ... The only thing that is certain is that ... not only have we had the petitions, we've had hundreds and hundreds of emails."

Cr Watson was not party to the discussions but said the council should be trying to keep the sauna in place at the campground as long as possible each year, and find an alternative site on the long beach for the Christmas holidays.

"The starting point should be this has been a huge, big success. The local people want it to stay ... Make that happen."

Short said alternative sites for the peak season were being looked at, such as within the regional parks network or involving land governed by the Hibiscus and Bays local board.

The chair of the local board was approached for comment.

The local board is set to discuss the sauna operation on 27 October.

MacKinnon told the council on Friday, "I really do appreciate the extension you have already provided and the work going into assessing the proposal.

"I completely understand your point that any extension does not create an ongoing right or entitlement to operate from the Holiday Park and that we need to continue meeting the compliance requirements that have been raised. I'm not asking for any different understanding around that."

It is understood it could be complicated for the private sauna business, that needs power and other amenities, to operate from reserve or park land.

The council's head of specialist operations Martin van Jaarsveld said, "As a Holiday Park, a primary focus is on providing an enjoyable holiday experience that meets the expectations from paying guests at what is a very popular regional destination.

World.title: Police tight-lipped on North Korean IT scammer and Kiwi accomplice
World.content:
Police will not say what they have done about a North Korean IT worker who duped a local company - or about the New Zealand citizen who helped them.

On Thursday, the National Cyber Security Centre revealed it had dealt with a remote worker earning foreign currency for the North Korean state by tricking a local company into hiring them.

They paid a local person to receive and operate the company's laptop.

The centre said police talked to that person. It also said the remote worker threatened to release commercially sensitive information when they were caught.

Police said they worked closely with the centre, but were unable to comment on the existence, status, scope or particulars of any investigation, including whether any individual was under investigation or what investigative steps might or might not have been taken.

"Police encourages any organisation that identifies suspicious remote IT worker activity, suspects it has inadvertently employed a DPRK IT worker, or experiences related fraud, cyber-enabled offending, or malicious cyber activity to report the matter to New Zealand Police or the NCSC as soon as possible," police said.

World.title: 18 babies dead as social stigma fuels Fiji's HIV emergency
World.content:
Berenadeta* was 23 when she tested positive for HIV.

She had lost weight and discovered boils that wouldn't go away.

She suspected she'd picked up an infection, one that was likely sexually transmitted.

Her father told her not to panic, suggesting she visit the sexual health clinic near where she lived.

"They tested me three times, and all came up positive," she said.

"I had to accept it."

But the same visit uncovered something else she didn't know - she was three months pregnant.

Berenadeta found out she was three months pregnant on the same visit she tested positive for HIV. ABC News

Her partner, who was also HIV-positive, had been on tablets to suppress the virus, but had stopped taking them and hadn't told her.

Berenadeta's father advised her not to blame herself or her partner, telling her the virus could be managed with medication.

But her wellbeing wasn't her only concern.

"That's the only thing I was curious about, was the baby's result, not mine," she said.

Her medication consisted of one tablet a day, which she never missed.

The antiretroviral tablet suppresses the virus to a level that protects the mother's own health and reduces the risk of passing it on to their baby during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding.

Berenadeta's medication consisted of one tablet a day, which she never missed. Getty Images / Michel Lunanga

When Berenadeta gave birth months later, doctors found no sign of the virus in her baby.

"When the result came out, they told me it's negative. I was so happy," she said.

Since then, Berenadeta, now 25 years old, has had a second child and is pregnant with her third.

The ABC has changed her name and masked her identity to protect her from the social stigma involved with being HIV-positive in Fiji.

The young mother has bottle-fed both her children on medical advice and kept them safe from the virus.

But others haven't been as lucky.

Last year, 59 babies were born with HIV at Fiji's largest hospital, 18 of which died before their first birthday.

Colonial Memorial Hospital is Fiji's largest hospital. Supplied / Australian High Commission Fiji

They were born to pregnant women living with HIV, many of whom weren't taking medication out of fear of being stigmatised.

National infection rates meanwhile are skyrocketing, with new statistics showing one in 60 adults are living with the virus.

Five years ago it was one in 167 people.

The crisis has prompted Fiji's government to declare a national HIV emergency, with officials predicting it would take "upwards of five years" to bring the epidemic under control.

Growing crisis

According to Fiji government figures, 2,016 people were diagnosed with HIV in 2025, representing a 27 per cent increase in positive cases from the previous year.

UNAIDS estimated that 9,100 Fijians were living with HIV last year and only 39 per cent knew their status.

Transmission between mothers and babies is also on the rise.

Priya Kaur, who leads Fiji's work on eliminating mother-to-child transmission of HIV, said the 59 babies who tested positive in 2025 was the highest number in a single year.

Priya Kaur is Fiji's national lead for elimination of mother-to-child transmission. (ABC News) ABC News

"They were born to about 332 women who were pregnant and had HIV infection," she said

"That puts a vertical transmission rate at 18 per cent."

Vertical transmission is the term used when HIV passes from a mother to her baby during pregnancy, childbirth or breastfeeding.

The World Health Organization's recommended rate is below 5 per cent where mothers breastfeed, and below 2 per cent where they do not.

Dr Kaur said Fiji's high transmission rates were preventable because HIV testing and treatment were free to access.

"If you are positive, go on treatment and your children will be negative," she said.

But many people aren't taking the medicine.

Social stigma

Nationally, only 22 per cent of people living with HIV are receiving antiretroviral treatment.

This means many people with HIV are unable to suppress the virus to a level that protects themselves and any baby they might be carrying.

A computer illustration of the HIV virus infecting human embryo. The embryo is eight weeks old. AFP

Berenadeta, who is due to give birth to her third child early next year, said accessing treatment was not always easy.

She said for many HIV-positive women, it could require multiple consultations and transportation costs.

"You have your first check-up, and then you go back home, and you are coming back in a week or two, provided you have bus fare to come and your husband has given you money and you don't have four other children to look after at home," she said.

Privacy and confidentiality are also issues.

In the antenatal clinic at Fiji's largest hospital, one-on-one counselling takes place in booths that seat four or five women next to each other.

The booths are divided by a partition, but Dr Kaur said much of what was said could be overheard by the person next to them.

She said the lack of privacy could deter women living with HIV from seeking treatment or getting tested because of the risk of being exposed.

Privacy can also be an issue at home, where it's common for women to live with relatives.

A bottle of tablets can invite unwanted questions from aunties, cousins, in-laws and grandparents, discouraging women from taking treatment and placing their babies at risk of infection.

Dr Kaur says the lack of privacy in hospital counselling booths can deter women living with HIV from seeking treatment. Supplied

"They don't want the other family members to know that they are taking this particular medication," Dr Kaur said.

Lethal injection

Stigma and a lack of privacy are not the only barriers driving Fiji's HIV crisis.

About half of all new infections are due to intravenous drug use, mainly methamphetamine, while the other half were linked to sexual transmission.

Fiji health authorities are rolling out more public messages raising awareness of HIV. ABC News / Sairusi Tabualuma

Much of it arrives in Fiji through international drug traffickers, who use Fiji as a transit point to access lucrative markets in Australia and New Zealand.

For many people who inject drugs, there is no easy, anonymous way to access clean needles.

Fiji sex worker Nora, who chose not to give her real name, said she contracted HIV after sharing a needle with her cousin.

She said many drug users shared needles and were unaware of the dangers.

"We just do it, and then wash it with the water, and then pass it to somebody else to use it," she said.

Fiji's government recently announced plans to introduce a needle and syringe program (NSP) as part of its response to the growing epidemic.

The program, which is used in more than 90 countries, will make sterile needles and syringes available to people who use drugs to reduce the risk of HIV transmission.

Meanwhile, a national sexual and reproductive health and HIV unit was created 18 months ago, and HIV testing is moving out of laboratories and onto cartridges, similar to the way Covid-19 tests work.

HIV testing is moving out of laboratories and onto cartridges, similar to the way COVID-19 tests work. AFP

Dr Kaur said a national list of HIV positive mothers had been developed so their treatment could be monitored.

"We know who they are, where they are, what phone numbers they have," Dr Kaur said.

World.title: Weather: School holidays to start with heavy rain, strong winds
World.content:
A series of cold fronts is forecasted to move up the country in a wet and windy start to the school holidays.

MetService said blue skies were seen in most of New Zealand on Thursday, but showers over the South Island would travel north and linger in the west on Friday and Saturday.

Sunday would be especially wet, it said.

Meteorologist Samkelo Magwala said it was a typical spring pattern.

"Which is why these fronts are moving through quickly, resulting in less rainfall accumulation despite the briefly heavy rain.

"Parts of the North Island will wake to frosts on Friday morning and we're forecasting showers from the southwest on both Friday and Saturday before the main band of rain arrives with the front on Sunday."

MetService said the east could expect warm and dry conditions as a feed of air from the northwest moved in, with temperatures in the upper teens and low 20s on Saturday.

It said Sunday would be the more active day of weather as a front moved up the South Island.

Heavy snow was possible above 600m for parts of Central Otago, Southern Lakes, and the Canterbury High Country in the morning.

Southwest gales were possible in coastal Clutha, Christchurch and along the Kaikōura coast.

Northwesterly gales would blow through Cook Straight and across into Wairarapa and southern Hawke's Bay as the front moved up the country.

MetService has issued a heavy rain watch for the Tararua Range from 5am to 3pm Sunday.

There was a moderate chance of it upgrading to a warning.

There was also a strong wind watch for Hawke's Bay south of Hastings, the Tararua District, and Wairarapa about and north of Masterton 9am to 4pm Sunday, and Horowhenua Kapiti Coast, Wellington, Wairarapa south of Masterton, and the Marlborough Sounds from 9am to 1pm Sunday.

World.title: 'Not happy': Secretary for Education Ellen MacGregor-Reid 'cannot explain' OIA comments
World.content:
Audio player for " Education Secretary on OIA avoidance allegations " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/education/1567188%2Fnot-happy-secretary-for-education-ellen-macgregor-reid-cannot-explain-oia-comments

Education Secretary on OIA avoidance allegations Morning Report Download MP3 8m

The head of the Ministry of Education says she is "not happy" with a manager caught on video appearing to suggest staff skirt the law, nor a scathing internal review of the culture in its curriculum division.

It has been a tumultuous week for the ministry, just six weeks ahead of the general election.

It began with a leaked video of senior official Dr Catherine Law telling staff not to put information shared with Education Minister Erica Stanford's office in writing because it could be made public under the Official Information Act (OIA). The leaker said was not an isolated incident.

Then on Thursday, a review prompted by staff concerns reported numerous issues, including allegations of favouritism, unprofessional workplace behaviours and a fear of speaking up.

Secretary for Education Ellen MacGregor-Reid told Morning Report on Friday she could not explain Law's comments.

"What she said was wrong, she should not have said it. And my expectation is that everyone within the Ministry of Education should be meeting the obligations under the Official Information Act, including that staff member."

MacGregor-Reid said she had commissioned another review and would be meeting with the chief ombudsman after the interview to provide him the terms of reference.

"I'll be providing the ombudsman with our OIA track record. We have responded to a wide variety of OIA's and I'll be fully working with the ombudsman into whatever matters he wishes to look into as well."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405522238112

She said to the best of her knowledge, no directive to avoid writing material down to escape potential discovery under the OIA had been made.

Host John Campbell put it to MacGregor-Reid that Law's instruction was a reminder of a "pre-existing concept", not a policy she was introducing herself.

"Is this video emblematic of our culture?" he asked.

"What Dr Law said in that video wasn't okay," MacGregor-Reid responded. "Dr Law is not a senior official. Dr Law is not a seasoned public servant. She's come into the ministry on secondment as a school principal for her expertise in education.

"I cannot explain what Dr Law was thinking, but what I can tell you is I have commissioned a review to ascertain whether there is a wider problem."

MacGregor-Reid said those claims had not been put to her, and did not want staff to fear speaking up.

"I always welcome people pushing matters of concern to me… I commissioned that review of the workplace because I could see the pressure the group has been under. It has been working extraordinarily hard. And I commissioned that review because I wanted to hear from people…

"They can speak to me. They will be safe. And if action is needed to be taken as chief executive, I will absolutely take it."

World.title: Brazil’s big-name squad meets mega hype from soccer fanatics
World.content:
As some of the world's most famous football players arrive in a city known for its love of another football code, soccer fans hope the hype might change people's minds.

The Brazilian soccer team landed in Townsville yesterday ahead of their friendly clash with the Socceroos tonight at North Queensland Stadium.

Legendary coach Carlo Ancelotti brought a squad of big names, including Vinicius Junior and captain Marquinhos.

Brazilian superstar Vinícius Júnior met with fans in Townsville to sign autographs. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

For the city's small and vibrant Brazilian community, their arrival has been a cause for celebration.

Enthusiastic fans wore jerseys and held signs, screaming out to the star-studded team, after they touched down in Townsville.

"We love to party, we love dancing, and we like to cheer for our soccer team," Tatiane Pinheiro said.

"Very loud, very excited, everyone is going to be so excited to watch the game."

Football fanatics came from far and wide to welcome both the Brazil and Socceroos teams. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

The friendly match is one of two games in the series, with the other scheduled for Brisbane on September 29.

It will be the 12th time the Socceroos and Brazil have met since their first match-up in 1988.

Australia has beaten the five-time World Cup champions just once, in 2001.

But a lopsided head-to-head has not tainted the excitement in Townsville, which has been decked out in green and gold in anticipation of the international game.

Brazilian community fires up

Ms Pinheiro, a Townsville resident and Brazilian national, said she was excited to welcome crowds of Brazilians from around the country to her city.

Tatiane Pinheiro expects to meet Brazilian fans who have flown in from around the country. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

"Everyone that we know from other cities is coming to watch the big game," she said.

Organisers said more than half of the sell-out crowd of 25,000 were visitors from outside of Townsville.

Louise Monteiro (right) came with friends and family to greet the Brazilian team in her new hometown of Townsville. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

Louise Monteiro and her family recently moved to Townsville, and she is originally from Brazil.

She said it was difficult for her to decide which team to support.

"I think I'll always support Brazil first," she said.

"If Socceroos play against another team, I'll be supporting Socceroos."

Socceroos vs Brazil, everything you need to know Everything you need to know as the youthful Socceroos take on a Brazil team on the rebuild under legendary coach Carlo Ancelotti in Queensland, with international friendlies in Townsville and Brisbane.

Townsville Brazilian community leader Ronie Reed said the occasion trumped every event she'd ever seen in Townsville.

She said the hype among her community had been building since the announcement, including gathering for pre-game events.

"The supporter part of Brazilian football is such a big thing," she said.

"All the Brazilians are so excited to go and support the team and just to be there."

Brazilian community leader Ronie Reed said the local community has been very excited about the game. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

Ms Reed has lived in Townsville for 14 years and organises many local events for the South American community, which is often made up of the many backpackers who visit North Queensland.

"We want to show our presence; we want to show the impact that we have," she said.

"We want everyone to know how good it is to have this community here."

The Brazilian team lined up for a photo in front of Cleveland Bay. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

A street party and festival in the city starts at 3pm, before entertainers and musicians lead the crowd to the stadium.

A different type of football

North Queensland Stadium is home to the NRL's North Queensland Cowboys, but soccer fan and local player Mark Gadzikwa hopes Brazil's appearance and performance at the stadium could help curb a "lack of interest" in the round-ball game.

Townsville resident Mark Gadzikwa is both a rugby league and soccer fan. (ABC News: Emily Anderson)

"Brazil has always meant football; there's no better team to do it," he said.

" When you think of football, you think of Brazil. "

Anotida Sandengu has watched soccer since he was five, but this will be his first time watching a team as skilful as Brazil.

Mr Sandengu said he was surprised Townsville was chosen for the international match, which was announced after the World Cup in June.

Townsville locals Anotida Sandengu and Jobe Waring. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

"I wouldn't have called it; I remember I heard the news around the World Cup when everyone was watching soccer," he said.

"It was just really exciting. This is a once-in-a-lifetime event; it probably won't ever happen again."

Brazil is the most successful team at the FIFA World Cup, having won five times.

The Socceroos last met Brazil for a friendly game in Melbourne in 2017, where they lost 4-0.

Kick-off in Townsville is 8pm.

World.title: Infantino calls for 'culture of dialogue' amid resignation calls
World.content:
FIFA's embattled president, Gianni Infantino, says he is committed to a fresh culture of openness at the football body that is "not about generating positive headlines".

Two months into a deep rift in global soccer over Infantino's now-dropped $4.2 billion ($6 billion) World Cup sell-off plan, he offered his critics this week an independent review of how FIFA is run and makes decisions.

"I have received positive messages about it from different parts of the world, and it is important that we keep listening to each other," he wrote in an Instagram post from Jeddah in Saudi Arabia, which is hosting the Arabian Gulf Cup.

Infantino will chair an October 15 meeting of the 37-member FIFA Council that will also be asked to approve consultation with the 211 member federations and six continental soccer bodies on "how to further strengthen FIFA's decision-making processes".

The 211 members already effectively own FIFA, a Switzerland-based not-for-profit that has at least $5 billion in cash reserves after a financially successful men's World Cup in North America.

FIFA's ruling council includes three vice presidents — European football leader Aleksander Ceferin, North America's Victor Montagliani and Asia's Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa — who have led opposition to Infantino during the furore over his proposal to create a commercial spin-off part-owned by investors fronted by Josh Kushner.

"There must be a culture of dialogue, of listening to each other and respecting one another," Infantino wrote on Thursday, local time, about the council meeting in Zurich. "This is not about generating positive headlines; it is about doing what is right for the game."

Infantino's presidency since 2016 has created most turmoil when proposing multi-billion-dollar commercial plans without fully consulting continental bodies like UEFA, which succeeded in stopping them.

Flying FIFA solo toward close ties to Trump

Gianni Infantino's close ties to Donald Trump have caused tension in the football world. (Getty Images: Chris Brunskill)

FIFA has often seemed an executive one-man leadership as Infantino built closer ties to US President Donald Trump around this year's World Cup. FIFA created a peace prize to award Trump last year and allowed United States striker Folarin Balogun to evade a mandatory ban at the tournament after intervention from the White House.

Infantino's secretive plan to sell at least 20 per cent of FIFA's commercial rights in a deal anchored by Kushner, the brother of Trump's son-in-law, provoked the soccer body's biggest crisis since anti-corruption arrests in 2015 that led to trials in New York.

The 211 national federations were offered $20 million each to approve the creation of the FIFA Forward Enterprise subsidiary. UEFA, North America's CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation countered by saying FIFA could afford to give each federation a $10 million dividend just from its reserves.

Now Infantino, who faces an election challenge ahead of a March 18 vote by FIFA members in Morocco, insists he is ready to listen to soccer officials.

"I have never been more determined and committed in doing that," he wrote on Instagram.

"FIFA is always engaged. I am always engaged, and I want to hear how we can continue to grow football for the benefit of everybody, everywhere."

AP

World.title: Incredible catch helps South Africa beat Australia in one-day clash
World.content:
Mitch Marsh could not hide his dismay at how Australia capitulated tamely in their opening ODI in South Africa, who were helped to victory by an incredible catch by Marco Jansen that needs to be seen to be believed.

The Aussies ended up succumbing to a 67-run defeat to the disappointment of their stand-in skipper after a succession of cheap dismissals in a sorry run chase in Durban.

Marsh himself seemed to have laid the foundations for victory with his blistering opening knock of 60, but after he had perished needlessly to the spinning wiles of Kehav Maharaj, none of his team could cement the partnerships to get them anywhere near the hosts' 298-run target.

After watching the world champs collapse to 230 all out off just 41.2 overs, Marsh sighed: "I'm pretty disappointed. South Africa outplayed us. It was a good game of cricket, but we fell well short.

"We had our opportunities. I am probably going to sound like a broken record speaking about having partnerships in our batting, but we weren't able to form many tonight."

Mitchell Marsh got Australia's run chase off to a fast start with a rollicking knock of 60, but his departure was followed by a collapse. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan)

The South Africans had set a challenging target after being inserted by Marsh, compiling 8-297 thanks largely to a brilliant 112 from Matthew Breetzke and a spectacular 75 off 59 balls from pace-bowling all-rounder Jansen.

Marsh, standing in as skipper again for the rested Pat Cummins, then led from the front in response with his 36-ball pyrotechnics, which featured three sixes, one of which sailed for 104 metres over the dressing room roof at Kingsmead and landed at the roadside.

He shared a blistering opening stand of 90 in just 9.2 overs with Travis Head, but like Head (36), Cooper Connolly, who'd looked supreme in making 38, and Matt Renshaw (44), he got out to an airy shot when the Australians were up with the required rate and under no real pressure.

The superb spinning of the two slow left-armers Maharaj (4-20) and Bjorn Fortuin (2-34) soon put them under that pressure, though.

Discomfited, Josh Inglis got out to a poorly executed reverse sweep on the eighth ball he faced and Australia lost their last six wickets for just 54 to allow the Proteas to draw first blood in the three-match series.

The key moment may have been when Jansen took a sensational running, diving, one-handed catch in the outfield, stretching out his long telescopic arm to scoop up the ball just above the turf to get rid of key man Renshaw off Gerald Coetzee. It left Australia on 7-215, and there was no way back.

So, after the three-match sweep of the Zimbabwe series, this really did feel like a proper test of Australia with the defence of their 50-over World Cup in southern Africa just a year away.

The first part of the reconnaissance mission demonstrated just how much they still have to work on, and the weakness against spin was again shown up even while South Africa had five top-line pace bowlers sidelined through injury.

Matthew Breetzke's brilliant 112 off just 106 deliveries allowed South Africa to post a score of 8-297 in the first innings. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan)

Man-of-the-match could easily have been Jansen, with his one wicket, four catches and big-hitting or the superb 36-year-old veteran tweaker Maharaj, but batting at No.4, Breetzke's superb 106-ball knock, before being run out by Connolly, deservedly won the day.

All-rounder Jack Edwards had an uncomfortable debut — 0-56 off 10 overs, followed by scoring five off 15 balls — but there was encouragement again in the display of paceman Nathan Ellis, who, fresh from his outstanding series against Zimbabwe, was again the bowling pick with 3-57.

All-rounder Cameron Green, back in the side after missing the series against Zimbabwe as he recovered from a shoulder injury, had a poor day with the bat, falling for five while trying to belt Maharaj over cow corner and getting caught in the deep.

The opening loss has really put pressure on Australia to turn the series round at The Wanderers in Johannesburg on Sunday, when Cummins is set to be recalled. They haven't won a bilateral series against South Africa since 2014.

AAP

World.title: Socceroos vs Brazil, everything you need to know
World.content:
The Socceroos will play their first internationals since the 2026 FIFA World Cup against five-time world champions Brazil in Queensland this week.

It is the team's first meeting since they played at the MCG in June 2017.

The Socceroos have only ever beaten Brazil once, a 1-0 victory in the 2001 Confederations Cup third-place play-off thanks to Shaun Murphy's 84th-minute strike.

Here's everything you need to know about the Queensland Series.

When are the Socceroos playing?

The Socceroos are back in action on home soil. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

The first game is on Friday, September 25 at Townsville's Queensland Country Bank Stadium.

The second is on Tuesday, September 29 at Brisbane's Lang Park.

For both games, kick-off is 8pm AEST, meaning Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, and the ACT.

In the Northern Territory and South Australia, kick-off is 7:30pm and in Western Australia, it's 6pm.

How can I watch the Socceroos?

Friday night's game in Townsville is available to watch across Network 10 on free to air and Paramount+, you just need to check your local guides.

Tuesday night's game in Brisbane is only available on subscription streaming service Paramount+.

Alternatively, you can follow both games in full on the ABC Sport live blog.

Who is in the Socceroos squad?

Lucas Herrington is back on home soil for the first time since his move to Hull. (Getty Images: PA Images/Annabel Lee-Ellis)

With July's Round of 32 penalty shootout defeat to Egypt in Dallas firmly in the rear-view mirror, coach Tony Popovic's eyes are now gazing forward towards January's AFC Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia.

As such, Popovic has called up seven uncapped youngsters: Dylan Leonard (19 years old), Marcus Younis (21), Kasey Bos (22), Kealey Adamson (23), Yaya Dukuly (23) and Eli Adams (24), while Riley McGree and Patrick Yazbek, who both missed the World Cup through injury, return.

Nestory Irankunda will hope to lead the line and test himself against some of the sport's biggest names.

Hull City centre back and Brisbane local Lucas Herrington has had a superb start to life in the Premier League and will look forward to play in front of his friends and family.

Only one player, Sydney FC's Aziz Behich, plies his trade in the A-League Men.

Mohamed Touré scored six goals in nine appearances in all competitions for Norwich this season before getting injured. (Getty Images: MI News/NurPhoto/David Watts)

Door not closed for Socceroos veteran despite another snub Mat Ryan's Socceroos days are not over, coach Tony Popovic insists, despite the decorated captain being left out of his first squad since the World Cup.

Vinícius Júnior headlines Brazil's squad. (Getty Images: Lars Baron)

The five-time Champions League-winning coach was adamant that he would not pick players based on reputation for the World Cup, only to surprisingly select a desperately out-of-form and unfit Neymar Junior, whose only contribution to Brazil's poor performances in the USA was to embarrassingly taunt Norway's goalkeeper Ørjan Nyland after slotting a consolation, stoppage time penalty in their 2-1 defeat.

"Friendlies are used to have a look at different players … players who I don't know really well," Ancellotti said this week.
