Tech.title: An OpenAI Agent Hacked Australia’s Health Service. Their Government Found Out Months Later
Tech.content:
OpenAI’s agent had been conducting internet based research into health statistics in a development project by an internal OpenAI research team. When it could not access certain information, the agent attempted alternative ways until it found a work around and gained unauthorized access. It also wrote files to the internal server, which the government is waiting on OpenAI for more technical information on. The government is also investigating whether the agent gained unauthorised access to three additional government websites it interacted with.

“There will obviously be legal consequences on it,” Albanese said as he disclosed the “unacceptable” incident. He said he had spoken with Altman over the phone earlier that day about his “extreme concern” about the incident and “disappointment” with the nature and length of time the company took to inform the government. While Albanese did not answer whether he had apologised, Altman “clearly accepted that the company had not done good enough,” he said.

The Australian government currently believes no one’s personal data was accessed, though investigations are ongoing. The website in question is a public-facing statistics portal that contains non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics such as spending. It was therefore behind much lower levels of security than personal data would have been, Marles said in Sydney. “The impact of the incident is actually relatively minor, but this is a serious incident, obviously, and one that is completely unacceptable,” he cautioned.

A number of incidents over the summer, including OpenAI agents’ hacking of HuggingFace—highlighting the threat of frontier model agents acting rogue—were raised at the United Nations General Assembly this week, with Secretary General António Guterres welcoming calls to control AI. Altman himself had warned the United Nations Security Council earlier on Wednesday about his concern that humans could lose control of these systems.

“It was a shock that it occurred, because it was real and serious,” Albanese said about the incident. “But it also, I think, was something that had been predicted, including by the AI companies themselves.”

Australia is establishing a task force to look at the incident and emerging AI cyber threats. It will consider possible law enforcement and legislative responses to ensure that incidents like this don’t happen again.

Tech.title: SeaWorld Wants to Make You Horny
Tech.content:
When you think of SeaWorld, you most likely think of orcas, school trips to the aquarium, or eating chicken fingers while contemplating the ethics of marine mammal captivity. But this Halloween, the theme park franchise wants to make SeaWorld synonymous with something else entirely: BookTok smut.

On September 11, SeaWorld Orlando officially opened its annual Howl-O-Scream event, an after-hours Halloween-themed immersive experience featuring various “scare zones” in the park. Scattered between the more expected spooky fare, such as a haunted “Woodrot Hollow” forest and an I Know What You Did Last Summer–themed haunted house is Just One More Chapter, a BookTok-inspired zone featuring the hunky tortured bad boys of romantasy lore.

In videos posted by Orlando-based influencers who got an early look at the park, young men with masks, floppy hair, and painted-on abs gallivant around wearing black denim, loitering next to brick walls, beckoning to park attendees, and gifting them with roses. And on Instagram, influencers posed around a central set piece, an oversized book open to a chapter called “The Cathedral,” emblazoned with the slogan “Good Girls Go for the Bad Boys.”

Some of the TikToks from the scare zone went viral, garnering mixed reactions. “Booktok dark 'romantasy' cancer is RUINING heterosexuality,” wrote one X user, “every little tasteful drop of eros has to be squeezed out of everything so it can be refined into pure concentrated fucking CRINGE.” The fact that the event took place at SeaWorld, an amusement park franchise that is perhaps most closely associated with a harrowing documentary about an orca, also lent to the absurdity.

But I did speak to one content creator present at the scare zone who had an entirely different reaction. “I wouldn’t say it was scary,” said the creator, who declined to provide their name because they did not want to “jeopardize their relationship with SeaWorld.” “But it did leave me with a good feeling—I guess you could say a sexy feeling, in a way.”

According to Jessie Kinsey, the art director at SeaWorld Orlando, that was precisely the point. She came up with the idea for the event last year, after seeing romantasy bestsellers like Lights Out and Haunting Adeline go viral on TikTok. She knew that a dark romance-themed scare zone was not necessarily “something that you would expect from a traditional horror event,” but she had a feeling it would resonate with the BookTok girlies. “I remember texting my production manager, saying, ‘Don't judge me, but I have an idea,’” she tells WIRED.

Tech.title: The Ovary Is Surprisingly Active After Menopause. Scientists Are Trying to Figure Out Why
Tech.content:
When Francesca Duncan decided to take a look at what was going on in postmenopausal ovaries, she assumed she wouldn’t find much of interest. In a woman’s reproductive years, the ovary is exceptionally dynamic, shifting form and function from day to day throughout her cycle. But after menopause, when egg supply has dwindled and hormone production has waned, the ovaries are often thought of as little more than empty sacks.

“I assumed it was just sitting there inert,” says Duncan, a reproductive biologist at Northwestern University, who was only looking at postmenopausal ovaries as part of a project to map a cellular aging process called senescence throughout the body.

Instead, Duncan found that aged ovaries were anything but stagnant. When looking at the protein composition of ovaries of postmenopausal women between the ages of 50 and 75 years old, her team found that the molecular signatures differed significantly across the decades. The oldest ovary looked nothing like a 60- or 70-year-old organ at the molecular level. She was shocked. “Clearly something is still happening,” says Duncan.

The question is: what?

A new wave of discovery is forcing researchers to recast the ovary not as an egg factory with an expiration date, but as an organ that impacts a woman’s overall health and may shape the trajectory of aging long after the fertile years have passed. What they are only beginning to understand is whether changes to the ovary after menopause are harmful, protective, or some combination of the two, shifting over time.

Tech.title: Why This Weekend’s Nor’easter Is Like a Hurricane
Tech.content:
A powerful nor’easter developing this week will bring wicked winds, rough surf, and heavy rains to coastal communities from North Carolina to Nova Scotia.

These types of storms are more synonymous with mid-winter than mid-fall. And true to form, this storm is a little different. It won’t drop snow or ice like a classic winter nor’easter. In fact, this system may bring a tease of tropical weather to an Atlantic basin that’s been devoid of hurricane activity so far this year.

An Impactful Nor’easter for the East Coast

Nor’easters are special types of low-pressure systems that earn their name from the fierce northeasterly winds that can lash coastlines.

The seed that’ll grow into this weekend’s nor’easter started developing on Wednesday a few hundred miles off North Carolina’s Outer Banks. The system will meander toward New England into this weekend before slowly winding down into early next week.

Forecasters expect strong, persistent winds to hit coastal locations from North Carolina to Nova Scotia. The strongest gusts will buffet New England through Friday and Saturday, when winds may reach 60 to 70 mph.

Communities throughout the region can expect coastal flooding, beach erosion, life-threatening rip currents, and dangerously rough surf. Isolated power outages are possible. Flight delays at New York's and Boston’s airports are also likely due to blustery winds and rain.

Computer models still don’t entirely agree on how close to the coast this storm will track, or how long it’ll linger in the area—both factors that are crucial to determining exact impacts. A slower track closer to the coast will plaster the region with stronger winds and heavier rainfall than a faster path or one that keeps the center of the storm farther out to sea.

Nor’easters Are Common in Late Fall and Winter

Nor’easters are most common between October and April as powerful jet streams sweep across North America. It’s unusual for such a potent nor’easter to develop this early in the season.

Nor’easters are considered non-tropical—or as meteorologists call them, extratropical—systems that typically draw most of their energy from intense upper-level winds. That’s different from hurricanes, which tend to feed on warmer-than-normal oceans. But low-pressure systems exist on a spectrum that sometimes makes it difficult to neatly define them as tropical or extratropical, and this storm is a prime example.

A Tropical Connection

Some computer models suggest that this week’s nor’easter may acquire some tropical characteristics as it intensifies off the Northeast coastline. Fully extratropical systems feature cold air throughout the entire core of the storm. This nor’easter, on the other hand, may briefly develop a shallow warm core, a phenomenon found in tropical storms and hurricanes. Cloud structure, the storm’s overall wind field, and thunderstorm activity near its center are other tropical characteristics to watch out for.

Even though it’s not likely to earn a name as a hurricane would, it’s important for residents throughout the region to pay attention to the threat of flooding, wind damage, and power outages.

It’s strangely fitting that a nor’easter may prove to be the most hurricane-like non-hurricane we’ve seen across the Atlantic basin this season. We’re now past the peak of hurricane season and the year remains historically quiet. Tropical activity here is running at less than 10 percent of normal for this point in the year. This is also the latest the season has gone without producing a hurricane since the satellite era began in 1966. A quiet hurricane season is a hallmark of an El Niño, when hot waters in the tropical Pacific create conditions in the atmosphere unsuitable for tropical storms to form in the Atlantic.

But winter is a different story, and this week’s storm is also a potential preview of what’s to come as El Niño gains strength. Strong El Niño events tend to influence an active storm track across the southern US during the cooler months, which may in turn lead to more coastal storms along the Eastern Seaboard.

Tech.title: Online CVS Shoppers Might Be Able to Cash In on a $20.5 Million Settlement
Tech.content:
Popular pharmacy chain CVS has been hit with a lawsuit that alleges the company sold data from customers who shopped on its websites (cvs.com and cvshealth.com) or the mobile app.

The lawsuit alleges that CVS disclosed private health information, browsing data and more from users to advertising company Criteo and other third parties, though the pharmacy denies any wrongdoing. It has settled to the tune of $20.5 million to avoid additional expenses by continuing the lawsuit and other business disruptions.

Email notifications (PDF) for potential class members were sent out earlier in September, but the deadline to submit the claim form is Nov. 16, 2026. If you’ve ever shopped on any of the CVS websites or mobile apps prior to July 27, 2026, you’re considered eligible to receive payment, but you must still submit a claim.

More from CNET

According to the official settlement website, customers who submit a claim without documentation may receive up to $5, and those who submit a claim with valid documentation of belonging to the class may receive up to $10, but the amount may be reduced depending on the number of valid claims submitted.

As is typical with class action lawsuits, potential class members may also opt out of the settlement. Opting out of the settlement will prevent payment, but will allow you to maintain your rights to directly sue the company yourself. The final date to opt out of the settlement is Nov. 1, 2026.

The final hearing is set to take place on Dec. 1, 2026, and if the court approves the settlement, payments will be issued 120 days after approval. Class members can be paid via check, PayPal, Venmo or Zelle.

Tech.title: Sliding Homemade Pizza Into a Hot Oven Isn’t Easy. This $26 Gadget Is Meant to Help
Tech.content:
If you have cursed in the vicinity of your phone while trying to launch a pizza into your pizza oven without inadvertently creating a calzone, chances are even better that Big Internet Brother has targeted you for a sliding pizza peel. If, after dozens of practice launches, you haven’t mastered the art of the traditional wood or perforated metal pizza peel, even with all-powerful semolina flour gliders, you may be very tempted by the ease promised by such a tool as a sliding pizza peel.

The Best Pizza Ovens, Tested by CNET See at CNET

But is it worth it? Or is it just the Temu-niverse capitalizing on your desire for a homemade pizza that doesn’t come with a side of anxiety and despair? Reader, the temptation was too strong. I checked one out, and here’s the lowdown on what you can expect from a sliding pizza peel.

How does a sliding pizza peel work?

A sliding pizza peel costs $30 to $40 on Amazon. Pamela Vachon/CNET

A sliding pizza peel is essentially a lightweight wooden pizza peel with a manual conveyor belt attached. Rather than thrusting a stationary peel under your entire pie, you only need a small edge of maneuverability to start. Once the sliding peel gets a little purchase on the raw pizza dough, you pull the cloth slide toward you by its handle while pushing the wooden board underneath.

More from CNET

To launch the pizza with a sliding pizza peel, reverse the process: Use the handle on the cloth glider to push, sliding the pizza into the oven while pulling the sturdy board out from underneath it.

Cloth, you say? Well, not exactly. The conveyor mechanism moves like fabric, but think of it more like a nonstick baking mat. Many are made of woven fiberglass with a polytetrafluoroethylene coating, which is nonstick but still grips enough to hold raw or cooked pizza dough. It’s frankly like a flimsier Silpat or not unlike an oilcloth table covering.

PTFE, in case you’re wondering, is related to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. Yes, we’ve worked hard to avoid PFAS; however, the material’s pliability doesn’t encourage chipping, and it is also replaceable. The wooden board itself admittedly also spares every expense without the heavy lifting required of other wooden pizza peels — this is made from raw, lightweight bamboo.

Sliding pizza peel best practices

I practiced with naked dough. Pamela Vachon/CNET

While a sliding pizza peel may seem like a cure-all, if, like me, you adore what your pizza oven offers but still struggle with pizza peel mechanics, it still requires practiceof its own —and caution. As with more traditional pizza peels, it cannot undo other mistakes, such as poorly constructed, too warm pizza dough or an overloaded pie. You can still calzone-ify your pizza, even with a sliding pizza peel.

Unlike a traditional pizza peel, which lets you push and pull simultaneously, the sliding pizza peel’s primary handle is also very short, meaning you kind of have to get (uncomfortably) close to the mouth of the oven to use it.

The fact that none of these seemingly magic wands are produced or branded by any major pizza oven manufacturer should serve as a caution. (Pizza oven manufacturers probably just want you to become a bona fide pizzaiolo, confidently using the legitimate tools of the trade; they are clearly not trying to encourage the use of these cheap devices.)

Various sliding pizza peels are purportedly heat-resistant up to a certain temperature (which varies). Many pizza ovens, however, can reach temperatures much hotter than those sliding peels are designed for.

Loading a raw pie into the oven is one of the trickiest parts of at-home pizza making. Pamela Vachon/CNET

More than one user on various online pizza oven forums reported that the nonstick belt of a sliding pizza peel melted onto the hot pizza stone. Others, however, called the device an absolute game changer. Either way, using a sliding pizza peel requires you to launch quickly, which again requires practice, probably best done outside your actual pizza oven. (Your oven-oven with a removable pizza stone? A much lower-stakes practice arena.)

My experience with a sliding pizza peel

Because of the peel’s modest length, you have to get uncomfortably close to the oven during launch. Pamela Vachon/CNET

I have been an enthusiastic pizza oven user since one came into my life, but I still haven’t mastered the mechanics of either a traditional wood or perforated metal pizza peel. I slightly prefer metal, but either way, pizza attempt number one always results in a folded disaster. My crime, apparently, is wanting the kind of thin pizza crust a 20-year-old New Yorker demands. The thinner the pizza, the harder to launch.

I can attest that the sliding pizza peel did make it easy to pull the pizza off the cutting board where I shaped the dough and applied toppings. Despite feeling cheaply made, the mechanics are inarguable. I achieved a crust thinness I truly couldn’t with the other models.

While you have to get close to the heat to deposit it, I haven’t earned any burns or scars from trying. Repeated launches in a very hot pizza oven also didn’t seem to affect the fabric slide, but then again, I was prepared to move extremely fast to avoid a crisis—and to get away from the heat.

Success, if not exactly centered. Pamela Vachion/CNET

In case it merits saying, a sliding pizza peel is entirely unnecessary for pulling pizza out of a pizza oven. In fact, I would caution against it since it really relies on setting the peel down on the pizza stone, never mind the fact that you really have to get your hand inside the oven in the starting position for pulling a pizza onto it. Once a pizza is fully cooked and the dough is sturdy, even a thin pizza can be collected with a more traditional pizza peel anyhow.

A traditional pizza peel is still best for pulling pies from the oven. Pamela Vachon/CNET

The verdict on a sliding pizza peel? Proceed with caution. And practice.

Ultimately, the average price of sliding pizza peels available online is about $30. Even with mixed reviews, it’s a fairly low-stakes gamble to see whether one improves how often you use your big-ticket pizza oven.

Tech.title: Microsoft’s New Surface Laptops Embody the PC-Phone Marriage Snapdragon Promised Years Ago
Tech.content:
On the stage for the second day of keynotes at Snapdragon Summit 2026, Microsoft Corporate VP of Surface Devices Brett Ostrum revealed new versions of the company’s 12-inch Surface Pro and 13-inch Surface laptops, both of which now run Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Elite X2 chips for improved performance and battery life. These chips had come to larger Surface devices earlier in the year, and arrived in the smaller sizes of Microsoft’s portable PC lineup.

Along with the chip upgrade, both of the updated Surface devices have increased RAM options of 16GB and 24GB (up from 8GB and 16GB in their predecessors).

But some hidden advantages of running Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Elite X2, which was introduced at last year’s Snapdragon Summit, are downstream of the years the company spent developing smartphone silicon.

More from CNET

The first Snapdragon X Elite chips were revealed in 2023 as Qualcomm’s big return to PC silicon, attempting to outdo Apple laptops in battery life and performance. A big part of the company’s pitch was using what it learned making phone chips to see benefits in the laptop space. Now, we’re seeing evidence of that DNA paying off.

For instance, Ostrum told me after the keynote that the new Surface devices have superior cameras to their rivals thanks to the image signal processing on the Elite X2 chips, inherited from phone camera hardware, that will make you look amazing on Zoom calls.

The 13-inch Surface Laptop and 12-inch Surface Pro received Snapdragon X2 upgrades, and the new Surface Mouse has haptics to buzz and pulse your palm. Katie Collins/CNET

Before, Apple had taken the crown of image quality in its laptop webcams, Ostrum said. But thanks to Qualcomm’s investment in ISP and the camera pipeline, the Surface devices have seen a big turnaround in the video quality captured by their webcams.

“With our [Surface] Pro and laptops that we announced earlier this year [with] Snapdragon X2 Elite, we took the No. 1 and No. 2 spots from Apple in terms of camera quality,” Ostrum said, referring to DxOMark’s laptop rankings. Those rankings currently place Microsoft’s 13.8-inch Surface Laptop and 13-inch Surface Pro in first and second place, above Apple’s MacBook Pro models, in camera quality.

It’s not the first thing consumers or commercial buyers look at when shopping for laptops and two-in-ones, but people now spend so much time in Teams and Zoom meetings that camera quality is more important than consumers might admit. And considering how much the bar has been raised by ever-improving phone cameras, it’s no surprise that people want and expect an improved webcam.

“You want to look good when you show up [on camera], and it’s important to us, it’s important to our customers. And so it’s a fairly straightforward approach for us to say we want to make this look as good as we can,” Ostrum said.

We’re not just talking about better camera hardware, either. Ostrum was quick to say that it isn’t the lenses or sensors that make the difference — it’s the image processing pipeline Qualcomm has refined.

“I can put the same sensors into multiple silicon platforms, but the best solution is going to come with a Qualcomm ISP,” Ostrum said. “If you compare an Intel-based one of our commercial devices to a Qualcomm-based solution, you will see the difference.”

Both the new 12-inch Surface Pro (left) and 13-inch Surface Laptop (right) pack Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Elite chips. David Lumb/CNET

Phone chip DNA doesn’t just help with cameras — it boosts battery, too

That’s not the end of smartphones’ influence on laptops. The older x86 chips may have been adapted to laptops, but they originated in a world where PCs plugged into walls, Ostrum said, implying that they struggled with battery life. But the Snapdragon phone chip DNA and its emphasis on performance per watt have noticeably extended the battery life on Surface devices while also delivering the fast speeds consumers need for their tasks.

“People raved about the first generation of devices from a performance perspective, but the thing that we heard unanimously that was just a huge delight was, ‘The battery life’s incredible. The battery life’s incredible. The battery life’s incredible,'” Ostrum said.

There’s more that goes into the battery life of the Surface Pro and Surface laptop than the chip, including redesigning the interior for better thermal management. Roughly speaking, better heat management means more time running at high performance and less energy spent cooling the device down, which means more battery life. It’s all connected.

“We oftentimes will see as much gen-over-gen performance improvement from the thermal design that we iterate on as we do from the chip improvement gen-over-gen,” Ostrum said.

Still, that’s combining what Microsoft does best with the advantages of Qualcomm silicon, at least as far as Ostrum sees it. Microsoft expects 22.5 hours of battery life from the second-gen 13-inch Surface laptop, which is slightly down from the 24 hours offered by its predecessor. We’ll see how those expectations bear out in our testing.

What is true is how much longer those expectations are than what they were before Microsoft switched to Qualcomm — the Surface Laptop 5 and 6 with Intel-based chips had 18.5 hours of expected battery life, though the internet is strewn with reports of units only lasting half that time, or even less. Switching to a chip that inherited priorities and design architecture from mobile silicon seems to have helped.

Editors’ note: David Lumb’s travel costs were covered by Qualcomm. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: Australia Says an OpenAI Agent Hacked Into a Government Health Site
Tech.content:
One of OpenAI’s agents went rogue and hacked an Australian health data website. It’s the first hack of a government system — that we know of.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese shared the news in a press conference on Wednesday that OpenAI’s agent tried to access a portal of Medicare statistics in June. It tried to bypass restrictions to gain access to restricted information. Specifically, he said it’s “a research project that has got into areas that it shouldn’t have.”

It’s the latest in a series of revelations that started over the summer when news broke that unreleased OpenAI models in an evaluation environment hacked the AI platform Hugging Face in a bid to cheat on the evaluation. In the two months since that disclosure in July, several similar incidents involving agents from OpenAI and other AI companies have come to light.

More from CNET

These incidents largely stem from unreleased models in testing environments that were not as well-secured as they should have been. One driver of the issue is that bots often won’t give up until they solve the problem or find the answer you’re looking for. Even if that means breaking the rules, going behind the digital red tape and hacking sites. That appears to be what happened with Australia’s government website.

Albanese said the Medicare Statistics Reporting Portal is a public-facing statistics portal that doesn’t have sensitive Medicare information, but is still conducting an investigation to understand what government systems were affected and get more information. A task force has also been created to review the hack and consider any law enforcement and legislative action. As of now, there’s no compromise to the Services Australia network or personal information, Albanese said.

How did this happen? One of OpenAI’s evaluation exercises was to find data showing how much the Australian government spends on medicine, according to Albanese. But when the agent wasn’t able to find that information on publicly available sites, it went beyond where it should have.

“It accessed public and non-public information within the portal, and Services Australia also advises that it engaged, in order to do this, it engaged in writing files as well to the internal server,” Albanese said.

Despite the hack happening in June, OpenAI didn’t spot the activity until August. According to Albanese, OpenAI didn’t notify the Australian government — by sending a message to a public mailbox — until Sept. 10. Albanese believes OpenAI understands better protocols are needed, especially since it understands the risks. He expressed his disappointment and concern to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

OpenAI told CNET in a statement that it is reviewing the case.

“As we’ve shared publicly, OpenAI is conducting an extensive review of misaligned model activity during training and evaluation and notifying third parties when our review identifies potential impacts to their systems,” the company said.

OpenAI also said that there’s no evidence that patient records were accessed, but aggregate health statistics and internal file names were.

“We notified the organisations and are providing technical information to support their investigations and help address potential security vulnerabilities. Our overall review is ongoing, and we remain committed to transparency about these issues and to sharing what we learn as that work continues,” said OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri.

Albanese said AI still has upside, despite the risk. “It is bringing enormous economic opportunity for growth, for productivity benefits, for breakthroughs in health, in innovation and other areas of science,” he said. “But AI also poses significant risks, and that’s why we need guardrails to protect our way of life. We want to make sure that we shape AI rather than AI shaping us.”

Tech.title: I Test Kitchen Tools for a Living. Most People Are Missing This $18 Essential
Tech.content:
As you spend more time in the kitchen, it becomes clear that having the right tools can have an outsized impact on your recipe success rate. Some gadgets out there aren’t worth the space they take up in a drawer, but many are essential without an obvious substitute or workaround. A high-quality knife collection, forgiving wooden cutting boards and a smattering of good pans fall squarely in this category.

Other, less obvious kitchen tools that chefs and home cooks deem essential exist. As a culinary school grad-turned kitchen tech writer, I have several. One, in particular, I can never count on finding in rental kitchens and Airbnbs, so I always take one along.

I used to travel to summer beach rentals with all manner of basic tools: tongs, a whisk, a rubber spatula, you name it, plus a fleet of knives, a good bottle of olive oil and bagged-up samples of my entire spice rack.

More from CNET

After a couple of years, I realized that most rentals, at least on the East Coast, were well-equipped, and I was happier not having to schlep the contents of my kitchen to feel empowered to make dinner. I might stash a chef’s knife, just in case, but more often than not, even that would stay tucked in my bag.

There is one tool, however, whose utility is so singular that it can’t be substituted; in my experience, it’s the key between a good dinner and a great dinner (and dessert), and, surprisingly, you can’t expect to find it in other kitchens.

My Microplane, myself

The Microplane is an essential tool I can’t count on finding in the drawers of an Airbnb. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Yes, it’s a Microplane. If you’re now puzzling over how a handheld zester of all things is that important a tool, well, some of you have never enjoyed scraped-together key lime pie for breakfast at the beach, and it shows.

But seriously. No other tool does what a Microplane does to the same degree. Using a paring knife to gingerly cut the rind off citrus fruits without taking the pith with it, then mincing it up? I’ve done it. Hard pass.

A box grater is not likely to do the trick. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Don’t start with me about some cheap grocery store zester that’s both ergonomically overcomplicated and entirely ineffective. A box grater you would typically use for cheese or carrots, with that one plane dedicated to zesting? Have you tried it lately? (Actually, has anyone ever? It just looks like a recipe for pulpy zest and bloody knuckles.)

Microplane Zester $18 on Amazon

Why the zester is an essential kitchen tool

Maybe your skepticism isn’t about the tool’s quality, but about why any kind of zester is so critical. So I challenge you: the next time you make salad dressing or pasta, enchiladas, pad thai, or anything that calls for citrus juice, add a hit of zest and see what it does to the outcome. Citrus zest adds several times the flavor, minus the sharp acidity. In a word, it adds vibrancy to whatever you’re doing, without the pucker. It’s a wow factor with the simplest execution. Not to mention: key lime pie for breakfast.

A hit of zest is like fairy dust for food. Pamela Vachon/CNET

And the economics are inarguable. Even in today’s economy, a lemon or lime can only set you back so far, but it contributes so much. And the Microplane itself? Is all of about $18.

Here I am waxing all poetic about citrus, but let’s also talk about two other cooking champions whose processing is made infinitely easier by a Microplane. Garlic and ginger — also cheap yet dynamic ingredients. A garlic press is a fine thing, but if yours is as difficult to clean after use as most I’ve owned have been, ditch it. The microplane can do that work for you, and basically rinses clean afterward.

A zester will inspire you to grate cheese over, well, everything. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Or, if you’ve been buying pre-shredded Parm or another hard cheese, here’s another taste-test challenge for you. It’s so quick to grab a hunk and shave directly into or onto whatever you’re making or eating, with the added bonus of leaving out the extra starches that act as anti-clumping agents in pre-shredded stuff. I could also make a point here about freshly grated nutmeg, but that would be extra. Suffice to say, I never make béchamel without it.

Microplanes of a different color

My go-to zester comes in more than a dozen colors.

If you’re convinced, I am partial to the Microplane brand here, whose handles are especially comfortable and which includes a protective sleeve for storage. Incidentally, you can also get a Microplane in over a dozen colors, and they are made in the US, if buying locally is a compelling argument.

If you’re already a Microplane evangelist and have made it this far, here’s an invitation to maybe upgrade yours. They don’t last forever, as the blades will dull over time. I recently switched out my 15-year-old model, and it has brought new life to my kitchen.

Pamela Vachon/CNET

For argument’s sake, I also checked out one of Amazon’s best-selling and least expensive models, the MasterChef version, which retails for only $10. It’s a little more generous in width, and its protective cover is admittedly a little easier to maneuver. Functionally, it works just like the Microplane, but is made in China for those keeping score.

Tech.title: Meta’s New AI Device Is This Tamagotchi-Like Muse Charm Keychain
Tech.content:
If you were overwhelmed by all the new Meta AI smart glasses at its annual Connect event on Wednesday, you’re not alone. CEO Mark Zuckerberg introduced many new glasses, including the reimagined Meta VR glasses that make the Quest 3 and Vision Pro look very old and bulky. But the keynote brought us one more AI device: Meet the Muse Charm.

This keychain looks like you took the face of an Apple Watch and tied a short phone strap to it. It’s a small, round device with a fingerprint sensor for you to activate it without needing a phone or laptop. The reason for it? To talk to your AI agent, Muse, whenever you want.

Muse is Meta’s AI agent, an autonomous bot that can assist you with tasks. Unlike chatbots, agents can take action and complete tasks independently. You can use Muse to send messages on Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp, for example.

The Muse Charm keychain isn’t available yet, but Zuckerberg said in the keynote that it will be ready by December — just in time for the holidays, if your loved ones are into that AI stocking-stuffer thing. You can 

Building Muse into a physical device

Muse has been relatively popular since its early September launch, with reports saying the agent’s app has been downloaded more than half a million times. This week’s reports of a serious zero-day cybersecurity vulnerability — now patched — haven’t seemed to dampen folks’ enthusiasm for Muse.

That is likely because agentic AI is largely seen as the future of AI. But it isn’t without risk. Privacy and security are huge concerns. Earlier this summer, AI agents from Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic escaped their digital testing environments and hacked real websites, including the popular AI platform Hugging Face and a system run by the Australian government. These incidents of so-called “rogue agents” — although they typically stemmed from poorly designed testing protocols — have prompted a lot of concern inside and outside of the AI industry, drawing the attention of governments around the world that are still struggling to create rules around AI.

Zuckerberg, for his part, has been clear that he doesn’t think a coordinated industry slowdown will be necessary. Every lab should be able to police itself, he wrote on X, citing the months Meta spent developing the tech behind Muse. But during those months, Meta was largely seen by the AI industry and investors as “falling behind in the AI race.” All the AI labs, including Meta, have significant financial incentives to develop the best AI quickly, even if that means safety falls to the wayside.

And safety will be key to the success of any AI device, including the Muse Charm. Meta, ironically, has already proven that. Its AI-enabled smart glasses drew widespread public backlash this summer after it was reported that Meta was considering adding facial recognition technology to the glasses. That built on mounting fears people had of glasses-wearers recording them with the camera in the glasses, without their consent, leading to Meta smart glasses being nicknamed “pervert glasses.”

Meta denied the facial recognition report despite the evidence and told CNET that privacy is important. But Meta still hasn’t provided many details on how it will protect wearers and bystanders. At Connect this year, Zuckerberg and the company left many of these questions still unanswered, as CNET’s Scott Stein reported.

Tech.title: So Many New Meta Glasses: Muse AI Everywhere, and Ray-Bans Without a Camera
Tech.content:
I talked to “Henry,” a Muse agent in my AI glasses, as I stared at a box of Kind bars. Henry was trained as if it were the assistant to a 38-year-old bodybuilding marketing executive. Henry told me whether I should eat Kind bars and also helped me plan my workout schedule.

This was me getting a preview of Muse, Meta’s AI agent that’s already on phones and Macs, but this time it was on Meta’s AI glasses. If you were concerned about AI on what many people are calling “pervert glasses” before, they’re about to get supercharged very soon.

But I also tried on a camera-free pair of Meta glasses that gave me audio assistance, meaning privacy-invading, pervy images aren’t an issue.

This was at Meta’s Connect developer conference this week, where the focus was on AI, VR and glasses and where Meta fired out a whole bunch of updates and many new designs. It was also getting a jump on the launch of Google and Samsung’s own AI glasses, which are just around the corner.

Some of Meta’s new glasses designs come with better battery life, some with added hearing assistance, and some, made by Thai rap star and actor Lisa, come with collectible charms. But amid all of this, there was very little about fundamental changes that would address the privacy concerns and fears surrounding a wearable category that so many companies are diving into.

Every time I wear or talk about smart glasses, people increasingly give me side eye. This has been a very bad summer for global opinions on AI-enabled and camera-equipped glasses, a category in which Meta is a leader. But with Google, Samsung and a ton of others – including Apple – expected to enter the fray next year, it’s going to get crowded and weird fast. Meta’s answer to all of this: more glasses, more features, including literally getting in our faces with its new agentic AI tool, Muse.

There is a new FDA-cleared hearing enhancement mode in Meta’s glasses that I tried, which costs $149 to activate. There are new Meta Ray-Ban Gen 3 glasses with slightly better battery life, and camera-free Meta Ray-Ban Audio glasses with even better battery life (up to 12 hours).

Muse could be the biggest news of all, especially as Meta goes head-to-head against Google and Samsung’s Gemini-infused wearables. But I was also surprised that no new fitness features were announced after Meta’s push into the space with Oakley-branded visors last year, and Meta’s prescription-challenged Ray-Ban Displays, while becoming available to order in more countries, have barely changed at all.

So, let’s break it all down. I’m still trying to digest it myself.

I tried Muse on Meta’s glasses at a single demo on Meta’s campus. Scott Stein/CNET

Meta’s putting its Muse AI agent on its glasses

Muse is an agentic AI system that’s been well-received by some early reviewers and in-app downloads since it emerged just a couple of weeks ago. Its appearance on Meta’s glasses now seems inevitable, especially since the faster-responding Muse Spark AI model has given them a performance boost.

The only chance I got to try Muse on glasses was a very quick and pretty canned demo, and the arrival timing for Muse on glasses is still unclear. Also unclear is exactly how capable Muse will truly be or how safe. The agentic AI can already tap into personal accounts of all sorts if you let it, and it can buy things for you or manage your data, but it doesn’t promise encryption or privacy. That’s why I’ve avoided connecting it to anything in my own life, and not all accounts will allow hook-ins: Amazon just blocked Muse from enabling shopping on its sites.

My Muse glasses demo showed very little of meaningful, deeper agent hooks to data I’d recognize, since it wasn’t my own being accessed. I did notice that Muse took a while to complete some actions when rescheduling workouts for the marketing manager Muse agent Henry was set up to serve. Muse worked over audio, with no sense of progress status for completing a task.

Meta is introducing some privacy updates to how its glasses handle data, promising a new Private Processing system in the future that will run on confidential virtual machines in the cloud, a system that Meta’s using now in WhatsApp and Meta AI but plans to extend to all tools for Meta glasses. It’s not here yet, though, and it doesn’t make me feel any more convinced that any of the systems can be trusted, though, and I certainly feel lots of anxiety about handing over any agentic control of my personal data to any system.

But the space is moving fast. Google Gemini can already handle a lot of agentic actions, and Samsung and Google’s glasses will be able to do them. Apple’s new Siri, meanwhile, also has increasingly agent-like actions in its connected AI and apps. And OpenAI could be introducing more wearables with direct support for its services, too. Everyone in tech seems to want something like Iron Man’s Jarvis for your face, and few actually have it. Meta’s casting its hat in the ring.

Meta’s two Ray-Ban Audio glasses models: Clubmaster (left) and Burbank (right) Scott Stein/CNET

There are camera-free Meta Ray-Ban glasses now

One way to avoid pervert glasses concerns? Not having cameras on glasses at all. I tried out the new line of camera-free Meta Ray-Ban Audio glasses, which promise 12-hour battery life (a notable bump from 8 to 9 hours on Meta’s recent glasses). There are just two designs for now: Clubmaster, which is a new look, and the more familiar square Burbank.

There’s not a lot new with Ray-Ban Audio glasses. They’re Meta glasses, minus the camera. A programmable action button on top of one arm still activates Meta AI, and one arm still has a touch bar for volume control. The audio sounded as good to me as Meta’s other models, but the battery boost could be a welcome addition. So could the social comfort of not having a camera on glasses.

But they’re not cheap. At $379 to $479, they’re actually more expensive than Meta’s recently launched line of self-branded smart glasses. Oddly, Meta didn’t make a non-Ray-Ban “Meta” branded (and likely less expensive) pair of audio glasses. Not yet, at least.

Nothing’s much changed on the camera front, either. A new landscape mode for photos sounded promising at first, but it works via digital cropping, and I haven’t tried it yet.

The phone app dashboard for Hearing Enhancement, which I got to demo briefly at Meta. Scott Stein/CNET

FDA-cleared hearing enhancement costs extra

In a move that mirrors a growing trend in hearing tech, Meta’s adding an FDA-cleared hearing assistance mode to its glasses, called Hearing Enhancement, which runs a hearing test to tune the experience for people with mild to moderate hearing loss. Apple’s AirPods Pro earbuds launched a similar feature two years ago.

Unlike Apple’s feature, though, you have to pay to enable Meta’s extra. It’s either $149, with a 30-day free trial to test how it works first, or included with a Meta One subscription that’ll run on glasses soon.

I hate subscriptions, especially for health features. A one-time cost feels more bearable. But it also pushes the total price up for a pair of Meta glasses as potential hearing aids.

To simulate how they work, Meta put foam earbuds in my ears while activating the mode during a conversation I had with Ravish Mehra, Meta’s director of research science. That’s far from a true simulation of actual hearing loss, but I got some sense of how the mode enhanced treble and clarity in sounds and conversations, like a more refined version of Meta’s existing Conversation Focus mode. Hearing Enhancement works in a targeted beam-forming mode that attends to a person, or more ambiently.

Mehra told me that the mode, when running, works for about 4 hours on Meta’s recent glasses models, but longer on the Ray-Ban Audio glasses. The extra fee could have been avoided (as Apple did), but Mehra cited R&D costs as one reason for the upcharge. I’m curious how AirPods and Meta glasses would compare for someone who actually needs the hearing assistance, something I couldn’t vet. With glasses, at least there wouldn’t be a need for any buds in your ears.

Meta Adventurer glasses in the new Lisa design are coming soon. Scott Stein/CNET

Lisa is making a pair of Meta Glasses too

I actually didn’t know who Lisa was, but she’s a famous rapper, actor and social media star who’s making her own custom-branded pair of Meta glasses, in the spirit of the Kylie Jenner glasses Meta launched in June. (My colleague Faith Chihil, one of CNET’s social media producers, flipped out at the Lisa news.)

The Lisa glasses come with a collectible charm, one of 14 types. They’re also decorated with stars on the arms. Lisa fans and collectors might be excited by this. I’m not.

But Meta’s also releasing a bunch more frame designs and colors, including some new Meta Glasses looks. Meta says there are over 100 designs and colors across all types now, and it felt that way when I browsed a bunch of new frames at Meta’s campus.

A new Aviator line of Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 smart glasses. Scott Stein/CNET

Gen 3 Meta Ray-Bans have new designs, slightly better battery

There are also new third-gen Meta Ray-Bans, but they’re not nearly as notable as the second-gen ones I wore last year. The battery boost on third-gen models is just an hour more than with Gen 2 — 9 hours total at best. That matches the claims for Google and Samsung’s imminent smart glasses, which is likely no coincidence.

There are a few frame designs, mostly variations on familiar looks. One pops, though: an aviator design that I tried out without my prescription added. They’re bold, kinda interesting, and…I felt a bit sinister wearing them.

The third-gen glasses are also more expensive, ranging from $449 to $529 without a prescription. Meta’s self-branded glasses, released in June, start at $299 and have nearly identical features, except for that tiny battery bump.

This is actually a virtual version of me in Meta’s new Hologram avatar. I animated it by talking on Meta’s Ray-Ban Displays. Scott Stein/CNET

Meta Ray-Ban Displays haven’t evolved much at all (except for Holograms)

Last year, Meta made a big deal with its display-enabled Ray-Bans and innovative neural band interface, a setup that seemed to push toward a future where full AR glasses lurk.

And yet, a year later, Meta has no significant improvements for Displays. They’ll be available in more countries this year, and may be easier to buy. But they still don’t work for a larger range of prescriptions, limited to just a -4 maximum. My eyes still won’t work with them.

Meta has been opening up more app development for its glasses and rolling out more features for Displays over the last year. Still, I expected Meta might find a way to blend its neural band with a smartwatch, perhaps one of Garmin’s models, since Meta and Garmin already have a partnership. But that didn’t happen either. The prices of the glasses are also still the same.

The most interesting thing about the Displays is the addition of Holograms, a hyper-realistic video chat avatar system that I tested out at Meta’s campus and was wowed by. It scans your face with a phone app and then projects your presence to the phone screen (or glasses, or VR headset) of whoever you’re calling, to surprisingly realistic effect. It’ll only be available to a limited test group at first in beta and will work on WhatsApp, but deliver the sort of simulated video chat on glasses that has been promised by Meta for years.

Besides camera-free Meta glasses (left), the design of Meta’s new glasses and camera design (right) remains the same. Scott Stein/CNET

Sorry, no watch, new fitness modes or major privacy improvements yet

Meanwhile, I was also surprised that Meta had no fitness updates at Connect, despite introducing Oakley-branded Vanguard visors last year and Garmin-connected workout features.

The Muse agent can connect to fitness and health functions, but a lack of new dedicated fitness features leaves a gap that Google might fill quickly with possibilities for Fitbit integration on its upcoming glasses, and an interconnection between WearOS watches and its glasses to act as a mini control dashboard and even preview photos.

Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth hinted to me last year that the neural band could evolve into a watch, but those plans haven’t yet materialized. Unlike Google and Apple’s wearables, Meta’s glasses are limited in how they connect to phones, using an app and, in the future, agentic hooks via Muse’s AI.

And also, biggest of all, Meta’s privacy issues feel barely addressed. It’s still as easy to take a photo in public as before, and nothing’s changed with how the glasses present themselves to others: They’re easy to confuse with regular glasses (to Meta’s credit, design-wise) and still just show a small LED light when recording.

And while Meta has promises of a private compute layer in the cloud for its future features, can they be trusted, and will third-party observers get access in any way? Will any of these new agentic features misfire unpredictably, as we’ve already seen with AI agents? The answer there feels like a “when” rather than an “if.”

But Meta won’t be alone in the pursuit of agentic AI wearables. It’s just the biggest and first in the door. There’s a lot of potential lurking in wearable AI, and lots of concerns. And Meta’s continuing to roll forward through all of it.
